News.title: Man killed by tiger died from 'multiple injuries'
News.content:
Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death."

Park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended but confirmed his death at the scene.

The senior coroner said her office was awaiting a more substantial report as to the extent of his injuries.

South Yorkshire Police provided a number of witness statements from the public and staff who were at the wildlife park at the time, the hearing was told.

Mundy instructed staff to contact Yorkshire Wildlife Park to ask them to keep any relevant CCTV and inform the coroner of any previous visits by Chapman to the park.

After opening the inquest, which Chapman's family chose not to attend, on Thursday morning, Mundy adjourned proceedings until 18 March 2027.

Speaking after the hearing, a neighbour of Chapman told the BBC he was "very polite and well-spoken" and a "lovely man".

Josh, 24, who lived in the same building as Chapman, said: "He'd always have a laugh and a joke. He was quite well kept, he'd look after himself physically. He loved his F1, he'd talk for hours about his F1 if he could."

Discussing the online comments and speculation in the aftermath of the incident, he said: "People didn't know him. If you don't know him, don't make a comment."

News.title: Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments
News.content:
On a different day in the ITV broadcast, Feeney is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area.

"There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film.

Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'."

Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look", before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

The BBC has contacted Campbell and Whelan, who has resigned as a councillor, for a response.

A Reform UK Solihull spokesman condemned Feeney and Whelan's "misogynistic and offensive comments" and confirmed they were no longer Reform councillors.

The spokesman said Campbell's comment "was a joke in poor taste but with no malicious intent", adding: "It's something that he deeply regrets, and the party will not be taking any further action."

Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election.

"We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there."

Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous."

ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments.

The BBC has contacted him for comment.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Reform should take "immediate and firm action against those who've been revealed to be making these abhorrent comments".

He added: "There is no place for any form of racism, antisemitism, discrimination in British politics, and we all should be relentless in repeating that and taking the firmest possible action."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "We should be asking why there's so many stories like this of people in Reform who are making these appalling comments."

Asked about one of the individuals being a former Tory councillor, she said: "It's not my problem anymore."

Badenoch added: "I don't want people like that in the Conservative Party. I'm glad they have gone."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

News.title: Fifty arrests in crime probe after fatal A66 crash
News.content:
A total of 50 people have now been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following a fatal crash.

The arrests have been made after the head-on smash on the A66 on Teesside which killed seven people, including two police officers.

Ten of the 50 arrested are alleged to be linked to the Volvo reportedly involved in driving into two properties in the early hours of 22 August, police said.

Det Ch Sup Helen Barker of Cleveland Police, said: "Over the last two months, we have identified 50 people who we believe are associated within criminal networks that seek to cause serious violence and harm within the community through the supply of drugs."

The force said shotguns, hand guns, machetes and ammunition had also been seized, as well as Â£60,000 worth of class A and B drugs and more than Â£30,000 in cash.

Barker said: "Our pursuit of this criminality will continue, and I want to take this opportunity to thank the community for their support and patience but also for the information that we keep receiving.

"I want to encourage you to keep on reporting behaviour that is related to drugs or organised crime - no matter how small - and be assured we will act."

News.title: Meet the curious billionaire behind the Bayeux Tapestry who began life as a refugee
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The lights are low in the British Museum when Igor Tulchinsky slips quietly into the room. There is no swagger, no entourage, no theatrical display of wealth. Slight, with a close-cropped beard and warm, enquiring eyes, he is dressed almost entirely in black, his leather jacket bearing the WorldQuant logo. He has the air of a man who would rather look than be looked at.

Observation is his instinct. He watches, asks questions, absorbs information and only then decides. It is a habit formed early, when, aged 11, he left the Soviet Union with his Jewish parents in search of a life beyond communism, antisemitism and the grey monotony of a society that offered little freedom or possibility.

Today, the Belarus-born American is a self-made billionaire and one of the most prominent arts patrons of his generation. He has committed £5 million to the British Museum’s exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry, one of the most anticipated cultural events since the Tutankhamun exhibition of the 1970s. Yet he seems less a tycoon surveying his investment than a man encountering something new. He is global philanthropist having founded the first digital university and giving tens of millions of dollars to endow universities. He also donated to Refuge when the Independent campaigned for homes for victims of domestic abuse.

He leans towards the tapestry. Nearly a thousand years old, the embroidered linen stretches for almost 70 metres, recounting the drama of 1066 in coloured wool. In the subdued light, it resembles a primitive strip of cinema. Horses rear, ships cross the sea, messengers carry news and armies prepare for battle. Harold Godwinson takes an oath; William of Normandy readies his invasion; then the killing begins.

open image in gallery Igor Tulchinsky is fascinated by the Bayeux Tapestry ( WorldQuant )

Tulchinsky studies it with almost childlike absorption. “I was struck by how new it looked,” he says, admiring the composition and the visual rhythm of its three horizontal registers. “It’s very visceral.”

He had not anticipated quite how cinematic it would be. “It tells a story in pictures,” he says. “Pictures [are] a thousand words.”

He is interested in who moves, who watches, who knows what is coming and who does not. The tapestry is a story of migration, calculation, chance and conflict; it is also a study in how people interpret information and act upon it. Few works could offer a more fitting introduction to a man whose own life has been shaped by movement and decisions made under uncertainty.

open image in gallery Igor Tulchinsky committed £5million to the project to bring the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum ( WorldQuant )

Tulchinsky’s parents were musicians. His father played the viola, his mother the piano and taught at a music school. They practised for hours each day, filling the family home with classical music. Although Tulchinsky never became a musician, it remained part of his intellectual landscape.

The family’s departure was neither an adventure nor an exercise in ambition. They wanted their only child to have a future they could not offer him in the Soviet Union. As Jews, they faced persistent antisemitism. “There were names called and chalk on the pavement,” he recalls. He learnt to keep his head down and avoid drawing attention to his identity.

Leaving was itself a risk. A Jewish organisation helped people emigrate, but applying for permission could mark a family as traitors. Refusal might cost his parents their jobs. They waited three or four months to discover whether they would be allowed to go.

At first, Tulchinsky resisted. He was 11, with friends and a familiar world he did not want to abandon. His parents, however, saw the choice in stark terms: darkness or light, deprivation or opportunity. They decided to stake everything on their son’s future.

The family travelled first to Vienna, then Italy, where they applied for refugee status in the United States, Australia and Canada. Money was scarce, and they sold possessions from their suitcases to survive. In a suburb of Rome, they stayed with a shoemaker. Tulchinsky remembers his father practising his viola while the shoemaker worked; when the music stopped, the hammering resumed.

Eventually, the family secured refugee status and flew to New York. Their first accommodation was a grey-stone hotel on the Upper West Side, where they stayed for two or three weeks. Tulchinsky remembers the cockroaches, which he describes as “humongous”, and the almost complete absence of English.

American television became his first language teacher. The family watched because they had to learn, and because immersion was the quickest route into a new world. Within a year, he could understand everything being said.

They moved to Astoria, Queens, settling in government-subsidised housing in a rough neighbourhood. His school had broken windows; furniture came from discarded belongings that were still clean enough to use. He carried a small dictionary to help with his homework.

It was an early education in resourcefulness: observe, absorb, work things out and find a solution. Complaining was of little use.

He also learnt that opportunity was unevenly distributed. One of his closest friends in Queens was Puerto Rican. Their circumstances were similar, but their lives diverged dramatically. Tulchinsky moved upwards through education and business; his friend remained in the neighbourhood.

The family’s experience was framed by an older, more harrowing history. During the Second World War, his paternal grandmother fled Belarus for Siberia while pregnant. She went because the Germans were unlikely to reach her there. Tulchinsky’s father was born in Siberia and did not see his own father until he was five. His grandmother understood the distinction between migration and war: immigration was difficult, she believed, but war was harder to survive. Tulchinsky has never forgotten that perspective.

His early academic record was unremarkable. He admits that he did not initially work particularly hard, and his grades reflected it. Then the family moved to Richmond, Virginia, where he sat an entrance examination for a good Catholic school and won a scholarship. Competition sharpened his ambition, and he rose to become the second-best student academically.

Mathematics and programming soon offered a different kind of education. Much of his technical knowledge came from computer manuals, first on an Apple and later on a Commodore 64. He taught himself BASIC, graphics and game design, learning by experimenting with systems and discovering their rules.

His first 20 jobs were less a conventional career ladder than a series of stepping stones. He made a card catalogue for a private library, washed dishes, prepared sandwiches, worked at a computer camp for disabled children, tutored English and held retail jobs at Target and Service Merchandise. He programmed software for hospital antibiotic dosages, designed computer games and wrote books, often studying while working and working while studying.

One employer gave him a list of names and asked him to turn them into games. One was called Blow the Whistle, a miniature football simulation with three players on each side. To Tulchinsky, the important element was not the entertainment but the underlying model. “It’s basically simulation,” he says.

The idea would prove foundational: understand a system, identify its rules and test what happens when they change.

At 18, he applied to an oil company and took a programming test. A month passed without a response, until an executive called to say he had never seen anyone programme like that. Tulchinsky went on to build the company’s general ledger, having acquired the necessary skills largely on his own.

At Bell Labs, he worked while completing a master’s degree that was supposed to take two years. He finished in nine months and, without immediately telling his employers, took three months of unpaid leave. But the slow bureaucracy of telephone-system programming soon frustrated him. Three lines of code a day, he recalls, was intolerable.

He began exploring other possibilities, taking the LSAT and GMAT and considering law school and business school. Traditional recruitment proved less successful. He was not as polished in interviews as the candidates competing for consulting and investment-banking jobs.

So he changed the method. He sent thousands of letters to chief executives, reasoning that a thousand letters might produce ten interviews and one or two offers. The calculation was simple, and it worked.

One letter led to the Harvard Institute for International Development and an assignment in Moscow, where he worked on privatisation. He became convinced that the system was compromised and decided to leave. One night, he walked away; two hours later, he was gone.

It was an early expression of a principle that would become central to his thinking: knowing when to cut your losses.

Tulchinsky subsequently worked for Thomas Peterffy, developing trading strategies, before joining Millennium. There he built quantitative frameworks and helped develop international research capabilities. The boy who had learnt English from television had become a man whose professional language was mathematics.

In 2007, he spun WorldQuant out of Millennium. The business expanded across China, India, Israel, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Vietnam, Singapore, South Korea and other markets. Today, he says, it has 28 offices in 18 countries, with Uruguay the latest addition. Its premise reflects a conviction formed long before he entered finance: talent is universal, but access to opportunity is not.

Quantitative investing also taught him the difference between intelligence and survival. In 1998, after Russia defaulted on the rouble, a pair-trading strategy he believed in lost heavily. He went into the red and spent more than a year recovering. His father advised him to quit. He persisted.

Then came the quant crisis. Tulchinsky recalls liquidating positions a day before the steepest fall and re-entering partway through the following day. Had he waited another day, he believes, the losses could have wiped him out.

The lesson was unequivocal: preserve the capital.

“When I’m scared, I run,” he says.

It is a strikingly unvarnished admission from a billionaire investor. There is little of the familiar mythology in which every decision becomes, in retrospect, an act of genius. Tulchinsky gives luck a substantial share of the credit. Asked to divide success between intelligence and luck, he puts it at “50-50”.

open image in gallery The self-made billionaire attributes his success to 50-50 luck and intelligence ( WorldQuant )

Wealth has given him something more valuable than the ability to accumulate further wealth: the freedom to choose what comes next. “Mainly, what changes [is] that you can do philanthropy the way you want to,” he says.

His first philanthropic commitments centred on scholarships, supporting disadvantaged students at universities in the United States and Israel. He also funded academic institutions and research, including a major endowment connected to Cornell.

But scholarships, he came to believe, addressed only part of the problem. If education had transformed his own life, why not expand access on a much greater scale? The question led him towards building a digital university, principally focused on Africa.

The ambition is consistent with his own experience. He arrived in America barely speaking English, acquired a language, gained an education and developed technical skills. Each new capability opened a door to the next opportunity. Education was not an ornament to success; it was the engine.

A digital university could challenge the assumption that geography should determine access to intellectual opportunity. A talented young person born far from an elite institution should not necessarily be excluded from the knowledge and networks that might change a life.

Here, his philanthropy becomes an extension of his biography. He is not merely redistributing the proceeds of one successful system; he is trying to build another, in which more people can learn, compete, experiment and try again.

open image in gallery Igor Tulchinsky in Davos ( Joe Short )

Tulchinsky’s life has not followed a grand strategic plan. “It came about as a sequence of tactical moves rather than strategic,” he says. Each day, he explains, you do whatever takes you closer to your goals.

Those goals have remained consistent: a certain amount of money, a certain amount of alpha, a certain amount of capital and a certain amount of philanthropy. The details change; the underlying method does not.

He is now writing a book, Cutting Losses, about recognising when something is no longer working and knowing when to stop. His life, he says, changes according to what he cuts. The challenge is to distinguish persistence from stubbornness, and ambition from attachment to a failing idea.

That combination of curiosity and pragmatism is what makes the Bayeux Tapestry such an apt encounter. Its grand narrative is one of kings, conquest and the making of England, but its details reveal a more uncertain world of messengers, individual risks and decisions taken without knowing the outcome. History, like markets, is shaped by the interaction of information, judgement and chance.

Tulchinsky recognises something familiar in that uncertainty. His own journey has depended less on a single master plan than on a succession of decisions: to leave, to learn, to try a different route, to persevere when the odds seemed unfavourable and to retreat when the risks became too great.

Back in the museum, he continues to study the tapestry. A man who built his fortune by searching for patterns in vast quantities of information is still drawn to the details others might overlook.

Has his search for the next opportunity finally ended?

“No,” he says. “I’m still looking.”

News.title: Yorkshire wildlife park announces reopening after fatal tiger attack
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Yorkshire Wildlife Park will open its gates again on Friday, almost a week after a young man was killed by a tiger in an enclosure at the Doncaster attraction.

The park, which has been closed since the incident, confirmed the reopening would include the “Land of the Tiger” area.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park on Saturday.

An inquest into his death opened on Thursday at Doncaster Coroner's Court.

The hearing was told that Mr Chapman had a history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

He had suffered previous bouts of psychosis, the court heard.

open image in gallery William Chapman died after being mauled by a tiger

His family expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services leading up to his death.

An initial post-mortem examination recorded multiple traumatic injuries as the cause of his death, the hearing was told.

City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation, the hearing was told.

The council said it would share the outcome of that investigation with the coroner.

The park, known as YWP, confirmed it will reopen on Friday following “engagement with the relevant authorities”.

In a previous statement on social media, the wildlife park said “many, many people” had contacted it about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident.

open image in gallery Altai will not be euthanised following the attack ( Yorkshire Wildlife Park )

It confirmed he is “safe and well” and will not be euthanised.

A statement said that Altai's “ongoing welfare at YWP remains a priority of our experienced animal care team”.

The statement went on to say: "We continue to assist South Yorkshire Police and other relevant agencies with their ongoing enquiries into the circumstances of this tragic incident.

"As we welcome visitors back, we would ask everyone to be understanding and respectful towards our staff team, who have shown tremendous professionalism and dedication during an exceptionally difficult time.

"We are providing specialist trauma support and ongoing care for those affected.

"As inquiries remain ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on circumstances at this time.

“We would like to thank everyone for their patience, understanding and support during this difficult period, and we look forward to welcoming visitors back to the park.”

News.title: Zelensky defies Trump over oil refineries attack after accusing US of ‘betraying’ Ukraine
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Volodymyr Zelensky has declared that Kyiv is “done” supporting a ceasefire on energy targets announced by Donald Trump after it was ignored by Russia.

Trump made the surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy, after which Kyiv suspended strikes on refineries while Russia continued launching air attacks across Ukraine.

"The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Mr Zelensky told the Financial Times, after Russian strikes on power stations knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of people.

It was the latest clear indication of Kyiv’s frustration with Trump, after the Ukrainian president said he felt betrayed by a decision to restrict the Ukrainian military’s use of SpaceX’s Starlink.

open image in gallery Zelensky is embroiled in a growing dispute with Trump ( Reuters )

By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on refineries, Mr Zelensky risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had "damn well better stop".

Ukrainians fear the growing rift between Washington and Kyiv could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by the US.

open image in gallery Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Officials in Kyiv have also reported that they have not received the usual warnings from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles, which rely on US satellite detectors.

At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.

White House sources and SpaceX owner Elon Musk have both denied being behind the restriction, but Mr Zelensky was clear that he believed it to be a policy decision, saying:"It was not a technical problem, it was the will.”

open image in gallery Musk blamed Trump for the decision to restrict internet in Ukraine ( Reuters )

Musk earlier blamed Trump for restrictions introduced on Starlink speed for members of the Ukrainian military.

The service delivers broadband internet and has been used for government and military communications by Ukraine in the war against Russia.

The outage came amid Trump’s demands for Ukraine to completely halt long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Polish foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski accused Musk of “playing politics” on Wednesday but the tech billionaire has now denied he was involved in the decision.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and POTUS,” Musk wrote on X in response to a post by Ukraine’s foreign minister Mykhailo Fedorov saying that the technology was “critical” for the country.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

open image in gallery Zelensky reacts during a meeting with Burnham at 10 Downing Street, 14 October 2026 ( Reuters )

He had previously said that “no ‌matter how much ⁠I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink ⁠will never turn off its terminals... We would never ‌do such ​a thing or ‌use it as ​a bargaining chip.”

Musk later retweeted a post by another X user that said among other things: “SpaceX is a private company with zero obligation to help Ukraine, yet it stepped up when governments dragged their feet.”

The X owner captioned the repost: “True”.

Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt betrayed by the decision in an interview with Piers Morgan and that the shutdown meant “people would die” as a result.

Several combat missions failed on Tuesday evening as a result of the shutdown, an adviser on military technology to Zelensky told The Guardian.

A US official told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved in the Starlink limitations.

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

“This is not the right side of history,” Zelensky said on Piers Morgan Uncensored. Asked if he felt betrayed by decisions made over the last week, he said: “Really, yes.”

open image in gallery A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line ( Reuters )

The outage came just as Ukraine was hit by ballistic missiles, despite Trump’s insistence that there is an energy ceasefire in place between the countries.

Poland has said that it pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscription, which is crucial for guiding long-range drone strikes that have severely disrupted Russian logistics.

“Hey, @elonmusk, ⁠big man, are you playing politics ​with ⁠your products again?” Sikorski wrote ‌in a post on X on Wednesday. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”

The restriction came amid Trump’s decision to lift sanctions against Russia and allow global diesel exports, with the US to buy 300,000 tons of the fuel.

He faced criticism from several corners, including from the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who told Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”

News.title: All the new driving licence rules introduced in October
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

New driving licence restrictions have come into effect, banning young people from carrying certain passengers at night and restricting when learner drivers can take a test.

The changes, which have been launched in Northern Ireland, are aimed at reducing fatal road crashes involving young people.

According to official figures, 17- to 23-year-old drivers were responsible for almost a quarter of all collisions in Northern Ireland in 2024. That is despite them only accounting for 8 per cent of licence holders.

Data also shows that 251 people were killed or seriously injured in collisions involving a young driver in 2024. In 65 per cent of cases, the young driver was at fault.

The changes come after the government announced in January that learner drivers in England and Wales could face a wait of six months between sitting their theory and practical tests.

Here are the changes that have been made to driving licences.

open image in gallery The photocard driving licence was introduced to the UK in 1998 ( PA )

What changes have been made in Northern Ireland?

Northern Ireland has become the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers.

Graduated driver licensing (GDL), for learner and newly qualified drivers, now applies to all new drivers, but the changes are aimed at those aged 17 to 23 years old.

Learners must spend at least six months getting driving experience before they can take a practical test, and those under 24 face restrictions on carrying young passengers at night.

The rule changes were announced in January 2026, and drivers who do not follow the restrictions could receive three penalty points or a fine of up to £1,000.

What proposals are being considered for drivers born after 2002?

As part of the Road Safety Strategy that was initially developed under Sir Keir Starmer's former government, drivers born after 2002 may face stricter measures.

Andy Burnham’s new government is weighing proposals to implement a "minimum learning period for learner drivers".

Learners, the majority of whom are in their late teens and early 20s, could have to wait six months between their theory test and practical driving test as part of the plans.

Drivers under the age of 25 represent 6 per cent of licence holders but were involved in 24 per cent of fatal and serious crashes in 2024, according to Government figures.

Ministers believe minimum learning periods could help to reduce such collisions by up to 32 per cent, based on evidence from other countries.

Currently, someone can start learning to drive from the age of 17 with lessons on the road.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

What has been proposed for drivers in their 70s?

Rather than take a whole new test, the proposal plans for drivers in their 70s to have their vision checked every three years to keep driving on UK roads.

This is also not a new policy announced by Mr Burnham but a policy which was first discussed in August 2025 during Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership, as part of a new road safety strategy.

The proposal went to consultation earlier this year between January and May.

What are the current rules for drivers over 70?

Currently, drivers aged 70 and over must renew their licence every three years and self-declare that they can meet the eyesight standards required to drive. Drivers also must declare any listed medical conditions.

However, the new proposal means drivers will no longer be able to simply say that their eyesight is good – instead, there will be mandatory eyesight tests as part of the licence renewal process.

News.title: Shooter, 16, kills 3 students and a teacher in Oregon elementary school rampage before armed bystander stops him
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A teenaged gunman shot his way into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, Thursday afternoon, killing three students and a teacher and wounding at least two others before an armed community member pursued and fatally shot him.

The 16-year-old shooter, armed with what authorities described as a “long gun”, shot the locked doors to gain entry to the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend and opened fire. At least four people — three students ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher — were killed in the attack before the gunman was shot and killed by a “bystander” who saw him enter the school with the gun, police said.

Officers were alerted around 1 p.m. local time after receiving a 911 call from a driver who said a person shot at his vehicle multiple times outside the school. Emergency crews transported victims to a local hospital. Within a minute of the initial call, law enforcement received dozens of 911 reports of an active shooter inside the building. Bend Police arrived at the scene by 1:02 p.m. — just two minutes after dispatch used a tone to alert all law enforcement in the area — and the shooter was down moments later.

Chief Mike Krantz confirmed during a news conference that the gunman forced his way into the building by firing through locked doors. A community member witnessed the gunman enter the facility, pursued him inside, and shot him before officers entered and confirmed the suspect was dead. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported to St. Charles Bend with critical injuries.

open image in gallery Details are beginning to emerge about the shooting in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old gunman forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday afternoon and opened fire, killing three young children and a teacher before being fatally shot ( AP Photo/Joe Kline )

The suspect’s identity has not yet been released, though officials confirmed he was a 16-year-old Bend resident. Krantz declined to specify the exact type of long gun used, how many rounds were fired or whether the suspect had any connection to the school, citing the ongoing investigation. Police are expected to hold another news conference Friday afternoon.

The incident prompted an immediate lockdown of the school while police vehicles, fire trucks, and ambulances swarmed the grounds. Bend-La Pine Schools buses transported students and staff from Silver Rail Elementary to a designated reunification point at Journey Church in Bend, Oregon.

Classes and other activities were cancelled across the school district on Friday with the streets around Silver Rail Elementary blocked off hours after the shooting.

“As you can imagine, the process of getting all of those people safely out of the building and down to Journey Church is a real challenge,” police told reporters during a news conference, asking for patience while officers thoroughly clear each section of the school. A large crowd of parents and community members gathered outside as the search and evacuation continued.

open image in gallery The incident prompted an immediate lockdown of the school while police vehicles, fire trucks and ambulances swarmed the grounds ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Authorities said the suspect forced his way into the building by shooting through locked entrance doors before firing on students and staff ( Reuters )

Speaking at the news conference on Thursday evening, Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, reflected on the shock felt across the district.

“Today, an unthinkable tragedy happened at Silver Rail Elementary School,” Cook said. “No community should have to do what we're doing right now. I don't have any words for what this community is feeling right now.”

Cook announced that all district schools and activities are canceled on Friday, and that crisis counselors will be available for students, staff and community members starting Friday morning at 9 a.m. at the Central Library.

open image in gallery Officers arrived at the building within two minutes of the dispatch alert, navigating an emergency response that local police had practiced during active threat training just two months prior ( Reuters )

open image in gallery State officials confirmed that the Oregon Department of Emergency Management is coordinating multi-agency support to assist the city and school district in the days ahead ( Reuters )

Bend Mayor Melanie Keibler called it “an awful day for our community” and said that a community vigil would take place Thursday night.

Federal authorities are also aiding local police with the response. FBI Director Kash Patel stated on social media that the bureau’s Portland field office is on the scene to support the investigation, adding that the agency “will make every resource they need available.”

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, speaking at the briefing, praised the community member who intervened to stop the shooter, calling it a act that prevented “further loss of life,” and confirmed that the Oregon Department of Emergency Management was coordinating support across state agencies.

“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.

The Bend Police Department is serving as the lead agency on the investigation.

News.title: Wildfire traps firefighters and volunteers in Indonesia’s Mount Bromo national park, killing 4
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Four people died and two others suffered severe burns while battling a wildfire in a national park on Indonesia's main island of Java, after they became trapped by thick smoke and rapidly spreading flames, officials said Friday.

The blaze erupted in recent days in the Mentigen and Pusung Lingker areas of the popular Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java’s Probolinggo regency.

The victims were among a 12-member firefighting team consisting of national park personnel, members of a community fire brigade and local volunteers trying to contain the wildfire on Thursday, said East Java police spokesperson Jules Abraham Abast.

Strong winds fanned the flames and caused the fire to spread quickly through dry vegetation. At about 1:30 p.m., firefighters operating outside the danger zone received an emergency call from colleagues who had become trapped by dense smoke and advancing flames, Abast said.

The fire follows a major blaze in August that scorched nearly 9 square kilometers (3.5 square miles) of grassland and vegetation, including protected edelweiss flowers, in the park.

Police launch an investigation into the incident

Rescuers later found three people dead and three others suffering severe burns at an evacuation point. One of those suffering burns died while receiving treatment, Abast said.

Two volunteers remained hospitalized with serious burn injuries after being transferred to Dr. Soetomo General Hospital in Surabaya for specialized treatment. Six others escaped unharmed.

“The incident occurred in a remote mountainous area, complicating rescue efforts,” said Probolinggo police chief Asmida Rizki Siregar, who joined emergency crews carrying victims on stretchers for about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) because steep terrain prevented vehicles from reaching the site.

She said authorities completed the evacuation late Thursday and have launched an investigation into the deaths, including whether negligence or criminal wrongdoing contributed to the tragedy. Investigators were collecting evidence and interviewing survivors.

Indonesian wildfires reignite transboundary haze concerns

The deaths came as Indonesia intensified efforts to combat forest and land fires that have worsened this year as El Niño intensifies a prolonged dry season. Contributing factors also include land clearance using fire in the Indonesian part of Borneo and regions of Sumatra Island, as well as water shortages that have hampered Indonesian firefighters, who have received assistance from Japan.

Indonesia's Forestry Ministry recorded 799 hotspots nationwide as of Thursday evening, up sharply from 372 a day earlier. More than three-quarters were concentrated in six fire-prone provinces on Sumatra and Borneo.

Toxic haze and smoke have caused a health crisis in neighboring countries as well. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) away.

The surge in fires has renewed concerns about transboundary haze across Southeast Asia. Malaysia on Friday ordered hundreds of schools closed in several states because of deteriorating air quality.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan rejected calls from some lawmakers to seek compensation from Indonesia, saying the crisis should be addressed through diplomatic engagement and ASEAN mechanisms. He said Malaysia was coordinating assistance for Indonesia and would push for stronger regional cooperation on haze management.

Singapore also called for closer cooperation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities were investigating companies allegedly linked to Indonesian forest and peatland fires that have worsened the haze and would pursue action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act where warranted.

Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry recorded more than 2,020 square kilometers (780 square miles) of burned land between January and July, almost three times Singapore’s size. The independent Nusantara Atlas project, which monitors fires using satellite imagery, estimated that nearly 8,960 square kilometers (3,460 square miles) of land had burned by the end of August in Indonesia.

___

Associated Press writers Edna Tarigan in Jakarta, Indonesia, and Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

News.title: Terrifying safety loophole exposed after man is thrown to his death from roller coaster
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A fatal accident on a Georgia roller coaster where a rider was thrown from the attraction has renewed scrutiny around amusement park safety as modern rides push for greater speeds and steeper drops.

Although fatal incidents on roller coasters remain exceptionally rare, authorities in Georgia have disclosed limited information regarding Monday's tragedy. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was ejected from his seat while riding the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia, hitting other park guests before landing below the ride.

Operating at the venue for two decades, Goliath uses a sheer drop from 200 feet (61 meters) to reach top speeds of 70 mph (112 kph), focusing on velocity and downhill plunges rather than turning riders upside down through loops or corkscrews.

open image in gallery A man's death on a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia has raised questions about ride safety and regulation ( AP Photo/Mike Stewart )

Following the death, Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar coasters across North America, stating it was acting out of an abundance of caution. The ride's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, said it is "actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened."

The US has a patchwork of rules regarding rides

Across the United States, roller coasters and other attractions at major theme parks such as Six Flags are exempt from federal regulation, leaving oversight entirely up to individual state governments.

Critics contend this has created an inconsistent patchwork of laws, with certain states maintaining rigorous standards while others enforce little to no oversight.

Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has introduced repeated legislation to close what he describes as a "loophole" in federal statute that allows officials to inspect mobile rides, yet bars the Consumer Product Safety Commission from regulating stationary park attractions.

Brian Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert, also maintains that stricter national guidelines are required.

"Who’s watching those in these organizations to ensure that they are adequately trained, that they are compliant, that they are monitoring these rides to the level in which the standards have established?" Avery said.

open image in gallery Operating at the venue for two decades, Goliath uses a sheer drop from 200 feet (61 meters) to reach top speeds of 70 mph (112 kph) ( AP )

Meanwhile, Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which handles annual inspections across the state, is "conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review" of the incident at Six Flags, spokesperson Garrison Bennett said.

Amusement park industry has set its own safety standards

Across the globe, theme park operators adhere to ASTM guidelines set by industry specialists. These standards dictate everything from ride design and construction to the maximum acceleration and forces a passenger may experience.

The sector relies on multiple layers of inspection, according to Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions. Operators face constant pressure from insurance carriers that could face major financial payouts if accidents occur.

"With the checks and balances that are put in place, theme parks are really one of the safest places to be on the planet," he said in a phone interview Tuesday.

According to the trade organization, the odds of sustaining a severe injury on a U.S. amusement park ride are 1 in 15.5 million.

open image in gallery Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which handles annual inspections across the state, is conducting an ‘in‑depth and comprehensive review’ of the incident at Six Flags ( AP )

Martin Lewinson, a roller coaster expert and professor at Farmingdale State College, said a mechanical failure on a coaster like Goliath is hard to imagine due to its engineering.

The attraction uses a pull-down lap restraint called a "clamshell," which operates via a ratchet device that clicks down over a rider's hips. The mechanism features redundant disks to ensure safety if one component fails, Lewinson noted.

"They’re dependable. They’re not so technically advanced that theme parks have difficulty with operations," Lewinson said.

Ride operator control systems also display a green signal for every seat prior to dispatching the train. Theoretically, the train cannot move unless every restraint is fully locked, Lewinson said.

Still, complete safety is never entirely guaranteed.

In 2022, a 14-year-old Missouri boy fell to his death from an Orlando attraction when his harness failed to lock properly due to his physical size.

In 2013, a 52-year-old Dallas woman died after slipping from her seat on the Texas Giant at Six Flags Over Texas. Six Flags subsequently added updated restraint padding, seat belts, and sample entrance seats so visitors can check their fit beforehand.

open image in gallery Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has introduced repeated legislation to close what he describes as a ‘loophole’ in federal statute that allows officials to inspect mobile rides ( AFP/Getty )

Nick Mendenhall, who has ridden Goliath more than 12 times in recent weeks, said staff verified restraints on every turn.

"There are two employees, one on either side of the train, and with their hands they push down and they make sure it locks every time. I’ve never seen them not do it," Mendenhall said.

States handle oversight in different ways

In California, the Department of Industrial Relations must approve new or modified rides. According to the agency’s website, officials monitor safety either through annual direct inspections of equipment and operations, or by relying on yearly reports submitted by owners.

Florida takes a different approach by exempting its largest theme parks, including Walt Disney World and Universal, from state safety inspections, though smaller carnivals and venues remain subject to oversight.

These major operators manage their own safety protocols, but they must report any injury or death to the state. Texas similarly relies on private inspectors hired by park operators or their insurers.

In Arizona, home to Six Flags Hurricane Harbor Phoenix, no state agency regulates rides or performs safety checks. State law instead mandates an annual private inspection, with local governments largely tasked with enforcement.

News.title: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia stays on track as safety fears grow amid Middle East conflict
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Asian Cup organizers have responded to increasing concerns over the safety of players and fans if the tournament goes ahead in Saudi Arabia by confirming plans for the Jan. 7-Feb. 5 continental championship remain on track despite ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation.

“Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” Saudi organizers said. “The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football.”

South Korea’s Professional Footballers’ Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

“The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly,” Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. “The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern.”

At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom.

South Korea, a World Cup semifinalist in 2002, is set to open against Yemen on Jan. 10 but only if, Lee added, it was deemed safe to do so.

“No competition’s value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans,” he said. “If safety cannot be sufficiently guaranteed, all possibilities — including whether the tournament should be held — must be carefully reviewed.”

An AFC Champions League game between Cristiano Ronaldo 's Al-Nassr and Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana was delayed on Monday in Riyadh after Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense issued a security alert.

Asian Football Confederation President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa told media in Zurich this week that — if necessary — the Asian Cup could be postponed by one year.

“We can wait until the end of November” to make a decision, Salman said. “Things can change very quickly for better or worse in the region, and it is a question of seeing what happens.”

“If we need to make a decision, then we will, but we could move it back a year to 2028 if we need to.”

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”

News.title: Ukrainian Vampire drones drop food on town besieged by Russian army
News.content:
On Ukraine’s front lines, drones are the deadliest weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal, hunting Russian soldiers one by one with chilling precision.

But across the Dnipro River, the same machines have been given a very different mission: keeping trapped civilians from dying of starvation.

Since March, Ukrainian drones have been flying food and medicine into occupied Oleshky, on the river’s left bank, where residents are surviving on grass and weeds.

The town is less than three miles from Kherson, a city battered by Russian drones and shelling.

Since December, Oleshky has been under an effective blockade. Its roads are mined and shops have closed, with no food arriving by road since late May. Humanitarian agencies are blocked from entering, and the health system has all but collapsed.

Only around 2,000 of its 24,000 pre-war residents remain. For them, the drones are now their only lifeline.

“With the onset of winter, the situation is only getting worse,” said Elvina Osmanova of the Kherson regional military administration. “Food supplies are running out. People are facing a life-threatening choice: risk their lives trying to find food outside the city or remain without food.”

News.title: Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle
News.content:
When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

News.title: Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six
News.content:
Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Second Ebola case confirmed in Kenya
News.content:
Kenya has recorded its second-ever case of Ebola after a relative of a patient who died last week tested positive for the virus, officials have said.

A 39-year-old man fell ill on Tuesday and has since been confirmed to be infected with Ebola, according to Kenyan health authorities.

The patient, who is now isolated, is a family member of Kenya’s first-ever Ebola case, who died in a hospital in Nairobi last Monday.

The index case, a 40-year old businessman, had travelled to Kenya from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of the deadly outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which has so far killed more than 4,300 people.

Kenyan authorities have identified 128 of his contacts and have successfully tracked down 113 of them, who are having their temperatures checked daily for a period of three weeks, the country’s Director-General for Health, Dr Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.

“There is no evidence of spread in the wider community,” the statement, issued on Wednesday, added.

However, questions remain over whether more cases will crop up in the coming weeks.

News.title: I tried Apple’s new smart home hub – the brand faithful will love it
News.content:
HomeView can control smart lights, heating, security cameras and video doorbells via touch or voice, but devices must support Matter – the cross-brand smart home standard. That means you aren’t confined to Apple-approved gadgets, but you are still limited – Ring video doorbells, for example, aren’t Matter-compatible, so they won’t work with HomeView, which could be a deal-breaker for even the biggest Apple fan.

But for anyone put off by the complexity of setting up a smart home, Apple is trying to simplify things. It has partnered with LG on Home Collection – a range of devices, including security cameras and a video doorbell – that connect with a single tap, just as AirPods do with an iPhone. They won’t be available until later in the year, but they could mark a major step towards making smart home set-up less complicated.

My early verdict

HomeView is built for the Apple faithful: set-up requires an iPhone or iPad, personalised AI features need a recent Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, and some apps work only when your phone is nearby. In a household split between iPhone and Android, Android users will get a much thinner experience, and Apple’s own services come first at every turn.

Still, HomeView is the most polished smart display I have seen. Face recognition makes it both a great shared and personalised device; the sound quality is excellent; and Siri AI is finally worth talking to, especially when it can draw on your personal context. I’ll need to live with it for a few weeks before giving a final verdict, but so far it’s a beautifully designed device I’d be happy to invite into my home.

News.title: Ed Miliband calls for ‘new deal on debt’ as developing countries face spiralling borrowing costs
News.content:
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has called for a “new deal on debt” as spiralling borrowing costs force developing countries to spend more on interest payments than on education or health.

In a speech in Bangkok on Wednesday, Mr Miliband warned that the global financial system is failing emerging markets, and promised to use the UK’s diplomatic heft to push for urgent reform.

He said: “The short-term repayments are crippling, and while many are not defaulting on their payments they are being forced, if you like, to default on the lives and prospects of future generations.

“So we need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space.”

Although public debt is not inherently problematic, servicing costs are at a 25-year-high – squeezing government coffers just as conflict, climate change and a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño push food and fuel prices ever higher.

Emerging economies in particular have little headroom: according to the Rockefeller Foundation, average interest payments now exceed 10 per cent of revenue in developing nations, while UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) analysis found 3.7 billion people live in countries where debt servicing costs exceed spending on health or education.

At the same time, overseas development aid (ODA) spending from wealthy countries has plummeted – hitting social, infrastructure and humanitarian projects, and disaster response.

The mounting global debt pile has dominated discussions in Bangkok this week, where some 15,000 people have descended for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.

This included the first meeting of the newly formed Borrowers’ Platform on Monday. A group of finance ministers and central bank governors from some 30 countries, it was formed to exchange ideas about how to deal with debt burdens – and how to avoid pitfalls.

Sports.title: Burnham forced to order wider probe of his dealings with Man City as details of SEVENTH meeting emerge
Sports.content:

ANDY Burnham was forced to order a wider probe of his dealings with Manchester City yesterday following The Sun’s investigation into his links with the crisis-hit club.

The PM has asked for a “manual trawl” of his previous engagements with the team’s bosses and Abu Dhabi owners — as details of a seventh meeting emerged.



Mr Burnham and his team began the week insisting he had held only one “significant” meeting with City chiefs — in 2021.

This was blown apart by our revelations he had been treated to two dinners with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in 2017 and 2018 while Manchester mayor, which had been deleted from the public record.



Mr Burnham’s relationship with City has come under fire after he expressed his “concern” that the UAE owners may leave the club, which has been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules.

At the PM’s instruction, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority issued a vague statement on Monday failing to mention the two dinners with Mr Al Mubarak.



The PM yesterday promised “full transparency”, saying: “I’ve asked them to do a more manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there. There’s no question about that — full transparency.”

But shadow minister Louie French is calling for an apology. He said last night: “The Prime Minister committed to the House of Commons that he would publish all of his Man City dealings on Monday afternoon.

“That did not happen and that is his personal responsibility. He must come to the House and apologise.”

As well as the two dinners, we can reveal that Mr Burnham met City bigwigs at least five other times.



Newly uncovered documents show the PM joined a round-table in China featuring City Football Group in September 2018. It was known he attended an event there for a club office opening, but not that he enjoyed a two-hour lunch with “senior representatives”.

Records released under Freedom of Information laws show Mr Burnham’s official itinerary for a four-day trip included a lunch billed as the “Manchester City Football Group Shenzhen Office Opening and CEO Tech Roundtable”.

The papers, stamped “Classified: Internal Personal and Confidential”, show the summit ran from 11.30am to 1.30pm on September 20, 2018, at One Shenzhen Bay.



The £4,796 bill for flights, hotels and costs was covered by the Manchester China Forum, a partnership to boost ties between the two areas.

In September 2019, Mr Burnham was pictured with Mr Al Mubarak watching Vincent Kompany’s testimonial match at the Etihad.

He then held what he called his only “significant meeting” with City’s chairman at the Government’s Global Investment Summit in October 2021.



In July 2023, he met City Football Group chief exec Ferran Soriano at an event to mark the completion of the Co-op Live roof in Manchester, the arena co-owned by the Blues’ owner Sheikh Mansour.

And in June 2025, Mr Burnham met Roel de Vries, City’s former chief operating officer, again at the arena, for a Brit Awards bash.

Image: Richard Dawson has been named assistant coach to Stephen Fleming in the England men's Test team

"Daws is a brilliant coach. He's been absolutely amazing for us," Crane said. "He has very high standards; he pushes you to become the best version of yourself, and we all sort of thrived off that.

"From a Glamorgan point of view, we'd obviously rather have kept him. But when you have someone like Daws as your coach, if we're if we're being brutally honest, I think you know at some point that he's going to go on to international cricket.

"He's such a brilliant manager of people. He'll be amazing in any role he does.

"It's amazing for England. And like I said, I'm sure one day he will be in a position to take over an international side. He's that kind of calibre of coach."

Crane on batting form - 'My confidence just grew and grew'

Crane's return to the England fold has as much to do with his hugely-improved form with the bat, as much as his performances with the ball.

Image: Mason Crane celebrates one of his two centuries for Glamorgan in the County Championship

Crane struck a maiden first-class century, swiftly following with a second, as Glamorgan finished safely in sixth place upon their first County Championship season in Division One since 2005.

"I've always believed I underperformed a bit with the bat," Crane said. "When I moved to Glamorgan and started playing a lot more regularly, I kind of realised I had a few more shots.

"My confidence just grew and grew. And then this year, to get a few big scores has been amazing.

"Ironically, that's helped my bowling because I'm now bowling in matches where I probably wouldn't be playing in to start with."

Crane claimed 34 wickets across 14 County Championship appearances in 2026, and 15 in 10 Vitality Blast outings. He also played three times for London Spirit in The Hundred, taking two wickets.

A couple of his dismissals went viral on social media, particularly those of Yorkshire batters George Hill and James Wharton as part of an eight-wicket match haul back in April, but Crane doesn't want to just be Insta-famous.

"I don't want to just be a highlights reel bowler, every now and then bowl a really good ball and just live off that," he added.

"I pride myself on trying to play to the situations really, trying to work out how I'm going to get the most out of a wicket and get a particular guy out.

"I've also given myself a bit more freedom, I guess, with the ball now. I try and bowl more variations, but I'm also better at bowling them now.

"It's about sort of adding as many strings to your bow. It's really important."

Sports.title: Rutter scores twice as Brighton win big and go top in Conference League
Sports.content:
Georginio Rutter scored twice and set up one as Brighton thrashed Kauno Zalgris 4-0 to get their Conference League campaign off to a winning start.

Brighton were dominant from the first whistle to the last against the Lithuanian Cup winners and took the lead through Rutter, but only after a VAR check. The ball had initially been deemed to have gone out of play before Ibrahim Osman's cut-back to the Frenchman, but the goal was awarded after review.

Image: Brighton and Hove Albion's Jack Hinshelwood (second right) is embraced by his team-mates

Rutter then turned provider as Brighton doubled their lead on the stroke of half-time when Hinshelwood - returning to the side for the first time since the Premier League opening weekend - slotted into the corner.

The third came after a lung-bursting run from Malick Yalcouye, who played Osman through to cross for Rutter to turn into the net with ease.

Matt O'Riley made it four with a header as he scored his first Brighton goal since August 2025. The Australia international should have got his second with another header late on, but was denied by an excellent save from Tomas Svedkauskas.

It is now five straight wins in all competitions for Fabian Hurzeler's side who host rivals Crystal Palace in the Premier League on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

Hurzeler: Disciplined performance sets us up

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler:

"We showed a good performance, a disciplined performance, a performance where we kept a clean sheet and a performance where a lot of players used the opportunities.

"This will be key for the season, that we can really rely on each other."

'Convincing win for Hurzeler's side'

Analysis from Sky Sports News' Sophie Evans:

"A convincing win for Fabian Hurzeler's side as they kick off the club's second chapter in Europe in style. The fans around the stadium are already confident of a strong run in this competition, chanting 'we're going to go to Istanbul'.

"The Brighton boss joined his team in applauding this evening's home support. He said that their energy would be crucial in making the Amex a fortress for the opposition this season.

"It's five wins in a row in all competitions for the Seagulls. They were already the favourites to win the Conference League and their dominant performance this evening will only drive that narrative."

Key moments from the Amex Stadium...

3: CLOSE! Costinha heads over from six yards out! Excellent early opportunity for Brighton.

14: SAVE! Gross shoots from the free-kick, but his effort is tipped over by the goalkeeper!

32: CLOSE! Dunk whips a shot at goal from distance that goes just over and lands on the roof of the net!

35: SAVE! Gross with an excellent delivery from the right for Hinshelwood who heads into the ground forcing the goalkeeper to make an acrobatic one-handed save.

43: GOAL! Rutter opens the scoring after turning in Osman's cross. The goal is awarded after a VAR check.

45+1: GOAL! Rutter turns provider and crosses for Hinshelwood who produces a tidy finish across the goalkeeper to double Brighton's lead.

49: SAVE! Gross picks out De Cuyper with a lovely ball, the substitute crosses on the volley for Hinshelwood whose header is tipped over.

53: GOAL! Rutter scores his second of the night after a quality ball from Yalcouye to Osman who cuts back for the Dutchman to apply the finish.

67: GOAL! O'Riley heads across the goalkeeper and into the net to make it 4-0 to the home side.

79: SAVE! Costinha with a header at the back post. Well saved by the goalkeeper!

82: SAVE! O'Riley's bullet-header is saved brilliantly by the Kauno Zilgris goalkeeper.

Dubois rose from the canvas twice to claim a stoppage victory in a tremendous battle with Wardley and win the WBO heavyweight championship in May.

The two will rematch at London's O2 arena this weekend.
