“And so, for us, we are very happy. The recent increment of salaries for members of the armed forces. I’m sure very soon the police and all others are being addressed, including those of the pensioners.

“Nobody is going to be left behind. Mr. President wants every Nigerian and every citizen to be happy with what is ongoing, and he is fully committed in the peaceful efforts on what we are doing today.

Musa added, “And we want Nigerians to put their hands together to make sure that Nigeria remains free. Security is everybody’s responsibility. It’s not only for members of security forces.

“Everyone has a role to play. And we keep on preaching. Whatever you see that is going wrong, even with our members that are not doing what is right, please, don’t hesitate to report. Action will be taken.”

World.title: President’s Choice of 12 States for Personal Campaign Signals Battlegrounds for 2027
World.content:
• APC releases nationwide schedule for rally

•Tinubu wants another term, but ashamed to face the people, Atiku mocks president

•He’s scared to face the electorate, says Makinde/Daura Campaign Organisation

Chuks Okocha, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Jonathan Eze in Lagos





The decision by President Bola Tinubu to personally lead the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign in 12 strategically selected states ahead of the January 16, 2027 election might have inadvertently revealed where the ruling party expects some of its fiercest electoral contests.

Beyond the appearances themselves, the choices offer an interesting insight into the president’s electoral calculations and the states considered critical to Tinubu’s re-election bid.

Of the 36 states of the federation, Tinubu has elected to personally campaign in Kaduna, Rivers, Plateau, Oyo, Borno, Enugu, Bauchi, Sokoto, Delta, Kano, Adamawa and Lagos, leaving the remaining 24 states and the Federal Capital Territory to the campaign machinery and other party leaders.

Although the president explained at Wednesday’s inauguration of his Presidential Campaign Council that governance must not suffer on account of electioneering, the states selected for his personal appearances appear anything but accidental.

Indeed, a closer examination of the results of the 2023 presidential election offers perhaps the clearest explanation for the choice.

Of the 12 states, Tinubu won only three — Rivers, Oyo and Borno — in the last presidential election. He lost the remaining nine to his principal opponents, namely Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso.

Instructively, Atiku defeated him in Kaduna, Bauchi, Sokoto and Adamawa, while Obi won Plateau, Enugu, Delta and Lagos. Kwankwaso, on his part, carried Kano, delivering nearly one million votes under the platform of the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP).

Put differently, 75 per cent of Tinubu’s proposed personal campaign appearances will take place in states where he suffered electoral defeats in 2023. This is hardly a coincidence that can be dismissed in the circumstances.

Take Kaduna, for example. The decision to formally flag off the campaign in the state on October 24 is particularly instructive. Atiku polled 554,360 votes there in 2023 against Tinubu’s 399,293, despite the APC controlling the state government.

With Atiku again seeking the presidency, this time on the platform of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Kaduna represents an important electoral contest, particularly given its political significance in the North-west.

The inclusion of Kano is perhaps even more revealing. In 2023, Kwankwaso secured 997,279 votes against Tinubu’s 517,341. But the political circumstances have since changed, with Kwankwaso now running alongside Obi on the platform of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC).

Thus, Kano is no longer merely about reversing a previous electoral defeat. It is also about confronting the combined political ambitions of two former presidential candidates, one of whom demonstrated considerable electoral strength in the state.

Sokoto presents a different calculation. Atiku defeated Tinubu there by just 3,235 votes in 2023, making it one of the closest contests between both candidates. Such a narrow margin naturally makes the state an interesting electoral territory for both parties.

Similarly, Adamawa, Atiku’s home state, where the former vice-president secured 417,611 votes against Tinubu’s 182,881, offers the APC another opportunity to test its political strength in an established opposition stronghold.

Bauchi also fits into this northern calculation, especially with the changing political alliances ahead of the 2027 contest.

In the South-east, the decision to visit Enugu is equally significant. Tinubu recorded a mere 4,772 votes in the state in 2023, compared with Obi’s 428,640. The difference was staggering and underscored the depth of APC’s electoral difficulties in that part of the country.

Enugu, therefore, presents not merely an opportunity to seek votes but also a chance for the president to make a direct appeal to an electorate that overwhelmingly rejected his candidacy four years earlier.

Plateau and Delta, which Obi also won in 2023, fall within the same broad electoral consideration, although their political circumstances and voting patterns differ considerably.

Then comes Lagos, arguably the most symbolic of the 12 states.

For a politician whose political influence has been closely associated with Lagos for decades, losing the state to Obi in 2023 was one of the election’s notable developments. Obi polled 582,454 votes against Tinubu’s 572,606, a difference of just 9,848 votes.

That Tinubu has chosen Lagos for the grand finale of his campaign on January 9, 2027, could therefore carry significance beyond the customary symbolism of ending a national campaign on familiar political territory.

It offers the APC an opportunity to demonstrate the strength of its organisation in a state that remains central to Tinubu’s political history.

However, the inclusion of Rivers, Oyo and Borno, which he won in 2023, suggests that the campaign strategy is not entirely about recovering lost ground.

Rivers remains politically important because of the influence of the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, and the state’s complicated political alignments.

Oyo has assumed additional significance with Governor Seyi Makinde’s presidential ambition, while Borno remains the political base of Vice-President Kashim Shettima.

These three states may consequently be seen as territories where the president considers reinforcement of existing support just as important as the pursuit of new votes elsewhere.

Taken together, the 12-state itinerary suggests a deliberate attempt to balance electoral recovery with political consolidation. Seven of the states are in the North, while five are in the South, ensuring that the president’s personal appearances cut across all six geopolitical zones.

Of course, the 2023 results cannot automatically determine the outcome of the 2027 election. Political alliances have changed, candidates have switched platforms, and the electorate will be judging Tinubu not merely as a candidate but as an incumbent with a record to defend.

Nevertheless, the campaign timetable has provided an early glimpse into the geographical priorities of the ruling party.

While the APC will campaign nationwide, the president’s decision to personally appear in these 12 states suggests that some electoral contests are receiving particular attention.

And if the itinerary is anything to go by, the battle for 2027 may already have its first identified battlegrounds — not necessarily by the opposition’s declaration, but by the president’s own campaign choices.

Meanwhile, the APC has released its nationwide campaign rally schedule for the 2027 presidential election covering 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

According to the timetable sighted yesterday, Tinubu is expected to lead the campaign for his re-election in 12 different states, including Kaduna, where the ruling party would officially flag-off the campaign on October 24, 2026.

This was as the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has said Tinubu was too ashamed to ask Nigerians for four more years, the reason he served a notice he would not go round the country to campaign.

At the same time, the Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has also said Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign.

In another development, Atiku’s Media Office has said the attempt by Vice President Kashim Shettima to portray him as a beneficiary of Bola Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged.

APC Releases Nationwide Schedule for Rally, Tinubu Leads Campaign in 12 States

The APC has released its nationwide campaign rally schedule for the 2027 presidential election covering 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

According to the timetable sighted yesterday, Tinubu is expected to lead the campaign for his re-election in 12 different states, including Kaduna, where the ruling party would officially flag-off the campaign on October 24, 2026.

President Bola Tinubu had Wednesday during the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) held at the Presidential Villa hinted that he won’t be available for all the campaign because he doesn’t want to abandon governance.

The campaign is scheduled to run from October 2026 through early January 2027, with Lagos hosting the major closing rally on 9th January 2027.

The schedule showed that President Tinubu would also lead the Port Harcourt campaign scheduled to take place on November 7.

He would also be on the campaign train to Plateau State on November 14, and would be in action in Ibadan, Oyo State on November 21.

Similarly, he would be available to captain the campaign train in Borno State on November 25, and he would also be on ground in Enugu on November 28.

The president is also expected to put on his campaign amour in Sokoto State on December 5, and in Asaba, Delta State on December 12.

Continuing,Tinubu would lead the campaign train to Kano, the votes hub on December 17, while Bauchi State would play host to the APC campaign train on December 29.

The president would lead the campaign to Yola, Adamawa State, the home state of his main challenger, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, on Monday, January 4, 2027, while the grand finale of the campaign would be held in Lagos State on Saturday, January 9, 2027.

Other campaign schedules include Owerri, Imo – 30th December; Akure, Ondo state – 11th November; Bauchi – 29th November; Katsina – 2nd December; Uyo, Akwa Ibom – 18th November; Makurdi, Benue State -30th November.

Others are Abeokuta, Ogun State, 3rd December; Awka, Anambra state -19th November; Gombe state, 3rd November; Kebbi state -17th November; Edo state – 12th November, Kwara state -10th December.

Also, Osun State will host the campaign on December 9, Abia State on December 7; Yobe State on November 16, Zamfara State on December 14; Bayelsa state on December 15, Niger State December 16, and Ekiti State November 5.

Ebonyi State is billedd for November 9; Taraba State or December 19, Jigawa State for November 10, Cross River for November 2; Kogi State December 8; Nasarawa State for November 8; and Adamawa State for January 4, 2027.

Meanwhile, President Tinubu has issued an order to the Director of Women Mobilisation of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, Dr. Betta Edu, and the party’s women leadership nationwide to galvanise the female electorate, consolidate grassroots support and spearhead an expansive mobilisation drive ahead of the 2027 general election.

The president gave the directive on Wednesday afternoon at the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council at the Banquet Hall of the Presidential Villa, Abuja, where he extolled the political significance of women and underscored their indispensable role in the party’s electoral calculations.

Recognising women as an influential constituency whose organisational dexterity, numerical strength and penetration of grassroots communities could substantially shape the electoral landscape, Tinubu charged them to convert their longstanding commitment to the APC into a formidable and meticulously coordinated political force.

The President pledged his support for legislative efforts to expand women’s representation in elected offices, assuring the gathering that his administration would sponsor the Women Reserve Seat Bill.

“You women are the greatest mobilisers, and I assure you a sponsorship of the Women Reserve Seat Bill. Go and work for it, it will come to fruition to increase the number of women representation at both National Assembly and subnational level. I assure you that,” Tinubu declared.

Tinubu Wants Another Term, But Ashamed to Face the People, Atiku Mocks President

Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has said President Bola Tinubu was too ashamed to ask Nigerians for four more years, the reason he served a notice he would not go round the country to campaign.

Instead, he claimed that the president chose to send governors, ministers and defectors across the country to defend the hardship of the past three and a half.

Also, the Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has corroborated this when it also said Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign, which is an aberration in a democracy.

This, nonetheless, the media office of Atiku has said the attempt by Vice-President Kashim Shettima to portray Atiku as a beneficiary of Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged.

A statement by the Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, stated that, “Tinubu says he may miss campaign rallies because Nigeria needs his attention. Where was that urgency when Nigerians pleaded for relief?

He has had three and a half years to govern. In that time, families have been forced to cut meals, postpone medical care and watch their earnings lose value before they get home.

“Now he wants another mandate. Before asking Nigerians for one, he must face them and account for the first term.

“Let him look a mother in the eye and explain what his government has done to make food affordable. Let him tell pensioners why they cannot afford their medicines. Let him explain to young Nigerians why years of study and hard work have still not brought them decent jobs.

“Tinubu says American creditors cannot wait. Nigerians cannot wait either. They have bills to pay, children to feed and lives to rebuild. They deserve a President who treats their suffering with the same urgency he gives creditors and investors.

“Instead, he is assembling a crowd of politicians to speak for him. He can fill every campaign stage in Nigeria. He cannot fill an empty pot with surrogates. He cannot send a politician into a market to persuade prices to fall.

“The people on his campaign council did not receive the mandate in 2023. Tinubu did. He made the promises. He took the decisions. He must face the questions.

“Nigerians will hear whatever his surrogates have to say. But when they vote, they will remember what they have lived through. No crowd of politicians can stand between Tinubu and his record.”

Tinubu Scared to Face Electorate, Says Makinde/Daura Campaign Organisation

The Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has said President Bola Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign.

Referring to himself as “Governor Tinubu” at the inauguration of his presidential campaign council, it said indicated a serious state of confabulation, disorientation and disconnection from reality underscoring his unfitness to govern.

In a statement by the Director of Strategic Communications of Makinde and Daura Presidential Campaign, Richard Ihediwa, said the campaign considered Tinubu’s decision not to accompany the “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition” to every state of the federation as a desperate attempt to evade public resentment, knowing that his government has renewed the “anger” of Nigerians, rather than their “hope” in the past three and a half years.

The Director of strategic communications further said the decision not only constituted a serious affront to the Nigerian electorate, but also made a caricature of democratic ethos.

“Mr. President’s decision and his confabulatory statement further confirmed fears by Nigerians that he is not fit to face the rigours of governing a nation like Nigeria.

“The decision not to campaign around the country also reinforces public apprehension that the All Progressives Congress (APC) is not ready for a free, fair and credible election but plotting to circumvent and compromise the process against the Will of the people.

“A president who believes he has performed well should be confident to defend his record before the people. However, having failed in all of his promises and having no meaningful achievements to boast of, President Tinubu is now fishing for excuses not to face the people.”

Attempt by Shettima to Portray Atiku as Beneficiary of Tinubu’s Political Generosity Misrepresents Historical Facts

Atiku Abubakar’s Media Office has said the attempt by Vice President Kashim Shettima to portray him as a beneficiary of Bola Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged.

In a a statement, the media office said, ‘’For Shettima’s education, the Action Congress (AC), on whose platform Atiku contested the 2007 presidential election, was not Tinubu’s personal political property.

‘’The AC emerged in 2006 from a coalition involving Tinubu’s faction of the Alliance for Democracy (AD), the Advanced Congress of Democrats (ACD), the Justice Party and other political interests.

‘’On the AD side were Bola Tinubu, Chief Bisi Akande, Aremo Olusegun Osoba, Otunba Niyi Adebayo and other prominent AD leaders.

‘’On the ACD/PDP breakaway side were Atiku Abubakar, Chief Audu Ogbeh, Chief Tom Ikimi, Alhaji Lawal Kaita, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, Alhaji Abubakar Rimi and former Speaker Ghali Na’Abba, among others.’’

The statement claimed that those were political heavyweights who came together to build an alternative political platform in the aftermath of the struggle against President Olusegun Obasanjo’s third-term ambition.

The Atiku media office further said it was a coalition of political interests, not a charity established by Tinubu to accommodate Atiku.

Accordingly, the Atiku media office said, “Indeed, Chief Bisi Akande, a central figure in the formation of the AC and its former National Chairman, acknowledged in his autobiography: “In 2007, we formed a party, the AC, with Abubakar Atiku.”

The Media office of the former vice president said, ‘’Akande also disclosed that the understanding was for Atiku to emerge as the presidential candidate, with Tinubu considered as his running mate. That proposal ultimately failed over objections to a Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket.

‘’Now, if Tinubu merely gave Atiku a political platform out of generosity, why was Tinubu himself being considered for the position of running mate? The answer is simple: they were political partners, not landlord and tenant.

‘’Atiku was already Vice President of Nigeria, with an established national political structure and considerable political influence, long before the AC was formed. Tinubu did not manufacture Atiku’s political relevance.

‘’Shettima should also remember that Atiku fought attempts to exclude him from the 2007 presidential election all the way to the Supreme Court and prevailed. As for Shettima’s attempt to ridicule Atiku by comparing him with Abraham Lincoln and Raila Odinga, what exactly is his point?”

World.title: W’Bank: $12.4bn Unrepatriated Oil Funds Eroded Nigeria’s External Surplus in H1
World.content:
• Portfolio investments hit $12.2bn, dwarfs $2.2bn direct investment inflows

•Lender identifies overlapping budget cycles as key weakness

•Calls for better expenditure forecast, credible budget calendar

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





Nigeria’s external accounts lost the benefit of a substantial inflow of foreign exchange in the first half of 2026, as unexplained transactions totalling $12.4 billion wiped out much of the combined gains from the country’s current account surplus and net financial inflows, the World Bank has said.

The unexplained outflows, recorded as net errors and omissions in the balance of payments, likely reflected, in part, oil export proceeds that were not repatriated into the country, according to the bank’s latest assessment of the Nigerian economy.

The development highlighted a persistent weakness in Nigeria’s foreign exchange market, where limited repatriation of export earnings and low Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) have left the country increasingly dependent on short-term portfolio investments to support foreign exchange supply and build external reserves.

However, the global lender did not say the $12.4 billion represented stolen funds or missing oil revenue. The figure only reflected a discrepancy between recorded external transactions and financial flows that could not be fully reconciled. It therefore requires further clarification from the government.

According to the World Bank, the gap likely reflected, in part, oil export proceeds that were not repatriated. Such proceeds may be retained in offshore accounts or used to meet existing obligations, including repayments under oil-backed financing arrangements, rather than returned to Nigeria through the domestic foreign exchange market.

“In principle, both current account surpluses and net financial inflows should support reserve accumulation, but large net errors and omissions of $12.4 billion in H1 2026 offset much of their combined total, likely reflecting in part oil export proceeds that were not repatriated.

“As a result, FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) has been a major driver of the continued rise in gross international reserves, which increased from $45.5 billion at end-2025 to $53.8 billion at end-August 2026,” the World Bank document titled: “Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Shaped State Priorities”, stated.

The World Bank also identified oil pledges as one of the factors limiting the repatriation of export earnings, although it did not establish how much of the $12.4 billion discrepancy was attributable to such arrangements.

The discrepancy nevertheless raises questions about the transparency and reconciliation of Nigeria’s export earnings, particularly in the oil sector, where foreign exchange receipts are critical to reserve accumulation and exchange rate stability.

Other possible explanations for net errors and omissions include incomplete reporting, differences in the timing of transactions and gaps in the recording of cross-border financial flows.

Besides, the World Bank report showed that Nigeria’s current account surplus rose to $12 billion, equivalent to 7 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), in the first half of 2026, compared with $5.5 billion in the second half of 2025 and $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

However, the country recorded net portfolio investment inflows of $12.2 billion during the period, an 80.8 per cent increase over the second half of 2025, while direct investment liabilities fell by 15 per cent to $2.2 billion.

The bank noted that, in principle, the current account surplus and net financial inflows should have supported a stronger accumulation of foreign reserves, but the $12.4 billion net errors and omissions figure offset much of their combined contribution.

Nigeria’s gross international reserves nevertheless increased from $45.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $53.8 billion at the end of August 2026, supported largely by portfolio investment inflows.

The World Bank, however, cautioned that the absence of a more recent net reserves estimate beyond the $34.8 billion reported at the end of 2025 limited its ability to assess the country’s usable external reserve buffers.

The growing reliance on portfolio investments also exposes the economy to sudden capital outflows whenever global financial conditions deteriorate or investors become less willing to hold assets in emerging markets.

Between January and August 2026, foreign portfolio investment accounted for 45 per cent of gross inflows through the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, almost entirely in fixed-income instruments, including investments attracted by high domestic yields and relative exchange rate stability.

The bank observed that although the functioning of the foreign exchange market had improved markedly since 2024, the supply of foreign exchange continued to depend heavily on short-term foreign portfolio investment.

It said foreign direct investment remained low, while the repatriation of export proceeds was still limited, partly because of oil pledges.

According to the report, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) had introduced reforms aimed at improving the operation of the foreign exchange market, including integrating bureaux de change into the official market through a centralised platform, standardising due diligence requirements and removing restrictions that previously constrained international oil companies from transferring their export proceeds abroad.

Other measures included granting unfettered access to domiciliary account balances, simplifying remittance procedures and raising the advance-payment limit for imports.

According to the bank, these reforms could encourage more stable foreign investment by improving the predictability and convertibility of the foreign exchange regime.

It also recommended progressively allowing banks to hold net open foreign exchange positions and improving the transparency of the CBN’s intervention framework to deepen the market and reduce exchange rate volatility.

The World Bank said sustained macroeconomic stabilisation and structural reforms capable of improving investment returns and reducing risks would be necessary to attract more durable foreign exchange inflows.

Beyond the external sector, the report warned that rising expenditure pressures could erode the federal government’s improved fiscal position and widen Nigeria’s consolidated fiscal deficit to about 3.5 per cent of GDP in 2026.

The warning comes despite an improvement in federal government revenue in the first half of the year, supported by higher distributable oil revenues, stronger corporate tax collections and increased independent revenues.

According to the report, federal revenue rose to N6.2 trillion, equivalent to 2.5 per cent of GDP, in the first half of 2026, from N3.6 trillion, or 1.6 per cent of GDP, in the corresponding period of 2025.

The increase, it stressed, helped narrow the federal fiscal deficit to N9.9 trillion, or 4 per cent of GDP, from N11 trillion, equivalent to 5 per cent of GDP, a year earlier.

However, the World Bank cautioned that the improvement should be interpreted carefully because reported federal capital spending remained unusually low.

Capital expenditure fell to N700 billion, representing 0.3 per cent of GDP, in the first half of 2026, compared with one per cent of GDP in the corresponding period of 2025.

At the same time, interest payments rose to N7.7 trillion, or 3.1 per cent of GDP, from N5.6 trillion, equivalent to 2.5 per cent of GDP, reflecting persistently high domestic borrowing costs.

Personnel expenditure also increased to N4.2 trillion from N3.7 trillion following wage adjustments.

The bank warned that the combination of recurrent expenditure obligations, high debt-service costs and the possible acceleration of capital spending later in the year could put additional pressure on public finances.

It also identified overlapping budget cycles, weak alignment between approved allocations and implementation capacity, and delays in expenditure reporting as persistent challenges undermining budget credibility.

At the federation level, the report showed that gross Federation Account revenues rose in nominal terms to N18.9 trillion in the first half of 2026 from N17.7 trillion a year earlier, although they declined as a share of GDP to 7.6 per cent from eight per cent.

Besides, distributions to the three tiers of government increased to N10.5 trillion from N7.6 trillion, supported partly by lower deductions from Federation Account revenues, the report stated.

The World Bank attributed the reduction in deductions partly to a February 2026 executive order that eliminated the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) management fee and Frontier Exploration Fund (FEF) deductions and redirected gas-flaring penalties to the Federation Account.

But despite the improvement in revenue distribution and the narrower federal deficit, the bank maintained that higher spending pressures were likely to widen the consolidated fiscal deficit for the full year.

It called for better expenditure planning, a more credible budget calendar and timely, comprehensive and consistently classified fiscal reporting to strengthen budget execution and improve public financial management.

World.title: FACC Disburses N2.428tn September Allocations as Federation Revenue Grosses N3.913tn
World.content:
• Inflation drops to 14.63% amid moderation in food index

•Severe in Imo, Enugu, Niger

Ndubuisi Francis and James Emejo in Abuja





The Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) has disbursed a total of N2.428 trillion to the federal, state, and local governments, as Federation Revenue grossed N3.913 trillion for the month of September 2026.

FAAC shared the amount during its October meeting in Abuja, yesterday, Director of Press and Public Relations, Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation (OAGF), Bawa Mokwa, said in a statement.

The N2.428 trillion September allocations surpassed the sum of N2.338 trillion shared in the preceding month of August by N90 billion.

That was the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures the rate of change in prices of good and commodities, declined to 14.63 per cent in September, from 15.39 per cent in August, National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said yesterday.

The drop was occasioned by falling food prices, which helped to moderate the cost of living, although underlying price pressures showed signs of renewed strength.

According to the CPI report for the month under review, headline inflation rate fell by 6.35 percentage points, from 20.98 per cent recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.

However, the relief remained uneven, with the core inflation rate, which excludes farm produce and energy, rising on a month-on-month basis, while urban inflation also accelerated during the review period.

Citing the communique issued at the meeting, Mokwa said from the N2.428 trillion distributable revenue, the federal government received N832.242 billion, state governments received N799.872 billion, while local government councils got N560.660 billion.

The sum of N236.049 billion went to oil mineral producing states as 13 per cent derivation revenue.

The N2.428 trillion total distributable revenue for September comprised a distributable statutory revenue of N1.672 trillion and distributable Value Added Tax (VAT) revenue of N756.587 billion.

Although gross revenue was N3.913 trillion in the month of September, total deductions for cost of collection stood at N131.758 billion, while total transfers, refunds, and savings accounted for N1.352 trillion.

According to the communique, gross statutory revenue of N3.096 trillion was received for the month of September 2026, an amount higher than the sum of N2.850 trillion received in the preceding month by N246.384 billion.

Value Added Tax (VAT) also posted a gross revenue of N816.872 billion in September, N17.972 billion, an amount less than the N834.843 billion recorded in the month of August 2026.

However, from the N816.872 billion gross VAT revenue, distributable VAT revenue was N756.587 billion from which the federal government received N75.659 billion, state governments got N416.123 billion, and local government councils received N264.805 billion.

According to the figures, state and local government councils received larger shares of distributable VAT revenue, while the federal government got a smaller share.

The communiqué also showed that gross statutory revenue rose in September, while VAT revenue declined during the period.

It equally emerged that gross statutory revenue stood at N3.096 trillion in September, up from N2.850 trillion in August, the N246.384 billion rise reflecting higher revenue available from statutory sources.

Overall, FAAC attributed the changes in revenue performance to increases in some tax and petroleum-related revenue sources, alongside declines in others.

Petroleum Profit Tax (PPT), Hydrocarbon Tax, petroleum royalties, import duty, Common External Tariff (CET) levies and excise duty recorded significant increases in September.

But Companies Income Tax (CIT), Capital Gains Tax (CGT), Stamp Duties Tax (SDT), VAT, mineral royalties, gas-flaring penalties, rental gas-flaring fees and miscellaneous oil revenue declined during the period.

Meanwhile, the CPI increased marginally to 146.38 points in September from 146.30 points in August, indicating that the overall price level continued to edge upwards, despite the slower annual inflation rate.

Month-on-month, headline inflation declined sharply to 0.06 per cent in September, compared with 0.71 per cent in August, NBS stated.

Average prices continued to increase, but at a substantially slower pace than in the preceding month.

Food prices provided the strongest relief during the period, as food inflation declined to 19.59 per cent year-on-year in September, from 20.16 per cent in September 2025.

Food inflation turned negative on a month-on-month basis, falling to -1.55 per cent from 1.02 per cent in August.

NBS attributed the development to changes in the average prices of several food items, including guinea corn flour, white maize flour, local short-grain rice, eggs, fresh onions, palm oil, fresh green beans, Irish potatoes, okra, fresh tomatoes, dried green peas and plantain.

The average annual food inflation rate for the 12 months ending September stood at 15.72 per cent, down from 28.37 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.

Despite the moderation, food inflation remained a major concern, with significant differences in price movements across states.

Core inflation presented a less encouraging picture, rising to 1.11 per cent month-on-month in September from -0.06 per cent in August.

Year-on-year, core inflation stood at 12.95 per cent, down from 22.11 per cent in September 2025.

The average annual core inflation rate for the 12 months ending September was 16.54 per cent, compared with 25.68 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year.

The divergence between falling food prices and the acceleration in monthly core inflation suggested that the easing in headline inflation was not broad-based across all components of the consumer basket.

Urban inflation also remained elevated, standing at 15.64 per cent year-on-year in September, while its month-on-month rate increased to 0.53 per cent from 0.28 per cent in August.

The average annual urban inflation rate for the 12 months ending September was 15.90 per cent, substantially below the 28.48 per cent recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.

Rural inflation stood at 12.46 per cent year-on-year, with the monthly rate falling to -0.89 per cent from 1.79 per cent in August.

The average annual rural inflation rate declined to 15.32 per cent from 25.67 per cent in September 2025.

At the state level, Imo recorded the highest year-on-year headline inflation at 30.04 per cent, followed by Enugu at 22.38 per cent and Niger at 22.05 per cent.

Taraba recorded the lowest annual headline inflation at 1.78 per cent, followed by Bauchi at 2.84 per cent and Adamawa at 3.66 per cent.

Month-on-month, Imo also recorded the highest headline inflation at 8.64 per cent, followed by Kaduna at 4.46 per cent and Sokoto at 3.01 per cent.

In contrast, Adamawa recorded the steepest monthly decline at -6.10 per cent, followed by Bauchi at -5.31 per cent and Kano at -4.49 per cent.

World.title: FG Flags Off N1.83tn Dangote-financed Niger Highway Project
World.content:
• Umahi: Over 5,500km of road projects ongoing across north-central

•Bago pledges to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election

•Dangote puts roads funded by his group at over N5tn

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





The federal government has commenced the reconstruction and dualisation of the 401-kilometre Lambata-Bida-Mokwa-Makera-Kontagora Road in Niger State, in a N1.83 trillion project expected to improve connectivity between communities, agricultural centres and commercial hubs.

The project, which is being financed by the Dangote Group through the federal government’s tax-credit scheme, is expected to ease the movement of people and goods across the state and adjoining areas, while opening up new economic opportunities along the corridor.

Niger State Governor, Umaru Bago, who performed the flag-off on behalf of President Bola Tinubu in Bida, described the project as a significant milestone in the development of the state and the renewal of hope for residents and motorists who depend on the road.

The project will involve the reconstruction and expansion of the highway, which runs from Lambata through Bida, Mokwa and Makera before terminating at Kontagora. According to the federal government, the intervention is expected to improve access to markets, facilitate the transportation of agricultural produce and stimulate commercial activities.

Speaking at the ceremony, the Minister of Works, David Umahi, said the Tinubu administration had initiated approximately 5,500 kilometres of road projects across the North-central zone, with Niger State accounting for more than 1,000 kilometres.

He attributed the scale of infrastructure development to the fiscal space created by the removal of the petrol subsidy, which he said had enabled the federal government to commit more resources to infrastructure nationwide.

Umahi said the Lambata-Bida-Mokwa-Makera-Kontagora project would be constructed using continuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP), a technology intended to provide a durable and climate-resilient road surface.

He described the choice of pavement as a measure to improve the road’s longevity, adding that the administration’s infrastructure programme required continuity to enable ongoing projects to be completed.

The minister also called for Tinubu’s re-election, arguing that another term would enable the president to complete the extensive infrastructure projects already underway across the country.

In his remarks, Bago who thanked Tinubu for approving the project, described the highway as a critical economic artery for Niger State and the wider region.

He pledged to mobilise support for the president’s re-election, promising to work towards securing victory for Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC) at all levels in the state.

Also, the Minister of State for Works, Bello Goronyo, recalled a recent assessment visit to the failed Dikko Junction-Maje Road, a seven-kilometre stretch linked to the major highway project.

He said Tinubu had approved immediate palliative works on the corridor, addressing a problem that had affected motorists and host communities for about a decade.

Goronyo expressed satisfaction that the intervention had eased the difficulties previously experienced by road users.

Besides, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, who spoke on behalf of other Niger State indigenes in the Federal Executive Council (FEC), said the federal government remained committed to accelerating infrastructure development and economic recovery.

He said the administration’s economic reforms were designed to strengthen the economy and support a broader transformation of the agricultural sector.

Idris also emphasised the importance of transparency in the implementation of government programmes and expressed optimism about continued support for the administration in Niger State.

The Chairman of the Senate Committee on Works, Senator Allwell Onyesoh, described the project as part of a deliberate policy to expand infrastructure development across the country.

“What is happening today is not novel; it is intentional on the part of Mr President to provide infrastructure across the country,” he said.

Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Works, Akin Alabi, said the highway was an important transport corridor connecting the northern and southern parts of the country.

He said its reconstruction would improve transportation, facilitate economic activities and strengthen the movement of goods and services, pledging adequate legislative oversight to ensure the project’s implementation.

Providing details of the project, the Director of Highways, Construction and Rehabilitation, David Yiltong, said the road would improve security, facilitate the movement of people and goods and enhance service delivery in communities along the route.

He said the 401-kilometre project would connect several communities and economic centres, strengthening access to agricultural areas and markets.

A representative of the Dangote Group, Mansur Ahmed, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to supporting infrastructure development through investments in the road sector.

He said the project would open up communities, expand economic opportunities, create jobs and stimulate commercial activities, expressing confidence that it would be completed within the stipulated timeframe.

Ahmed put the group’s investment in road infrastructure development across the country at more than N5 trillion.

He also cited the ongoing establishment of a rice mill in Wushishi, Niger State, among the group’s other investments and development initiatives in the state.

The Senior Special Assistant to the President on Community Engagement for the North-central zone, Abiodun Essiet, called for sustained collaboration among the federal and state governments, private-sector partners and local communities to ensure that infrastructure projects met the needs of residents.

Similarly, the Secretary to the Niger State Government, Abubakar Usman, thanked Tinubu for approving the road project and other infrastructure interventions in the state, while acknowledging the Dangote Group’s role in its financing.

The Etsu Nupe and Chairman of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers, Yahaya Abubakar, also expressed appreciation to the president, saying the highway had the potential to improve transportation, expand economic activities and enhance the welfare of communities along the corridor.

World.title: EU, UN Push Nigeria to Mobilise More Local Funds as Joint Projects Top $500m
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja





The European Union (EU) and the United Nations (UN) have called on the Nigerian government to mobilise more domestic resources to bridge the country’s development and humanitarian funding gaps.

Both organisations warned that international assistance must be matched with stronger national ownership and more effective project delivery.

The call came as EU disclosed that its partnership with the UN supported projects worth more than $400 million annually in Nigeria, with a portfolio of about 32 EU-funded projects valued more than $500 million, being implemented in collaboration with 16 UN agencies.

EU Ambassador to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Mignot, speaking after a meeting to review the partnership, said the two institutions were committed to improving the impact of their interventions amid mounting questions about international solidarity, development assistance, and the future of multilateral cooperation.

Mignot said the review was aimed not only at renewing the partnership but also identifying implementation gaps, improving coordination, and ensuring that assistance translated into tangible benefits for ordinary Nigerians.

He said, “This meeting was a clear indication that we need to work together and have the government of Nigeria increase its engagement and mobilisation of domestic resources to address the development gap and the humanitarian assistance need in the country.”

The appeal placed domestic financing and government ownership at the centre of discussions about how Nigeria could sustain development programmes, respond to humanitarian emergencies, and make better use of international support.

According to Mignot, EU-UN partnership combines European financial contributions and grants with United Nations’ technical expertise and operational presence on the ground.

He said the arrangement also involved Nigerian authorities at both federal and state levels to ensure that projects aligned with the country’s development strategies rather than being operated independent of national priorities.

He stated, “Beyond even the financial support, which in Nigeria translates into projects that value more than $400 million a year, we are still having a strong strategic partnership.”

Mignot explained that the collaboration had become increasingly important as the international landscape changed and multilateral institutions faced questions about their ability to sustain cooperation, development assistance, and humanitarian support.

He said EU and UN remained committed to international solidarity and collective action, adding that periodic reviews are necessary to address challenges and strengthen the delivery of joint programmes.

Providing details of the partnership, Mignot said EU and UN had reviewed a portfolio of approximately 32 projects worth more than $500 million, involving 16 UN agencies.

The projects brought together EU funding and UN’s technical and political expertise, with Nigerian authorities participating in the broader partnership.

He said the objective was to ensure that the resources committed to Nigeria translated into effective interventions and measurable benefits for citizens.

The official did not provide a breakdown of the portfolio by sector or clarify the period covered by the more-than-$500 million valuation. The figure, therefore, represents the reported value of the project portfolio, rather than a confirmed annual disbursement.

Mignot also did not provide a breakdown of the more than $400 million in annual project value by programme, beneficiary group, or state.

Nevertheless, he stressed that the effectiveness of the partnership would ultimately depend on its ability to deliver results on the ground.

“We are strong believers in a multilateralism that delivers, that delivers for the people and is efficient on the ground,” he said.

The EU official said the bloc’s investment priorities in Nigeria were guided by its Global Gateway Strategy, which seeks to mobilise investments while supporting sectors considered essential to sustainable development.

He identified education, governance, democracy, human rights and security as important enablers of investment.

Mignot stated that economic opportunities required an environment in which institutions functioned effectively and communities could benefit from development.

The emphasis on security also reflects its importance to the implementation of projects and the ability of development partners to reach intended beneficiaries.

The official said EU would continue to work with UN and Nigerian authorities to support the priorities, with the partnership serving as a mechanism for combining funding, technical capacity, and coordination.

He added that the relationship went beyond financial assistance, providing a strategic framework for responding to development and humanitarian challenges through international cooperation.

The call for increased domestic resource mobilisation signals the importance the partners attach to Nigeria’s capacity to complement external assistance with resources generated within the country.

While international funding can support projects in education, governance, and humanitarian response, the sustainability of such interventions also depends on national financing, effective institutions, and coordination between governments and development partners.

The EU official said the review was intended to determine where the partnership needed improvement, which challenges remained unresolved, and how both institutions could strengthen implementation.

He said cooperation with federal and state authorities was central to ensuring that projects reflected Nigeria’s priorities and addressed the needs of citizens.

The meeting also reaffirmed EU and UN’s commitment to multilateralism at a time when international cooperation and development assistance faced growing scrutiny.

For ordinary Nigerians, the central test of the partnership will be whether its substantial project portfolio translates into better access to essential services, stronger public institutions, improved livelihoods, and more effective humanitarian assistance.

Mignot said the partners would continue to work towards more effective delivery. He stressed that the ultimate purpose of international cooperation was to produce tangible results for people rather than merely sustain agreements between institutions.

World.title: NCC Moves to Strengthen Security in Internet Usage, Inaugurates Working Group
World.content:
Emma Okonji





Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), yester-day in Lagos, held its inaugural symposium on “Inter-net Governance”, designed to strengthen security around the use of the internet and build resilience for all internet users in Nigeria. This is to keep internet us-ers safe while browsing the internet in today’s digital era.

To drive the process of Internet Governance on a na-tional scale, the commission used the symposium to inaugurate the Internet Governance Working Group (IGWG), drawn from industry experts, with the man-date to enforce consumer protection and online safe-ty, drive digital inclusion and meaningful last-mile connectivity with affordable pricing, and promote global participation in surfing the internet from any convenient location, among others.

Speaking at the symposium, Executive Commissioner, Technical Services at NCC, Abraham Oshadami, who represented Executive Vice Chairman of NCC, Dr. Aminu Maida, said the Internet Governance Fo-rums (IGF) at national, regional and global levels had shown the value of bringing different voices to one table to discuss how the internet affected networks, opportunity, trust, security, and the rights of the people who use it.

Oshadami stated, “That responsibility is becoming more urgent. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and access services. It also creates new questions about harmful content, fraud, privacy, accountability and the protection of children and other vulnerable users. These questions cannot be answered by one institution alone. They require informed dialogue and cooperation across the communications sector and beyond.”

Oshadami also spoke about the Internet Code of Practice (ICOP) 2026 implementation guideline, issued by the NCC to network operators, which, according to him, provides a framework for promoting a safer and more responsible online environment.

He said its success would depend on clear expectations, meaningful engagement with affected stakeholders, and consistent implementation.

Oshadami equally spoke on the Cyber Resilience Framework for the Nigeria Communication Sector (CRF-NCS), which mandates network operators to strengthen the security and resilience of the infrastructure on which digital services depend.

According to him, these efforts speak to a simple obligation: Nigerians should be able to use the internet with greater confidence.

He added that the symposium was an opportunity to hear from one another, identify practical priorities, and strengthen the communications sector’s contribution to internet governance.

Presenting the fact sheet on internet governance and why it matters, Assistant Director/Head of Internet Governance Unit at NCC, Ibiso Angela George, said the symposium would link global internet governance discussions to Nigeria’s priorities and turn them into commitments stakeholders could act on.

According to her, a central focus of the symposium is strengthening private sector participation in internet governance.

George said the discussions will examine what held organisations back, what other regulated sectors could learn, and how participation could become more consistent and meaningful.

She said internet governance would help address is-sues around critical internet resources, such as the .ng country domain, help to secure Nigeria’s Domain Name System (DNS), and tackle domain name abuse.

George stated, “Nigeria’s communications sector has an important voice in the internet’s future. The symposium brings those voices together and builds lasting participation in the decisions that shape Nigeria’s digital development.”

World.title: Senate Moves to Modernise Farming, Establishes Agriculture College in Borno
World.content:
• Ndume: Shani institution will promote modern techniques, boost productivity

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja





Senate has initiated legislative action to strengthen agricultural productivity and promote modern farming practices, with the passage of a bill seeking to establish a Federal College of Agriculture in Shani Local Government Area of Borno State.

The upper chamber passed the bill for Third Reading on Thursday after adopting the recommendations contained in the report presented by its Committee on Agricultural Colleges and Institutions.

Sponsored by Senator Mohammed Ali Ndume (Borno South), the proposed institution is expected to promote agricultural education, improve farming techniques, and facilitate the adoption of modern technologies to enhance food production in Nigeria.

Ndume said the college would address one of the major challenges confronting the country’s agricultural sector: the continued dependence on traditional farming methods that limit productivity and make farming more difficult than necessary.

He said, “One of the fundamental challenges facing agriculture in Nigeria is our continued reliance on crude farming methods.

“We have not made sufficient progress in improving productivity and making farming easier through modern technology.”

He stated that establishing the college would provide farmers and other agricultural practitioners with access to improved knowledge, modern techniques, and better crop varieties, ultimately strengthening agricultural production and supporting national food security.

According to him, the proposed institution would serve as a centre for agricultural learning and development, equipping farmers with the skills and knowledge required to improve yields and respond to the changing demands of modern agriculture.

Ndume said the initiative was particularly significant because of Shani’s agricultural potential and its strategic location within a region with substantial farming opportunities.

He stated, “For those who may not know Shani, it is a local government area in Borno South. It is known for agriculture, particularly the cultivation of rice, tomatoes and onions, and shares boundaries with Adamawa and Bauchi states, which are also agricultural zones.”

He maintained that locating the college in Shani would help harness the agricultural potential of the area while extending the benefits of modern agricultural education to neighbouring communities and states.

The senator expressed satisfaction with the passage of the bill, describing it as a significant milestone in his legislative career and an opportunity to contribute to agricultural development in his constituency and the country.

Ndume said, “I am excited about this achievement. I consider it one of my lifetime achievements in the National Assembly, especially as we approach the end of our legislative session.”

He added that the proposed college would provide a platform for transferring agricultural knowledge, improving farming practices, and encouraging the application of technology to agricultural production.

The initiative comes amid persistent concerns over Nigeria’s food production capacity, the need to improve agricultural productivity, and the importance of equipping farmers with the knowledge and tools required to increase output.

With the proposed institution, Shani is expected to become an important centre for agricultural training and knowledge-sharing, subject to the completion of the legislative process and the eventual establishment of the college.

President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, commended the committee for its work, and Ndume for sponsoring what he described as a development-oriented initiative.

Akpabio said the proposed institution would contribute to agricultural development in Nigeria. He expressed support for efforts aimed at strengthening the country’s agricultural sector through education and institutional capacity-building.

The passage of the bill marks an important legislative step towards establishing the college, although the institution cannot be established through the senate’s approval alone.

In line with parliamentary procedure, the bill will be transmitted to the House of Representatives for concurrence. If approved by the House, it will subsequently be forwarded to President Bola Tinubu for assent.

The proposed college is expected to focus on agricultural education and the dissemination of improved farming techniques, with the broader objective of strengthening agricultural productivity and supporting food production in Borno State and beyond.

World.title: The playful South African kid’s song that ended up in Equality Court
World.content:
The year is 1962, and Ag Pleez Deddy is a cheerful tune about suburban kids nagging their dad for a trip to the drive-in. Firstly, how did it become the best-selling single in South Africa that year? Secondly, why did a song about peanuts and popcorn end up causing so much offence? It was eventually banned by the national broadcaster, the SABC. And it even ended up in the Equality Court.

AG PLEEZ DEDDY

If you’re unfamiliar with Ag Pleez Deddy, singer and songwriter Jeremy Taylor tells the story behind it HERE. For context, Taylor was born in England and educated at Oxford. He moved to Johannesburg in 1959 to teach. He later explained he was ‘enchanted’ by the way his pupils in the southern suburbs of Joburg spoke.

The areas’s unique blend of English and Afrikaans, with slang all of its own, inspired him to write Ag Pleez Deddy. It was also known as The Ballad of the Southern Suburbs. The seemingly harmless song became the showpiece of the revue Wait a Minim!, which opened in Johannesburg in January 1962. A live recording was released by Gallotone as a single.



A SMASH HIT

Originals are selling on Ebay for several hundred US dollars. Image: Ebay

No one could have predicted how successful Ag Pleez Deddy would become. The single reached number one on the LM Radio charts in June 1962. This earned Taylor a gold disc for more than 75 000 copies. It outsold Elvis Presley, and every other domestic single in South Africa at the time.

However, the Apartheid-era SABC proceeded to ban the song, along with most of Taylor’s work. The offence was not the racial slur describing one particular sweet, which did eventually end up in the modern-day Equality Court. Instead, it was Taylor’s mixing of English and Afrikaans that forced the ban. At the time, keeping the languages separate was official broadcasting policy, and linguistic purity carried political weight.

STIRRED STRONG FEELINGS

However, there’s perhaps more to Ag Pleez Deddy than initially meets the ear. Taylor himself said the song stirred strong feelings long before it was banned. “A lot of people were offended by it. The song held up a mirror to white middle-class suburban life and its sort of mongrel speech. Some felt it mocked their language and class,” said Taylor.



Nevertheless, as is so often the case, the ban couldn’t stop it. In fact, it emboldened people to get hold of the record and sing along to the chirpy chorus around the braai. It’s just one of those songs that South Africans of a certain generation know by heart. And others are happy they’ll never hear again …

But what do you think? Have you heard Ag Pleez Deddy before? Are you offended when you hear it today? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: Transfer news: Orlando Pirates hold talks for R18.7 million wonderkid
World.content:
Cape Town City FC chairman John Comitis has confirmed that talks with Orlando Pirates over the potential transfer of teenage sensation Emille Witbooi have taken place, although no deal has been agreed.

The 18-year-old winger is reportedly valued at €1 million (approximately R18.7 million) and has attracted interest from several clubs, with the Buccaneers among his admirers.

Orlando Pirates have been looking to strengthen their attacking options following Relebohile Mofokeng’s reported departure for Belgium in July, with Witbooi emerging as a potential target.



Speaking to KickOff, Comitis confirmed that the two clubs had held discussions but were unable to reach an agreement.

“We decided to keep Emile Witbooi to assist us this season. There is still a lot of interest, and we may still do something before the end of the season,” Comitis said.

“We saw a lot of media frenzy around the kid. We were very happy to listen to offers. We did speak to Orlando Pirates, but nothing materialised.”

Despite the interest in the young winger, Cape Town City are currently prioritising their promotion push and want to retain his services for the remainder of the campaign.

Orlando Pirates eyeing Witbooi

Comitis is confident that the club will eventually secure the right value for the highly rated youngster, should a transfer materialise.

“At this stage, we are very focused on keeping him here so that he can assist with the promotion battle. Everybody knows the value of the player, and we will get the value. We are not concerned about that,” he added.



“The team is settled now. There is nothing happening. We are just focusing on matches, game by game. We will see how it goes, one game at a time,” Comitis concluded.

For now, Witbooi remains at Cape Town City as the club pursues promotion, but Comitis’ comments suggest that the door remains open for a possible transfer before the end of the season. Orlando Pirates will need to pounce fast if they are to sign the wonderkid.

Should Pirates sign Witbooi?

World.title: R10 million winger made Kaizer Chiefs sign R16 million player
World.content:
According to Sukazi, Kaizer Chiefs failed to meet his R10 million valuation for the 22-year-old Mahlambi. The Rockets chairman revealed the story during a candid chat on Andile Ncube’s Sports Night Amplified show on Metro FM.

The Soweto giants would later land Phili from Stellenbosch who was valued at R16 million.

KAIZER CHIEFS OFFER FOR SELULEKO MAHLAMBI

Asked whether TS Galaxy has had any offers for Mahlambi considering his ability, Sukazi said: “There has never been any monetary offers outside Kaizer Chiefs. Kaizer Motaung Jr tabled a R4 million offer. I thought really, it was not good enough in my view. For a player like that.”



“At least he should be on those R10 million and above, at least…For that player. He is young. Kaizer Motaung was not prepared to budge. R4 million was the number and he stood his ground.”

Meanwhile, Mahlambi is yet to find the back of the net or an assist in six games this season. Last season he delivered six goals and six assists in 37 games last.

LANGELIHLE PHILI RATHER THAN MAHLAMBI

Following the failed bid to land Mahlambi, Kaizer Chiefs landed the services of Phili, 21, from Stellenbosch FC on an undisclosed fee. The transfer included Ashley Du Preez and Given Msimango joining Stellies.

Phili, who was valued at R16 million, arrived at Naturena after nine goals and one assist in 39 games for Stellenbosch last season. After scoring one goal in three games for Amakhosi, Phili sadly suffered an ankle injury in August.

Kaizer Chiefs’ full list of signings included Thabo Moloisane (central defender), Renaldo Leaner (goalkeeper), Adolf Mtasingwa (midfielder) and Faiz Abrahams (winger).

The Soweto giants, sitting in fourth place, are yet to taste defeat in the league this season with five draws and three wins in eight games.

World.title: R4 Million not enough for Mahlambi! Sukazi explains Kaizer Chiefs’ transfer failure
World.content:
TS Galaxy chairman Tim Sukazi has revealed that Kaizer Chiefs made a R4 million offer for winger Seluleko Mahlambi, but the bid was rejected.

The 22-year-old has impressed with his performances in the Betway Premiership, establishing himself as an important player for TS Galaxy over the past two seasons. His displays have also attracted interest from Soweto rivals Kaizer Chiefs and Orlando Pirates.

Speaking to Andile Ncube on Metro FM, Sukazi confirmed that Amakhosi had made an offer for the talented winger but insisted that the amount was not enough to secure his services.



Chiefs fail to sign Mahlambi

“There’s never been an offer in monetary terms outside Kaizer Chiefs,” Sukazi revealed.

“Yes, Kaizer Junior tabled a R4 million offer. I thought, really? It wasn’t good enough in my view. At least he should be R10 million and above, as he is young.”

Sukazi explained that Chiefs were unwilling to increase their bid, while TS Galaxy remained firm on their valuation of the player.

“Kaizer was not prepared to budge and he stood his ground, and we stood our ground,” he said.

Having failed to secure Mahlambi’s signature, Kaizer Chiefs strengthened their attacking options with the signing of Stellenbosch FC winger Langelihle Phili.

Phili has made a positive impression since arriving at Naturena and has been regarded as one of the club’s standout signings this season.



Amakhosi also secured the services of Faiz Abrahams on loan from Stellenbosch FC. The winger has impressed in his opportunities, scoring in his first start for the Soweto giants.

While Chiefs have added fresh attacking talent to their squad, Sukazi’s comments reveal the financial gap that prevented the club from reaching an agreement with TS Galaxy for Mahlambi.

World.title: From Madlanga to 'Clock it': South Africa's words of the year revealed
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Madlanga Commission has been named South Africa’s Word of the Year for 2026, while “Clock it” has won in the social media category. The expression “Oh, I see” was named Sign Language Word of the Year.

The Pan South African Language Board (PanSALB), in partnership with media research company Focal Points, announced the winners after unveiling the shortlist earlier this week.

The six shortlisted entries in the main category were the Madlanga Commission, illegal immigration, Gender-Based Violence, March and March, xenophobia and femicide.

The social media category featured “Clock it”, “Nikhona”, “Gone Kanje”, “Diabolical”, “Abahambe”, “Aura farming” and “Ashwagandha”.

According to PanSALB, the South African Word of the Year is a word, term, expression or sign that best reflects the year through language.

“To qualify for consideration, the word(s) must capture the ethos, mood, or preoccupations of 2026. There must be evidence that the usage of the word or expression has significantly increased across a broad range of media in the past 12 months,” the organisation said.

PanSALB said this year’s shortlist reflected issues dominating public discourse, including the Madlanga Commission, which has brought allegations of deep-seated corruption within law enforcement into the spotlight.

Other prominent issues included illegal immigration, the March and March movement, gender-based violence and femicide.

Several shortlisted expressions have also moved beyond social media and entertainment into everyday vocabulary, particularly among younger South Africans.

“Gone Kanje”, popularised by Amapiano singer Scott Maphuma, is one example of a phrase that has gained traction beyond music and entered the lexicon of younger audiences.

Another notable entry is “Nikhona +27?”, an expression commonly found in social media comment sections, particularly on TikTok. The isiZulu and isiXhosa word “Nikhona” is used to ask whether someone is present or around.

Flament's Toulouse and France teammate Emmanuel Meafou has also been ruled out for the four games next month, including a mouth-watering tie against South Africa on November 13.

World.title: Asian stocks rise as tech bounces from rout, eyes on Warsh
World.content:
HONG KONG - Most Asian markets bounced on Friday after the previous day's tech rout fuelled by concerns over the AI boom, with traders also awaiting comments from Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh at the IMF's annual gathering.

Seoul and Tokyo enjoyed healthy gains in early exchanges, with chipmakers SK hynix and Kioxia among the best performers -- having been pummelled Thursday as investors bailed out of the once-dominant AI sector.

The selling had been fuelled by forecast-beating US inflation data that ramped up bets on more Fed interest rate hikes, as well as concerns about the financial health of data centre operator CoreWeave owing to its huge debt pile.

The New Jersey firm -- which has borrowed heavily to finance hefty purchases of pricey semiconductor chips from Nvidia -- tanked 15.5 percent Wednesday as yields on some of its bonds soared, reflecting heightened angst over its future.

That added to concerns about the whole AI-tech complex, but Nvidia chief Jensen Huang on Thursday lifted spirits by defending the company and its health.

"CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," he told Bloomberg. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."

CoreWeave's shares climbed almost six percent.

Huang's "defence of CoreWeave's financial position was enough to pull the NeoCloud complex off the floor, drag AI equities higher and give the broader market something resembling a pulse", wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.

"One moment the market was pricing the possibility that the AI financing machine had started eating its own tail, the next it was listening to the high priest of the boom explain that the patient was getting stronger.

"AI Jesus had entered the trading room and, for a while at least, the machines found religion again."

Seoul jumped more than two percent and Tokyo around 1.8 percent, though they slumped 7.6 percent and 4.9 percent respectively Thursday.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei and Manila were also well up.

Traders are now awaiting comments at the International Monetary Fund's gathering in Bangkok, with hopes that he will give some insight into policymakers' thinking following this week's inflation-busting consumer inflation data.

The reading was the highest in five months and saw investors push up bets on a second-successive rate hike this month.

World.title: Using AI to help find Mexico's legions of missing children
World.content:
MEXICO CITY - Veronica Rosas is one of tens of thousands of Mexican mothers looking for a child that has disappeared into a vortex of violence fueled by brutal cartel turf wars.

Now artificial intelligence may be able to help the loved ones of Mexico's legions of disappeared.

Two new AI tools are being developed to help in the search for the more than 134,000 people being sought.

Rosas' son, Diego, went missing at the age of 16 in the central town of Ecatepec in September 2015 after leaving his home to meet some friends.

The state prosecutor's office said he was kidnapped by a criminal gang but have not established which group, why, or whether Diego is still alive.

"It's been 11 years and I still don't know where Diego is. There's no line of investigation leading us to find out what happened to my son," Rosas, 52, told AFP at one of the demonstrations held regularly in Mexico City to demand justice.

Cases like Diego's have prompted two universities to develop AI tools they hope will provide answers.

Regresa (Return) was developed by Mexico's main public university, UNAM. It uses anthropometry -- human body measurements -- to create an image of how the faces of minors, which remain frozen in time in missing persons posters, may have changed over time.

With investigations generally dragging on for years, these updated likenesses are a recurring demand of the families.

Countries like the United States, India and China already use facial recognition and age progression software to search for kidnapped children.

In Mexico, some prosecutors' offices use the technology but most software relies on open-source photo databases that don't reflect typical Mexican traits.

Regresa's developers took a different approach.

They created their own image bank from hundreds of photos and data from 75 Mexican volunteers to make portraits that feature more typically Mexican features.

Anthropologist Ana Juarez, one of the project's founders, explained that Regresa also uses different technology to age the children.

"Many software programs only work with facial contours or textures, or add filters that simulate wrinkles. We seek to develop a scientific approach that shows how a person grows in craniofacial terms," she explained to AFP, referring to imaging that predicts the development of the skull.

World.title: Ailing UK director Mike Leigh wishes he could make '100 more films'
World.content:
LONDON - British filmmaker Mike Leigh told AFP he regretted he could not make "another hundred films" because of ill health, as he attended the London premiere of his prize-winning latest work.

Leigh (83) has myositis, an autoimmune disease that affects the muscles, and now uses a walking stick.

"It's only because I have a medical condition that makes it difficult to do stuff, but otherwise I'd love to make a hundred more films," he told AFP on the red carpet at the London Film Festival ahead of the screening of his film, "Tender Loving Care".

"But it may not be possible, just from a practical point of view."

Leigh won the top prize last month at the San Sebastian film festival for the drama about social workers supporting vulnerable people, expected to be his last feature.

He won top prize at the Cannes film festival in 1996 for "Secrets and Lies" and at Venice in 2004 for "Vera Drake".

Actress Alice Bailey Johnson, one of the new film's stars, said she was "heartbroken" at the prospect that this could be the socially engaged filmmaker's final work.

"But if it is, then I can't express how honoured I feel to be part of it," she told AFP before the screening.

"It's just a wonderful moment, and I will treasure it forever."
