Four ⁠ANC Youth League⁠ members have been killed and three other people wounded in ⁠Katlehong⁠. Police say a former ward councillor has handed himself over. The ANC has called for stronger police visibility; the EFF cautions against treating an unproven political motive as fact.

Former police boss ⁠Shadrack Sibiya⁠ remains in custody after the ⁠Randburg Magistrate's Court⁠ postponed its bail decision. The State raised concerns about possible witness interference and referred to an alleged attempt by an associate to persuade a complainant's father to withdraw charges. These are allegations before the court, not findings against Sibiya.

The⁠ AKA and Tibz murder⁠ trial was adjourned after an air-conditioning failure in court.

The⁠ NPA and KwaZulu-Natal police⁠ have rejected claims that arrest warrants were issued for March and March leader ⁠Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma⁠ and her husband, Xolani Zuma.

SPORTS

PSG beat Manchester City 4-2, while Real Madrid fought back to defeat Roma 4-3.

Mamelodi Sundowns look ahead to domestic and continental fixtures, with Carling Knockout pairings announced.

The Proteas have dropped Tristan Stubbs and called in Matthew Breetzke ahead of the second Test.

Listen to ⁠News Bite⁠ with Marcelle Gordon. More at enca.com and on eNCA, DStv Channel 403.

World.title: Raila's spirit: Anniversary turned into battlefield of bruised egos, bitter divisions and open rebellion
World.content:
Late Raila Odinga Family, friends follow proceedings during the remembrance service at Migwena ground. [Michael Mute, Standard]

It was an event that many had hoped would be the turning point to unite all the political orphans of the late Raila Odinga and breathe new life into a region, a support base and a party in discord.

But if Raila had hoped in his grave that his first anniversary would be the uniting factor, he is probably turning in his grave in disappointment as fissures of division among his former troops deepened in a politically charged anniversary at the historic Migwena grounds in Bondo.

World.title: From 'Chogo' to senator? Winnie Odinga steps into her own political spotlight
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

From Raila Odinga’s shadow to her own political path, Winnie sets her sights on the Nairobi Senate seat in 2027. [Courtesy]

The hat was more than a hat. Literally.

As Raila Odinga’s body made its final journey home from India, his youngest daughter, Winnie, held tightly to his familiar cream-coloured fedora. It was one of the few things she could still protect, a small piece of a man whose presence had filled her life and Kenya’s political imagination for decades.

The image of Winnie carrying her father’s hat was deeply personal. The country was mourning a political giant, but she was mourning her father.

A year later, on the first anniversary of Raila’s death, Winnie has announced her intention to contest the Nairobi Senate seat in the 2027 General Election.

The timing is poignant. On a day devoted to remembering her father, she has declared her own political ambitions, signalling a shift from being one of the most recognisable faces of the Odinga family to a politician seeking a mandate in her own right.

“As Edwin Sifuna seeks a higher office, I see an opportunity in Nairobi, which is why I have decided I will vie for Senator of Nairobi County,” she said.

And just like that, the conversation shifted from the daughter who carried Baba’s hat to the politician who wants a seat of her own.

The last-born girl

To many Kenyans, Winnie is Chogo, the last-born child of Raila and Ida Odinga. The nickname carries the familiarity of family life, a reminder that behind the powerful surname is a daughter who grew up in a household where politics was never far from the conversation.

Her father was no ordinary political figure. His name could summon crowds, ignite debate and divide opinion. His decades-long career placed the Odinga family at the centre of Kenya’s political story.

Growing up as Raila’s youngest daughter meant sharing him with a country that claimed a piece of his time, energy and, eventually, his final goodbye.

Yet Winnie was not simply a spectator in her father’s political world. She worked around his campaigns and communications before stepping into politics herself, eventually winning a seat in the East African Legislative Assembly.

In November 2022, Parliament elected her to represent Kenya in the regional legislature, where she took office in December that year. Based in Arusha, Tanzania, she became part of the East African Community’s legislative institution, serving a five-year term running to 2027.

The EALA offered Winnie a political platform beyond her father’s immediate circle and an opportunity to participate in regional affairs. Her current tenure has also given her experience in legislative politics before her proposed move into elective politics at home.

The Nairobi Senate bid would take her into a different contest, one in which voters will have to decide whether her experience, ideas and political programme merit their support.

The hat she could not let go

For years, Raila’s trademark headgear had been part of his public identity, appearing at political rallies, meetings and public ceremonies. But in Winnie’s hands, it became something else: a personal possession tied to the final journey of a daughter and her father

She explained how protective she had been of it throughout the journey, describing it as one of the few things she could still hold on to.

The image captured a kind of helplessness that public figures’ families rarely get to show. Crowds could mourn Raila, politicians could speak of his legacy, and supporters could debate who would inherit his political movement. Winnie, however, had been left with the painful task of bringing her father home.

The symbolism of the hat has since acquired another layer. At a ceremony in Bondo earlier this month, elders placed a traditional hat on Winnie’s head in a symbolic gesture associated with the possibility of her carrying forward her father’s political mantle.

Winnie’s political journey has not started with this Senate announcement.

Her election to the East African Legislative Assembly placed her among Kenya’s representatives in a regional institution whose work concerns cooperation among East African Community partner states.

The role gave her a platform in regional legislation while her father remained a central figure in national politics.

The Senate is responsible for representing counties, participating in lawmaking on matters concerning counties and exercising oversight over revenue allocated to county governments. A Nairobi senator must therefore make a case on issues that touch residents directly, from public spending and service delivery to the accountability of county leadership.

The capital is also a demanding political terrain. Its electorate is diverse, its concerns immediate and its contests fiercely competitive.

A famous surname may open doors, but it cannot replace a convincing programme on jobs, housing, transport, healthcare and the management of public resources.

Winnie will have to demonstrate that she understands Nairobi beyond its place in her father’s national political story.

Can she translate the loyalty associated with Raila into support for her own agenda? Can she persuade voters that she is more than the daughter of a political icon?

Those questions will follow her into the campaign.

The Odingaism

Political inheritance can be both an advantage and a burden.

Raila’s name carries a formidable history of opposition politics, democratic reform and a loyal support base. It also invites comparisons that few politicians have to contend with.

Winnie’s challenge will be to honour that history without allowing it to become the entirety of her political identity.

Raila’s death left a space in the Orange Democratic Movement and among supporters who had looked to him for direction through decades of political contests. The question of who will carry his legacy has inevitably turned towards his family and the wider political movement he helped build.

Winnie’s Senate bid will require her to turn recognition into a political proposition that voters can interrogate. Her experience at EALA gives her a legislative starting point; the Nairobi contest will demand that she demonstrate how that experience can serve residents of the capital.

She must also navigate the expectations attached to her father’s name while making room for her own ideas, priorities and leadership style.

There is a temptation to see Winnie’s future entirely through the lens of inheritance. She is Raila’s daughter, the last-born known as Chogo, the woman who carried his hat and the politician whom some supporters hope will continue his legacy.

But she is also a woman making a decision about her own future.

The Senate bid offers her an opportunity to define what that future means, beyond the grief surrounding her father’s death and the weight of a name that has shaped Kenyan politics for decades.

The hat remains an unforgettable image from Raila’s final journey home. A daughter attempted to protect the last tangible thing she could hold on to.

The Senate will demand something different: a political vision, a campaign and the votes of Nairobi residents.

Chogo has announced her next move. Will Winnie Odinga turn the memory of Baba into a mandate of her own?

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Gift for Putin as fears grow that Trump is turning the screws on Ukraine
World.content:
Ultimately, you have to wonder what it is that Vladimir Putin says to Donald Trump when they are on the phone.

A week ago, a call between the US president and his Russian counterpart seemed to be about an urgent clarification over a possible outbreak of plague in Siberia. Instead, a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel emerged, prompting fury from Ukrainians, and then Trump demanding they get a new president. For days, fears grew across Europe this may spill into the real world of the US limiting military aid and intelligence for Ukraine, and in the past 48 hours, that might be spilling into reality.

Twice now, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has declared Kyiv was not given the usual warning about Russian ballistic missile attacks from its partners.

The US, whose satellites and other methods are the early warning mechanisms for Russian launches, normally provide Ukrainians a vital few minutes to run to the shelter before the missiles hit. Thirty-nine slammed into Ukraine last night. President Trump has openly rejected the idea he has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, saying Tuesday: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel.” But that does not preclude the possibility less intelligence is being shared, or it is less in real time.

With the dead from Russian strikes often in the dozens, as Moscow seeks to yet further widen the envelope of what civilian carnage it will impose, a sudden withdrawal of these early warnings would mean many Ukrainians will likely die. It is possible there is another reason for Zelensky’s messaging – that he is pre-emptively posturing, or that poor weather or technical issues prompted the lack of warnings.

The second withdrawal of assistance that appeared to beset Ukraine Wednesday also suggests Trump is squeezing them harder.

Ukrainians watch over an apartment building damaged by a Russian attack in Kyiv on Wednesday. Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

Starlink space-based internet antennae – assisting Ukrainian medium and longer-range drones to hit their targets, and interceptors to tackle Russian loitering drones – have had significant speed limits imposed on them. This may amount to the removal of a bonus capability negotiated by the former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov with Space X’s owner, Elon Musk. It is important to note it is not comparable to Musk’s decision to entirely stop Starlink functioning inside Russia, which significantly hampered Moscow’s frontline operations in the summer of last year. But it is a palpable snub with operational significance, and one that Ukrainian officials have said would only have occurred at the behest of the White House.

For days, European and Ukrainian officials have warned the US was threatening to limit intelligence and other cooperation if Kyiv did not stop hitting Russian diesel facilities. Trump has – somewhat misleadingly – stated Ukrainian targeting of Moscow’s oil facilities is behind a surge in pump prices in the United States, choosing to ignore the role the Strait of Hormuz has played in this global economic calamity. It is possible the Starlink slowdown and lack of ballistic warnings shows this threat coming to life.

Smoke rises over Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft’s oil refinery near Moscow on June 18. Russian and Ukrainian forces have increased attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure. AFP/Getty Images

President Trump has denied this is the case, but that is not in of itself definitive proof it is not happening. Trump has also – since he spoke to Putin – again swung from deciding to finally allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot interceptors, a high-profile and vital move long-prevaricated over, to deciding the true obstacle to peace is Zelensky, the president of the invaded country, who has been asking for an immediate ceasefire for over a year.

It does not appear to influence Trump’s thought process when Putin attacks Ukrainian energy facilities in the middle of Trump’s self-declared “energy ceasefire.” Or when Putin’s operatives plot to murder a dissident in Washington DC. Or when US businesses are relentlessly hit in Ukraine. There are moments when Trump simply appears bent on hurting Ukraine and damaging its position. We may never learn why, or what it is that Putin says to him to cause this relatively frequent flip in Trump’s worldview.

Conjecture might revive the old trope that Trump the real-estate dealmaker seeks to pressure his subcontractors (here, Ukraine) to get the deal to go through or forge a price more palatable to his end consumer (Putin), who he has correctly assessed is in the driving seat of the war and therefore any peace deal. But the timing of this pressure rarely comes when a deal is close, or appears supported by logic. Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, by most analysis, won’t impact prices at the American pump before the mid-terms, but will likely flood the Kremlin’s coffers with badly needed cash.

Zelensky and his European allies have seen this vacillation enough times to be inured to its emotional impact, and perhaps even relaxed about how long it might sustain. Perhaps more Trump-whispering by France’s Macron, or another call from NATO’s Rutte, or visit from Italy’s Meloni, will see the US president flip back again. Indeed, Zelensky was in London Wednesday, and the topic has surely come up.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky (left) and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (right) inspect a damaged building in Kyiv on October 4. Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images

But Trump’s persistent sympathy for Russia’s position remains a mystery of our time. Critics say it is unlikely to achieve his apparent goal of a peace deal, incompatible with the long-term security interests of the United States, and oblivious to Moscow’s role in assisting Iran , which continues to embarrass Trump and injure American servicemen.

There is an inherent risk in the current state of affairs, however, to both Trump and Putin.

First, Trump might create such acrimony in his transatlantic relationships, that his allies simply zone him out for the 18 months after the mid-terms, and wait for him to depart. That could leave Trump further hamstrung when dealing with an intractable conflict, spreading in the Middle East.

There is risk for Putin too.

Europe and Ukraine being forced to forge ahead without the United States, fashion resilience, find new methods, and surge funding into their defense, does not leave the Kremlin in a dominant position. The more Moscow antagonizes Europe, the more it arms up, and the greater, in the long-term, the (defensive) threat Europe’s armies pose to Russia.

Ukraine has shown extraordinary inventiveness and capability. That is unlikely to stop, and likely to again reshape the landscape of warfare in the coming years. Similarly, Russia’s capacity to absorb pain is immense. Yet its breaking point is rarely publicly visible, and tends to surge menacingly from the deep without warning, as when the frustrated chief of Russia’s infamous Wagner mercenary force launched a short-lived rebellion in 2023.

In the immediate term however, the risk of this current strategy is born entirely by Ukraine. Its children and mothers are dying from nightly strikes. Its cities are sleepless. And its military aid is prey to two powerful men’s curious bromance.

World.title: Inside the Kenyan manufacturer betting on Africa’s industrial future
World.content:
In a central Nairobi factory, a steady stream of household, hair and skincare products rolls off the production line.

HACO Industries makes around 90 products designed for African consumers. Its brands reach more than 3 million families across the continent, while raw materials are sourced from more than 500 farmers in Africa.

For Mary-Ann Musangi, whose family launched HACO more than 50 years ago, the opportunity lies in making products on the continent for people whose needs the business recognizes.

“How do we reach African consumers with products that they want and need, manufactured by a company that understands them — understands African skin, African hair and African needs?” she said.

HACO currently exports to eight African countries. Kenya is its largest market, but it also has a presence in Uganda, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia. “Distances can be a challenge and African logistics is one of the key challenges in terms of penetrating across the continent,” Musangi said.

The company’s plastics plant, which produces the packaging for its products, has the capacity to produce 5 million components a month, according to its manufacturing director, Peter Ndichu. A separate plant has the capacity to process and pack 1,365 metric tons of products monthly.

HACO is trying to strengthen its supply chain by buying more ingredients within Africa. The company works with small and medium-sized suppliers of natural oils, offering technical support to help them meet its quality standards.

Shea butter is now sourced from Uganda or Ghana. Ndichu said HACO previously imported it from the United States for 5,000 Kenyan shillings ($38.50) per kilogram, compared with 1,000 shillings ($7.70) per kilogram from Uganda.

HACO is now looking to automate more of its operations. “In terms of packing, we are currently achieving 3,000 pieces in an hour,” said Ndichu. Automated machinery could quadruple that to roughly 12,000 items an hour, he said, adding that HACO plans to build a new factory to accommodate the upgrades.

Hubs and partnerships

To support its goal of exporting to 30 African countries by 2030, HACO plans to establish five regional hubs across Africa. Ghana is set to become its West African manufacturing base, from which products can be exported to neighboring markets.

Musangi said collaborating with local companies will be essential for expansion.

“Africa is so fragmented in many ways: the countries, the boundaries, our taxation laws, our policies, our culture, our language, our money, currency. We’ve got to see, how do we reduce these points of fragmentation?” she explained. “The only way I see we can do it is through these partnerships, working with local people.”

HACO Industries makes around 90 household, hair and skincare products. CNN

In Ghana, HACO is partnering with Ayewa Labs, a product development and manufacturing firm specializing in making goods from African ingredients. Founder Nanayaa Bates said the African Continental Free Trade Area — which came into effect in 2019 and is the world’s largest free-trade area by number of countries — is helping the company attract clients from other African countries.

HACO supplies raw materials for Ayewa, which then manufactures products for other companies beyond Ghana. Bates said the partnership had increased Ayewa’s manufacturing output tenfold.

Making more in Africa

Manufacturing is seen as an important route to economic growth and job creation across Africa, yet in many countries it accounted for less than 15% of gross domestic product in 2023.

Musangi argues that African countries should retain more of the value generated by their raw materials. “It is unacceptable that we continue to simply extract raw materials from Africa and send them out to the West for them to manufacture and send us the finished product to consume at much higher prices,” she said.

“We have the technical skills,” Musangi added. “Our youth are highly skilled and highly educated. We need to make sure that we develop and continue developing the manufacturing sector so that we can add value to these raw materials.”

World.title: OpenAI accuses former employee of leaking intel on AI device to Apple
World.content:
OpenAI is accusing a former employee of stealing intellectual property related to an unreleased device and later sharing some of the information with Apple.

The employee, OpenAI alleges, had previously worked at Apple, then joined OpenAI for six months, before going back to Apple, according to a court filing from OpenAI on Wednesday.

The company said the employee downloaded over 100 highly confidential files to his personal accounts before rejoining Apple. The transferred files include “detailed images of the unreleased device(s), as well as highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s),” according to the filing. The last file was sent in June on the employee’s final day, OpenAI alleges.

OpenAI went on to claim the former employee, who it did not name, “made a presentation about OpenAI’s product plans to Apple’s senior leadership, including Apple’s vice president of operations in Asia.”

“That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI wrote in the filing.

Apple told CNN it has found no evidence to support the allegations and that it has strict policies in place to make sure new employees don’t use confidential information from previous workplaces. The company also said it would work with OpenAI to remediate any of OpenAI’s information found on Apple’s systems.

Apple accused OpenAI of trying to create a distraction from the original claims of their case. The allegations came as part of a filing in an ongoing lawsuit that Apple brought against OpenAI in July, alleging the AI company stole the iPhone maker’s trade secrets to develop its own gadgets. Apple alleged in its original filing that former employees who went to work for OpenAI downloaded confidential files, and urged job candidates to bring Apple parts to interviews at OpenAI. OpenAI has denied the claims, saying Apple hasn’t been able to identify any stolen trade secrets and has sought to dismiss the case.

Both companies are racing to create AI-enabled devices. This week, Apple announced HomeView, its biggest push into the smart home market in nearly a decade with a revamped version of Siri, making it a critical piece of Apple’s AI strategy. OpenAI is working on an AI-enabled device, reported to be a small screen-free smart speaker. Last year, OpenAI brought on former Apple product design chief Jonny Ive and his company, io, to take over design and creative responsibilities across the company.

While engineers and researchers regularly switch companies in Silicon Valley, Apple said in a court filing that OpenAI has hired more than 400 of its former employees.

CNN’s Lisa Eadicicco contributed to this report.

World.title: Harry and Meghan make first joint appearance since returning to the UK
World.content:
London —

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have made their first joint public appearance in Britain since moving back to the country.

Prince Harry and Meghan were greeted by well-wishers as they arrived at the Community Recording Studio (CRS) in Nottingham on Thursday morning.

Crowds gave the couple balloons and flowers, Britain’s PA Media news agency reported, with Harry and Meghan stopping to greet onlookers and pose for selfies. Meghan told one woman in the crowd: “It’s great to be back.”

The CRS, which Harry has visited before, is a charity that teaches film, video and music skills to young people. Inside the studio, Meghan joined a group of girls for a confidence-building and bracelet-making workshop.

When asked what makes them feel most like themselves, one participant said she liked doing gymnastics, to which Meghan replied: “Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it,” according to PA Media.

The duchess, whose Netflix lifestyle “With Love, Meghan” show centered around hosting and cooking, added: “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I’m cooking. I love doing that. I love to cook.”

The couple’s second stop while in Nottingham on Thursday was at Himmah Hub, a food poverty community action group. While there, they participated in cooking classes and packed food parcels for donations.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub in Nottingham on Thursday. Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

A crowd of about 50 people gathered at the gates to try and catch a glimpse of the Sussexes, according to PA Media.

In a surprise announcement this summer, the couple revealed that they would be leaving their home in California to resettle in the UK, together with their two children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. The family landed in August, ahead of the start of the school year last month. They returned as private citizens and are not resuming any official duties on behalf of King Charles III.

The engagements in Nottingham come more than six years after the couple departed the United Kingdom for the United States and the years since have seen a public falling out with some members of the royal family.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrive at Himmah Hub in Nottingham on Thursday. Dominic Lipinski/Getty Images

Harry and Meghan had cited tabloid intrusion, racism in British institutions, online abuse and complex family dynamics as among the reasons behind their 2020 departure.

Harry and Meghan’s Nottingham visit is not an official royal engagement.

Last month, Harry’s father, King Charles, issued a letter in which he clarified that the couple should be treated as “private citizens.” The missive is said to have caught the Sussexes off guard.

According to the letter, sent by the UK’s Lord Chamberlain – the most senior officer of the British royal household – all charitable work carried out by Harry and Meghan is a “personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.”

The letter also made clear that any operational issues involving them should be directed to the relevant police authorities. Harry has continued to push for the UK Home Office to reinstate his family’s taxpayer-funded security, which was downgraded when the family left for North America in 2020.

The last time the Sussexes appeared together in public in Britain was four years ago, at the funeral of Harry’s grandmother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, in September 2022.

While living in the US, Harry made several trips back to the UK, including for the funeral of his grandmother Queen Elizabeth II in 2022 and the coronation of his father King Charles III the following year.

CNN’s Lauren Said-Moorhouse and Max Foster contributed reporting.

World.title: Egypt, Tunisia discuss cooperation in Non-Banking Microfinance Regulation
World.content:
Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) is keen on strengthening cooperation with Arab and African countries prioritizing the exchange of expertise and knowledge-sharing, FRA Chairman Islam Azzam said. FRA chairman made the remarks during a meeting with Mahmoud Montasser Mansour executive director-general and founder of Tunisia’s Microfinance Control Authority and his accompanying delegation to discuss ways to enhance cooperation and exchange regulatory and supervisory expertise in non-banking finance.

The meeting was attended by FRA Assistant Chairman Rehab Taha.

The Tunisian delegation’s visit aimed to gain first-hand insight into Egypt’s legislative and regulatory frameworks governing financing for medium, small and micro enterprises, particularly given the relatively close timing of regulatory developments in the sector in both countries.

Azzam welcomed the Tunisian officials to Egypt, describing non-banking finance for enterprises as one of the key sectors supervised by the FRA, given its relevance to a broad segment of the population.He said the sector directly supports financial inclusion, one of the main objectives of Egypt Vision 2030 and the government’s plan to advance the national economy.It also has the potential to improve the livelihoods of vulnerable groups and contribute to sustainable economic and social development, he added.

Azzam said outstanding financing balances for medium, small and micro enterprises in Egypt exceeded 101 billion Egyptian pounds in the second quarter of this year, benefiting around 3.5 million people through approximately 4,400 outlets operated by licensed companies, associations and institutions nationwide.

He also said the FRA had recently placed especial emphasis on improving the financing experience for beneficiaries, especially microenterprise owners, by tightening assessments of borrowers’ repayment capacity to reduce defaults, ensuring transparent information and data protection, and encouraging providers to develop innovative products that meet customers’ needs.

The authority seeks to ensure that customers can effectively use available grievance and complaints mechanisms and to assess the actual impact of financing on their livelihoods and economic activities, he added.

Azzam pointed to recent regulatory decisions aimed at tightening oversight of debt collection practices to prevent abuses, strengthening customer identity verification, improving the FRA’s ability to detect risks early and reducing individual borrower defaults.

The measures also seek to improve the financial solvency of licensed financing providers and encourage the development of new products using financial technology to keep pace with market developments and changing customer circumstances.

The aim is to expand access to financing, particularly in poor and remote areas, alongside ongoing awareness campaigns conducted in cooperation with various government entities, he said.For his part, Mansour reviewed the development of Tunisia’s microfinance sector since its regulation in 1999, initially covering associations, followed by a restructuring of the sector in 2011 that brought commercial microfinance institutions under regulatory supervision.

He also outlined the authority’s role since 2012 in regulating pricing and monitoring financing costs, as well as measures introduced last year, including reviews of the prices of certain products offered by seven licensed microfinance companies and 289 licensed microcredit associations.

Mansour said more than 856,000 clients currently benefit from microfinance in Tunisia.

Last year, financing worth around 2.7 billion Tunisian dinars, equivalent to 47.1 billion Egyptian pounds, was extended through more than 524,000 financing transactions, reflecting the sector’s continued expansion.The meeting also addressed the development of financial products and diversification of financing instruments, as well as the two countries’ experiences in digital transformation, financial technology applications and the use of artificial intelligence in supervisory tools.

Participants also discussed modern approaches to risk management, compliance and consumer protection to improve the efficiency of activities overseen by both authorities.

World.title: IMF, World Bank launch global roadmap to combat online financial fraud
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank unveiled a global roadmap to fight online financial fraud as increasingly sophisticated scams undermine confidence in digital finance.

The “Bangkok Blueprint” developed in coordination with the Bank of Thailand and released during the institutions’ annual meetings on Wednesday in Bangkok sets out 12 policy considerations to help countries identify vulnerabilities and develop comprehensive and coordinated responses, Thai central bank chief Vitai Ratanakorn said.

“The framework calls for a whole-of-ecosystem response, stronger cross-border cooperation, and sharing practical experience to inform evolving global standard setting,” Vitai said during the report launch, adding that it drew experiences from Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. Asia accounted for 67 per cent of global fraud losses in 2024, he said.

Scam operations have been proliferating across South-east Asia in recent years, particularly in border regions adjacent to Thailand, which has become a transit hub for human trafficking linked to scam compounds.

The initiative comes as Thailand’s efforts to crack down on scam operations have uncovered sophisticated ways in which proceeds of cyber fraud become a major part of broader illicit financial flow, Vitai said.

World.title: WHO confirms Egypt as first country to retain Hepatitis C gold status
World.content:
Egypt has become the first country in the world to retain the World Health Organization’s (WHO) gold-tier status on the path to eliminating hepatitis C, following a review of its national prevention, testing and treatment programmes.

The WHO confirmed the recognition on Wednesday after assessing Egypt’s progress between 2023 and 2025. The assessment was approved by the organization’s regional validation committee in July 2026.

Egypt first achieved gold-tier status in 2023 after reducing hepatitis C prevalence from around 10 percent to less than 0.38 percent in just over a decade.

The achievement follows Egypt’s nationwide 100 Million Healthy Lives campaign, which screened more than 60 million people and provided treatment to over 4.5 million hepatitis C patients.

According to the WHO, Egypt has since moved from large-scale screening campaigns to a permanent healthcare system that provides routine hepatitis C testing, diagnosis and treatment.

The country has also expanded hepatitis services through primary healthcare and universal health insurance while improving disease surveillance, laboratory standards and blood safety measures.

These efforts are supported by a national plan to sustain progress towards eliminating viral hepatitis, including measures covering 2025–2030.

The WHO said that it had provided technical support to Egypt throughout its hepatitis C programme, helping improve prevention, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.

World.title: FM, Thai deputy PM discuss trade, investment cooperation
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, to discuss strengthening economic, trade and investment cooperation between the two countries.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of a dinner hosted by Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul for heads of delegations attending the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group.

The two ministers stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade and investment, exchanging expertise in economic and financial reforms, and attracting further investment.They also discussed strengthening cooperation through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), building on the cooperation agreement signed between Egypt and the regional bloc in 2016.

Both sides expressed their commitment to expanding economic partnerships and advancing mutual interests.

World.title: Liberia’s Rural Women Feed the Nation, Build Peace, But Remain Locked Out of Opportunities
World.content:
MONROVIA — Madam Esther David Yango, Executive Director of the Women’s NGO Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL), has called on the Government of Liberia(GoL) to take concrete steps to address the challenges facing rural women, warning that despite their contributions to food production, local economies, and community peacebuilding, many continue to face barriers to economic opportunities and meaningful participation in decision-making.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

Her call comes as Liberia joins the world in observing the International Day of Rural Women on October 15, a day dedicated to recognizing rural women’s contributions and drawing attention to the challenges they face.



Across Liberia, rural women help feed families, sustain local economies, and resolve community conflicts. Yet many continue to struggle with limited access to land, financing, education, healthcare, technology, and leadership opportunities.

From farming and trading in local markets to caring for families and mediating community disputes, rural women play a critical role in the country’s economic and social development. Their contributions also extend to peacebuilding, reconciliation, and efforts to strengthen relationships within communities.

Despite these responsibilities, many rural women face barriers that limit their ability to expand their businesses, improve their livelihoods, and participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their communities.

The observance provides an opportunity for the government, development partners, civil society organizations, and traditional leaders to move beyond celebrating rural women and take practical steps to address the challenges they face.

Rural Women at the Center of Peacebuilding

Beyond their economic contributions, rural women play an important role in maintaining peace and social cohesion across Liberia.

In communities throughout the country, women help resolve disputes, encourage dialogue, rebuild relationships, and bring people together across social and cultural divisions.

Their involvement in community peacebuilding demonstrates that sustainable peace requires more than formal agreements and government initiatives. It also depends on the participation of people who understand the challenges facing their communities and work daily to address them.

Rural women also support survivors of violence and contribute to efforts to prevent violence against women and girls. Through community networks and local leadership structures, they help create spaces where difficult issues can be discussed and conflicts addressed.

However, their contributions to peacebuilding must be matched by meaningful participation in decision-making, particularly in processes concerning local development, security, land rights, and reconciliation.

Recognizing women as peacebuilders means ensuring that they are not merely invited to meetings but are given opportunities to influence decisions and shape policies affecting their lives.

Limited Access to Resources Remains a Challenge

Despite their role in sustaining households and communities, rural women continue to face significant economic and social challenges.

Limited access to land, financial services, markets, education, healthcare, and technology can make it difficult for women to improve agricultural production, establish businesses, and achieve financial independence.

These barriers can also affect their ability to support their children’s education, access essential services, and contribute more effectively to local economic development.

For women who depend on farming and small-scale trading, access to affordable financing, agricultural tools, reliable markets, and skills training can make the difference between struggling to survive and building sustainable livelihoods.

Addressing these challenges requires deliberate investment in rural communities, policies that protect women’s rights, and programs that provide women with the resources needed to improve their economic circumstances.

Calls for Greater Government Commitment

As the International Day of Rural Women is observed, the Government of Liberia and its development partners are being urged to strengthen support for rural women by improving their access to economic opportunities, essential services, and leadership positions.

Civil society organizations, traditional leaders, and other stakeholders also have a role to play in ensuring that rural women are included in development planning and community decision-making.

Support must extend beyond public recognition to practical interventions that improve women’s access to land, credit, education, healthcare, agricultural resources, and markets.

Equally important is the need to protect rural women’s rights, strengthen their participation in peacebuilding, and create opportunities for them to lead community development initiatives.

Investing in rural women can produce wider benefits for Liberia. When women have the resources to increase their income and improve agricultural production, households can become more financially secure, communities can become more resilient, and food security can improve.

Their participation in peacebuilding and local governance can also strengthen social cohesion and promote more inclusive development.

Empowering Rural Women Is Essential to Liberia’s Future

The International Day of Rural Women is observed annually on October 15 to recognize rural women’s contributions and highlight the challenges they face.

For Liberia, the observance is a reminder that the country’s development cannot be separated from the well-being and empowerment of the women who sustain rural households, contribute to food production, and help maintain peace within their communities.

Rural women should not be viewed merely as beneficiaries of development programs. They are farmers, entrepreneurs, caregivers, community leaders, and peacebuilders whose knowledge and experience are essential to national progress.

Ensuring that they have access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making spaces is not simply a matter of recognition; it is an investment in Liberia’s economic growth, social stability, and long-term development.

As the country marks the day, the challenge is to translate recognition into action by protecting rural women’s rights, investing in their livelihoods, amplifying their voices, and ensuring their meaningful participation in decisions affecting their future.

When rural women thrive, Liberia thrives. When rural women lead, peace grows. And when rural women are empowered, Liberia moves closer to a more inclusive and prosperous future.

World.title: Liberia: Rubber Transshipment Ban Draws Complaints From Truckers and Shipping Stakeholders
World.content:
Stakeholders Urge Boakai to Reconsider Executive Order No. 166, Citing Reported Business Losses and Idle Trucks

MONROVIA — Liberia’s Executive Order No. 166 prohibits the transshipment of specified forms of unprocessed natural rubber, including natural latex, coagulum, cup lump, tree lace, bark scrap and ground scrap, according to the government’s description of the measure.

By Obediah Johnson

The Executive Mansion has said the order is intended to promote domestic industrialization, create jobs, increase government revenue and encourage value addition by keeping more rubber-related economic activity in Liberia.



Truckers and other stakeholders in the shipping and logistics sectors, however, say the policy has reduced the movement of Guinea-origin rubber through the Port of Monrovia and affected businesses that depend on cross-border cargo.

The stakeholders’ account has not been independently verified through port, customs or shipping records reviewed for this report.

They claim that the Guinea-to-Liberia rubber transit trade previously generated between 100 and 150 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) per month. That figure was provided by stakeholders and could not be independently confirmed. It is also unclear whether it refers only to unprocessed rubber, all rubber products, or total related cargo.

Stakeholders say cargo volumes declined after the order took effect, leaving some transport operators with fewer loads. The number of affected businesses, the value of any losses and the extent of the decline have not been independently established.

Shipping Stakeholders Report Reduced Business

Layee Sheriff of the Truckers Union Association of Liberia said the restrictions had affected export-related business associated with the movement of Guinean rubber through the Port of Monrovia.

“Major export business previously generated by the transshipment of rubber from Guinea through the Port of Monrovia has declined since implementation of the order,” Sheriff said.

His statement is a stakeholder claim. No port or shipping data was provided to substantiate the reported decline.

Sheriff said Guinea had used Liberia’s maritime corridor partly because of the proximity between rubber-processing facilities and the Port of Monrovia. He also said both unprocessed and processed rubber from Guinea had moved through Liberia for onward shipment to international markets.

The extent of that trade, the proportion involving unprocessed rubber and the number of shipments affected were not provided.

“The decline in cargo volumes means fewer containers for shipping companies and reduced revenue from export-related services,” Sheriff said.

That statement describes an expected or reported business effect, but no financial figures were cited. The article could not independently determine whether shipping lines experienced a measurable reduction in revenue or container utilization.

Shipping and logistics companies can be affected when cargo volumes fall, but the specific impact on companies operating through Monrovia remains unconfirmed.

Truckers Report Idle Vehicles

Sheriff also said some truck operators and owners had complained that their vehicles were remaining idle for several days because of reduced haulage opportunities.

This account was not independently verified, and no records were provided showing the number of idle trucks, the duration of inactivity or the number of operators affected.

Adam Deok, a trucker, said the consequences could extend beyond the immediate loss of transportation contracts.

“For truck owners and drivers, the issue extends beyond the rubber trade itself. Reduced cargo movement can affect fuel consumption, driver employment, vehicle maintenance, port-related services and the wider logistics chain,” Deok said.

Deok’s statement identifies possible effects, not verified outcomes. The number of jobs affected, changes in fuel consumption, maintenance losses and impacts on port-related services have not been established.

The reported concerns are consistent with the way reduced cargo activity can affect transport businesses, but the specific consequences in Liberia require supporting evidence from trucking companies, workers, port operators and government agencies.

Government Cites Industrialization and Value Addition

The government’s stated rationale for Executive Order No. 166 is to encourage domestic processing and value addition.

According to the Executive Mansion, the measure is intended to create jobs, increase government revenue and ensure that more rubber-related economic activity takes place within Liberia.

Those are government objectives. The available information does not establish whether the order has already produced additional jobs, increased revenue or expanded domestic processing.

The order’s precise application is also important. The available material describes a prohibition on the transshipment of specified unprocessed rubber, but it does not provide the full text of the order or clarify whether all foreign-origin rubber in transit is covered, whether exceptions exist or how processed rubber is treated.

Stakeholders argue that the measure has affected businesses handling goods originating outside Liberia. The government has not, in the information reviewed for this article, publicly provided data on the order’s effects on cross-border trucking, shipping services, employment or port revenue.

The policy therefore presents two competing claims: the government says it is intended to promote domestic value addition, while stakeholders say it has reduced regional transit business. Neither the claimed economic benefits nor the reported losses have been quantified in the available information.

Trade and Transit Rules Raise Legal Questions

The order has prompted questions about Liberia’s obligations under regional and international trade arrangements, particularly if it applies to foreign goods passing through Liberian territory.

Article V of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade addresses freedom of transit and the movement of goods through the territory of a member country. The World Trade Organization’s Trade Facilitation Agreement also contains provisions concerning transit procedures and the facilitation of cross-border movement.

These provisions establish a legal framework for international transit. Their existence alone does not demonstrate that Executive Order No. 166 violates Liberia’s obligations.

A legal assessment would require the full text of the order, information about how authorities are enforcing it and an analysis of the relevant treaty provisions and exceptions.

It would also be necessary to distinguish between a restriction on the export of rubber produced in Liberia and a restriction on foreign-origin rubber merely passing through Liberia. The available information does not establish how the order treats each category.

No legal challenge or formal finding of noncompliance was identified in the material reviewed for this article.

ECOWAS Context

Liberia is a member of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), whose regional framework includes objectives related to trade liberalization, the removal of non-tariff barriers and the movement of goods among member states.

Those broad objectives do not, by themselves, determine whether the rubber restriction is inconsistent with a specific ECOWAS obligation.

The article’s source material states that ECOWAS launched the Interconnected System for the Management of Goods in Transit (SIGMAT) involving Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea and Liberia in November 2025. That date and the scope of the launch should be confirmed through ECOWAS or national customs records before publication.

SIGMAT is intended to improve customs coordination and facilitate the movement of goods in transit. Its existence provides regional context, but it does not establish that the executive order conflicts with the system or with any ECOWAS rule.

Stakeholders say Liberia’s treatment of Guinea-origin rubber should be reviewed in light of regional efforts to reduce trade bottlenecks. That is their policy position, not a verified legal conclusion.

AfCFTA and Mano River Union Context

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) seeks to liberalize trade in goods and services and advance economic integration across Africa. Its general objectives do not, without further legal analysis, establish how the agreement applies to the specific rubber-transshipment restriction.

The Mano River Union (MRU), comprising Liberia, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d’Ivoire, has pursued initiatives related to regional connectivity, trade facilitation and cross-border movement.

The source material refers to an MRU Roads Development and Transport Facilitation Programme and other efforts to streamline border and corridor procedures. The details and current status of those initiatives should be confirmed with the MRU before publication.

These regional frameworks provide context for the debate, but they do not independently verify the reported decline in rubber traffic or demonstrate that Liberia has breached a regional commitment.

Stakeholders Ask Boakai to Reconsider the Order

Stakeholders, including representatives of truckers and other transport-related businesses, are calling on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to reconsider Executive Order No. 166 and lift or revise the restriction on the transshipment of unprocessed natural rubber.

They say the government should consider the reported effects on truck owners, drivers, shipping companies and other businesses involved in cross-border cargo movements.

The appeal is based on stakeholder accounts. The article did not identify a formal petition, written submission or official meeting record documenting the request.

A review of the policy could examine whether Liberia can pursue domestic processing while preserving legitimate transit operations. It should also assess the order’s legal scope, its effects on foreign-origin goods in transit and the availability of exemptions or alternative arrangements.

Reliable evaluation would require verified data on rubber cargo volumes before and after implementation, the number of affected trucks and businesses, employment effects, port revenue and the order’s contribution to domestic processing.

The government’s position remains central to the issue. Further responses from the Executive Mansion, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Liberia National Port Authority, customs authorities and relevant maritime agencies would help clarify the order’s scope, the evidence supporting it and whether any review is under consideration.

For now, the verified facts are that Executive Order No. 166 prohibits the transshipment of specified unprocessed rubber products and that the government says the measure is intended to promote domestic value addition. Claims that the order has reduced cargo volumes, caused financial losses or left trucks idle have been attributed to stakeholders but remain unconfirmed by independent data.

World.title: Liberia: In Bomi, Women Turn World Bank Support Into Businesses, But Call For More Help
World.content:
BOMI COUNTY — Women in Gbojay, Bomi County, say financial support from the Liberia Women Empowerment Project (LWEP) is helping them build small businesses, pay their children’s school expenses, and ease financial pressures in their homes. But they are calling on the government and its partners to extend the assistance to other women still struggling to make ends meet.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

The women made the appeal Wednesday, during a field visit by representatives of the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MGCSP), the World Bank, Plan International, and other project partners to assess the impact of the initiative on local livelihoods.



For beneficiaries, the support has provided more than access to money. It has created opportunities to save, borrow, invest in small businesses and contribute to household expenses. However, women who have not benefited from the program remain a concern for those already receiving assistance.

Oretha Cooper, secretary of the Walekerma Village Savings Group, said the financial support had helped members develop better money management skills and use loans to strengthen their businesses.

Speaking on behalf of the group’s chairlady, Cooper said the revolving fund had helped women understand the importance of saving, investing, and repaying loans so that other members could also access the money.

“Before, some of us did not know how to manage money or operate businesses. But today, this support has helped us learn how to save, borrow, invest, and repay our loans,” Cooper said.

The group has 25 members and received US$8,000 in revolving funds, disbursed in two instillments of US$4,000 each, according to Cooper and the project coordinator.

Cooper said the money had helped members improve their businesses and meet family responsibilities, including their children’s educational needs.

But she said the benefits should not stop with the current group.

“We want you to help other communities and women who have not received this opportunity. We are benefiting from the support, and we want other women to have the same chance to improve their lives,” she added.

Single Mother Uses Support to Feed Her Family

For Satta Massalay, a beneficiary of the project, the assistance has provided an opportunity to earn an income through gardening and small-scale trading.

Massalay said she divided the money between her farming activities and the purchase of goods for resale, allowing her to generate income to support herself and her children.

“I used the money to work in my garden and buy goods to sell. The profit I make helps me solve problems for myself and my children,” she said.

Another female beneficiary also praised the government and its partners, saying the assistance had helped her establish a small business.

The experiences reflect how livelihood support can help women build income-generating activities and contribute to their families’ daily needs.

According to the LWEP Project Coordinator, village savings groups receive up to US$8,000 in revolving funds, while individual enterprises receive grants of up to US$2,500.

The support is intended to help women establish businesses, expand existing enterprises, and improve their financial independence.

Man Says Women’s Economic Empowerment Can Ease Family Tensions

The impact of the program, beneficiaries say, extends beyond business and household income.

Momo Mah, a male community member, said women’s economic empowerment could help reduce financial pressure within households and improve relationships between couples.

Mah explained that when husbands are expected to meet nearly every household expense, repeated financial demands can sometimes create tension. But when women earn their own income, they can contribute to family needs and ease that pressure.

“When a woman starts doing something small and earning money, it brings fresh air into the home,” Mah said. “As a husband, when I see that my wife is doing something to help the family, I also feel encouraged.”

He urged the government and its partners to provide more women with opportunities to earn income, arguing that stronger financial independence could contribute to more stable households.

His remarks highlighted the connection between women’s economic empowerment and efforts to reduce tensions that may arise from financial hardship.

Women Demand Wider Access to Support

Fatu Sonnie, another beneficiary, said the project had helped women generate income to support their children’s education and meet other household expenses.

However, she raised concerns that some women in the community had not benefited from the program, despite facing similar economic challenges.

Sonnie appealed to the project partners to extend assistance to more women so they could also establish businesses and improve their living conditions.

The appeals from Cooper and Sonnie point to a challenge facing community-based empowerment programs: ensuring that opportunities reach women beyond the initial groups selected to benefit.

Government Urges Beneficiaries to Expand Opportunities

Julius Sele, executive director of the Liberia Agency for Community Empowerment (LACE), said the initiative forms part of broader government efforts to improve livelihoods through small businesses and community-based agricultural activities.

Sele said the program brings together government institutions, the World Bank, and implementing partners to support women and communities facing economic challenges.

He encouraged beneficiaries to use the funds responsibly and demonstrate that the assistance could produce lasting results.

“Those of you who have the opportunity now should demonstrate your ability to do better, so that tomorrow other women who are not part of the group can also have access to similar opportunities,” Sele said.

He also urged the savings group to consider extending credit opportunities to women outside its membership.

Sele noted that while the group had 25 members, the wider community had more than 100 women, making it important to explore ways of spreading the benefits.

His appeal placed responsibility on both project partners and current beneficiaries to help ensure that more women can access economic opportunities.

World Bank Praises Women’s Collective Efforts

Robert Chase, the World Bank’s Practice Manager for Social Policy, said he was encouraged by the women’s experiences and their willingness to discuss challenges affecting their lives.

Chase, who was visiting Liberia for the first time in connection with the project, said he had followed the initiative for years and welcomed the opportunity to observe its implementation in the community.

“I was very impressed to see the way the SASA! group is talking about difficult issues and trying to open up conversations to empower women and the community,” Chase said.

He also highlighted the importance of Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), which enable women to save together, access loans, develop businesses, and discuss issues affecting their households and communities.

Chase said the experiences and ideas emerging from Bomi County could offer lessons for other communities across West Africa.

Project Reaches Six Counties

The Liberia Women Empowerment Project is a government initiative implemented by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection with financing from the World Bank.

It supports women’s economic empowerment through livelihood activities, improved access to basic services, community participation, and efforts to prevent violence against women and girls.

The project operates in Bomi, Gbarpolu, Grand Cape Mount, Grand Gedeh, Montserrado, and River Cess counties.

The Wednesday field visit also included activities under the Rural Economic Transformation Project (REALISE) in Queenie-1 Town, Suehn Mecca District, Bomi County.

According to the Ministry of Gender, REALISE has supported 33 participants in Queenie-1, including 28 members of an agricultural livelihood group and five Community Oversight Committee members.

The farming group has planted 39 acres of rice, with harvesting ongoing, while a community-selected rice mill has been installed and is operational.

The broader field visit was intended to assess implementation progress, hear directly from beneficiaries, and identify areas requiring further action.

For the women in Gbojay, the support has opened doors to small businesses, improved household contributions, and greater financial independence. But their appeal is clear: the opportunities helping some women move forward should also reach those still waiting for a chance.

The experiences shared in Gbojay show how LWEP, under MGCSP’s leadership and with World Bank financing, is helping women grow businesses, meet their children’s school expenses, and contribute more to household needs. Savings groups and community dialogue are also providing spaces for women to strengthen their financial skills and discuss issues affecting their lives.

The challenge ahead is to sustain these gains while addressing the needs of women yet to benefit. For Gbojay’s beneficiaries, progress carries a shared hope: that the opportunities helping them build greater financial independence will also open doors for other women in their community.
