World.title: A Tamaulipas teen built a fire extinguisher that puts out flames using sound
World.content:
A 17-year-old from the northeastern state of Tamaulipas is competing at an international science fair in Indonesia this week with a device she spent a year developing — a fire extinguisher that snuffs out small flames with sound instead of water or chemicals.

Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández is representing Mexico at the International Science and Invention Fair with Vortex Tech, a prototype developed with the help of her uncle, José Arturo Hernández Muñoz.

Her school, CETis 78 in Altamira, Tamaulipas, announced her participation in the fair being held this week at the University of Indonesia in Depok, near Jakarta.

Photographs shared by Mexico’s federal technical education agency showed Venegas wearing traditional Mexican clothing at the fair.

Venegas told the newspaper El País that a video of a large, roughly 4-meter (13-foot) sonic cannon extinguishing a flame — with air movement, not water or chemicals — inspired her to investigate whether she could build a smaller device.

She and her uncle, who holds a master’s degree in science, according to the Tamaulipas Education Ministry, spent about a year developing five prototypes, building on earlier experiments by others.

Just to create the first prototype — one that could extinguish a candle — took two months, not including preliminary research, she told the newspaper.

Vortex Tech uses a 12-volt battery, a frequency generator set to 30 hertz, an amplifier and a speaker. A modified bucket channels the output toward a flame.

According to Venegas’ explanation, the sound generates swirling rings of air that disrupt the oxygen supply sustaining combustion, extinguishing small flames within seconds.

The technology remains experimental. The newspaper El Universal reported that it works on small, nearby flames and does not replace conventional extinguishers for large fires.

Tamaulipas education officials said the project also includes thermal sensors designed to detect a developing fire and automatically activate the sound-based extinguishing system.

The state Education Ministry said Venegas advanced through regional, state and national competitions before qualifying for Indonesia. It also pledged support for her and her uncle/adviser’s participation.

With reports from El País, El Heraldo de México and El Universal

World.title: 2,500-year-old astronomical observatory in Puebla confirmed to be the oldest in Mexico
World.content:
A pre-Hispanic solar observatory in the municipality of Teteles de Ávila Castillo in the Sierra Norte region of Puebla has been confirmed to be the oldest in Mexico, dating back more than 2,500 years.

According to research carried out by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), a monumental architectural complex named “Grupo E” functioned as a solar astronomical observatory and is the oldest of its kind in Mexico.

Researchers believe the settlement’s inhabitants incorporated astronomical observations into the planning of their ceremonial buildings more than two millennia ago.

Heritage Daily —a digital publication specializing in archaeology, anthropology and palaeontology — says the discovery “provides remarkable evidence of sophisticated astronomical knowledge among ancient Mesoamerican civilizations.”

INAH says it is the first discovery of its kind outside the Maya region and is comparable to the observatory at the archaeological site of Uaxactún in Petén, Guatemala, which has been identified as the first and defining archetype for ancient Maya astronomical observation complexes.

While both the Uaxactún and Teteles complexes are believed to date to the Middle Preclassic (from 1200 to 400 BCE.), the Uaxactún structure is approximately twice the size of the one in Puebla.

Researchers have confirmed that the original layout of the “Group E” settlement (also known as Tetelihtic) and the orientation of its pyramidal structures are based on an understanding of celestial bodies.

Archaeologist Alberto Diez Barroso said the ancient settlement is an outstanding example of pre-Hispanic urban planning — shaped by the observation of the surrounding landscape, such as the nearby mountain peaks, as well as the astronomical horizon — making it “a significant point of reference for Mesoamerican studies in this field.”

Tetelihtic consists of a quadrangular courtyard flanked by two platforms at its eastern and western ends. The eastern platform is elongated (90 m from south to north by 40 m from east to west), while the western structure is smaller (46 m from north to south by 27 m from east to west) and served as an observation point.

The elongated platform does not mark the equinoxes at its center, however.

“It apparently served to establish the beginning of the pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican calendar in February and the harvest period in October, making it a complex and unique feature,” Diez said.

However, the eastern platform did function as a solar calendar; observations have confirmed that, from its front, one can track the sun’s path at dawn during the equinoxes and solstices.

Archaeologists believe the finding could provide insights into the cultural relationship between the Huastec and Maya groups during the early stages of human settlement in the Sierra Norte as it serves to confirm the Maya ethnolinguistic roots of the Huastec groups.

A Maya presence at Teteles may date back as far as 3,000 years — a possibility suggested by the Puebla observatory.

With reports from INAH, Heritage Daily and Ambas Manos

World.title: Mexico targets cheap Chinese bicycles with six-month anti-dumping duty
World.content:
Mexico has imposed a provisional anti-dumping duty of US $68.60 per unit on adult bicycles originating from China, after the Economy Ministry preliminarily determined that Chinese bicycles were being sold below fair market value, harming domestic manufacturers.

The measure, which took effect on Oct. 13, will remain in place for six months and will apply to adult bicycles with a wheel size larger than 20 inches, including urban and mountain models, with or without gears, as well as unassembled units. Electric bicycles and racing or road bikes are excluded from the measure.

The decision traced back to an anti-dumping investigation requested in April 2025 by the National Association of Bicycle Manufacturers and the companies Mercurio, Veloci, Benotto and Línea Siete. The investigation formally began in August of that year.

According to preliminary results, Chinese bicycles accounted for 95% of Mexico’s imports of adult bicycles in 2024. Apparent national consumption of Chinese bicycles rose from 53% in 2022 to 61% in 2024, while the average price of imports fell 35% during that period.

In 2024, Chinese bicycles cost 27% less than their domestic counterparts. According to the Economy Ministry, this difference pressured the Mexican industry to reduce prices by 4% to stay competitive.

As more low-cost Chinese bicycles entered the country, Mexican manufacturers saw a significant drop in business. The Economy Ministry found that between 2022 and 2024, adult bicycle production fell by 34% and domestic sales declined by 32%. Meanwhile, employment dropped by 29%.

Sales revenue in the domestic market fell by 36% in the same period, while the industry’s operating profits swung into the red, a 111% drop. These figures led investigators to conclude that low-priced Chinese imports caused material harm to Mexican manufacturers.

During the six months that the preliminary duty will remain in effect, interested parties may submit evidence for or against the measures, while the investigation continues to determine whether to establish more permanent duties.

The provisional anti-dumping duty is part of a broader trend toward increased trade protection in Mexico. According to data from the Economy Ministry, imports falling under the 1,463 tariff classifications subject to new levies — approved in December 2025 — declined by 23% between January and May 2026, compared to the same period the previous year.

China, the primary supplier of the goods subject to duties, was the hardest hit, as its tariffed goods fell by 28% — from $10.1 billion to $7.2 billion.

With reports from Milenio and Diario de Tabasco

World.title: American Airlines is the latest carrier to drop service to Tulum
World.content:
American Airlines is dropping flights from Miami to the Yucatán Peninsula destination of Tulum as part of its cutback of several international routes, including its Charlotte-Los Cabos service.

American (AA) — the largest U.S. airline by passenger numbers — joins other major carriers, including Aeroméxico and Volaris, in dropping or pausing routes to the resort town on the state of Quintana Roo’s Caribbean coast.

AA had already announced that its Miami-Tulum route would be on seasonal pause through Nov. 19, after which it would continue again until Dec. 1. The current plan is to then resume service one last time from Dec. 17 to January 5, 2027, before stopping it completely.

Los Cabos is also slated for service cuts

AA ended its service to Tulum from Charlotte, North Carolina, in February, 2025, less than a year after its launch. Next year, the only AA route from the U.S. to Tulum will be from or through the Dallas/Fort Worth hub.

American has also announced plans to remove its Charlotte-San José del Cabo route from its future schedule, after its current seasonal pause. The route was originally planned to return to normal operations in November, but the schedule now reportedly shows only sporadic operations.

That limited service will end in August of 2027. A possible motive for the discontinuation is that the route’s flights on average were just 73.69% full between June 2025 and June 2026.

With reports from Simple Flying

World.title: Rachel death toll rises to 8 in Baja California as newly formed Hurricane Trudy heads for Jalisco coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

While Pacific Coast residents are still reeling from the passage of Polo, Rachel and Simon, the newly formed Hurricane Trudy threatens to bring more chaos and disruption to the region.

Eight deaths have been attributed to Hurricane Rachel, while at least four people remain missing and the military has been actively carrying out search and rescue operations. And Simon, lurking near the Jalisco coast south of the tip of the Baja California Peninsula, is expected to remain a Category 1 hurricane through Friday.

In light of the devastation, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Thursday activated the Defense Ministry’s DN-III emergency protection plan and the Navy’s “Plan Marina.”

Sheinbaum also ordered the Interior Ministry to stay in close contact with the Baja California governor in order to provide any support that may be needed, especially as Simon is expected to move toward the peninsula on Saturday.

Last month, Polo — the second most-intense Pacific hurricane on record — made consecutive landfalls on the peninsula and then mainland Mexico on Sept. 29.

Now comes Trudy, which became a hurricane before dawn Thursday.

The storm system was located about 300 miles (480 kilometers) southwest of Acapulco and 445 miles (720 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo, Colima, while registering maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h), with gusts of 93 mph (150 km/h).

According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC), Trudy is undergoing a period of rapid intensification as it moves northwest at 9 mph (15 km/h) and is expected to bring heavy rains to Oaxaca and Guerrero today (Thursday).

Forecast models project it will become a major hurricane as it approaches the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico this weekend, bringing rainfall of 4 to 8 inches (101 to 203 millimeters) through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco states.

Meanwhile, Simon remains virtually “frozen” a few hundred kilometers west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, and is expected to continue orbiting in place with sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h) and gusts of 95 mph (150 km/h).

Sustained winds were about 130 miles (210 kilometers) per hour as the week began, and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the Jalisco coast.

The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper Simon’s intensity and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC said. Still, as the storm system weakened from a Category 4 to Category 1 it delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, Colima.

With reports from La Jornada, The Associated Press, El Economista, Meteored and CNN en Español

World.title: International tourist spending grows 8% in August despite a dip in arrivals
World.content:
International tourist arrivals in Mexico declined year over year in August for the first time in almost a year, according to official data, even as total expenditure by international tourists increased by over 8%.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported Wednesday that 3.76 million international tourists came to Mexico in August, a decline of 0.5% compared to the same month of 2025.

International tourists are classified as foreign residents who spend at least one night in Mexico during their visit to the country.

In August, 1.39 million of the 3.76 million international tourists flew into the country, a decline of 6.5% compared to a year earlier. International tourist arrivals by air declined during every month between February and August.

The remainder of the international tourists in August entered Mexico by land, with most of that cohort staying within the northern or southern border region. INEGI’s data shows that two-thirds (67.1%) of the tourists who came to Mexico in August and traveled beyond the border regions are residents of the United States.

The year-over-year decline in international tourist arrivals in August was the first annual decrease since September 2025.

Humberto Molina, an expert in tourism economics at the consultancy firm Grupo Empresarial Estrategia, attributed the decline to a range of factors, including the presence of sargassum on Mexican beaches, insecurity and a lack of tourism promotion.

International tourist expenditure increased 8.1% in August

While in Mexico in August, international tourists collectively spent US $2.16 billion, an increase of 8.1% compared to the same month of 2025.

Each international tourist spent $573.30 on average, up 8.6% from August 2025.

Individual expenditure by international tourists who flew into Mexico was more than double that amount at $1,269.60, an increase of 15.2% compared to August 2025.

International tourists who flew into Mexico collectively spent $1.77 billion while in the country, a figure that accounts for 82% of total international tourism expenditure.

Despite decline in international tourists, international traveler numbers reached a record high in August

While international tourist numbers declined 0.5% year over year in August, international traveler numbers increased 1.3% to reach 7.98 million, the highest figure on record for the month of August.

INEGI’s international travelers category includes international tourists and international day-trippers (excursionistas internacionales). The latter enter Mexico by land or sea but don’t stay the night. International day-trippers include cruise ship passengers and people who spend a few hours in Mexico after entering the country via border crossings with the United States, Guatemala and Belize.

Just over 4.2 million international day-trippers came to Mexico in August, an increase of 3% compared to the same month of last year. Around 81% of the international day trippers (3.43 million) entered Mexico by land, while 785,558 came into the country by sea. Sea arrivals increased by 12.3% compared to August 2025, while land arrivals rose 1.1%.

Total spending by international travelers in Mexico in August was $2.4 billion, a 7% increase compared to a year earlier. International tourists spent 90% of that amount, while international day-trippers contributed the other 10%.

While expenditure rose in dollar terms, it declined 5.51% annually in real peso terms, according to Banco Base analysts, who took inflation and the USD:MXN exchange rate into account. The USD:MXN exchange rate was 17 at the end of August compared to 18.66 a year earlier.

More than 32 million international tourists came to Mexico between January and August

INEGI data shows that 32.68 million international tourists came to Mexico in the first eight months of 2026, a year-over-year increase of 3.9%.

International traveler numbers rose 6.3% annually in the same period to reach 67.69 million.

In a statement, Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez said that data from the first eight months of the year indicates that “Mexico could end 2026 with a record in international tourist arrivals.”

“Mexico is in vogue and we’re continuing to work so that more people visit us, get to know our cultural and natural wealth and contribute to the well-being of communities,” she said.

Total expenditure by international travelers in Mexico was $24.15 billion between January and August, an increase of 0.9% compared to the same period of last year.

Mexico is one of the world’s 10 most visited countries, ranking sixth or seventh in recent years. One of the goals of the federal government’s Plan Mexico economic initiative is to make Mexico one of the world’s top five tourism destinations by 2030.

With reports from El Economista, La Jornada and Reporte Indigo

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Brugada’s big plans, a sinking city and methane mitigation
World.content:
In this week’s MND Local for CDMX, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada touted her administration’s accomplishments and outlined future priorities during her second annual “state of the city” address. Meanwhile, new research highlights the capital’s ongoing sinking problem, and officials are pursuing efforts to reduce the city’s methane emissions.

Let’s get into it.

Mayor Brugada delivers 2nd ‘state of the city’ address

Earlier this month, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada delivered a “state of the city” address, touting her administration’s accomplishments across various sectors, including social services, security, infrastructure and healthcare. It was Brugada’s second such address since she assumed office on Oct. 7, 2024.

The theme of Brugada’s speech was “utopias,” which she said are the cornerstone of her administration’s policies.

“We want to build the city of Utopias, the city where all possible utopias fit: the utopia of well-being, democracy, social justice, fraternity and freedom,” Brugada, who belongs to the ruling Morena Party, said.

She touched on several future priorities and projects the administration intends to carry out, including criminal justice reform that centers on reintegration, establishing three new public universities outside Mexico City’s core, and constructing five new high schools that serve the city’s Indigenous population.

Utopian visions

Meanwhile, she touted myriad accomplishments over the past two years, such as a 48 billion peso (US $2.6 billion) investment in the city’s metro system, resulting in 100 kilometers of electric bus routes. She also pointed to 1 million square meters of public space that have been reclaimed, 600 new public women’s spaces, a 1 billion peso (US $54 million) investment in agriculture, and an 85% increase in social programs, which now cover 2.6 million people across the capital, among other things.

“Let’s continue building all possible utopias,” Brugada said during her address, per La Gazzetta DF. “Let’s strive for more, for much more. With the memory of those who fought before and the hope of those who will come after. This is our city, this is our time, this is our history, and we are writing it together.”

While Brugada’s approval rating currently stands at 60%, according to the most recent polling from El Financiero, her tenure has not been without controversy.

During her speech, Brugada touted a significant reduction in crime over the past two years, including a 24% dip in “high-impact crimes” and four consecutive months with homicides at historic lows. However, her administration’s failure to hold anyone accountable for the assassinations of two of her deputies in 2025 continues to dog her legacy.

Mexico City is sinking … still

A new study published Oct. 12 in “Nature Cities” suggests that areas of Mexico City are sinking as much as 8.5 inches per year, while the citywide average sits somewhere around 0.3 inches per year.

The study, led by Shengli Tao and Xie Hu of Beijing’s Peking University, used high-resolution satellite data collected over nine years, from 2014 to 2023. Of the 465 cities across 107 countries that were surveyed, Mexico City recorded the fastest localized sinking.

The 8.5-inch figure hovers around a similar analysis published in May, which found that Mexico City is sinking by nearly 10 inches (about 25 centimeters) a year and has sunk by nearly 40 feet over the past century.

That study relied on NASA satellite data from NISAR, a joint U.S.-India satellite project. NISAR uses advanced radar imaging — effectively a microscope in space — to measure changes in Earth’s land, ice, sea level rise and groundwater.

It’s a different approach from Tao and Hu’s team, which used satellite interferometric synthetic aperture radar, which basically functions like a ruler that measures ground movement over time.

Mexico City details methane mitigation efforts

Meanwhile, Mexico City is attempting to tackle a significant driver of global warming — methane emissions.

Earlier this month, the city hosted Mexico Climate Week, which included a session dubbed “Accelerating Methane Action in Mexico City.” The event brought together domestic and international stakeholders representing government, academia, civil society and the private sector.

According to Ricardo Cepeda of the U.S.-based nonprofit C40 Cities, methane mitigation efforts are one of the best, most demonstrable ways to slow climate change in the near future.

“The objective is not to create more strategies, plans or projects,” Cepeda said. “The objective is to reduce methane emissions.”

Despite Cepeda warning governments off endless strategy meetings, Maritza Florez, who works with Mexico City’s Environment Ministry, did just that, detailing the capital’s methane mitigation strategy. It includes preventing food waste, expanding composting infrastructure and developing four additional treatment facilities for organic waste.

While much of the infrastructural onus lies with city leaders, residents are encouraged to develop composting and food waste prevention initiatives in their own communities.

“Methane mitigation is the brake for climate change,” said Mexico City Environment Ministry Secretary Julia Álvarez Icaza, adding that better waste management and separation systems are key to controlling the capital’s methane emissions.

“When waste is not mixed, it can be valued and utilized. When it is mixed, it becomes garbage,” Icaza said.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Man accused of burglarizing YWCA and Divine Mercy Church, acting as his own attorney, asks Magistrate to recuse herself after she previously convicted him in case overturned by High Court
World.content:
Man accused of burglarizing YWCA and Divine Mercy Church, acting as his own attorney, asks Magistrate to recuse herself after she previously convicted him in case overturned by High Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A burglary trial involving Denfield Lemott has been left in limbo after he requested that the Magistrate hearing his case recuse herself because she had previously convicted him of burglary in a separate matter, a conviction that was later overturned on appeal.

Lemott, who is representing himself, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, October 15, where his case was adjourned to November 17, 2026, as the court considers how to proceed.

The trial had already commenced in Court #4, with evidence taken from the complainant, when Lemott raised concerns about the Magistrate’s involvement and requested her recusal. The matter was subsequently transferred to Court #5, leaving unresolved questions about how the partially heard trial should continue.

The dispute follows Lemott’s successful appeal of a 2025 burglary conviction for which he had received an eight-year prison sentence. High Court Justice Candace Nanton subsequently quashed the conviction and set aside the sentence, allowing him to regain his freedom.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Lemott later faced two additional burglary charges involving the alleged theft of $130 from a program officer and $350 from a teacher at the YMCA building in Belize City. He pleaded not guilty to those allegations.

In another case, Lemott was charged with allegedly stealing $2,000 from Divine Mercy Church in July 2026. He also pleaded not guilty in that matter and was denied bail.

During Thursday’s appearance, Lemott informed the court that he had misplaced his original disclosure documents and requested another copy.

The Magistrate adjourned the current burglary case to November 17 for mention, when the prosecution is expected to clarify its position on how the trial should proceed following the transfer between courts.

World.title: Jamie Young’s murder trial delayed again, rescheduled for Friday
World.content:
Jamie Young’s murder trial delayed again, rescheduled for Friday

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder trial of Jamie Caesar Young, accused of fatally shooting his former girlfriend’s new partner during a high-speed pursuit along the Philip Goldson Highway in 2024, has been postponed yet again.

Young was scheduled to stand trial before High Court Justice Candace Nanton on Thursday, October 15, but the proceedings could not begin due to unforeseen circumstances. The matter was adjourned to Friday, October 16, at 9:00 a.m.

Young, who is represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones, is charged with the March 16, 2024 murder of 30-year-old former Belize Defence Force soldier and bus driver Damion Dominique Baptist of Burrell Boom.

According to police, Baptist was travelling with Young’s former girlfriend when Young allegedly pursued them in a grey pickup truck along the highway near Ladyville.

Investigators allege that Young repeatedly pulled alongside their vehicle and fired shots, eventually striking Baptist in the head and causing him to lose control of his red Ford Fusion, which crashed into a lamppost near Our Lady of the Way RC School.

Baptist was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Young was subsequently arrested and charged with murder and aggravated assault against the woman.

The latest adjournment follows an earlier postponement on October 5, when the trial could not proceed because Young’s attorney was reportedly ill. BBN previously reported on that delay.

The case is now expected to proceed on Friday morning.

World.title: Belize City teen takes rap and gets 2 years in jail for unlicensed Glock 17 so his sister can go free
World.content:
Belize City teen takes rap and gets 2 years in jail for unlicensed Glock 17 so his sister can go free

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man who pleaded guilty to possessing an unlicensed Glock pistol, resulting in the withdrawal of a firearm charge against his older sister, has been sentenced to two years in prison.

Aaron Ayren Pitter, of Pitter Street, was sentenced on Thursday, October 15, before a Magistrate in Court #5 at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court. His sentence was ordered to take effect from August 18, 2026, the date he pleaded guilty.

The conviction stems from a police search conducted on August 17 at a residence on Pitter Street, where officers from the Violence Prevention and Enforcement Team discovered a Glock 17 Gen 4 9mm pistol wrapped inside a pair of blue short pants hidden in a hole beside a bathtub.

The firearm was fitted with a black magazine and red extension, but police confirmed that the gun and magazine contained no ammunition.

According to police, Pitter arrived home while officers were conducting the search and admitted that the firearm belonged to him, telling officers, “Da feh me, big man. I have knowledge that was there.”

Pitter and his 20-year-old sister, Gregoria Veronica Pitter, were initially jointly charged with keeping a firearm without a gun licence. However, after Aaron accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty, prosecutors withdrew the charge against his sister, allowing her to walk free.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, the Magistrate initially encouraged Pitter to seek legal advice before accepting his guilty plea, but the teenager insisted on taking responsibility for the weapon so his sister could go free.

During Thursday’s sentencing, Pitter offered no mitigation. Although he had initially faced a possible five-year prison term, the Magistrate imposed a two-year sentence, retroactive to August 18.

World.title: “I just want to be your mother-in-law”: Daughter-in-law drops harm charge against ‘ma-lee’
World.content:
“I just want to be your mother-in-law”: Daughter-in-law drops harm charge against ‘ma-lee’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City woman who was arrested on a bench warrant after repeatedly missing court appearances has been spared further legal trouble after her daughter-in-law, who accused her of causing harm more than two years ago, asked the court to withdraw the charge.

Angela Copious appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Wednesday, October 14, after being detained over the holiday weekend for failing to attend previous court hearings.

Copious was charged with causing harm to her daughter-in-law following an alleged altercation on July 26, 2024.

In court, Copious explained that she had been seriously ill and claimed her daughter had emailed medical documents to explain her absences. However, the court had no record of receiving those documents.

The matter took an unexpected turn when the daughter-in-law appeared and informed the Magistrate that she had forgiven her mother-in-law and no longer wished to pursue the case. She requested that the charge be withdrawn so both women could move on with their lives.

Faber also asked that they be bound over to keep the peace, but the Magistrate did not impose such an order.

With the charge withdrawn and her bail not revoked, Copious was allowed to leave court.

Before departing, a relieved Copious turned to her daughter-in-law and told her, “I just want to be your mother-in-law.”

The emotional exchange brought an end to a criminal complaint that had been pending since July 2024.

World.title: Belize participates in U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State
World.content:
Belize participates in U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State

By Zoila Palma: Today, Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, is participating in the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue, hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

The Ministry says that the high-level dialogue provides an important platform to strengthen regional partnerships and advance shared priorities in security and defense coordination, strategic economic growth, disaster response, and regional health cooperation.

CEO Arnold is joined by the Ambassador of Belize to the U.S., Nestor Mendez, and Counsellor, Alexya Perez.

“Belize remains committed to constructive engagement and regional collaboration with the Caribbean and its partners,” the Ministry said.

World.title: Belize City man fined $55 for riding bicycle up-stop on his own street
World.content:
Belize City man fined $55 for riding bicycle up-stop on his own street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 26-year-old Belize City man found himself in trouble with the law after police caught him riding his bicycle against the flow of traffic on the very street where he lives.

Jermaine Lewis, a resident of King Street, was detained on Saturday, October 10, 2026, after police observed him riding his bicycle in the wrong direction along the one-way street.

Lewis was escorted to the nearby Precinct 1 Police Station, also located on King Street, where he was charged with causing a bicycle to proceed up a one-way street.

He appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, October 13, and pleaded guilty to the traffic offence.

The Magistrate imposed a fine of $50 plus $5 court costs, giving Lewis until November 30, 2026, to pay or face one week in prison.

Riding a bicycle against the designated flow of traffic is an offence under Belize’s traffic laws, and similar violations have resulted in fines and, in some cases, imprisonment for unpaid penalties.

World.title: International News: Strong El Niño raises global concerns over wildfires, food security and power shortages
World.content:
International News: Strong El Niño raises global concerns over wildfires, food security and power shortages

By Zoila Palma: An exceptionally strong El Niño weather cycle is contributing to drought, wildfires, power shortages and growing food security concerns in several parts of the world, with scientists warning that its effects could intensify as the phenomenon approaches its expected peak in December.

In Indonesia, prolonged dry conditions have contributed to fires in forests and plantations in Borneo and South Sumatra, triggering a regional haze crisis that has affected neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.

Authorities and conservation groups have rescued dozens of orangutans from the fires. Meanwhile, Brazil’s Amazon region has also experienced widespread fires, with Amazonas state recording nearly four times as many fire hotspots in September as in the same month last year.

In Myanmar, authorities have warned of possible electricity outages as unusually high temperatures increase power demand, while the Philippines is preparing for higher energy consumption and potential declines in hydropower production. The impacts are also raising concerns about food security, with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva expressing concern about the global consequences and saying the IMF is preparing to support countries that may struggle to cope.

The World Meteorological Organization has warned that El Niño is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the world and alter rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of droughts and floods.

World.title: Wrong And Strong: ‘Dads’, 61, fined $110 for riding bicycle up-stop and upstarting police
World.content:
Wrong And Strong: ‘Dads’, 61, fined $110 for riding bicycle up-stop and upstarting police

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 61-year-old Belize City man who was caught riding his bicycle against traffic on a one-way street ended up facing two charges after allegedly refusing to cooperate with a police officer.

Jose Augustine August appeared unrepresented before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 14, where he pleaded guilty to causing a bicycle to proceed against the designated direction of a one-way street and obstructing a police officer.

According to police, the incident occurred on Sunday, October 11, on Cemetery Road, where August was intercepted for riding his bicycle in the wrong direction. He subsequently obstructed a female corporal while she was executing her duties.

August admitted both offences and did not dispute the prosecution’s allegations. When given an opportunity to offer mitigating circumstances, he remained silent.

The Magistrate imposed a fine of $50 for each offence, along with $5 court costs on each charge, bringing his total penalty to $110.

August was given until November 30, 2026, to pay the fines or face one week in prison for each offence.

World.title: DOMESTIC DISPUTE TURNS FATAL
World.content:
Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey who reportedly committed suicide after stabbing his wife who was taken hospital where she is said to be battling for life.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — The usually quiet community of New Market Oval in Savanna- la-Mar has been left in shock following a violent family dispute that left a nurse battling for life in hospital and her husband dead.

The husband, Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey, was from a neighbouring community. Police report that the couple had been involved in a dispute at their home when the woman was allegedly stabbed by Anderson.

Following the attack, Anderson used a ratchet knife to inflict stab wounds to his abdomen about 10:30 am Thursday.

He was rushed to hospital where he was pronounced dead. The Jamaica Observer was told that the couple, who had been together for more than a decade, has three young children.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the children witnessed the incident. When the Observer visited the community, police were processing the scene, while residents shied away from speaking publicly about the matter.

President of the Cooke Street Benevolent Society Bishop O’Neil Russell said he spoke with Anderson just a few days ago and that the incident came as a complete shock as the family was known to be quiet.

“We had a conversation because, you know, there were some things that the benevolent society was supposed to do for him.

We are always in constant dialogue, but he had not shown any sign of depression. It is so shocking. It comes as a shock to see really what took place,” stated Russell.

Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division), who visited the scene, expressed sadness over the tragedy.

“It’s not anything to rejoice over. We all have issues, and we all have problems. We all go through things,” stated Chang.

She noted that the community, which was devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October, is already under stress and attempting to rebuild.

“We understand the constraints, but you know, we have to deal with our problems better than this, instead of taking our own lives or taking the lives of others,” stated Chang, who joined Russell in calling on people having problems to seek help.

Domestic violence, it can affect anyone regardless of our income, education, or social status. It stretches across all socio-economic backgrounds. We just have to understand that it is right in our midst and we should not be ashamed of it.

We should seek help. And I implore the persons in the Savanna-la-Mar Division, or anywhere for that matter in Jamaica, to seek help because I’m sure there are telltale signs even before it occurs,” Chang said.

She also emphasised the need for community sensitisation to stop judging victims and instead offer support, “because we all deserve to be safe in our own homes”.

World.title: Protecting Palisadoes
World.content:
An overhead shot of the Palisadoes Peninsula.

SPURRED into action by the warning from Hurricane Melissa which lashed sections of the island last year, the Cabinet has approved a US$56-million ($8.9 billion) coastal protection system for Palisadoes main road in Kingston which leads to Norman Manley International Airport and Port Royal.

The Category 5 storm, which hit Jamaica on October 28, 2025, reached wind speed of up to 190 miles per hour and devastated sections of the island’s southand north-western coasts, leaving several communities inaccessible.

With the pain from Melissa still fresh in Jamaicans’ minds, Minister of Energy, Telecommunications and Transport Daryl Vaz on Wednesday told a post-Cabinet media briefing that the Government is moving to provide even more protection for Palisadoes, the narrow approximately 14.2-kilometre strip of land that serves as a protective barrier for Kingston Harbour.

“The Government is advancing efforts to strengthen coastal protection along the Palisadoes Peninsula and Port Royal, safeguarding the Norman Manley International Airport, the main road that links from Harbour View to Port Royal, and surrounding communities against coastal erosion and storm surges,” Vaz said.

“The initiative represents a coordinated effort to protect critical transportation infrastructure, preserve access to Port Royal, and strengthen Jamaica’s resilience to coastal hazards.

So this is a far-reaching project that is going to once and for all protect the airport and access all the way to Port Royal,” added Vaz.

He underscored that over the last few years the Government has made efforts to protect the strip, which included approximately 4,500 metres of revetment work.

“We started back in 2007 when we did all of those boulders on the stretch.

As a result of Melissa and realising that, had Melissa come closer to Kingston, the access to the airport and, of course all the way to Port Royal, would be non-existent…

and seeing the work that has been done and what needs to be done, the Government has completed a comprehensive shoreline protection project [study] covering approximately 14.2 kilometres,” added Vaz.

He explained that proposed works will include strengthening revetments, rehabilitating dunes and mangroves, revegetation, and 12.1 kilometres of dunes [while] improving vulnerable road sections and installing coastal monitoring systems.

Underscoring that the country’s airports must also be built with resilience, Vaz noted that this project will be undertaken by the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authorities (NaRRA) under its work programme, with funding expected from its designated project pool.

He said with the project being under NaRRA, the Government will ensure that the procurement process is fast-tracked, which will result in it being completed in a timely manner.

“I just want to impress again, with all the noise that is being said about NaRRA, here is a project out of my ministry which has been approved by Cabinet as a NaRRA project.

Just to indicate that the noise is not always what you must listen to; you must watch the sale.

Here is a good sale.

Money that is going to be well spent [so] that if we have another catastrophe, God forbid, and it comes closer to Kingston, we will be able to respond how we responded to Melissa to get all the flights in with relief within hours,” Vaz told the media briefing.

The revetment work on Palisadoes came after Hurricane Ivan passed close to Jamaica’s south coast on September 10, 2024, leaving behind a trail of destruction not seen in the island since the passage of Hurricane Gilbert in 1988.

Ivan generated storm surge that caused the sea level to rise pushing mountains of sand and stones on the Palisadoes, leaving the vital roadway impassable.

The sand had also formed what was later referred to as the Palisadoes New Beach, essentially strips of land on the Kingston Harbour side up to 50 metres wide.

In 2007, sea water from storm surges associated with Hurricane Felix, which passed south of the island on September 3, flooded a section of the Palisadoes, making it impassable for several hours.

World.title: Insurers set to gain investment flexibility
World.content:
WILLIAMS... announced during the 2026/27 Budget Debate that the Government intended to simplify Regulation 47 to make it easier for life insurance companies to invest in corporate debt

Insurance companies could gain access to a wider range of investment opportunities under proposed changes to rules governing the sector, with the Senate’s Regulations Committee raising no objections to a measure that would remove a requirement for four conditions to be met simultaneously before certain investments qualify.

Deputy executive director of supervision at the Financial Services Commission (FSC) Nicolette Jenez told the committee on Thursday, during a virtual sitting, that the amendment to Regulation 47 of the Insurance Regulations is intended to widen insurers’ investment choices, which she said have been restricted by the existing rules.

Under the proposed change, insurers would be able to invest in certain obligations issued by solvent institutions if they satisfy any one of four conditions rather than having to meet all four at the same time.

The criteria include investments secured by adequate collateral and meeting prescribed fixed-interest requirements; investments rated as investment grade by an agency recognised by the FSC; obligations meeting prescribed earnings-coverage requirements; or obligations listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange or another stock exchange recognised by the commission.

Jenez said the existing requirements, introduced through amendments in 2022, had limited insurers’ ability to diversify their portfolios, invest in corporate debt, and support infrastructure financing.

“While intended as prudential safeguards, this cumulative application of requirements has significantly restricted the range of investments available to insurers, limiting diversification opportunities, asset liability matching, participation in corporate debt markets, and infrastructure financing,” she said.

Asset-liability matching refers to ensuring that an insurer’s investments can provide the money needed to meet future claims and other financial obligations.

The FSC expects the amendment to broaden investment opportunities, support the development of Jamaica’s capital markets and make it easier for insurers to direct funds towards productive sectors of the economy.

The proposed change also forms part of the commission’s regulatory modernisation programme and its efforts to align Jamaica’s insurance supervisory framework with international standards.

Jenez stressed that the reform would not weaken the FSC’s oversight of the industry.

“What this amendment will not do is to reduce the FSC supervisory authority or existing prudential safeguards,” she said.

She pointed to other provisions in the Insurance Regulations, including 72(B), 72(G), 72(J), and 72(K), which set out requirements relating to insurers’ investment management and the handling of risk.

The amendment follows concerns that the existing rules have made it difficult for insurers to invest in some otherwise eligible corporate obligations because those investments must satisfy several conditions at once.

Finance Minister Fayval Williams announced in March, during the 2026/27 Budget Debate, that the Government intended to simplify Regulation 47 to make it easier for life insurance companies to invest in corporate debt.

The Government has argued that the existing requirements restrict investment choices and limit the development of the domestic corporate debt market.

After 50 years on the market, the delicious, creamy drink that ‘boosts you up’ is a household name in Jamaica.

World.title: Prison officials deny reported fight between P Diddy and Dudus
World.content:
American rapper P Diddy and Jamaican drug lord Christopher 'Dudus' Coke a

Prison officials are reportedly denying a reported physical altercation between American music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs and convicted Jamaican drug lord Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke, which resulted in the rapper being rushed to hospital on Wednesday.

A TMZ report on Wednesday said the confrontation reportedly erupted after Combs allegedly caused trouble that resulted in disciplinary action against fellow inmates. The Bad Boy for Life singer reportedly sustained a head injury and was subsequently transported to an outside medical facility for treatment.

But the Federal Bureau of Prisons is denying that the fight took place.

“While, for privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any individual in our custody, we can tell you that the story you are referring to is false and did not happen. Sean Combs is in the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons and is incarcerated at the Federal Correctional Institution Fort Dix. Beyond this, we have no additional information to provide,” a spokesman for the Federal Bureau of Prisons was quoted as saying in a statement to The Daily Mail.

Combs was sentenced last year to just over four years in federal prison after being convicted on prostitution-related charges involving two of his former girlfriends.
