World.title: JC appeals ISSA sanctions over Jamone Lyle, says procedure was unfair
World.content:
Jamaica College forward Jamone Lyle. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica College (JC) has appealed sanctions imposed by the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) over the eligibility of footballer Jamone Lyle, with the school’s Board of Management Chairman Lance Hylton describing the penalties as “unsupportable, extreme and excessive”.

In an update to the school community, seen by Observer Online on Thursday, Hylton said JC lodged its appeal within 24 hours of the disciplinary hearing on October 13 and is awaiting the outcome ahead of Friday’s Walker Cup final.

The sanctions followed a ruling that JC fielded an ineligible player after Lyle was found to have a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

JC was subsequently removed from the Walker Cup, banned from next year’s competition and ordered to forfeit its Manning Cup second-round match against St Catherine, which it had won 3-2. The result was reversed to a 3-0 victory for St Catherine.

READ: JC booted from Walker Cup for fielding ineligible player Jamone Lyle

The decision also paved the way for Kingston College (KC) to face Mona High in Friday’s Walker Cup final, after Mona lost to JC in the semi-final on penalties.

Hylton said the school received a letter from ISSA on October 12 informing Principal Wayne Robinson that a complaint had been made concerning Lyle’s eligibility. The hearing was scheduled for the following day at 2:00 pm.

According to Hylton, the letter provided no prior notification of the complaint and did not identify the complainant or provide further particulars of the charge.

He said the school’s leadership, football management and coaching staff immediately mobilised to prepare written submissions for the hearing, with assistance from the Jamaica College Public Relations Committee.

Hylton added that ISSA’s rules did not permit the school to have a lawyer or anyone other than the coach or his replacement to accompany the principal to provide representation or support.

“ISSA’s harsh ruling followed with blinding speed…We consider the sanctions unsupportable, extreme and excessive,” he said.

Hylton said the school intends to address aspects of the hearing as part of its appeal, although he did not disclose the details of its submissions.

JC is challenging both the application of ISSA’s rules and whether Lyle’s purported contract with Waterhouse constitutes a valid and enforceable agreement.

Hylton said the school’s interpretation of the relevant rule is that it prohibits players from being under contract with clubs, whether through professional agreements or other contractual arrangements. However, he argued that the rules have not been consistently enforced over the years, pointing to what he described as widespread contractual arrangements involving schoolboy footballers.

He also said JC does not concede that a valid contract exists in Lyle’s case and intends to pursue that argument on appeal.

“We regard the treatment of JC as unfair,” the board chairman said. “In our view, the treatment of both the school and the player, who appears to have entered into the purported contract without independent representation, is particularly harsh when many well-known contractual arrangements have attracted no sanctions.”

He said JC had lodged complaints concerning other contractual arrangements.

A central part of the school’s position is that it was never informed by Waterhouse that Lyle had signed a professional contract or that the club was restricting him from playing for JC.

The dispute follows a disciplinary letter from Waterhouse dated October 9, in which the club said it had fined Lyle $60,000 for unauthorised participation in a Manning Cup match on October 7. Waterhouse alleged that Lyle ignored instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and General Secretary Richard McCallum not to play for JC, in breach of his professional contract and the club’s rules.

Hylton said JC was particularly concerned that a professional club would have a minor sign an agreement purporting to prevent him from continuing to play for his school.

Lyle, who turned 17 in July, has represented JC since he was 12 and was at a significant stage of his schoolboy football career, Hylton said.

The chairman added that the school had seen no indication that Lyle received independent legal representation during the process. He also said information available to JC suggested that the player did not have a parent or guardian in Jamaica supporting him through the process, including a disciplinary hearing with Waterhouse.

Hylton stressed that the school had received no written communication informing it of the purported restriction or instructing it to stop the player from participating.

He further questioned whether the restriction could be enforced against a minor, citing legal precedents concerning contracts entered into by minors, including a case involving former England footballer Wayne Rooney.

JC intends to pursue that issue as part of its appeal.

Hylton has called on Waterhouse president Donovan White to withdraw and retract a statement that the school had been informed about Lyle’s contractual status. He said the principal was adamant that he had received no telephone call or other communication from White on the matter.

Hylton also called on the Waterhouse president to identify whom he claimed to have informed, when the communication took place and how it was delivered.

According to Hylton, the school has received no response to that request.

The chairman also addressed questions from stakeholders about why the school had not sought an injunction to challenge ISSA’s ruling.

He said the disciplinary letter referred to ISSA’s rule against members taking the association to court, adding that the school had previously been warned that seeking an injunction could result in a ban from all sporting activities under ISSA’s jurisdiction.

Hylton described the restriction as constitutionally objectionable and cited the cases of Butler v KSAFA and Royale Lakes Football Club Limited v St Catherine Football Association in support of the school’s position on access to the courts.

Quoting from Chief Justice Bryan Sykes’ judgment in Butler v KSAFA, Hylton argued that membership of an association should not require individuals to surrender their fundamental right to seek judicial redress.

He said, however, that the school faces a difficult decision because court action could trigger an immediate ban while proceedings continue, potentially affecting students across all its sporting programmes.

“For now, we have decided that it is not a risk worth taking at this stage,” Hylton said in the update, while making clear that court action remains an option.

Hylton said the immediate priority is the appeal lodged within 24 hours of the October 13 hearing, with the school awaiting a decision ahead of Friday’s final.

The chairman maintained that JC had been treated unfairly and expressed regret that the controversy had overshadowed the school’s football achievements.

He thanked members of the school community for their research, assistance and support, while urging stakeholders to continue submitting questions and suggestions.

World.title: Guilty by report?
World.content:
CHUCK... questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck has questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s (IC’s) practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption, even when those matters do not result in findings of wrongdoing.

Speaking at Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Integrity Commission Oversight Committee, Chuck argued that reporting such figures could create an impression of widespread corruption even when investigations might not lead to charges.

“You must say how many investigations you have started and so on, but when you start, if you see in your report that you’re investigating permanent secretaries, you have… 18 or so permanent secretaries, even if you have three where you’re investigating, all of them come under scrutiny, and so when you say you’re investigating six, nine parliamentarians, every single one of us come under scrutiny,” he expressed.

The minister questioned whether the commission’s reporting approach was helping or hurting Jamaica’s efforts to fight corruption, arguing that the public needed to see clear results from investigations, rather than repeated references to matters still being examined.

He also questioned whether the country was getting value for money from the anti-corruption body, given the resources spent on its work and the need to demonstrate progress in tackling corruption.

“Because all I’m really saying is, yes, if there is corruption, expose it, find it, but… far too many of your reports are actually saying you are investigating, and at the end of the day nothing comes of it, or you don’t hear about it, and I am concerned, because when people speak about corruption, they should at least be able to say we have investigated these, we have charged so many for failing to report,” Chuck said.

However, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the suggestion that the commission should be blamed for the effects of its reporting, arguing that public accountability required it to explain the work it was doing and the progress of its investigations.

Robinson said the commission had to report on the nature of matters referred to it, while the public should also question why so many matters were being brought to its attention.

“As far as I know, you get to an investigation, having gone through a process, and you have met a particular threshold to determine that somebody

should be investigated. Part of your accountability mandate must be to report where you are in a process, which means whether it is public officials, parliamentarians, you must indicate of the number, how many have reached so-and-so, so I don’t share the view that the issue is with the Integrity Commission. If there are a lot of people under investigation, then the issue must be why are there so many people under investigation?” Robinson questioned.

The debate prompted director of investigation at the Integrity Commission Kevon Stephenson to explain the distinction between matters referred to the commission and cases that proceed to a formal investigation.

Stephenson said not every complaint or referral led to an investigation, as each matter had to be assessed before a decision was made. He told the committee that only a small fraction of matters referred to the commission proceeded to investigation.

“I think the public could appreciate that when matters are reported to the commission as under [Section] One of the Second Schedule, there is no guarantee that those complaints will be investigated, because an assessment has to be done on each of those complaints for a decision to be made under Section 47 of the legislation as to whether an investigation will be conducted,” Stephenson said.

He added that investigations could also be discontinued if the evidence did not provide a sufficient basis to continue. In those circumstances, the director of investigation was required to issue findings to the commission, but those findings were not made public.

Stephenson said reports reached Parliament when a completed investigation found a breach of a code, policy or law. He also explained that the annual report’s description of matters referred to the commission should not be interpreted as a list of cases actively under investigation.

Stephenson suggested that if Parliament is dissatisfied with what the law required the commission to include in its annual report, any change in policy would need to be reflected in legislation.

In the meantime, committee Chairman Pearnel Charles Jr said the concerns about reputational damage had to be considered without restricting the commission’s work.

“The commission must fearlessly carry out its work. But fear perhaps can be spelled in two ways, F-E-A-R and F-A-I-R. So as you fearlessly carry it out, it must be fair to the persons who you may have thoughts of, but not established evidence about,” Charles Jr said.

Furthermore, director of information and complaints at the commission Joeth Jones also criticised the media for what she described as a failure to give sufficient attention to positive compliance findings in the commission’s reports.

Jones said parliamentarians had performed relatively well in meeting their statutory obligations, but argued that this aspect of the commission’s work was not receiving adequate coverage.

“The media does not pick up that,” Jones told the committee, referring to the group’s compliance performance.

World.title: Secret location
World.content:
CHANG... we handed them over to The International Organisation for Migration and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE location of the first batch of 22 third-country nationals (TCNs) that arrived in the island on Monday will remain concealed says National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang.

Responding to questions posed by journalists at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, Chang maintained that though he is aware of where the TCNs are being housed, it’s not his “privilege” to announce where they are.

“I cannot give you their housing. We handed them over to International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay. The officers were in Jamaica and they looked at a number of hotels; they now have the responsibility of where they are to stay. In fact, they can move them at anytime,” said Chang.

The group, which arrived under an agreement signed between the Jamaican and United States (US) governments in June this year, comprises of 15 males and seven females, representing seven nationalities.

According to the Government, under the agreement, up to 25 asylum seekers who have unresolved migration cases in the US will temporarily transit through Jamaica en route to their home countries every two weeks.

But Chang on Tuesday shared that he is unaware of when the next batch of TCNs will arrive.

“I cannot tell you when others will arrive. We have a 14-day gap. As I’ve indicated, we can get another trip after 14 days, but there’s no guarantee. It’s not like these are designated numbers as we have with the involuntary returned migrants that we receive — our own citizens. Every two weeks, we know we get a batch, a flight, anywhere from 50 to 75 individuals. The TCNs depend on the number which might penetrate the barrier getting into the United States, as well as where they are from and what the State Department will decide or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will decide where they’re sending them and to which country,” he said.

According to Chang, no limitations will be placed on the TCNs during their stay in the country.

“They are individuals from different cultures, and what they do is up to them. They are here as visitors and they are working closely with the IOM in terms of conveying relevant information. The IOM will extract the information they require to prepare them for transit to their home country. They are free to do as they wish, like any visitor to Jamaica.

“They are individuals, who just like you in this room are regular working people who have sought to migrate, but done so illegally to the United States. The ones we accept, there are no criminals in there. They’re just families looking for a better life and we are accommodating their transition back home,” Chang reiterated.

Responding to concerns about the number of people who may want to seek asylum, Chang told journalists that the issue is not one of the Government but that of the institution which deals with the applications.

“The commissioner that deals with asylum or refugee status is a public body. It’s like a court. The documents are available. And I’m not saying we’ll not say how many…It’s their right to do so. And if they do so, it will be established. The asylum committee will sit, and the public will have access to it,” he said adding that the process can be lengthy, but the Government will notify the public as the numbers are available.

“They may ask to stay without going to asylum. It’s their freedom to do so. They are here as visitors, and if they have a skill set that is in high demand, they may. Doesn’t mean we have to accept it, but they can apply for that as well as apply for refugee status. They have a number of options,” he said.

According to Chang, their options will be discussed with them by the IOM.

“The IOM will interrogate and not only make arrangements for their movement, if they seek other alternative arrangements, then the IOM will inform us and we take it from there. But that is an important part of the nature of the IOM. As indicated, the United Nations body, they do this kind of activity globally as a trusted organisation in humanitarian relief activity. And, therefore, we allow them to proceed without any interference,” he said.

World.title: EU summit runs out of gas
World.content:
It’s been a packed agenda at the European Council summit, with little sign of progress on key issues. EU leaders continued to argue over the bloc’s long-term budget, with energy supply and security taking up much of the discussion … including questions over strategic gas reserves and the future of the Emissions Trading System.

The war in Ukraine looms large over the summit. Earlier this week, President Trump alarmed European leaders and horrified Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy by announcing a deal to release Russian diesel onto the U.S. market, apparently in an attempt to lower fuel costs for American consumers.

Host Sarah Wheaton unpacks developments late into the night with colleagues who have been reporting on the summit. She’s joined by Chief EU Correspondent Zoya Sheftalovich, Chief Political Correspondent in Europe and the U.K. Tim Ross and Gregorio Sorgi, financial services reporter.

World.title: Are the Brexit wars back?
World.content:
Customs union, single market, rejoin, second referendum. It’s all feeling a little Ground Hog day in Westminster after Andy Burnham reopened the Europe question at Labour Party conference.

Hosts Sascha O’Sullivan and Pat Baker find out how the row over Europe will play out in the next few years, with Reform MP Danny Kruger and Labour MP Stella Creasy.

Sascha speaks to Cecilia Malmström, former EU Trade Commissioner during the Brexit negotiations, who says any new deal with the EU would need to be “Nigel Farage-proofed” in case Reform wound up in Downing Street.

UK-EU reporter Jon Stone explains what Burnham is hoping to gain from the EU summit next month, and whether Britain’s friends in Brussels care about Westminster looking again at Britain’s relationship with the trading bloc.

World.title: Britain’s Lib Dems are having a mini-meltdown. Here’s what’s going on.
World.content:
The botched coup comes as the Liberal Democrats try to answer a more existential question: what are they actually for and how do they make an impact in Britain’s fragmented political landscape?

POLITICO’s Poll of Polls shows the Lib Dems coasting along. After getting 12.2% in the 2024 general election — and bagging a record 72 members of parliament as a result — the party has slipped down, polling between 9% and 11% since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

POLITICO explains why Lib Dems are now openly discussing Davey’s future; how much danger he is in; and exactly how the man known for a cheery demeanor and eye-catching paddle-board stunts could be capsized.

1) Why is Davey’s future in the headlines?

The surprise resignation of the Lib Dems’ Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard a week ago triggered the latest round of soul-searching about the leader’s future — but the grumbling goes back a bit further.

Maynard’s resignation followed costly tax-cutting pledges from Davey at the party’s conference in September and came hot on the heels of sharp responses — including from 2024-intake Lib Dem MPs Tom Gordon and Vikki Slade — to the way Davey defended an existing guarantee on state pensions. Some MPs believe the party isn’t adequately representing younger voters by opposing changes to the so-called triple lock, now targeted for reform by Burnham.

The immediate threat looks to have receded. Maynard’s resignation has gone down badly among a host of colleagues.

World.title: Marine Le Pen’s EU dream is a nightmare for Brussels
World.content:
Other buildings in the EU Quarter of Brussels (or, as it’s now known, the 21st arrondissement) have not been so lucky. Most have been razed to the ground. Some have been occupied by disgruntled former EU staff, who are refusing to leave and have set up a working group to discuss a future roadmap that will feed into a discussion on how to bring back a European Union that Le Pen has largely destroyed.

Largely, but not completely. There is still an official EU office; the corner table in the branch of sandwich shop Exki near the Schuman roundabout (ironically, Le Pen used some of the money saved from dismantling the EU to finish the roundabout as planned). It is staffed 24/7 by Maroš Šefčovič, and he has a plentiful supply of leaflets.

Le Pen had more in store for the EU after her crushing 2027 presidential election win over Kylian Mbappé (who won a primary against Raphaël Glucksmann to be the unity centrist candidate, which was decided by who could do the most keepie-uppies).

The phrases “non-paper,” “stakeholder” and “trilogue” have been consigned to la poubelle de l’histoire. The European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee were closed down within weeks of Le Pen taking office, which shocked millions of Europeans who had no idea they ever existed. The European Parliament building is still there but is now occupied by a strange breed of zombie-like creatures wandering aimlessly through the corridors in search of something to do. No one can tell the difference.

Von der Leyen was, as Le Pen promised would happen, sent back to Germany where — in a somewhat unexpected move — she has become chancellor, succeeding Angela Merkel, who herself came out of retirement and orchestrated a coup to bring down current Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Anyway, back to 2026 and an EU reeling from a Le Pen speech in which she pledged to turn the Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries, and scrap some institutions altogether.

World.title: In Europe, the Trump shock factor is wearing off
World.content:
According to the Financial Times, EU officials plan to urge Zelenskyy to tone down his increasingly sharp remarks about Trump, fearing they are only inflaming the situation. Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, is positioning himself as someone who can “lay the ground” for a reconciliation, he explained to the House of Commons Wednesday.

Nonetheless, the calmer reaction to Trump’s maneuvers stands out, acknowledges Daniel Fried, a former senior U.S. diplomat who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian Affairs under U.S. President George W. Bush.

“The Europeans seem to have taken Trump’s measure,” Fried told POLITICO. “They want to avoid the worst. They want to mitigate the damage over the next two years while Trump is in office. They do work with people in the Trump administration with whom they can work. And there are such people.”

Speaking from Warsaw, fresh from attending a recent security conference in the Polish capital, he said the Europeans understand now that much of what Trump does is performative and has a short life span — like the Russian diesel deal, which has a shelf life of two or three days, he said. “I’m not sure it’s going anywhere as it is utterly impractical and legally questionable, and it isn’t clear the Russians actually can supply the diesel,” he said. In other words, why get worked up about it?

Daniel Fried, Atlantic Council speaks at The 2017 Concordia Annual Summit at Grand Hyatt New York on September 19, 2017 in New York City. | Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Concordia Summit

Fried said in his conversations with European leaders and officials, he has detected increasing exasperation with the overall inconsistency of the American position: “Trump wants Europe to do more militarily, but it must buy American,” he said. “But we can’t sell to the Europeans because of our needs, so they will have to wait even though they can’t build it themselves. Nonetheless, they have to carry the load in Ukraine without us. That’s utterly inconsistent, and they are exasperated by it.”

And they’re just tired of having Trump jerk them around, Fried added. “One thing they are trying to avoid is having Trump snap his fingers and they come flying. Because then it looks like they are at Trump’s beck and call and are his supplicants, and they don’t want to do that. Besides, if they fly out and talk him into something, how long will what he agreed to last?”

Of course, the Europeans can also console themselves with the high chance of Trump reversing himself. “There is a pattern,” said Kuleba. “He launches a cavalry attack … and then retreats. That’s what we saw in February last year. That’s what we saw in November 2025. And that’s what we will see this time too.”

World.title: Budget showdown slips to November as Costa pushes for quick deal
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron gave a big boost to the European Council president’s plan to end the negotiations by the end of the year.

BRUSSELS — EU leaders will go back to the drawing board in November as they race to finalize a deal on the bloc's next seven-year budget by the end of the year.

During the first day of a two-day summit in Brussels on Thursday, European Council President António Costa announced he was convening an additional gathering on Nov. 26 in a bid to overcome disagreements and lay the ground for a final deal in December. To bring the sides closer to an agreement, he will present new budget figures before the meeting, according to an EU official, who was granted anonymity to discuss the confidential planning.

Costa is pressing leaders to finalize negotiations by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks.

World.title: Trump and Putin’s ‘terrible’ alliance threatens to strain EU’s resolve on Ukraine
World.content:
A U.S. proposal to unfreeze some of the Russian assets and transfer them to a U.S.-controlled entity so Washington could use them as leverage in peace talks with Moscow also attracted strong criticism.

Merz told reporters that the assets had been frozen in Europe and “should remain frozen in Europe … That is our business, and we will decide on it.”

‘Try again’

Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told POLITICO as the summit began: “The best solution would be that we will have a solution on how to use frozen assets … We have to try again.”

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo speaks to journalists at the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Sept. 14, 2026. | Jouni Porsanger/AFP via Getty Images

Sweden is also backing the move to re-examine options on using the assets to help Ukraine’s future funding needs. “Doing nothing is not an option,” Swedish EU Affairs Minister Jessica Rosencrantz told POLITICO. “The Commission is looking into different financial options, and we need to get them on the table quite soon,” she said.



Leaders at this week’s summit should “be really honest that Ukraine needs increased financing” and that the EU “must really step up,” she added.

Zelenskyy met Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the main opponent to a deal on assets, for talks on Thursday and thanked him for his country’s support so far.

Speaking to reporters after the first day of the summit, De Wever said the assets should be looked at as part of a future peace agreement. “Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: Yes there are,” he said. “Are they in this building? They are. Are there outside this building? Yes there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don’t.”

World.title: Costa angers EU leaders as splits mar summit
World.content:
The showdown over the Emissions Trading System — both the current one, and the second iteration which is already legislated and will put a carbon price on heating and transport from 2028 — became so bogged down it forced Costa to cancel the summit’s planned press conference and delay further talks until after dinner, because they had become a “mess,” three EU diplomats told POLITICO.

With German Chancellor Friedrich Merz incensed by what Berlin saw as his Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni’s intransigence, fiery negotiations pitted a coalition made up of Germany, Spain, France, Portugal, the Nordics and the Netherlands against a stubborn bloc of Italy with Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Poland (known as the Visegrád Four). Rome and the V4 group wanted the EU to postpone ETS2 because of the burden it would place on energy bills, according to five diplomats.

Leaders were fuming at Costa for allowing talks to go off the rails, two EU diplomats from different member countries said. While the pre-summit conclusions didn’t point to any rethink of ETS2, the countries tried to unpick the legislation in the summit room, leaving Costa flustered, one of them said.



Costa “wants to have conclusions ready from [pre-summit meetings of ambassadors] and not to open them during EUCO,” the diplomat said. “He is not a fan of drafting on the spot.”



Another said there was “huge frustration,” calling the tug-of-war over the wording of the energy policy “insane chaos.”

“They just went on with Italian drafts and disregarded texts that were handed in before by others, seemingly not understanding the political nuances of the whole ETS discussion,” they added.

Another accused Costa of “losing control of the room,” saying he had failed to keep track of proposed amendments and present them to EU leaders in time for the discussions. As a result, leaders were left debating without them, contributing to negotiations going on past midnight.

One diplomat and one EU official separately compared Costa with his immediate predecessors, Charles Michel ― who governments frequently criticized for a lack of dealmaking know-how ― and Donald Tusk, who enjoyed broad support throughout his term in office.

World.title: Extreme weather is decimating Europe’s crops. These farmers have a solution
World.content:
Almonds decimated by frost, tomatoes disrupted by heat, and Halloween pumpkins shrunk by drought: it’s been a punishing year for agriculture in Europe.

 

The hot, dry summer – which would have been “virtually impossible" if it weren’t for climate change – reduced the continent’s forecast grain harvest by an estimated 16.7 million tonnes, costing farmers more than €3 billion, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).

“After this summer, many European farmers are on the brink,” says Josefine Herz, managing director of the European Alliance for Regenerative Agriculture (EARA).

“One year prices collapse because they grew too much; the next, drought punishes them for growing at all, and each swing hands a bigger share to the same few processors and retailers who are increasing prices on the consumer side.”

French vegetable growers’ association Légumes de France warned in July that losses in some sectors could reach 50 per cent.

Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggered by the war on Iran, have added to pressure on fuel and fertiliser supplies, while drought has restricted cargo traffic on some European waterways. Together, these supply-chain problems are adding to concerns about the cost of farming and the security of food supplies.

But could changing the way we farm pave the way for a more certain future?

Diversification of crops helps farmers weather the extremes

At Curly Creek Ranch in Spain’s Basque Country, tomatoes – one of the farm’s highest earners at €7/kg – stopped flowering in the extreme heat.

“Imagine the length of the tomato plant and the middle third has a gap without fruit. We never saw that before,” says farmer Meghan Sapp, who is also EARA’s external relations director. Flowering has since resumed, and she hopes a later-than-usual season will make up some of the shortfall.

A lack of water has also affected the farm’s Halloween pumpkins, which are smaller than usual this year, while high temperatures left corn with “early signs of burning on the leaves, which we’d never seen before”, says Meghan.

The heat also exposed weaknesses in the local water supply, including leaky infrastructure: Curly Creek Ranch repeatedly received less than its expected daily allocation, forcing authorities to deliver 50,000 litres by tanker.

But diversification has helped spread the risk.

“Many years we don’t get a single aubergine due to lack of heat and yet we plant them anyway, just in case,” Meghan explains. “This year that bet paid off… for the first time ever we had a huge crop.”

Farmer Yanniek Schoonhoven: Owner of La Junquera farm and co-founder of the Regeneration Academy. Yanniek Schoonhoven via Commonland

It’s a tactic that’s also working for farmers further south in Spain.

“Historically, our farm depended heavily on cereals,” says Yanniek Schoonhoven, who owns La Junquera farm in Murcia. “We have gradually diversified… looking for systems that are better suited to an increasingly unpredictable climate.”

Aromatic plants like rosemary, lavender, sage and oregano are particularly well adapted to dry Mediterranean conditions. They also fetch good prices: around €2,000 per hectare, with costs of about €1,000, according to Yanniek. Pistachios, which also cope well in a dry climate, bring in even more: around €2,350 per hectare with similar costs.

But frost during a critical period wiped out La Junquera’s almonds, a “very significant loss” of around €700–€1,050 per hectare.

The challenges of branching out from commodity crops

Despite the attractive margins on certain drought-resilient crops, it’s not a simple switch.

While aromatics can be distilled into essential oils, a higher-value product than grain, “these markets require processing, investment and reliable buyers”, explains Yanniek.

Cereals and oilseeds, by contrast, are commodity crops: standardised products sold in bulk, with prices largely dictated by wider markets. Farmers may have established buyers for their harvests, but have little leverage to charge more for climate resilience. At La Junquera, wheat brings in around €600 per hectare against roughly €500 in costs, according to Yanniek.

Subsidies tend to favour these crops, though. The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) pays basic income support by hectares farmed, not by crop type or output, so more funding naturally flows to large-scale farms which often grow commodities. The EU also steps in if market prices for commodity crops fall below a certain threshold.

Yet commodities are not immune to extreme weather. On Gut Weimarschmieden, a 700-hectare organic conservation agriculture farm in Fladungen, Germany, summer barley and winter wheat struggled in the heat, says manager Maximillian Krimm, while the cornfields produced about 17 tonnes instead of the usual 25 to 30.

Spelt and canola fared better. Maximillian is also considering emmer, an old wheat variety whose yields are 20 to 30 per cent lower than conventional wheat, for only a slightly higher price. “In general we don’t grow much that’s lower value because the prices don’t justify it,” he says.

EARA farmer Maximillian Krimm manages Gut Weimarschmieden in Fladungen, Germany, producing rapeseed and flax oils alongside arable crops and an agritourism operation. Maximillian Krimm via EARA

Restoring soil health can turn things around for Europe’s farmers

Commodity farming also favours intensive methods that deplete soil and generate emissions, not least from synthetic fertiliser – and crop choice alone won’t fix that.

“A drought-tolerant crop planted into dead, compacted soil in a biodiversity dead zone will still struggle, because there’s nothing left to hold the water when it comes,” says Lily Maxwell-Lwin, head of advocacy at international non-profit Commonland.

Her team works with local communities across more than 50 countries to restore degraded landscapes using a holistic approach that blends social impact, biodiversity restoration, financial return and pride in place.

Lily Maxwell-Lwin is head of advocacy at Commonland , an international non-profit that works with local people to restore degraded landscapes using a holistic approach. Commonland

“For most arable farms in our region, years of tillage, monoculture and synthetic input use has turned the soil into hard, dry land with low soil organic carbon, limiting the soil’s ability to infiltrate and retain the rain when it does come. Instead it runs off, creating erosion,” explains Meghan.

Healthier soil can raise yields, cut the need for costly synthetic fertiliser and hold more water, easing drought and flooding alike. “We’ve watched degraded landscapes turn around in a decade: soil that crusted over starts absorbing rain again, hillsides that shed water start acting like sponges,” says Lily.

At La Junquera, ponds, swales, vegetation cover and keyline design slow runoff and increase infiltration. “For us, adapting to drought isn’t about finding more water. It’s about making much better use of every drop of rain that falls,” says Yanniek.

That is what gives resilient crops “a fighting chance”, says Lily. “If we want farmers to take the risk of switching to lower-yield, climate-resilient varieties, we have to invest in restoring the land underneath them first, not just hand them a different seed and call it done.”

What support do farmers need from governments?

The EU’s CAP subsidy scheme does reward regenerative practices like crop rotation, cover cropping and planting nitrogen-fixing crops, which produce natural fertiliser and improve soil health. But farmers still largely bear the costs and responsibility of implementing these measures alone, with little recognition for the benefits they create for food security, biodiversity and human health.

“We need policies that make it less risky for farmers to adapt,” says Yanniek, pointing to better insurance against drought and frost, and financial support during the years it takes to establish perennial crops.

Meghan wants regional policymakers to move fast and fund the move to regenerative land management, through advisory services, transition insurance and co-investment in new machinery.

EARA farmers achieve equal or better harvests with less water and fewer inputs, says Josefine, yet “neither the market nor the CAP pays for the resilience built”. She calls for “a fair market and a CAP that pays for outcomes, not just practices and hectares, so resilience stops being a cost farmers absorb alone”.

Meghan Sapp is founding farmer and external relations director at EARA, and a farmer at Curly Creek Ranch in the Basque Country in Spain. Meghan Sapp via Commonland

One of the alliance’s farmers, Gunnar Thelin of Västra Gatugård, a five-hectare holding in Vederslöv, Sweden, sketches how that could work: satellite measurements over the season would check that photosynthesis is above an agreed level for the region, and bare ground and soil temperature below agreed levels.

Meet them and you receive CAP money; miss them and you don’t. “That’s the incentive to go regen,” he says.

Not everyone is convinced. Maximillian says he’s “not a big fan of subsidies” and believes farmers must simply adapt through regenerative farming. Better prices alone, he says, won’t solve the underlying problem.

But for many, a fair market remains the missing piece. “Growing a drought-resistant crop is only half the solution,” says Yanniek. “Farmers also need a market that pays enough to make growing it worthwhile.” Without one, Josefine warns, “Europe loses hundreds of farms a day this way, the very farms holding the solutions to regenerating it.”

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 16th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: These are the world’s best destinations for ‘golden hour’, according to a meteorologist
World.content:
Even amateur photographers know that the best time to get snapping is during “golden hour” – but not all are created equal.

 

Some are far longer than an hour, others shorter; clouds can get in the way of the effect, as can rainfall; and light pollution can have an impact, too.

Luckily for us, travel company Kuoni has teamed up with meteorologist Jim Dale from British Weather Services to create a ranking for the world's best spots for golden hour.

Having analysed 165 destinations against metrics including cloud cover, light pollution, rainfall, artificial brightness, wind speed and average sunset duration, 20 places made the final list.

Greece dominated the rankings, with four places making the cut – ahead of Namibia with three, and two each for the US, Australia and Botswana.

“There’s something about that soft, warm light of golden hour that makes a destination feel truly unforgettable, whether you're watching the sun dip below the Acropolis in Lindos or over the dunes of the Namib Desert,” Marco Rocha, the product, commercial and operations director at Kuoni, said.

“What's interesting is that the best golden hour locations aren't always the most obvious ones – clear skies, low light pollution and a bit of local knowledge often matter more than a destination's reputation.”

Golden hour destinations you need to know about

Jordan’s Wadi Rum came out on top overall, with little cloud cover and almost no rain, followed by Sossusvlei in Namibia, the desert landscape with no light pollution and sunsets that last an average of 27.9 minutes.

Namibia has three locations in the top six. As well as Sossusvlei, Damaraland placed third, with Etosha National Park in sixth.

Chile’s Atacama Desert came fourth, with Kuoni noting that wildlife like flamingos, alpacas and Andean foxes make a visit here even more special, while Wahiba Sands in Oman rounded out the top five.

As for Europe, Lindos Acropolis in Rhodes narrowly made it into the top 10, with Kuoni noting that its perch 116 metres above the sea gives you uninterrupted golden hour views most evenings.

Next up was Paphos in Cyprus, coming in 16th, followed by Rhodes Town (17th), Cape Sounion in Athens (19th), and Zante’s Navagio Shipwreck Beach (20th).

World.title: Risk of electric battery fire: VW recalls thousands of cars again
World.content:
A few weeks ago it was a faulty screw; now a suspected battery defect means VW has to recall thousands of cars once again. In the worst case, there is a risk of fire.

 

Recall campaigns are already reported to be under way in the United States and the United Kingdom, and models in Germany are now also being recalled. According to the authorities, around 22,000 ID.4 electric cars are affected in the US.

VW prepares recall in Germany

With recalls already under way in the US and the UK, VW is planning and rolling out recall campaigns in Germany and other markets.

Some battery cells in Volkswagen electric cars are defective. Internal quality checks have revealed the problem, according to Handelsblatt. A Volkswagen spokesperson told the outlet that several thousand vehicles are affected.

VW cited production faults at suppliers as the cause of the faulty battery cells. The issue is limited to a specific production period.

Because of the defect, the batteries may be exposed to increased thermal stress, according to the information available. In extreme cases, a fire in these electric vehicles cannot be ruled out, VW said.

According to Handelsblatt, the VW ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID Buzz and Cupra Born models produced between 2023 and 2025 are among those affected. The company has not yet confirmed this list of models.

The recall is being prepared in close coordination with the relevant authorities, the spokesperson said. It has not yet appeared in the databases of Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).

VW sets out immediate measures

To prevent possible damage and incidents, the group is now recommending that potentially affected cars be charged only to a maximum of 80%. The manufacturer plans to recall some of the vehicles to service centres to check the batteries. Once the batteries have been inspected, the charging limit will be lifted for cars in which no fault is found.

If a defective battery is identified, the high-voltage battery module would not necessarily have to be replaced and could potentially be brought up to date with a software upgrade.

Customers whose vehicles are affected will be contacted by the company, according to the report. Owners will receive a letter informing them of the next steps.

A damaged screw led to a recall of around 2.86 million VW and Audi vehicles worldwide in September. The component could have caused the steering to fail, the KBA warned.

20% of VW deliveries are electric

VW’s electric-car business is strongest in Europe compared with the rest of the world.

The share of battery electric vehicles in Volkswagen Group’s European deliveries rose to 20% in the first three quarters of 2026, meaning one in five vehicles delivered was fully electric.

Overall, the group is grappling with falling demand worldwide, with business in China in particular slumping. In Germany, VW continues to dominate both the market for new electric car registrations and the used EV market.

World.title: Income after rent: How much is left across European cities?
World.content:
Many European countries face a housing crisis, with a shortage of homes and rising prices. Rents also continue to increase, and city centres are particularly expensive. A single salary is no longer enough to cover the rent for a family-sized flat in the heart of a major city for many European households.

 

But what if a couple both work and share the rent? Is that enough? How much money would they have left each month after paying rent? And how do European cities compare globally?

The Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute, sheds some light on the topic. It looks at two people earning a local net salary and deducts the rent on a three-bedroom apartment in the given city centre. What remains is the household’s disposable income after rent.

Among 28 European cities, the disposable income after rent ranges from €253 in Lisbon to €9,140 in Zurich.

Swiss cities lead the ranking

Zurich has the most expensive rent (€5,502) among the 28 cities. But it also has the highest net salary (€7,321). As a result, a couple in Zurich has the most money left after rent (€9,140).

In addition to Zurich, Geneva is far ahead of the rest. In Geneva, a couple has €8,783 left each month after rent. This is thanks to the second-highest net salary (€6,516).

Luxembourg is third with €5,890. It has the third-highest net salary (€4,548). Its rent is also high (€3,206), but lower than in cities such as London, Dublin and Amsterdam. This leaves couples with more money at the end of the month.

Birmingham follows with €5,238, just ahead of Copenhagen with €5,233.

Birmingham vs London: Rent makes the difference

A couple in Birmingham has €5,238 left each month after rent. In London, the figure is €3,148. That means couples in Birmingham have €2,090 more each month.

Salaries are lower in Birmingham, but rent is much cheaper. A city-centre flat costs €1,949 in Birmingham, compared with €4,362 in London.

Couples also have more than €4,000 left after rent in Oslo (€4,936), Frankfurt (€4,786), Munich (€4,575) and Amsterdam (€4,431).

Amsterdam’s rent is among the five highest (€3,542), but a high net salary (€3,986) makes up for it.

Vienna (€3,709) and Stockholm (€3,674) are very close to this level.

Berlin beats Paris thanks to lower rent

Salaries in Paris are higher than in Berlin (€3,171 compared with €2,946). Yet couples in Berlin have more left after rent (€3,554 compared with €3,336). The reason is rent. A city-centre flat costs €3,005 in Paris but €2,339 in Berlin.

Dublin has a higher net salary (€3,455) than Paris, Berlin, Vienna and Stockholm. But couples there have less left after rent than in all of these cities (€3,038). Rent in Dublin is the fourth-highest in Europe (€3,873), and it is higher than one net salary.

Southern Europe is at the bottom

Cities in southern Europe have the lowest income after rent. Lisbon and Milan are the hardest cities for couples. In Lisbon, just €253 is left after rent. The net salary there is €1,408, but the rent is €2,561.

In Milan, only €697 is left. In Madrid, a couple has €1,905 left each month. In Barcelona, they have €1,832. The figure falls to €1,265 in Rome and €1,148 in Athens. In Athens, the rent (€1,164) is slightly higher than one net salary (€1,156).

Istanbul follows Lisbon at the bottom of the European list with €353. The net salary there is €1,027, but the rent is €1,701.

Central and Eastern Europe do better than the south

Some cities in Central and Eastern Europe perform better than those in Southern Europe. In Prague, a couple has €2,054 left after rent. In Warsaw, they have €1,985, and in Budapest €1,548. All three are above Rome and Athens.

It is important to note that rent is the only cost included. Couples still need to pay for food, bills and transport.

Is one salary enough to pay the rent?

The answer is no in many cities. In 11 cities, rent is higher than one net salary. These are Athens, Barcelona, Budapest, Dublin, Istanbul, Lisbon, London, Madrid, Milan, Prague and Rome.

Lisbon has the biggest gap. The net salary is €1,408, while rent costs €2,561, which is 82% more than one salary. In Milan, a net salary is €1,940, compared with rent of €3,184.

In Prague and Budapest, rent and one net salary are almost the same.

How does Europe compare with the rest of the world?

Europe performs well in the global ranking. Zurich (€9,140) and Geneva (€8,783) top the list of 69 cities, ahead of San Francisco (€7,992). Seven of the top 10 are in Europe.

No European city is in the bottom 10. All of them are in Latin America, Asia and Africa. In six, rent costs more than two net salaries. Manila (-€882) and Bangkok (-€759) are at the bottom.

In Moscow, a couple has €313 left after rent. The net salary is €1,570, but the rent is €2,827.

Several European cities also do better than New York (€1,921).

Younger generations in Europe have lower homeownership rates than earlier generations. In 2026, house prices and rents continue to rise across Europe, outpacing inflation in many countries.

World.title: Wind Sled, Spanish invention to cross Antarctica without emissions: 'Unique in the world'
World.content:
Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is set to lead a scientific expedition that will travel around 3,400 kilometres across the interior of Antarctica over roughly 80 days, without using fossil fuels for transport. The Wind Sled Antarctica 2026-2027 project will carry instruments to conduct 16 research projects (source in Spanish) in some of the most inaccessible regions on the planet, with the aim of expanding knowledge about ice, climate change and polar ecosystems.

 

"The wind sled is, in a way, completely unique in the world," Larramendi tells 'Euronews' in an interview in Madrid's central Plaza de España. The explorer believes that the vehicle he has designed is an exceptional combination of traditional techniques and advanced technology, conceived to cover long distances without combustion engines or aerial resupply.

The expedition will leave Spain on 18 October and is scheduled to return in early February. The route will start near Russia's Novolazarevskaya base, in Queen Maud Land, and end at the French-Italian Concordia station on Dome C, after crossing the Pole of Inaccessibility and skirting the vicinity of the Pole of Cold.

Route of the Wind Sled Antarctica 2026-2027 expedition. Tierras Polares / Trineo de Viento

A wind-powered vehicle to cross Antarctica with zero emissions

The Wind Sled is a polar exploration platform that uses kites to harness the power of the wind and solar energy to power scientific equipment. Its design, inspired by Inuit culture, as Larramendi explains, is the result of around 25 years of development and testing, during which he has travelled more than 28,000 kilometres over ice on different expeditions.

"This sled combines Inuit techniques, which may look old-fashioned and a bit strange compared with modern technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but tremendously efficient," says the explorer, who sees sustainability as one of the fundamental pillars of the project.

The vehicle is made up of four modules and is 15 metres long. It can carry up to 2,100 kilos of cargo, although on this occasion it will initially transport around 250 kilos of scientific instruments.

Related Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979

The crew will have 20 kites, with surface areas ranging from five to 150 square metres, which they will deploy according to the weather conditions. In favourable winds, the sled can reach speeds of up to 80 kilometres per hour, with an average cruising speed of around 25 kilometres per hour.

The absence of fossil fuels reduces both the environmental impact and the logistical needs of the expedition. As a point of comparison, the Transantarctic Scientific Expedition of 2011-2012 covered a similar distance using tracked trucks, snowmobiles and sleds, consuming around 170,000 litres of fuel in two months.

Larramendi hopes this campaign will demonstrate the vehicle's potential as a scientific platform for future crossings. "Other systems powered by renewable energy may emerge to cross Antarctica, but none will be more sustainable or have a smaller footprint than the Wind Sled," he argues.

Spaniard Ramón Larramendi drew on Inuit culture to design his kite-powered sled. Tierras Polares / Trineo de Viento

Sixteen projects to study ice, pollutants and microbial life

The expedition will carry out 16 scientific projects selected through a call coordinated by the Spanish Polar Committee. The research, involving centres from CSIC, CIEMAT, INTA, six Spanish universities and international organisations, will provide direct measurements in areas where hardly any data exist, complementing information gathered by satellites and permanent stations.

Among the studies is a project from NASA's Ames Research Center, led by Spaniard Alfonso Dávila, which will examine whether conditions favourable to microbial life can arise inside salt rocks exposed to Antarctica's extreme cold. Sensors will measure temperature, relative humidity and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could have formed inside them despite the low temperatures and the arid environment.

Another project, called Dinglac and led by glaciologist Francisco Navarro of the Polytechnic University of Madrid, will use ground-penetrating radar to analyse the first ten metres of snow. The measurements will help to understand how snow layers accumulate and move and to improve estimates of how the Antarctic ice mass is evolving in the context of climate change.

The campaign will also investigate the presence of microplastics, persistent pollutants and possible microorganisms and viruses, as well as studying Earth's magnetism and the performance of Europe's Galileo navigation systems. Some of the experiments will use equipment linked to space exploration.

For Larramendi, the value of this work also lies in the fact that it will take place in territory that is virtually unknown from a scientific point of view. "It takes place in an area for which there are practically no data," he explains. The system makes it possible to venture into regions where the difficulties and costs of conventional operations mean research campaigns are particularly complex.

Four people isolated for 85 days: an experiment for future space missions

The expedition team will consist of four Antarctic veterans: Larramendi himself; Hilo Moreno, polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki, a researcher at the University of Maine in the United States; and Javier Selva, photographer, documentary maker and head of technical image direction. Selva already accompanied Larramendi on an Antarctic expedition between 2011 and 2012.

In addition to taking part in the fieldwork, the four explorers will themselves be the subject of study. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre from the University of Cádiz, will analyse the effects of prolonged isolation on the crew's psychological responses, sleep and social dynamics. "We are part of the research project and yes, we do feel a bit like guinea pigs, but we are happy," Larramendi jokes.

We are part of the research project and yes, we do feel a bit like guinea pigs, but we are happy Ramón Larramendi Leader of the Wind Sled Antarctica 2026-2027 expedition

The research aims to generate knowledge applicable to future long-duration space missions, in which astronauts will have to face conditions of confinement, danger and extreme distance from Earth. Antarctica is one of the most suitable environments on the planet for studying these factors and testing instruments destined for future planetary exploration.

"We ourselves are the experiment. Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent," Larramendi acknowledges. The explorer explains that there are two projects in which the members of the expedition themselves are the subject of research.

Portrait of Ramón Larramendi during one of his expeditions. Tierras Polares / Trineo de Viento

Self-sufficiency will be one of the keys to the journey. The team will carry all the supplies and equipment needed to remain for weeks without outside support, although they have an evacuation plan in place in case of a medical emergency or any other exceptional situation.

A pioneering route with an eye on future expeditions

The journey, which can be followed live on the website tierraspolares.es (source in Spanish), is the culmination of decades of work on the Wind Sled and will test its capacity to carry an unprecedented scientific payload on Larramendi's Antarctic expeditions. The four team members will set up five scientific stations along the route, with extended stops to collect samples, run experiments and take measurements.

On arrival at Concordia, the explorers will leave the continent by air, while the scientific equipment will return to Spain with French support. The sled will remain dismantled at the base, ready for a possible future journey in the opposite direction.

The aim is to repeat the expeditions so that the data gathered on different campaigns can be compared, something essential for identifying changes in the ice and the climate. "Repeated data collection is absolutely key to seeing the variations," Larramendi points out.

The journey, integrated (source in Spanish) into the 40th Antarctic Research Campaign, which marks the 40th anniversary of Spain's polar expedition, aims to consolidate a low-impact scientific exploration route in the interior of the continent. It offers an alternative that combines research in one of Earth's most extreme regions with the development of technologies that could contribute to future space missions.

World.title: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon elementary school shooting
World.content:
Three children and one teacher were shot dead at an elementary school in the northwestern US state of Oregon on Thursday, police said, adding that the assailant was a 16-year-old who was killed by an armed bystander.

 

Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary school in Bend, a city of about 100,000 people.

Mike Krantz, police chief of Bend, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun.

Dozens of emergency calls then reported that a shooter had entered the school and all law enforcement in the area were called to the scene, Krantz said.

Officers arrived at 1:02 pm local time (2202 CET) within minutes of the calls, said the police chief.

People leave a family meeting area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, 15 October, 2026 Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

"Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him," Krantz continued.

"Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead."

Officers performed emergency aid on the victims. The three children who died on the scene were aged five, eight and 11, the police chief said.

One teacher was also pronounced dead.

Krantz said one seven-year-old and one 54-year-old teacher with critical injuries were transported by medics to a local hospital.

He added that the shooter was a resident of Bend.

Krantz stressed that the investigation was in its early stages, but told a press conference it appeared "the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors."

'Unthinkable tragedy'

Between 400 and 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary, where more than 40 staff work, a police spokesperson had said earlier.

After a lockdown, Bend-La Pine School District said law enforcement was escorting students in buses to a separate location, where families could reunite with their children.

The district's superintendent, Steve Cook, tearfully called the day's events "an unthinkable tragedy."

"We are heartbroken. We are horrified. This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here," he told reporters.

Parents were anxiously waiting at the site near a church, where parent Drew Sharp told CBS News: "I have faith that he's okay and that he'll be alright."

People gather for a candlelight vigil held in Drake Park in Bend, 15 October, 2026 AP Photo

Sharp said his son was a fifth grader, the highest grade in the school, and that children were disembarking from the bus youngest to oldest.

"Which makes sense," Sharp said, but "it's just more time waiting."

Friday classes at schools across the district along with activities and athletic events were canceled, Bend-La Pine said in a statement.

The elementary school is approximately 270 kilometres southeast of the city Portland. It serves primary-age students in kindergarten through fifth grade.

'Cannot keep accepting this'

The United States, where firearms are readily available, is a frequent scene of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.

The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on 16 April 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot.

"Our hearts are with the terrified children and the families anxiously waiting to hear that their loved ones are safe," GIFFORDS, a gun safety organisation, said on X.

"We cannot keep accepting this as a fact of life."

Thursday's shooting was followed by a painfully familiar chorus of calls for action on gun control, pleas that have resulted in little meaningful change.

In the face of decades of massacres akin to Thursday's, the powerful US pro-gun lobby has given millions of dollars to primarily conservative politicians in a successful bid to keep gun laws loose.

"They're killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear," said Janelle Bynum, an Oregon congresswoman, in a statement.

"This continues to happen," she said later, speaking on CNN.

"And it seems as if the adults don't care."

World.title: Albania: Violent protests rock Tirana for third straight day
World.content:
Demonstrators hurled stones, firecrackers and other objects at riot police, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Fires broke out in the city centre, engulfing trees and a roadside structure as firefighters worked to contain the flames.

 

Footage shows protesters racing through smoke-filled streets, tearing down police barriers and throwing tear-gas canisters back at officers. Shops and banks were damaged, some looted, while police reported vandalism targeting ATMs, cameras, vehicles and fencing. Burnt-out vehicles, smashed windows and wrecked offices were left behind across the Albanian capital, where residents and workers began clearing debris as demonstrations continued.

What began three days ago as student protests over the cost and quality of higher education has become a broader challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama's government. Students demanding better university conditions, financial support and job prospects have joined the Flamingo movement, which opposes a luxury resort project linked to Jared Kushner and is calling for Mr Rama's resignation over corruption allegations.

World.title: Carney says US trying to break Canada amid vote for Alberta independence referendum
World.content:
The oil-rich province of Alberta will vote to decide if it wants to remain a Canadian province or start the legal process toward separation. Carney warned that the US was trying the divide-and-rule tactic.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned the people of oil-rich Alberta that the United States was trying to break Canada so it could "own us."

Carney was speaking at a pro-Canada rally in Calgary, ahead of a vote which will decide if the disgruntled western province will begin a legal process towards separation from Canada.

"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," he said, without naming the US or its president, Donald Trump.

This is not the first time Carney has made such a claim. His warning comes as Washington and Ottawa are in the middle of a trade war and Trump has threatened to make Canada the 51st US state.

Meanwhile, Carney's push towards making Canada less dependent on the US has irked Trump.

How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is is Alberta voting for?

Monday's vote in Alberta is not a direct referendum on independence. Rather, the province, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote to decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process towards a referendum on separation.

Albertans have long held grievances with liberal governments in Ottawa, from concerns about immigration and federal power to oil industry management. While Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has attempted to address frustrations, a lot stands to be resolved.

Mark Carney grew up in Alberta Image: Mike Sturk/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," Carney said, adding that Ottawa had made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own."

However, he urged the public there to not use the vote as a "message" to the federal government.

"Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty."

Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP that US interests "don't play a role" in Alberta "until we win and become a government." At that point, he would ensure free-flowing trade.

"There is no animosity towards America here," he said, adding that he didn't see a reason to stop trading with the world's largest economy.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders have held several meetings at the State Department.

World.title: Oregon school shooting: Gunman kills 3 students and teacher before being shot dead by community member
World.content:
A 16-year-old gunman opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing three children and a teacher. Two others were wounded. A community member pursued and killed the suspected shooter, authorities said.

A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher and wounded two others in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday before a community member pursued and killed him, authorities said.

"The deceased at the scene include three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters. Another child and a teacher were injured and taken to a hospital.

The first 911 call came in around 1 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone carrying a long gun, Krantz said.

Additional 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. Officers arrived within minutes.

"Seconds later, we received word over the radio that the suspect in this incident was down," Miller said.

Students evacuated as police respond to shooting

Bend is a ​city of some ‌100,000 people in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

Students were evacuated from the school and the buildings were cordoned off Image: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

An updated post later said law enforcement was escorting students by bus to a separate location, where they could reunite with their families. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly children aged ⁠5 to ​11. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek thanked the community member who "heroically intervened to ​stop further loss of life."

"No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have ​to live through ‌this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to ‌cry privately," Kotek said.

US grapples with recurring mass shootings

The United States, where firearms are widely available, experiences frequent gun violence, with thousands of people killed each year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among high-income countries.

Emergency personnel directed people away from the school Image: Rob Kerr/REUTERS

The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007. South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 365 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter.

World.title: Bus, train collide, injuring 19 at Channel Tunnel terminal
World.content:
A minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a freight train near the Channel Tunnel entrance in France, injuring 19 people, two of them severely. Authorities launched an inquiry into what caused the accident.

A minibus collided with a stationary train near the entrance to the Channel Tunnel in northern France on Thursday, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, authorities said.

Two people, including the bus driver, were seriously injured and airlifted to a hospital in Lille, but none of the injuries were life-threatening, the local prefect said, revising down earlier reports of five people seriously injured passengers. The other injured passengers were brought to nearby hospitals for treatment.

The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities preparing to board a shuttle train through the tunnel. LeShuttle carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.

Pas-de-Calais Deputy Prefect Agathe Cury said an inquiry was launched to determine what caused the accident.

"This is the first time an incident of this type has occurred" at a Eurotunnel loading platform, she said.

Eurostar and freight service to continue

Eurostar, which runs passenger train services between mainland Europe and the UK, said the collision would not impact its services.

"An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel tonight, not involving Eurostar. This incident does not impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected," the company said in a statement.

The last two trains between Paris and London were canceled. Eurostar said this was due to engineering work, not the accident.

The 50-kilometer (31-mile) Channel Tunnel is the longest infrastructure of its kind in the world. It has linked Coquelles in northern France and Folkestone in England since 1994. Operated by Getlink, the tunnel is used by several hundred trains every day.

Eurostar operates high-speed passenger trains between the UK and mainland Europe through the Channel Tunnel [File photo] Image: Aurelien Morissard/AP/picture alliance

Eurostar, which is a separate entity, has held a monopoly on cross-Channel passenger rail services for decades, said it carried 11.8 million passengers in 2025.

World.title: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges
World.content:
Maduro and his wife were charged with leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro appeared in court on Thursday, where he rejected newly unsealed torture charges against him and his wife, Cilia Flores.

He said the indictment represented "false accusations" against him.

Maduro was combative in court as he was asked to enter a plea to the charges, condemning allegations of torture as "false accusations and false testimony."

Ultimately, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein interjected to declare that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro."

Flores told the judge through the Spanish interpreter: "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."

The court appearance was the latest for the pair, who are currently in US custody in New York City, now eight months since they were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a nighttime raid.

The new torture charges against the couple have been added to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced.

Maduro and Flores' trial is set to begin June 14, 2027, according to a schedule approved by the judge Thursday.

What are the torture charges?

Maduro and his wife have been accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans, during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

They are said to have committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.

Security forces have been accused of torturing prisoners with electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Maduro stands accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims' treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner's child as a form of psychological torture.

For her part, Cilia Flores has been accused of helping develop the repressive system and ordering the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.

Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but the US indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

Maudro has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents, but the court has not served him with a warrant.

Torture is considered a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside of the nation where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims' nationality.

But in the US, the prosecution of foreign officials is exceedingly rare. The only recent cases include the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad's Syria.
