See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch cycling team Picnic-PostNL has been silently struggling with an oppressive atmosphere and culture of intimidation, according to an investigation published by broadcaster NOS and cycling platform In De Waaier.

Many of the team’s former members have been left traumatised and described a “culture of fear” and “unsafe working conditions”.

Reporters confidentially spoke with 71 current and former employees of the team, which competes in the World Tour, the sport’s top division. It currently employs around 120 people. Many people described how management would punish criticism and ignore mental health complaints.

One interviewee described the management structure as a “dictatorship” and another said team members were treated as “puppets”.

This began after the team’s successes in the Tour de France in 2013 and 2014, when German rider Marcel Kittel won stages as a sprinter. After that, the managers became paranoid about losing control of the team, one person told NOS.

More rules were established and people were told “everyone is replaceable.”

After Dutch racer Tom Dumoulin won the 2017 Giro d’Italia, one of cycling’s three Grand Tours, the managers became even more “radicalised”, according to another interviewee.

Dutch rider Martijn Tusveld described how he was dropped from major races for questioning the team’s tactics. He became so anxious he considered harming himself. He left the team and said he is still mentally unwell.

Another, who was suffering mentally, said he was told by sports director Rudi Kemna “I don’t believe in psychologists” after he asked for help.

The Dutch professional cyclists’ association VVBW told NOS it had heard similar accounts over the past 18 months, with some riders calling in tears.

NOS has asked the team owner Iwan Spekenbrink for a comment but he has so far refused to reply to any allegations in person or in writing.

World.title: MPs move to curb small schools amid cost and curricula concerns
World.content:
MPs and the cabinet want to curb the growth of small, independent schools in the Netherlands, after a school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) opened with just four pupils, according to broadcaster NOS.

A 2021 law made it easier to set up state-funded schools based on new educational ideas or on religious or other “worldview” beliefs. Since then, more schools have opened every year, a large share of them Islamic.

The “Renaissance School” in Almere, which opened in August, was approved partly on the basis of market research showing around 350 people were positive about it.

MPs from both coalition and opposition parties said the research amounted to little more than an online survey, and that respondents often did not know what kind of school was planned. It is linked to the far-right FVD party.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen told parliament on Wednesday she would look at whether that part of the law should be tightened or scrapped. She had already written to MPs that keeping so many small schools going was “no longer sustainable”.

Tielen said she saw no reason to intervene at the Renaissance School for now. It must have at least 139 pupils by the start of its fourth school year or close.

The law originally was a VVD initiative, which the FVD voted against it at the time.

The debate comes a year after research by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur found that a number of orthodox Protestant and Islamic schools were teaching messages at odds with democratic values, such as rejecting same-sex relationships or teaching that women should be subordinate to men.

All schools in the Netherlands are legally required to stick to democratic values, including equality and non-discrimination. The schools inspectorate said it would investigate where necessary.

World.title: Dronten wreckage identified as British WWII bomber
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Aircraft wreckage uncovered four years ago in Dronten has been identified as a British WWII bomber, according to local officials.

Discovered in what is now the Van Veldhuizenbos forest in Dronten, the aircraft is said to be a British Avro Lancaster Mk III that was shot down by German forces on the night of September 27-28, 1943, while attempting to target Hanover, Germany.

The aircraft, run by the Canadian 405 Pathfinder Squadron stationed near Cambridge, England, crashed into what was then the Ijsselmeer.

The plane was carrying seven crew members – four Canadians, one Australian, and two Britons – whose bodies were never recovered. But human remains were found in 1959 and buried in the Jonkerbos War Cemetery in Nijmegen.

Additional human remains were discovered and are now being examined by the Ministry of Defence’s Recovery and Identification Service to see if they belong to the slain crew members.

“Behind every plane wreck lies a human story,” said Dronten mayor Jean Paul Gebben, who said the aircraft’s identification was of great historical significance.

Some of the recovered wreckage will be loaned to museums and foundations.

The government estimates that some 5,500 aircraft were lost over the Netherlands during the Second World War. Annually, a maximum of three aircraft recovery operations are carried out in the country, with the costs mostly covered by the national government.

World.title: Police urge Ahold to file a report over cybersecurity breach
World.content:
Dutch police and the Public Prosecutors Office have asked Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Albert Heijn, to file a report on what the company is still calling a “cybersecurity incident”.

“There is currently no criminal investigation into the incident,” the police said in a press release issued on Wednesday. “Police and the OM have been in contact with Ahold Delhaize. The company has been invited to file a report.”

“In order to successfully track down and prosecute, it is crucial to always get information from victims as quickly as possible.”

Although Ahold did report the incident, which began on Sunday night, to the National Cyber Security Centre as required by law, a criminal investigation can’t be started without a formal police report.

The company says it will “work with all relevant authorities”, but it gave no explanation as to why it hasn’t filed a report and said it is not currently making any further statements.

The incident hit other Ahold chains Etos and Gall & Gall, leading the company to shut down several of its IT systems that has continued to make online shopping and deliveries impossible.

Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad, on condition of anonymity, that the crisis is costing Ahold Delhaize “tens of millions” of euros a day. Ahold told the paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

Fresh produce took a particularly hard hit, with the supermarkets’ fruit and vegetable sections very low on stock.

Albert Heijn said on Thursday that its distribution centres are running again, but its website and delivery services are still not operating, meaning customers still can’t place orders online or via app. Deliveries of fresh products were also said to be resuming as of Thursday night, while delivery of non-perishable products has been fully restored.

“This is a positive step forward in the recovery of our supply chain,” said the company. “The investigation into the nature and cause of the cybersecurity incident is ongoing. At this time, there is no indication that any customer or employee data has been involved in the incident.”

Bad actors

“We can no longer see cybercrime as a collection of separate crimes, but as a criminal ecosystem,” said a police statement. “Behind almost every attack lies a chain of cooperating perpetrators, resources and criminal services that reinforce each other: a criminal supply chain.”

Several foreign servers are known to be used in the attack, including in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that’s where the attacks are coming from as traffic can be routed through other countries.

Ahold supermarkets in Belgium (Delhaize) and the US (Stop & Shop and Food Lion) have also been affected.

The Albert Heijn incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France.

World.title: Dutch cabinet wants AI to help slash civil service: Telegraaf
World.content:
The cabinet is planning to slash the civil service with the help of new AI technologies, which could save hundreds of millions of euros, the Telegraaf reported on Thursday.

Sources told the paper that Eric van der Burg, the VVD junior home affairs minister, will soon present targets for cutting staff numbers, although estimates are not yet known.

Experts told the Telegraaf the rise in civil servants, which went from 140,000 in 2021 to 170,000 last year, that things are not improving. One said the government is being stifled with ever more rules and subsidies.

Policy officials in particular, who have almost doubled to 20,000 in the past decade, are putting needless pressure on the government, one analyst said.

Insiders said using AI could save an extra €200 million in both 2028 and 2029. A further €200 million has been planned for the interior ministry’s budget for the following year, rising to €1 billion a year from 2035.

Van der Burg is reported to be partly following the thinking of an advisory committee on the future of the civil service, which is due to present conclusions this year.

Ahead of a meeting with MPs, the committee said digitalisation and AI can make government more efficient, but only if the build-up of rules and checks is also tackled.

Government economist Jos Blank wrote that the state had been underperforming for decades, and that a constant stream of new rules, subsidies and mergers was making public services worse.

Former senior civil servant Roel Bekker criticised growing “policy overload” and called for the number of policy officials to be cut by 20% to 30%.

World.title: Unemployment remains at 4%, 408,000 out of work
World.content:

Over 408,000 people were out of work in September, national statistics office CBS said on Thursday.

The number of jobless people rose by an average of 5,000 a month over the past three months. The number of people in paid work stayed level.

Unemployment returned to 4% in July after dipping slightly in June. A year ago, 409,000 people were out of work, also 4% of the workforce.

The recent rise is mainly down to fewer unemployed people finding work rather than people losing their jobs.

Benefits agency UWV was paying out 197,100 unemployment benefits at the end of September. The UWV figures are not directly comparable with the CBS total, which counts everyone without paid work who is actively looking for a job.

A further 3.2 million people aged 15 to 75 are not counted as part of the workforce because they have not recently looked for work or cannot start straight away. Most are retired or unable to work because of illness or disability.

World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two. The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war. At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population. Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026 Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″. Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”. “Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.” “True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery. At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers. Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”. “This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.” Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war. In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant. “This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.” ❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱 Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026 Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project. PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant. However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis. The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year. Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation. According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule. The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026 Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts. The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called. Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign. When will the election take place? Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023. Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible). It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term. How does voting work? The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list). The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat. How is a government formed? A government can only be formed if it has the support of a majority in the Sejm. After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence in the Sejm. If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm. Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister. That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023 If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. If that does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called. Who is likely to form the next government? At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture. According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%. Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%. If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition. It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun. However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside. The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law. There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government. PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult. All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation. What about the Senate? The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset. It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO). In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies. In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition. To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023. What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest. What role will Nawrocki play in all of this? Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work. Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition. During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right. But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together. In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections. Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition. What issues are likely to feature in the campaign? A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer. Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump. On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland. While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims. Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024. The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues. As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy. The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation. World.title: Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march. Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall. His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city. Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026 Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people. In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”. However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did. "I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024 The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”. “I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.” Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments. Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch). During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed. When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would. However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków. In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union. The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries. Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue. Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46). The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”. Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”. World.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. World.title: New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president. Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions. PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M — Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026 Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in. The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so. Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge. Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present. The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK. The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present. The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding. 1294/2026 Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo — Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026 Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him. However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government). Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions. Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal. Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK. Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026 Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry. Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”. However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”. This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force. ❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX — Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Man charged with plotting attack on Polish PM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot. The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist. Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”. On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences. “The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years. Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns. Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect. Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force. At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026 Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts. On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”. "Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026 In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty. A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison. “He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine. “In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre. 🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane. ✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych. 🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026 The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries. Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries. Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation. “The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.” The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”. Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors. Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe. “Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine. World.title: The Czech Republic’s Tallest Structures Have Been Torn Down
World.content:
Two 355-meter radio transmission towers in Liblice were brought down in a controlled demolition on October 15, ending nearly half a century as the country’s tallest structures.

The towers collapsed at 11:15 a.m. local time after demolition crews used approximately 4.5 kilograms of Semtex explosives to sever supporting cables, iDNES.cz reported.



Hundreds of spectators gathered to watch the demolition, some bringing binoculars and folding chairs. Several residents were visibly emotional as the towers fell.

“We’ve lost our beacon and a symbol of home,” local residents told the outlet.

The Liblice B transmitter entered service in December 1976 and was once the most powerful radio broadcasting facility in Central Europe.

Czech Radio stopped using it for medium-wave broadcasts at the end of 2021, while Country Radio continued operating there until March 2025.

Some locals had called for the towers to be preserved as part of Czechoslovakia’s engineering and broadcasting heritage. Others viewed them as obsolete structures dating from the communist era.

With the towers gone, the 347.5-meter Krašov television and radio transmitter has become the tallest structure in the Czech Republic.

Crews are expected to spend approximately 20 more days clearing the collapsed steel structures.

World.title: Brno Burger Brand Pickle Plans Up to Seven Locations in Prague
World.content:
A burger brand recently launched in Brno is preparing to expand into Prague, where it plans to open up to seven restaurants.

Pickle also has ambitions to enter other Czech and Slovak cities before expanding across Europe and eventually Asia.

The first Pickle restaurant opened in Brno in June 2026.



Co-founder Peter Szamuhel now plans to establish the brand in Prague and Bratislava before launching a franchise network. If preparations proceed as planned, the first franchise locations could open in early 2027.

The company is considering six or seven restaurants in Prague and two or three in Bratislava. Other potential locations include Ostrava, Olomouc, Hradec Králové, Liberec, Nitra and Trnava.

Pickle aims to have its franchise model ready by the end of 2026. Although prospective partners have already expressed interest, the company is not yet signing agreements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pickle Brno (@pickledoublecheese)

The same burgers at every location

Maintaining consistent quality will be a major challenge as Pickle expands. The company plans to use regular inspections, mystery shopping, regional managers and ongoing staff training to ensure that customers receive the same food and service at every restaurant.

Ingredient supplies are another priority. Meat, buns and other key products must match those used at the original Brno location.

The restaurant currently prepares approximately 1,000 to 1,300 burgers a day, according to Szamuhel. Expanding the chain will require a supply network capable of supporting substantially greater demand.

Global ambitions within ten years

Pickle aims to establish ten locations across Czechia and Slovakia within three years, followed by another ten restaurants in other European countries over the next five to six years.

Its longer-term goal is to operate hundreds of locations worldwide within a decade, with Asia among its eventual targets.

World.title: Do You Really Need 10,000 Steps a Day? A Doctor’s Guide to Walking in Prague
World.content:
Walking is part of daily life in Prague, but how much is enough to benefit your health?

A doctor at Charles University explains why 7,000 steps a day may be a more realistic target.

Living in Prague often means walking to the tram, crossing the city centre on foot or taking a stroll through one of its parks. But does this add up to enough physical activity to improve your health? And is reaching 10,000 steps a day really necessary?

According to research published in The Lancet Public Health in 2025, walking around 7,000 steps a day may be enough to deliver significant health benefits.



The study found that people taking approximately 7,000 steps daily had a 47% lower risk of premature death and a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease compared with those walking around 2,000 steps a day.

These figures represent associations rather than guarantees, but they suggest that the widely promoted 10,000-step target is not a requirement for better health.

Why walking matters

Regular walking can help strengthen the heart, improve circulation, regulate blood pressure and blood sugar levels, and support muscle and joint health.

Its benefits are not limited to physical fitness. Spending time outdoors and walking regularly can also help reduce stress, improve mood and support better sleep.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week. This can include brisk walking for around 30 minutes a day, five days a week, to meet the minimum recommendation.

The pace matters, too. Brisk walking should make you breathe slightly harder while still allowing you to hold a conversation comfortably.

Where to walk in Prague

Prague offers plenty of opportunities to incorporate more walking into daily life without joining a gym or travelling outside the city.

Stromovka is a good option for beginners and those looking for longer walks on relatively flat paths. The extensive park provides a break from traffic and the busy streets of the city.

For a more demanding route, Divoká Šárka offers hills and woodland trails that provide a more strenuous workout while remaining within Prague.

Vyšehrad is suitable for a shorter walk, combining gentle climbs with views of the city and the Vltava River. Its location also makes it a practical option for those who have limited time.

For a longer weekend outing, Prokopské údolí offers walking routes through valleys and green spaces away from the city centre.

How to keep walking during winter

Shorter days, cold temperatures and icy pavements can make walking less appealing during the winter months. However, the arrival of colder weather does not mean abandoning a regular routine.

Dressing in layers, wearing shoes with good grip and choosing well-lit, cleared paths can make outdoor walks safer and more comfortable.

Even a 10- to 15-minute walk during a lunch break can be worthwhile. When pavements become icy, slowing down or choosing a safer indoor alternative is advisable.

Small changes can make a difference

Building more walking into everyday life does not require a major change in routine. Getting off the tram one stop earlier, taking a walk during lunch or using the stairs when practical can all help increase daily activity.

Those who currently walk relatively little can start with 10 to 15 minutes a day and gradually increase the duration as their fitness improves.

Rather than focusing on a fixed target, people who track their steps can aim to increase their usual daily total over time.

About the author

Darren Andrew Noronha, MD, is a medical doctor and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, with a research focus on cardiovascular health and disease prevention.

World.title: Czech Republic to See Sharp Weekend Cooldown and Possible Snowfall
World.content:
The Czech Republic is set for a change in weather this weekend, with temperatures expected to fall and snow possible in mountain areas, according to the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute (CHMI).

The colder conditions will follow several relatively mild autumn days, when daytime temperatures are forecast to reach 17 to 18 degrees Celsius.



By the weekend, however, increased cloud cover and precipitation could bring the first signs of winter to higher elevations.

The transition will come after a frosty start to the week. Meteorologists expect the coldest night of the week to have already passed, meaning temperatures should remain more moderate over the coming days.

Sunshine is forecast across much of the country during the remainder of the working week, although mornings will stay chilly. Local fog and showers may develop in eastern parts of the Czech Republic.

The outlook for the weekend remains uncertain, but forecasters expect a general cooling trend, accompanied by extensive cloud cover and periods of rain.

Mountain regions are most likely to see wintry conditions. As temperatures fall, rain could turn to snow at higher elevations, particularly in the mountains. Some locations may also experience temperatures below freezing.

However, significant or lasting snowfall is not currently expected. Any snow that falls is likely to be limited to light dustings or scattered flakes, with accumulations unlikely to persist for long.

World.title: David Duchovny Brings New Album to Prague This Thursday
World.content:
David Duchovny, best known for his acting career, will perform in Prague on October 15, 2026, presenting songs from his upcoming album Prince of Pieces at Archa+.

Tickets are on sale through GoOut.

Duchovny has spent the past decade developing his career as a songwriter and recording artist, releasing music that combines melodic rock with introspective lyrics.

Prince of Pieces is his fourth album and brings together a small group of musicians and longtime collaborators.

The new record follows Hell or Highwater, Every Third Thought, released in 2017, and Gestureland, released in 2021. According to the album’s press release, the latest project is his most cohesive and collaborative work to date, reflecting the relationships he has built with fellow musicians over the years.

Duchovny’s music has received positive reviews from critics.

AllMusic described his sound as “eloquent, alt-rock-kissed country-folk in the vein of Wilco and the Wallflowers,” while The Boston Globe praised his voice for its “parched resonance and just a hint of rasp,” adding that he sings with feeling.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by David Duchovny (@davidduchovny)

The actor has said that the arrangements on his records are shaped by the mood and rhythm of each song, rather than following a single formula.

“The arrangements of the songs have always been in service of either the groove or the emotion,” Duchovny said. He added that he looks for sounds that complement the melody, including horns, bells and harmonies, while also experimenting with rhythms and beats.

World.title: Czech Doctors May Soon Prescribe Museum Visits to Prevent Depression
World.content:
Doctors in the Czech Republic could soon recommend museum visits, dance classes, singing and creative workshops to people at risk of depression, anxiety or social isolation.

The program, known as Art on Prescription, aims to connect healthcare providers with museums, galleries, libraries and other cultural institutions.

Rather than replacing medication or psychotherapy, these activities would complement existing treatment and help prevent mental health problems.



The National Institute of Mental Health (NUDZ) is preparing a National Platform for Prevention through Culture to bring together cultural organizations, healthcare providers, social services and schools. The goal is to make existing cultural activities more accessible to people who could benefit from them.

The initiative is not intended to turn cultural institutions into medical facilities. Instead, it seeks to use local resources to support mental well-being and strengthen social connections.

Research highlights benefits of cultural activities

International research suggests that participating in cultural and artistic activities can improve well-being, strengthen social ties and reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety.

According to Dominika Grygarová, a researcher at NUDZ, an analysis combining studies from more than 20 countries found significant reductions in symptoms of both depression and anxiety.

The benefits depend not only on exposure to art but also on active participation, Grygarová said. Creating something, learning a new skill, sharing experiences and interacting with others can help people focus on something beyond their difficulties and develop a sense of belonging.

However, the programs are intended primarily as a preventive and supportive measure, not a substitute for professional treatment. Researchers also want to assess their effectiveness and economic value, with preliminary analyses suggesting that some initiatives could be cost-effective.

Czech project looks to Northern Europe

NUDZ plans to build on similar programs already operating in several countries, particularly the United Kingdom and Northern Europe.

The Czech initiative intends to follow the so-called Baltic model, with researchers planning to work with Danish colleagues next year on a European project to introduce the approach more widely.

World.title: Who Is Petr Hlaváček? The Architect Set to Become Prague’s Next Mayor
World.content:
Petr Hlaváček is seeking to become the Czech capital’s next mayor after his political movement, STAN, won the municipal elections.

STAN received 23.16 percent of the vote, securing 17 seats in the Prague City Assembly and putting the movement in a strong position to negotiate the next governing coalition.



Hlaváček, currently deputy mayor for territorial and strategic development, has indicated that he wants to take the top job at City Hall.

His priorities include expanding housing construction, redeveloping former industrial sites and improving transport infrastructure.

A key role in Prague’s new zoning plan

Hlaváček’s main achievement as deputy mayor has been his involvement in preparing Prague’s new Metropolitan Plan, which replaced the previous zoning document from 1999 when it came into effect in September 2026.

The plan sets out where construction can take place and establishes rules for future development. It identifies capacity for up to 350,000 new homes, primarily through the redevelopment of brownfield sites.

One of the main projects is the transformation of Bubny-Zátory, an underused area expected to provide housing for around 20,000 people.

Hlaváček has also backed the Prague Development Company, which manages municipal land and aims to increase housing construction. According to him, the company could facilitate the development of up to 70,000 homes while helping prevent city-owned land from being sold off.

Transport and housing at the top of his agenda

If appointed mayor, Hlaváček wants to continue work on major transport projects, including Prague’s inner ring road and the Prague Ring Road. He also supports expanding public transport and reforming parking policy, arguing that parking in the city is often too cheap.

Before the elections, he said STAN would welcome continuing the existing coalition at City Hall but wanted a more prominent role, depending on its electoral support.

From architect to deputy mayor

Born in Zlín on July 31, 1961, Hlaváček graduated from the Faculty of Architecture at the Czech Technical University in Prague. He later established his own architectural studio, taught as a visiting professor at the University of Michigan and served as vice-dean at his alma mater.

His professional work includes the renovation of the Czech Embassy in Brasília, Brazil.

In 2015, he became director of the Prague Institute of Planning and Development. He was dismissed the following year amid criticism over delays to the Metropolitan Plan, a decision that prompted protests from institute employees.

Hlaváček entered Prague politics after the 2018 municipal elections and became first deputy mayor for territorial development and spatial planning in November 2021. He remained in the city leadership after the 2022 elections and took responsibility for territorial and strategic development in February 2023.

World.title: Sinatra Tribute Pairs Frank Sinatra Classics With 1930s Dining at Prague’s Mánes
World.content:
Prague’s Art Restaurant Mánes combines live performances of Frank Sinatra’s best-known songs with a three-course dinner inspired by traditional Czech cuisine of the 1930s.

The functionalist building offers views of the Vltava River and nearby Žofín Island, providing the setting for an evening dedicated to the music and style of Sinatra’s era.



The Sinatra’s Tribute musical programme features acclaimed soloists, including baritone Daniel Klánský and jazz singer Sophie Lamoš. They perform some of Sinatra’s best-known songs, including *My Way* and *Fly Me to the Moon*, accompanied by a group of musicians.

Rather than simply imitating the legendary American singer, the Sinatra Tribute offers its own interpretation of his musical legacy.

One of the programme’s highlights is a restored 1897 Steinway & Sons grand piano, an instrument once played by Czech composer and pianist Jaroslav Ježek.

The music is complemented by a three-course dinner served before the concert.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sinatra Tribute Koncert & Večeře / Sinatra Tribute Show & Dinner (@sinatratributeprague)

Created exclusively for the programme by Mánes Restaurant head chef Jaroslav Zahálka, the menu draws inspiration from Prague’s culinary traditions of the 1930s, reflecting the period associated with the evening’s musical theme.

Visitors can contact the venue for current dates, ticket prices and reservations.

World.title: London analysts share when Hungary could join the eurozone
World.content:
Hungary could still adopt the euro in 2032 despite a worsening budget deficit and rising public debt, according to the Eurasia Group. The risk consultancy expects drought damage and geopolitical shocks to put further pressure on public finances in the short term, but believes the country could enter the EU’s exchange rate mechanism by 2030.

Hungary’s budget deficit could rise to around 7.7–7.8% of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, according to a new assessment presented by Eurasia Group, one of the world’s largest political and economic risk consultancies, in London on Thursday.

The consultancy said the greatest pressures on the budget, particularly high oil prices and the damage caused by prolonged drought, stem from factors beyond the Hungarian government’s control.

Markets have already begun reacting to weaker deficit expectations over the past month. One indication is the rising cost of credit default swaps (CDS), financial instruments used to insure against the risk of a sovereign debt default, according to the group’s analysis.

Illustration created by artificial intelligence.

Hungary’s public debt could approach 77% of GDP

Eurasia Group expects Hungary’s public debt-to-GDP ratio, which stood at 75.6% in the middle of the year, to approach 77% by the end of 2026. However, the consultancy noted that the need to borrow on the market to pre-finance European Union payments would also contribute to the increase.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar is reluctant to introduce policy measures that would be felt directly by voters. As a result, he is likely to favour additional taxes on large companies, broadly following the approach taken by his predecessor, Viktor Orbán.

The key difference, according to Eurasia Group’s London-based analysts, is that Magyar would present these measures as temporary sacrifices necessary to secure eurozone membership.

His target would be for Hungary to join the European Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) by 2030, a mandatory step towards adopting the euro.

If you missed it: An exact date of Hungary adopting the euro emerged with new roadmap proposed

Could Hungary join the eurozone by 2032?

Eurasia Group considers it likely that Hungary will enter ERM II by 2030. If that happens, it could pave the way for eurozone membership in 2032, as countries must spend at least two years in the mechanism before adopting the single currency.

Entering ERM II by 2030 would be a “major political success” for Magyar, the consultancy said. Adopting the euro in 2032 would also “cement Hungary’s position within the EU”, according to its assessment.

The group added that such a timetable could have positive effects on financial markets. For example, yields on Hungarian sovereign debt denominated in forints and euros could converge further, potentially lowering the cost of borrowing.

Other major London-based financial analysts have published similar assessments of Hungary’s public finances in recent reports.
