World.title: Hajduk Beats Ajax 2-1 at Poljud to Open Conference League Campaign!
World.content:
Hajduk opened their Conference League group stage with a 2-1 win over Ajax at Poljud on Thursday, as goals from Bamba and Šotiček saw off the four-time European champions in a match halted for 12 minutes by Torcida’s flares.

Hajduk reached the group stage of a European competition for the first time in 16 years after eight qualifying matches. Their European campaign began in the first qualifying round of the Europa League, where they knocked out Slovakia’s Žilina before going out to Cypriot side Pafos over two legs in the next round. That sent Hajduk into Conference League qualifying, where they comfortably beat Lithuania’s Žalgiris and then got past Poland’s Raków after extra time in both legs.

The draw paired Hajduk with Ajax for their opening league-phase match. The two clubs have a long history. They have met three times in friendlies and four times in competitive matches. Hajduk won all three friendlies, each played at the Stari Plac: 3-0 in 1974, 1-0 in 1977, and 4-2 in 1979, shortly before the club moved to Poljud.

Their first competitive meeting came in the first round of the 1993 Cup Winners’ Cup. With war in Croatia, Hajduk played their home leg at Ljubljana’s Bežigrad stadium and won 1-0, but Ajax won the return leg 6-0. The sides met again in the quarter-finals of the 1995 Champions League. The first leg at Poljud finished goalless, and Ajax, who went on to win the competition, took the second leg 3-0.

Hajduk have never lost to Ajax in Split, across four meetings.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silić, Hrgović, Hadžikadunić, Marešić, Acapandie, Fayad, Del Moral, Dalisson, Šotiček, Bamba, Šego

Ajax: Ter Stegen, Kehrer, Baas, Bouwman, Torrents, Amrabat, Klaassen, Brandt, Ouazane, Tsygankov, Tolu

Match report

The match got under way at Poljud with Ajax in possession and Hajduk sitting in a mid-block, looking to build their attacks down the right through Bamba.

Ajax almost scored within seven minutes. They broke quickly, and Arokodare got clear of Hadžikadunić to run through on Silić. The Hajduk goalkeeper was already on the ground, but Hadžikadunić recovered with a superb last-ditch sliding challenge to make up for his own mistake.

Hajduk began to push higher. In the 11th minute Šego sent Bamba away down the wing, but Torrents stopped his run, and from the 12th minute the home side were pressing aggressively whenever Ajax had the ball. A minute later Dalisson won possession and tried to play Bamba through on goal, but the Ajax defense reacted well.

Bamba won Hajduk’s first corner in the 17th minute, and their first shot followed straight after. Hrgović timed his run to beat the offside trap onto a Dalisson through ball and shot from a tight angle into a defender, leaving Šego frustrated that he had not crossed. By then the Poljud stands were shaking with the noise from the home supporters.

Šotiček sent in a dangerous cross in the 23rd minute, but Šego was penalized for a foul in the challenge for the ball. A minute later Dalisson beat his man with a fine dribble and shot from around 20 meters, a comfortable save for Ter Stegen.

Hajduk kept coming. In the 29th minute, Hrgović played a superb ball over the top for Šotiček, but Klaasen read it well. Ajax countered in the 35th minute, only for Arokodare to be caught offside.

Two minutes later Hajduk took a deserved lead with a deadly counter-attack. Klaassen was dispossessed, Šotiček played in Bamba, and he finished to make it 1-0 in the 37th minute! The stands erupted into a chant of “Ja te volim Hajduče”.

Ajax looked for a quick response, and in the 43rd minute Klaassen’s header from eight or nine metres was saved by Silić.



Hajduk kept up their high press after the restart, but Ajax punished them as soon as they dropped deeper. In the 53rd minute, with Hajduk sitting in front of their own penalty area, Kehrer crossed, and Klaassen timed his run to drive the ball in under the bar for 1-1.

The equalizer stood for only three minutes. In the 56th minute Hajduk won the ball back with more excellent pressing. Šego pounced on a dreadful pass from Torrents and, rather than shoot from a promising position, laid it off to Šotiček, who took a touch and scored to make it 2-1!

Šego was booked in the 60th minute. Three minutes later, Bamba beat Torrents and tried to go past Baas as well, but the defender stopped him and cleared the ball out of the box. Bamba went down, but there was never a case for a penalty.

Hajduk’s tempo dropped slightly as the hour mark passed, and García turned to his bench, bringing on Dendoncker for Del Moral in the 70th minute. A minute later, Dalisson sent in a dangerous cross, but it struck Šego and rebounded straight into Ter Stegen’s hands.

Ajax made a quadruple substitution in the 76th minute, as Leonardo, Gloukh, Rosa and Mokio replaced Cigankov, Klaassen, Ouazane and Torrents.

Two minutes later, the match was stopped. Torcida lit flares in the 78th minute, and the smoke became so thick that nothing on the pitch could be seen, so the players were taken to the dressing rooms under UEFA protocol. Even then, the fans kept letting off bangers.

In the 86th minute, the stadium announcer warned that the match was at risk of being abandoned.

Play finally resumed after a 12-minute stoppage, on the understanding that any further pyrotechnics would see the match abandoned. The clock picked up from the 78th minute.

Ajax almost made the most of it. In the 80th minute, Gloukh struck the crossbar from a cut-back, though the flag was already up for offside.

Ajax was now much more dangerous and pinning Hajduk back. In the 84th minute, García made a double change, bringing on Melnjak and Šutalo for Hrgović and goalscorer Bamba.

Hajduk defended desperately as Ajax laid siege to their goal in the closing minutes. In the 90th minute, Bouwman shot over from around ten meters. At least five minutes of stoppage time were signaled.

García used his final changes in the first minute of added time, bringing on Van Hoorenbeck and Martin for Fayad and Šego. Hajduk held firm through the remaining minutes, and at the final whistle they had beaten Ajax 2-1 to start their first league-phase campaign in 16 years with a win!

Hajduk coach Gonzalo Garcia addressed the press after the win.

“What can you say to the players after this win? First game in Europe after 16 years. The way they performed, their personality with the ball, their pressing. Everything. Ajax is an amazing team with an amazing coach. You can only be proud in this moment. We never gave up, and it showed.

Our players are brave. They want to improve every day, every game. Ajax did not underrate us tonight; they knew it was going to be a hard game. But we showed from the first moment that we wanted it. We didn’t give them space to breathe.

We worked together. We were intelligent. We controlled a big part of the game. Even when we conceded a goal, we knew how to come back and play smart. The team is increasingly mature with every game.

Even if we have bad moments, we will push, and we won’t give anything for free to anyone.”

World.title: Will Croatia Prevent Montenegro EU Accession?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Croatia has multiple conditions for entry into the bloc, but could it go as far as to block the Montenegro EU accession?

Croatia has very clearly warned neighbouring Montenegro that a series of unresolved bilateral issues could slow its planned entry into the European Union by 2028. Among the open topics are war crimes, property restitution and the definition of the border, Index reports.

This week, Zagreb sent a document to the other EU Member States listing eight demands that Montenegro must fulfil before the conclusion of accession negotiations. Montenegro is otherwise widely regarded as the front-runner among the candidate countries and hopes to become the 28th member of the Union by 2028. Nevertheless, long-standing disputes with Croatia, which mostly date from the time of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, represent an obstacle to those plans.

blockade progress

“Croatia sincerely wishes to close this painful chapter of our shared history and to build a future-oriented relationship with Montenegro. However, mutual trust and genuine and lasting reconciliation cannot be achieved without resolving these issues,” the Croatian document states. On Monday, Montenegro advanced in its negotiations with the EU after closing the chapters on statistics, economic policy and employment. This brought the total number of closed chapters to 21 out of 33.

Croatia, however, is blocking progress in four other areas: transport, external relations, fundamental rights and internal affairs. Every member state has the right of veto over the enlargement process, which gives Zagreb significant influence over Montenegro’s path to membership. The document elaborates in detail the objections that the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs already put forward back in July, which largely stem from the wars of the 1990s.

a list of croatia’s open issues

One of the most sensitive demands concerns compensation for around three hundred Croatian citizens who were detained and abused in the Morinj concentration camp in Montenegro from October 1991 to August 1992. During the conflict, Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly taken to that camp. Croatia also demands that the memorial plaque at the site of the former camp remain permanently visible. The plaque was enclosed in a metal structure after protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups. Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people who are still listed as missing from the Homeland War.

Zagreb is therefore asking Montenegro for help in locating their remains and describes this as an important humanitarian issue that has not yet been resolved. Croatia also demands that in the cases of already convicted war criminals for crimes against civilians in Morinj, command responsibility be taken into account.

long-standing disputes from the 1990s

Zagreb also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes from the early 1990s concerning Croatian families whose property was confiscated without adequate compensation. The document notes that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region with a predominantly Albanian minority, which “raises concerns about unequal treatment in similar cases.”

Zagreb also seeks the return of the “Jadran” vessel which has been under Montenegrin control since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991. Finally, Croatia demands the resolution of territorial disputes over the land and maritime border in accordance with the decisions of the Arbitration Commission on Yugoslavia. Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although that did not prevent it from joining the European Union back in 2013.

“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve the open bilateral issues and at the same time has actively supported its entry into the EU. Despite Croatia’s constant efforts and constructive approach, none of the open issues has yet been resolved,” the document concludes.

World.title: How Will Croatia Actually Benefit From the €50 billion Data Centre?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – In what way will Croatia actually concretely benefit from the giant €50 billion data centre in Topusko that has many deeply concerned about the environment and water?

The previously announced construction of the huge and very controversial Pantheon data centre in Topusko, whose value is estimated at as much as €50 billion, raises a series of questions about the real benefits Croatia could gain from such an investment. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this gigantic project recently took another step towards realisation. Sisak-Moslavina County has initiated amendments to the spatial plan in order to create the conditions for the construction of the centre and the accompanying infrastructure.

Although a series of procedures and the obtaining of the necessary permits still lie ahead before construction can begin, below we provide answers to some of the key questions about the project, its possible benefits and costs. For the purposes of this text we also received an expert comment from Tomislav Vazdar, an expert in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

intended for large tech companies with little care for anyone else

According to Ryan Rich, executive partner of Pantheon AI, who wrote about the project for the Wall Street Journal, the centre is intended for large technology companies that need enormous computing capacity for continuous operation and the development of artificial intelligence. Rich also stated that the infrastructure would be available to European defence, intelligence and commercial users.

Pantheon representatives were asked about who specifically will use the future data centre and whether there are already agreed tenants, but we had not received a reply by the time this text was published. Project manager Mario Gudelj explained to Večernji list in July that the final value of the investment will depend on the requirements of future users, whom he described as large technology companies developing artificial intelligence. According to the announcements at the time, the first users should start using the centre’s capacities at the beginning of 2029.

Vazdar explained to us who the most common users of such data centres are. “The largest users are global cloud service providers, companies developing large artificial intelligence models, and increasingly the defence and security sector. In a centre of this scale, AI models would primarily be trained and run. Money is earned by renting out capacity, most often through long-term contracts with a few large clients,” Vazdar commented for Index.

is there any benefit to anyone outside of big tech?

Part of the investment will relate to construction works and infrastructure, and a significant part to the purchase of computer and other technological equipment. The value of the campus construction is estimated at up to €12 billion, while the total investment, including IT equipment, should exceed €50 billion. One of the possible long-term benefits is the construction of electricity infrastructure. In addition to the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant, for which cooperation with the international energy group Greenvolt has been announced, according to project representatives’ announcements, the construction of approximately 280 kilometres of power lines and a new substation is planned, and the investment would be financed by the investor.

The built infrastructure should then pass into the ownership of the Croatian Transmission System Operator. “The benefits won’t come by themselves; all of that has to be contracted in advance. So, a share of capacity for domestic companies, universities and the public sector, engagement of domestic contractors and investment in the network that remains with the state. Equally important is control over the data. If data is processed in Croatia but control over it remains outside the European legal framework, the state bears the risk and does not gain digital sovereignty,” Vazdar said.

are there any benefits for croatian companies?

One of the concrete opportunities for Croatian companies is linked precisely to the construction of the mentioned electricity infrastructure. At the end of April, Končar signed a non-binding letter of intent on cooperation on the Pantheon project, which envisages the participation of several companies from its group, including Dalekovod. One of the investors, entrepreneur Jako Andabak, claimed on HRT back in April that the majority of the works during the construction and equipping of the centre should be carried out by Croatian companies, using domestic knowledge and workforce.

what about new employment opportunities?

As announced at the project presentation, more than 3,000 workers should be engaged during construction, around 1,500 people employed after the centre starts operating, while the project could indirectly contribute to the creation of a further 6,000 jobs. Andabak stated that approximately half of the 1,500 permanently employed should have higher education qualifications. That would mean around 750 highly qualified jobs, primarily linked to the operation and maintenance of complex technological infrastructure.

It is not yet known how many of the employees will be from Croatia, and especially how many jobs could go to residents of Topusko and the surrounding area. “The most jobs are created during construction, and once the centre is up and running there are few permanent employees, although these are highly qualified positions. Realistic expectations should be based on signed commitments, not on announcements,” Vazdar said.

how will pantheon help croatia’s own tech sector?

One of the potentially greatest long-term benefits of the project could be the development of Croatia’s technology sector, especially companies dealing with artificial intelligence. Large computing capacities are needed for the development and training of advanced artificial intelligence models, and access to such infrastructure could open new opportunities for domestic companies, universities and research institutions.

Project manager Mario Gudelj spoke to N1 in May about the ambition for Pantheon to bring the industry of the future to Croatia and position it among the leading countries in digital transformation. Vazdar said more about the importance of Pantheon for the development of artificial intelligence and the domestic technology sector. “The significance is potentially great, but only with clear access conditions for domestic companies and scientists. Without that, the centre can operate at full capacity for foreign clients, while the domestic sector gets almost nothing from it,” he added.

how much will the state and the local community benefit financially?

In addition to employment and the engagement of domestic companies, one of the more important potential benefits of the Pantheon project relates to tax and other public revenues. The Municipality of Topusko has particularly high expectations. Its mayor Ivica Kuzmić stated on HRT in May that the realisation of the project could increase the municipality’s revenues three to four times. He emphasised that the additional funds would primarily be used to improve communal infrastructure.

However, a detailed financial projection showing how much the state and the Municipality of Topusko would earn annually from the centre’s operations has not yet been publicly presented. The amount of tax revenues will depend, among other things, on the centre’s business results, the number and salaries of employees, and the way in which the business of the companies involved in the project is organised.

will electricity prices shoot up?

One of the more important questions relates to the high consumption of electricity and water and the possible consequences for the general public, for whom a giant data centre represents little but a deep worry. As Gudelj announced, Pantheon in full operation would consume around five terawatt-hours of electricity per year, 1.5 times more than Zagreb and a little more than a quarter of Croatia’s consumption.

However, he stated that electricity would not become more expensive for citizens because of the centre. According to his announcements, the centre would primarily be supplied from renewable sources, and the investor would also finance the necessary electricity infrastructure. “A data centre of this scale consumes as much electricity as a large city, and continuously. That means great pressure on the electricity system and a risk that the cost of adapting the network will spill over onto all users if the rules are not set in advance,” Vazdar adds.

“Cooling data centres down also requires significant amounts of water, so it is necessary to transparently determine how that will affect local sources. All of this must be publicly and independently assessed before any decision,” Vazdar says.

data centres and their devastating environmental impact

The impact of Pantheon on the environment is a separate and extremely important topic that deserves an analysis of its own. We have already written about this in detail on Index, and here we will only recall that part of the public is mainly concerned about the high water consumption, noise, waste heat, interventions in the space and potential consequences for the local ecosystem.

Vazdar warns for Index that cooling a data centre requires significant amounts of water, which is why it is necessary to transparently determine the possible impact on local sources and to assess everything publicly and independently before any decision is made. Gudelj says that the final solution has not yet been chosen. Pantheon, as he emphasised, will not connect to the public water supply or use water from rivers and streams, and hydrogeological research is being carried out. Earlier, the investors claimed to Index that the impact on the environment would be negligible or non-existent. In any case, the strategic environmental impact assessment and the assessment of acceptability for the ecological network are only part of the procedures that must precede construction. Therefore it still remains to be determined what consequences the project could have for the environment and what protection measures will be necessary.

World.title: Split High on Quality of Life in Relation to Costs Ranking – But Should It Be?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Split has occupied a high position in terms of quality of life in relation to costs of living, being above Stockholm and and Copenhagen, but should it rank this highly?

Two of Croatia’s largest cities also made it into the aforementioned quality of life ranking. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that according to this research, Zagreb and Split are cities with above-average, even high, quality of life, but at the same time they are extremely expensive relative to the median salary.

does split really offer a better life than 94% of other european cities?

The analysis shows that Split offers a better life than 94 percent of other European cities, including Copenhagen, Prague, Stockholm and Madrid, but in order to enjoy its benefits and advantages one needs to earn 29 percent more than the net median salary, which in Croatia back in July amounted to 1,346 euros. The median salary means that half of employees received a net salary lower than 1,346 euros, and half received at least that much or more.

Zagreb fared somewhat worse, or better, depending on which parameter on the chart you look at. In the capital, the chart says, the quality of life is significantly lower than in Split: Zagreb is better than 64 percent of other European cities (for example Graz, Rome, Berlin and Milan). On the other hand, the mentioned standard is also significantly more accessible and one needs to earn only three percent more than the net median salary.

the worst quality of life is in belgrade

The best and most affordable life, according to the research, is lived in Vienna, Helsinki and the Dutch cities of The Hague and Eindhoven. And the worst and most expensive in Skopje, Belgrade, Sofia and Bucharest. That is at least how it was calculated by Alessandro Palombo, an Italian entrepreneur and doctor of legal sciences, who published the research in the form of several charts on social networks and his website.

Of course, what immediately catches the eye on the chart is the paradox that Skopje is more expensive than Paris and London, and that Oslo and Geneva are cheaper than Zagreb. However, Palombo did not take into account absolute living costs, according to which the largest European cities are certainly expensive, but the ratio of costs to the median salary in those cities. The contradiction is nevertheless only apparent: a city can be very expensive, but the local median salary can be sufficient for an excellent standard of living. Likewise, a city with relatively low prices can be difficult to afford for local residents with low salaries.

numbeo deemed “an unreliable data source”

The fundamental problem that largely calls into question the validity of the research is the source of the data. As usual when it comes to such analyses, Palombo uses data from Numbeo, an online database that, based on user inputs, collects and compares information on living costs, prices, salaries, safety, quality of life and other indicators in cities and countries around the world.

Numbeo is often quite unreliable as a source because anyone can enter data in a certain category. Although there are automatic filters for suspicious values, its data and analyses should generally be taken with a large dose of caution. For this reason, Palombo himself does not present his comparisons as infallible. In a discussion on X he admitted that he considers the quality of such data limited and that some components of quality of life are inevitably subjective.

Specifically, according to the October data on prices on Numbeo, for Split in the previous 12 months data was submitted by 37 different participants, and for Zagreb by 156. Dozens of voluntary participants are not a representative sample for a display on a map with seemingly precise coordinates. Numbeo’s standard quality-of-life index includes eight factors: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, property prices relative to income, cost of living, commute time, pollution and climate.

Palombo states that he calculated quality of life without Numbeo’s price-related indicators. What remains are the criteria of safety, healthcare, traffic, pollution and climate, which at Numbeo to a large extent rest on the perception of the website’s users rather than on official statistics. Financial affordability is shown separately by Palombo on the horizontal axis.

croatia’s housing structure makes a major difference

However, quality of life in this research does not take into account other important criteria at all, such as the quality of education, employment opportunities, availability of kindergartens, cultural offer, social protection and the real possibility of finding long-term housing.

It should also be borne in mind that the research is based on a single person who earns the median salary and lives in a rented one-bedroom apartment outside the city centre. That in no way corresponds to the financial status of the majority of the population. For Croatia specifically, this difference is particularly important. According to Eurostat data, in 2024 91 percent of Croatia’s inhabitants lived in their own property. A person living in their own paid-off apartment, a young tenant, a married couple with two salaries, a four-member family and a pensioner have completely different relationships between income and living costs. This clearly shows how much the author’s model differs from reality.

It is also not explained by what criterion these particular 79 cities were selected. It is not entirely clear whether the author of the research took into account the median net salary in the entire country, the region or only in the specific city.

osijek finds itself (surprisingly) on the list

Interestingly, Palombo also offers another interactive map that, according to the same criteria, compares 322 world cities. Among Croatian cities, Osijek is the biggest surprise. It is at approximately the 99.7th percentile of quality of life, which places it among the highest-rated cities, even slightly ahead of Vienna, Helsinki, Split and Rijeka. The only problem is that the basic (and entirely bizarre) assumption is an annual gross income of 86,000 US dollars, which is deeply unrealistically high for Croatian standards. Only a few thousand employees in Croatia receive such a salary.

World.title: Estonia's €50m planned island e-ferry passes first model tests with flying colors
World.content:
A scale model of Estonia's planned €49.93 million electric ferry has passed its first tests in Germany, reaching 14 knots where the contract requires 12.

The boat, once built, will be the fifth ferry in the fleet serving Saaremaa, Muhu and Hiiumaa, and is planned for the Virtsu–Kuivastu route. It will be Estonia's first shore-charged electric ferry.

The week-long tests at the Schiffbau-Versuchsanstalt Potsdam center evaluated the vessel's seagoing and hydrodynamic properties and checked energy efficiency and propulsion solutions, the State Fleet said. Ice model tests follow in Finland in late November.

Model testing allows planned solutions to be checked and improved before construction begins. The tests used an 8.2-meter scale model of the hull matches the planned vessel's shape and proportions exactly, fitted with accurate scale copies of its drives and propellers.

Eero Avi, a shipbuilding engineer and chief specialist with the State Fleet's (Riigilaevastik) ferry project, attended the tests and said they showed good work had been done on the hull design. Energy consumption is low for the vessel's size and remains within contract limits, with some margin.

The scale model during testing in Germany. Source: State Fleet

"The tests showed that although the construction contract sets the vessel's maximum speed at 12 knots, the model was able to reach 14 knots, with some power reserve still remaining," Avi added.

Ice model testing takes place at the end of November at Railotech's ice model basin in Helsinki, checking the hull and propulsion system's performance in level ice of varying thickness and in brash ice, meaning an accumulation of floating sea ice or river ice made up of small fragments not more than 2 meters across.

The project is co-financed by the EU Modernization Fund, whose terms require the new vessel to be significantly more energy-efficient than existing ones.

The full-sized ferry will have a 3 MWh battery, allowing fully electric operation in normal conditions on the route. Biodiesel generators will keep service running in heavier seas and emergencies, and its range without refuelling is at least 1,000 nautical miles.

The actual ship when build will be close to 100 meters in length and able to accommodate up to 380 passengers and up to 110 passenger vehicles, or eight trucks.

The model is a little over 8 meters in length. The finished ferry will be over 10 times that length. Source: State Fleet

The vessel will be built by Polish shipyard CRIST S.A. and designed by subcontractor LMG Marin France, which also designed the ferries now operating the route. The contract is worth €49.93 million, with €28 million from the EU Modernisation Fund and the rest from Estonia's national CO₂ quota sale funds.

The Virtsu–Kuivastu route links the mainland with Muhu and, via a causeway, Saaremaa, and is one of Estonia's busiest ferry crossings. The fifth ferry is part of a wider fleet renewal and is due to enter service at the end of 2028.

A cold spell at the start of this year led to thick sea ice and falling sea levels and caused problems with island ferry connections, with cancellations and some of the smaller islands cut off from the mainland.

World.title: Elisa to shut down 2G network in 2028, competitors hold back for now
World.content:
Phone operator Elisa is to shut down its 2G mobile network in 2028, Sakala reported .

The service will be phased out region by region, and the closure will leave older phones and devices that rely only on 2G or 3G without a connection, as Estonia's 3G network has already shut down.

Elisa spokesperson Toomas Polli said the technology dates from a time when a phone's main job was calling and sending messages, and that the role of networks has changed beyond recognition.

Competitors Telia and Tele2 said they will be closing down their 2G networks too, but not before 2029-2030 – Tele2 spokesperson Tanel Sarri said security devices and gate systems still depend on 2G.

Elisa network services development director Kristo Kork said the 2G closure will happen in phases by region, but the exact timetable and order of regions is still being drawn up and with customers noted in good time - Elisa would not say how many devices on its network are 2G-only, but said most already support 4G and 5G.

The original Sakala piece is here.

Elisa stated on its own website it shut down 3G at the end of 2024, and while most calls and data already run on newer networks, some devices in Estonia still rely on 2G.

Alongside older phones, these include security and alarm systems, electricity and water meters, payment terminals, and industrial and property automation equipment.

Polli said most people won't need to do anything, but devices with a longer lifespan than phones need attention. "Some surveillance, measurement or automation devices may have been installed ten or even more years ago and are still operating on a 2G network," he said.

2G networks, which launched in Finland in 1991, are also being phased out in other North European countries. Sweden and Norway set are to do so in 2027, while Iceland already did so last year. Further afield, G networks have already been shut down in Australia, Japan, and the U.S. Elisa recommends travellers with concerns check whether their device supports 4G and/or VoLTE.

World.title: Estonia mulls allowing dual citizenship in certain circumstances
World.content:
The coalition parties want to allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The opposition questions what problem the change is intended to solve.

On Wednesday, the Reform Party and Eesti 200 parliamentary groups in the Riigikogu jointly introduced a bill that would allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The bill would allow Estonian citizens by birth to apply to have their Estonian citizenship restored even if they had previously lost or renounced it after acquiring citizenship of another country.

Under the Constitution, Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. However, the Citizenship Act stipulates that people who are Estonian citizens by birth but also hold citizenship of another country must choose between the two when they turn 18.

Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said at a government press conference that this was the wrong approach. "There is no reasonable justification for this whatsoever," she said. Pakosta argued that if an 18-year-old receives a letter telling them to choose between U.S. and Estonian citizenship, for example, but wants to retain both, they are fully entitled to do so.

Dual citizenship would be possible only in the case of select countries

According to Pakosta, this is precisely why the law needs to be brought into line with reality. The countries with which dual citizenship would be permitted include European Economic Area member states, as well as the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Switzerland. These countries are home to large Estonian communities.

The opposition does not understand what problem the proposal is intended to solve. Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. Vadim Belobrovtsev, deputy chairman of the Center Party's parliamentary group, suggested that the coalition was trying to push through a proposal ahead of the elections that actually requires more extensive debate.

He said that because the bill applies only to Estonian citizens by birth, it would give some people an advantage over others.

Military service one potential stepping stone

Evelin Poolamets (EKRE) said the bill would create further confusion, particularly regarding compulsory military service. She explained that questions would arise over whether a young person should complete military service in Estonia or another country and which country's military reserve they would be assigned to.

Poolamets noted that the Citizenship Act contains various provisions affecting citizens, including matters related to social security and pensions. "Perhaps the goal is precisely to give dual citizens more opportunities," she said. However, Poolamets added that there was no guarantee a person would contribute equally to both countries.

Valdo Randpere (Reform Party) said times and circumstances have changed, with many young people living abroad and that citizenship is one way to maintain ties with Estonia. Randpere hopes the bill will secure the necessary 51 votes this time.

"I've spoken with both unaffiliated MPs and opposition representatives and I haven't received a firm no," Randpere said. He has not discussed the issue with EKRE representatives. "They would definitely say no," Randpere explained. He hopes at least one opposition party will allow its MPs a free vote.

World.title: Estonian ex-soldier jailed in Russia after visiting his wife
World.content:
A former Estonian Defense Forces member is currently in a Russian prison, accused by the FSB of planning to fight for Ukraine — a charge his family says was forced out of him.

Artur Kirmjõe, 30, is married to a Russian national who is banned from entering Estonia, leaving him to travel to Russia to visit her. He had done so over 10 times before he was detained on April 29.

In a video published by the FSB — Russia's main internal security organ — in the Vladimir oblast in June this year, a man with his face concealed states he got in touch with Ukrainian contacts and asked to join Ukraine's armed forces.

"My attitude towards the war in Ukraine became sharply negative. On my own initiative, I contacted Ukrainian contacts and asked them to help me join Ukrainian military units to fight on their side against Russia," the man is heard to say.

Relatives confirm it is Artur, but say he was induced to say what he does in the video.

"He said what he was forced to say, but it is all lies. It is not true. He was just reading it, I don't know, from a screen or from a piece of paper," said his brother, Jüri.

Artur Kirmjõe served in the EDF'Scout's Battalion. Source: ERR

Artur's mother, Inga Allikas, points out the absurdity of the charges given how and why her son had traveled there. "If a person wants to go and fight on Ukraine's side, they don't take big suitcases and a cat and travel to Russia to their wife," she said.

The "Pealtnägija" report was the first time Jüri and Inga have spoken publicly on the episode under their own names and faces. The family had not drawn attention to the case earlier, hoping it was a misunderstanding which would resolve itself. Now they want international attention drawn to the situation: the 30-year-old Estonian citizen faces 7 to 12 years in prison based on what they call a trumped-up confession.

Artur was born in Tallinn and grew up in nearby Maardu. He is bilingual and studied in Russian for his first eight school years, and in Estonian after that. After high school he studied at the maritime academy, was conscripted, and stayed on as a regular EDF member — serving as a paramedic in the Scout's Battalion at Tapa from autumn 2018 to the end of 2020.

The chain of events leading to his current plight began shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In late March that year, a couple arrived from Russia — a married couple, aged just over 20, referred to in the report as Lina and Sergei. In early April 2022 they applied for international protection in Estonia, saying life in Russia was dangerous for them due to their anti-war views.

"Lina was persecuted because of her political views, which were clearly opposed to the Russian state," said her lawyer, Merili Laansoo.

Indrek Aru, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border guard bureau, said not all circumstances could be commented on, but that the grounds given were checked and no sufficient basis for protection was found.

Artur with his wife Liina (name changed). Source: ERR

When the PPA refused protection, Sergei and Lina appealed. Tallinn Administrative Court found they were not in real danger in Russia: no criminal cases had been opened against them, they were not on any wanted lists, and the likelihood of attracting the authorities' attention was low. The pair appealed to the Supreme Court without success. In November 2023, they were banned from entering Estonia for three years — a detail that matters much in respect of what followed.

"He was quite shocked. You could see he was very uncomfortable, because he started crying. Just uncontrollably," said their friend Lars-Eerik Väina.

While the court cases were unfolding, a romance unfolded too, between Artur and the still-married Lina. The pair were working as security guards at the Kauplus Aasia club in Tallinn. Lina divorced Sergei in summer 2023.

Since Lina had to leave Estonia a few months later, in November 2023, Artur and Lina married in Russia on June 1, 2024, at a registry office in Vladimir, 200 kilometers from Moscow. The couple said they hoped the entry ban would now be lifted, but the PPA refused again — seeing it as suspicious that the application to live in Estonia had come so soon after the marriage, which in turn had followed soon after the entry ban.

As a result, Artur shuttled between Estonia and Russia more than ten times between 2023 and 2026 to see his wife. The lawyer representing them repeatedly pointed out that traveling to Russia could be dangerous, particularly as Artur was a former serviceman, but the PPA downplayed any danger.

"A significant number of Estonian citizens live permanently in Russia. In this case, the specific person has traveled back and forth to Russia repeatedly. Yes, at certain stages our wording may not have been the best. I admit that in hindsight," Aru said. He added that the official information presented at the time was not meant to encourage Estonians to travel to Russia, and that it was an unfortunate choice of words.

"I think those decisions are made en masse; everyone gets the same reply under their application. Nobody looks through the files, nobody looks at the applicant's background, whether it is genuinely safe for them or not," Inga said.

Artur in EDF uniform with his mother, Inga Allikas. Source: ERR

Inga now lives in Helsinki and works as an accountant, but she previously spent years working as a translator for the PPA. She believes official indifference cost her son his freedom. Separation from his wife has caused Artur mental health problems, the family says, and in April this year he traveled to Russia again, after six months apart.

"I lived with him for about 20 years. And the fact that he went there means love told him that it was the only thing worth going for — love," said his brother Jüri.

At the end of April, the FSB arrested the Estonian citizen in Lina's kitchen. Then in June the video appeared on the FSB Vladimir office's Telegram channel and spread to other outlets. In it, Artur appears to confess to anti-Russian activity.

Relatives, who can only communicate with Artur by letter via Lina, believe the video statements are entirely fabricated. "Artur has never been to Ukraine, not even out of tourist interest. To comment on what the charge is based on — some correspondence that was found, maybe. I don't know," said Inga.

Aru said the family's view is now seen differently in light of the arrest and detention. "But in hindsight, would that change anything? We cannot change the past. It is, unfortunately, a tragic story," he said.

Lina says she is currently not facing persecution, but, citing her safety, declined to appear in the report and asked that her real name not be published.

Artur's family has hired a lawyer in Russia and recently appealed to the Estonian Foreign Ministry for help, so that consular officials can assist and diplomats can perhaps pull international strings. "I know Estonia should somehow contact the United States — I don't know which institution — and start negotiations to have Artur added to an exchange list, so he might get home sooner than if he serves all those years," Inga concluded.

World.title: Tartu prison director: Dissatisfaction with prison life hardly out of the ordinary
World.content:
Tartu Prison Director Merle Ulst acknowledged that renting out prison space is a new situation for all parties involved, requiring both the Estonian Prison Service and the inmates brought to Estonia to adapt.

The inmates complained that prison officials did not speak English well enough and that they had been sent to Estonia against their will. Among other things, the inmates were unhappy that the two televisions in their cells were positioned side by side, that the beds lacked guardrails and that they had no privacy when washing.

Ulst noted that the visit by the Office of the Chancellor of Justice took place nearly two months ago when the vast majority of Swedish inmates had been at Tartu Prison for just two days. Most of the issues and concerns raised at the time had already come up in the prison staff's daily work.

"Addressing these issues is part of the prison's day-to-day work. We explain the rules and procedures to inmates, listen to their feedback and make adjustments based on practical experience where reasonable and possible. When new procedures are introduced, it is only natural that some arrangements need to be refined and improved based on initial experience," Ulst said.

She emphasized that inmates cannot expect all the comforts they are accustomed to outside prison and that certain restrictions are an inevitable part of prison life.

"Our task is to ensure humane conditions, respect for inmates' rights and a safe environment for everyone in our custody. These principles also guide us when making changes. We take legitimate needs into account, but not every request warrants changing existing procedures," Ulst said.

The Tartu Prison director noted that the issues raised by Swedish and Estonian inmates regarding everyday living conditions, restrictions and prison procedures are fairly similar.

"Dissatisfaction with certain aspects of prison life is not unusual and addressing such concerns is part of the prison's daily work. Regardless of an inmate's background, we follow the same principles: We ensure their rights and humane conditions while maintaining clear boundaries necessary for the prison to function," she said.

World.title: Eesti 200 to decide Sunday on running with Greens at Riigikogu election
World.content:
Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas is to propose at Sunday's party board meeting that the party run alongside the Greens in the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.

The Greens (Rohelised) will discuss the merger at their own general assembly later in the month. Both parties are polling far below the 5 percent threshold required to win seats, at 1.2 (Eesti 200) and 0.7 percent (Greens), even though Eesti 200 is in office with Reform at the national level.

Media reports that the two parties were considering joining forces emerged late last month.

Kallas, who is also education minister, told ERR she will make the proposal at Sunday's meeting and was unwilling to comment further on the possible merger, or her own political plans before then.

Rasmus Lahtvee, one of the Green party's leaders, said the exact date for their discussions is still not set, but the merger with Eesti 200 will certainly be talked about..

"There is talk [with Eesti 200]. We have been feeling out various possibilities and what the two parties have in common. It is clear that something has to change on the Estonian political landscape," Lahtvee said.

"The merger certainly has to be decided by the general meeting, and that will stay at the end of October," he went on.

Asked whether the parties' possible decisions would be followed by more serious merger talks in November, Lahtvee said some clarity must come soon, as the president will declare the Riigikogu elections by December 6 at the latest. Polling day is set for March 7, 2027.

Eesti 200 has been struggling with very low ratings for several years now. A Norstat poll published this week put support for the party at 1.2 percent, with the Greens at 0.7 percent. The latest ERR-commissioned Emor poll in September put Eesti 200 at 1.9 percent and the Greens at 1.1 percent.

Eesti 200 was founded in 2018 and won 14 Riigikogu seats in 2023, entering government with Reform and, until spring last year, the Social Democrats (SDE). Lauri Hussar, a former Eesti 200 chair, has held the Riigikogu speaker position since April 2023, while Margus Tsahkna is its Foreign Minister.

Eesti 200's rating started to collapse soon after the 2023 election, however, after a donations to Ukraine scandal engulfed a former MP. Another MP, former Green leader Züleyxa Izmailova, who herself had replaced the disgraced MP, returned to her original party, SDE, in 2024. Then in late summer this year, high-profile MP and former Riigikogu Defense Committee chair Kalev Stoicescu quit the party, to join the non-parliamentary Parempoolsed. This left the ruling Reform-Eesti 200 coalition as a minority government.

Eesti 200 has also approached SDE and also the Free Party (Vabaerakond) about mergers, but without success. The Greens in fact have more members now — 705 to Eesti 200's 579 — but their candidates mostly cannot afford the €946 election deposit, which is part of what Eesti 200 could offer.

A party needs a minimum of 500 members to be legally registered.

World.title: Foreign minister: One must ensure one's own survival when inflicting pain on Russia
World.content:
Estonia's decision to keep a Russian supplier to Silmet off the EU sanctions list was necessary to protect European industry, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said, but stressed that the company must end its dependence on Russian raw materials or face further sanctions.

Estonia has been a leading advocate of sanctions for years. Now it turns out that we have nevertheless been feeding the Russian war machine through Silmet. How is that possible?

Estonia has been and will continue to be one of the most active advocates of sanctions and supporters of Ukraine in Europe. And just on Monday, we imposed sanctions on 1,600 companies and individuals. But my question is rather the other way around: How is it possible that, in the fifth year of the war, Europe remains so dependent on Russia, particularly for rare earth elements, for example? And that is not a question for Estonia. Rather, the question is how actively Europe has been working to eliminate these dependencies. We know that we are buying less energy, but Europe still continues to consume Russian energy.

What we are doing now is setting out our conditions for Silmet. And now that Silmet has also received notification from the European Commission that it has been included on the list of strategic companies, this provides a basis for obtaining European funding. But that funding must come with conditions and one of those conditions must be that the company eliminates its dependence on Russia.

But Estonia has held itself up as a moral beacon in the European Union when it comes to doing business with Russia. How can we now point fingers at others who want to do business with Russia or refuse to impose sanctions?

I would not exaggerate this position of being Europe's moral beacon quite so much. We have simply been very exemplary in our actions and we have absolutely never discussed...

This particular case shows that we have not been exemplary.

Yes, but this particular request also came from the European Commission. We also have to ask the question the other way around: If Russia were to stop supplying these raw materials to Europe altogether, European technology companies, including those in the defense industry, would be in very serious trouble.

So this is not a question of our being a moral beacon. We will continue in that role. Unfortunately, there is still a great deal of lobbying going on in the corridors of the European Commission, not specifically on strategic issues where Europe is dependent, but also purely in the interests of business. This is something that Estonian viewers do not usually learn about.

But we will continue our work as advocates of sanctions and Silmet's owners have also been told very clearly that they have a certain amount of time to eliminate their dependence on these raw materials. And this particular company will be added to the sanctions list at Estonia's own initiative.

How exactly did Silmet's supplier, a Rosatom subsidiary, end up on the proposed sanctions list? Who put forward that proposal?

We do not know how this particular company ended up on the list. Estonia has also made a great many different proposals concerning both companies and individuals. And in a sense, that is the problem with the European Commission's procedure: Before a draft reaches the member states' ambassadors, quite a few names and companies disappear during the process.

That happened this time as well. In fact, of those 1,600, I estimate that more than 50 have disappeared. We do not know who made those proposals, which is not even such a big problem. But we do not know at whose request those individuals and companies were removed from the list.

Now, Estonia acted very honestly and clearly. When the draft was already complete, the Commission pointed out that this particular magnesium plant was very directly connected to Silmet's supplies and that Silmet accounts for a very large share of what Europe needs for its industry. They asked us to look into it and it turned out that Silmet was dependent on this particular plant in its supply chain.

Did Estonia ask for Silmet's supplier not to be included on the list?

On the Commission's recommendation, we said that this particular proposal should be removed from the draft until the supply problem involving Russia had been resolved.

Did that proposal come from the Estonian government or from Silmet?

No, the proposal came to us from the Commission and I, as foreign minister, acting under the existing government mandate, confirmed that this would indeed have real consequences for European industry and that, until the supply problem was resolved, this company would not be included on the sanctions list.

We have been working for several years to find some kind of solution, but Silmet is not a state-owned company. Silmet is a private company. Silmet's owner is Neo Group, which is listed on the Canadian stock exchange.

Now that we have a real means of leverage, for example through funding, we can set our conditions directly for Neo Group. And that is what we have done.

I hope this problem will be resolved next year and that this particular company in Russia will also be on the sanctions list. It is not that easy to change the mines from which these raw materials originate. The issue is not only that there is enormous global competition, but, according to Silmet, it also requires changes in technology, and that is precisely why investment is needed.

Four and a half years have passed since the start of the war. Have you previously spoken with Silmet's management about the fact that importing these materials from Russia is not a particularly sensible thing to do, given that they would inevitably be sanctioned at some point?

We have discussed this repeatedly and we have also discussed how to attract investment here so that this specialized industry can develop in Estonia. Our goal, in fact, is to bring rare earth production, magnet manufacturing and the entire research, development and innovation center to Estonia. There is enormous competition for this around the world.

Silmet and Neo are the world's largest producers of rare earth elements outside China. So, for example, we are currently negotiating with the United States to conclude a memorandum of understanding. The European Union has already done so with the United States.

And we have been working to get Silmet and Neo included on Europe's list of strategic companies, which happened last week, and to bring European Union investment here.

Incidentally, a Neo magnet plant opened in Narva last year and the European Commission has already invested in it. So there are enormous opportunities here for Estonian industry and for our own economy.

But one specific problem that remains unresolved in Europe is this dependence on Russia and it must now be addressed as quickly as possible. It certainly will not be easy, but the only thing the Estonian government can do is apply pressure. We do not actually want to lose our own industry either.

By the way, are raw materials still being shipped from Russia's Solikamsk Magnesium Plant to Estonia today?

We are in contact with Neo's representative and my understanding is that another shipment still needs to be made. They have already factored that in. This morning (Wednesday — ed.), they also issued a public press release announcing their intention to use the available opportunities to end Russian supplies and eliminate this dependence.

Four and a half years after the start of a war that everyone has long known about. Can we trust them? And what happens if they still have not found a new supplier by the end of this year or the beginning of next year? Will national sanctions be imposed or what happens then?

If Europe has taken the necessary steps to make this technological change possible and Silmet, for example, still does not make that change, then it is no longer our responsibility. In that case, this particular company must be added to the list.

We have simply provided an opportunity for this change to take place. And this is not something that began because the company appeared on a proposed sanctions list. Work on this issue had already been underway.

Let's clarify one more thing about the timeline. Did the prime minister know that Estonia did not want to impose sanctions on a Rosatom subsidiary?

This was part of the normal working process and it was handled at my level. We bring individual decisions to the government when, for example, we are going to block a sanctions list.

That is what almost happened with the sanctions against individuals when two oligarchs were removed at France's request. If we had decided, for example, to be the only country to vote against the list and the entire list of 3,000 individuals headed by Putin had ultimately been left without sanctions, decisions of that kind would go through the government.

The prime minister is certainly aware that Silmet depends on Russian raw materials or that European industry depends on Russian raw materials. But this particular process is managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

But the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee did not know about this either?

That Europe depends on Russian raw materials? I think that...

Were they aware that Silmet imports raw materials from Russia?

I think the entire Estonian public knows that because, as far as I know, Silmet's story has been discussed for more than 10 years.

As for the working process, this is actually how it operates because there is constant work going on between the member states and the Commission on these sanctions lists, proposals and everything related to them. That is precisely the work of our diplomats.

Why was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' initial reaction that this information should not have become public?

I do not know where the idea comes from that this information should not have become public.

That initial reaction, suggesting that this was some kind of retaliation against Estonia, that we had done something and now information had become public about which company in Russia might face sanctions?

Everything that happens in the Committee of Permanent Representatives, or Coreper, is not some kind of state secret. In that sense, I cannot say what the big secret here is.

Perhaps it is even a good thing that this has become so public and that Estonian society as a whole and Europe more broadly are recognizing that we still have a very significant strategic dependence on Russia.

What is even worse is that Europe is actually dependent on China, and, to be frank, I do not see any solution whatsoever to that problem.

We will resolve this Russian problem, or rather, the company must resolve it, not the Estonian state. But I think Europe's dependence on China will remain for a very long time.

In your assessment, did the Ministry of Foreign Affairs act correctly? Was its reaction in the first few days exactly what it should have been?

I think the reaction of the Estonian public was entirely...

The ministry's reaction.

The Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs is doing its job and we have never concealed what we are working on.

If I were in the same situation I was in a few weeks ago, I would make exactly the same decision because we are talking about European industry, we are talking about Estonian industry and we are talking about the need to eliminate our strategic dependence on Russia.

So there is no need to look for any conspiracy theory here. Communication has been very open.

But perhaps we should openly acknowledge that, in certain cases, we have no other choice. This company is so important to our economy that, in some cases, exceptions have to be made and imports from Russia have to continue.

In certain cases, when supply problems have not been resolved and these are existential issues for us, then inevitably that is how things are.

But that does not mean we should in any way abandon our support for Ukraine or stop applying additional pressure on Russia, which we have no intention of doing.

In a sense, I am even pleased that Estonian society is so uncompromising that we do not accept any such deviations or alternative interpretations.

Unfortunately, that is not the case across Europe. Increasingly, we are seeing that it is becoming harder and harder to agree on new sanctions packages. In fact, when you start working on something, you often have to take several steps back.

How can Estonia demand that other countries adopt these sanctions packages when we ourselves seemingly cannot even comply with them very well?

We can comply with them very well. Estonia has called for a complete trade embargo. Just today, at my decision-making meeting, I approved new proposals and this changes absolutely nothing about our course.

This is completely normal work for other member states as well. When issues like these come up, they are raised. This is not just about Estonia's interests or anyone's business interests. It is actually a European problem.

These matters must be discussed openly and, as foreign minister, I have no problem explaining them because any reasonable person in Estonia can understand this.

This is not some kind of moral competition. We are talking about how to inflict as much pain as possible on Russia while also ensuring our own survival.

And the question should rather be asked the other way around: How is it possible that Russia holds such powerful leverage over the whole of European industry?

What do you think the answer is? Why has Europe backed itself into a corner when it comes to raw materials?

It is not just Europe. This is actually a broader global issue and it is not just about Russia. China's influence is even greater.

In this context, perhaps what is unfamiliar to Estonia is that this particular rare earth industry and magnet industry are of such enormous importance to the entire world, especially Europe.

Europe has simply been unable to respond in the way many other countries have. And if we look, for example, at what President Trump is doing in this field today, the sums of money involved are enormous and so is the political influence.

We will get to Trump, but I want to ask one final question on this subject. You met with your Ukrainian counterpart on Monday. How could you look him in the eye in light of all this?

I looked him in the eye the same way I always do.

They are facing a very difficult winter, during which they will need very substantial assistance from Europe.

By Monday, it was also already clear that Trump had once again put Ukraine under pressure.

So I think we should focus on what the truly existential issues are and how we can help Ukraine survive this winter.

Those are the issues we actually discuss with our colleagues from Ukraine and Europe.

Eesti Ekspress reported today that there are 22 kilometers of spare gas pipeline in southeastern Estonia intended for Russia. Should Estonia maintain a gas pipeline intended for Russia in working order?

If that is what you mean, then it can be kept in working order, but not open.

Keeping it in working order also costs money.

Well, that is some kind of international obligation, since it is an international gas pipeline. But the question is whether the pipeline is open. It is not open.

It has been open on certain occasions?

Exactly, and that is why I met with the prime minister this morning and our climate minister has also been given the relevant instructions.

In fact, the valves are located in Latvia and a large part of the infrastructure is in Lithuania.

This is a European Union issue, but it is certainly one of the ways, let's be frank, that we could put pressure on Russia at some point because gas and gas transit are not subject to EU sanctions.

Let's talk about Trump and Putin. As we know, the U.S. president struck a so-called diesel deal with Putin. Why has the U.S. president begun bringing Vladimir Putin out of isolation?

First of all, this is not the first time that many people who sympathize with Ukraine have suffered what you might call a nervous breakdown, gone gray or lost a few brain cells.

But I think these questions should, of course, be put first and foremost to U.S. President Trump.

I think the answers are primarily connected to the midterm elections, which are fast approaching.

What is Estonia's position on this?

We have stated very clearly that this is a step in completely the wrong direction, considering that it allows Putin to earn additional revenue.

But this has now also been accompanied by pressure that goes beyond buying diesel. What is particularly serious is the pressure on Zelenskyy to stop his attacks on oil refineries.

That is actually where Putin and his capabilities can be significantly weakened.

Ultimately, the volume involved is not decisive in terms of either the global market or U.S. consumption.

And this is largely a political game aimed at his own voters, in response to a situation of his own making in which oil and gas prices have risen very sharply.

Has Estonia communicated its position to the United States in any way?

We have stated it completely publicly and our positions are well known.

Going back to the beginning of the interview, we criticize Trump, saying that this move is wrong. Yet through Silmet, we ourselves are feeding that same Russian war machine. Isn't that hypocritical?

These are two completely different issues.

One is whether you go and offer a deal to buy diesel or propose that kind of cooperation.

The other is when you are trying to eliminate your own strategic dependence.

These are not comparable issues.

How has this company been trying to eliminate that dependence for four and a half years without succeeding and now we are hoping it will manage to do so in just a few months?

That is what they say and I think the company's representatives should come on this program and explain to you what they have done over the past four and a half years.

By the way, have you been in contact with Silmet's CEO again over the past week?

I have been in contact with him before, personally.

But not recently?

I have. I spoke with him on Friday and our people are in contact.

Perhaps as a result of this pressure, the company, as a publicly traded company, also issued a press release this morning, which I recommend reading.

Returning to Trump, is Trump now so angry that, for the Ukrainians, this means receiving less intelligence, none at all or receiving it with a delay?

Today, I met with NATO Secretary General Rutte who was visiting Estonia and this was one of the questions we discussed.

NATO is very well informed and as of today, the United States has not restricted its intelligence sharing.

I hope that remains the case.

So this appears to be primarily political pressure, but who knows? Trump is unpredictable.

So, as things stand, at least according to NATO's assessment, the Americans have not started reducing the intelligence reaching Ukraine or causing any delays in its delivery?

Yes. The information our secretary general had was that intelligence sharing has not been reduced.

Military assistance provided through the PURL mechanism has also not been reduced or suspended.

I hope that remains the case.

Finally, a little about Estonian domestic affairs. President Alar Karis criticized the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, meaning you, in his latest speech. Do you accept the criticism?

I think Alar Karis should now move on with his life, just as he appeared to be doing in the photo he posted on Facebook, sitting in a comfortable chair by the sea.

Tomorrow, I am meeting with the new president, Ülle Madise. We have also sat down together since her election by the Riigikogu and our team is working very well with her.

So I would not go down the path of commenting on the views of a president who is already leaving office.

But what will communication between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the presidency as an institution look like now? Will cooperation with Ülle Madise be better?

Just as cooperation was excellent during President Karis' term, it will also be excellent with Ülle Madise.

--

World.title: Estonia still importing Russian food products
World.content:
Estonia's trade with Russia has dwindled since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but imports of food products have continued alongside rare earth metals.

Tespi, a wholesale warehouse store, imports Russian and Belarusian food products that are not subject to sanctions into Estonia. Some of these products are also sold by other grocery stores. The retailers are reluctant to discuss Russian goods.

Apart from certain chemicals and rare earth metals, for which Estonia sought special permission from the European Union to supply Silmet, food products now account for most imports from Russia to Estonia. In August, for example, imports of Russian food products and animal products totaled around €1 million, although last year there were months when the figure reached €3 million. Imports have declined since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but not significantly.

"The fluctuations in food import figures are due to the size of the shipments transported by sea," said Ursula Riimaa, deputy director general for customs at the Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA).

Overall, however, little remains of Estonia's trade relations with Russia.

"Trade with Russia has changed significantly, both in terms of imports and exports. Before the war, Estonia imported approximately €2.2 billion worth of goods from Russia. In the first eight months of this year, imports totaled around €40 million. We're talking about volumes that have fallen more than tenfold," Riimaa said.

The European Union's sanctions policy has primarily targeted sectors of the Russian economy that fuel its war machine, such as exports of petroleum products and mineral resources. Product categories that generate less revenue for Russia have so far largely been excluded from the restrictions.

"Food products and medical supplies have been the two main categories of goods that have largely remained exempt from sanctions so far. However, certain food products classified as luxury goods are subject to restrictions on both imports from and exports to Russia," said Kadri Elias-Hindoalla, director general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' sanctions department.

Compared with prewar levels, EU exports to Russia have fallen by 60 percent, while imports have dropped by 90 percent. Additional restrictions are being introduced with each new sanctions package.

The most significant measure set to take effect next year is a restriction on imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG), which several European countries continue to purchase from Russia.
