World.title: Indonesian stocks dive 11% as MSCI weighs market reclassification
World.content:
Jakarta – Indonesian stocks plunged more than 11 percent Friday as index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain the country’s emerging-market status, fuelling fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

The US firm said earlier this year that investors had raised concerns about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities in Jakarta said in April they had completed reforms, hoping to avoid the downgrade, which could deal a blow to government efforts to kickstart Southeast Asia’s biggest economy, and have a significant impact on investment decisions.

But on Friday MSCI said investors had indicated the “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”.

“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.

“Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate and is launching a consultation on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a Standalone Market.”

“A reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognise the depth of the market problems,” it said.

A standalone classification could force investment funds tracking the MSCI’s emerging market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings.

Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg.

The Jakarta Composite Index collapsed eight percent at the open, sparking a trading halt. When trading resumed it was down 11.1 percent, its heaviest fall since early 1998 and sitting at its lowest level since 2020.

The index has now fallen more than 40 percent since the start of the year.

– Rupiah weakens –

In reaction to the news, the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said it “respects MSCI’s independence in assessing and determining market classification based on its proprietary methodology”.

“However, considering the various progress and reform measures that have been taken, the IDX will request further clarification from MSCI regarding the basis for the considerations and assessments behind this announcement.

“We also need to emphasise that this MSCI announcement is still part of the consultation process, with input being accepted until April 30, 2027, and does not constitute a final decision.”

The rupiah dropped about 0.8 percent against the dollar to sit at around around 18,060, having hit 18,209 in June, its weakest level on record.

Erwin Gunawan Hutapea, the Indonesian central bank’s head of monetary management and securities, said the bank would take action to ensure stability of the rupiah, which had already tumbled around eight percent this year to a record low.

“Amid rising global risk-off sentiment, which has driven US dollar strengthening and put pressure on domestic financial markets, capital outflows from domestic portfolio assets are expected to continue.

“Bank Indonesia is committed to maintaining a presence in the market to uphold Rupiah exchange rate stability in line with its fundamentals and to ensure that market mechanisms function properly.”

The central bank had carried out several rate hikes earlier in the year to shore up the rupiah, after it came under pressure over the state of Southeast Asia’s biggest economy.

The bank is due to hold its next monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.

New York-based MSCI produces international indexes used by investors as a benchmark to balance their portfolios.

It has a significant impact on investment decisions through its flagship emerging markets index, which contains 1,200 companies with a market capitalisation more than $10 trillion.

Fund managers worldwide keep a close eye on what countries are included or excluded in MSCI’s indexes as that can trigger adjustments to their portfolios.

World.title: Iraq’s parliament approves new cabinet ministers
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — On Thursday, Iraq’s parliament confirmed 11 cabinet nominees and three deputy prime ministers, including Laith al-Khazali, a key member in Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq who faces US terrorist sanctions.

The nomination is a politically risky decision for Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, whose administration is dealing with strained regional ties and severe economic challenges as a result of the continuing US-Israeli war against Iran.

Al-Khazali is the brother of Qais al-Khazali, the commander of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, which Washington listed as a foreign terrorist organization in 2020.

Both brothers were classified as specially designated global terrorists, and the US Treasury sanctioned them individually in 2019 for suspected participation in violence against Iraqi demonstrators.

Their US designations also included references to assaults on American troops, such as a 2007 operation that killed five US soldiers.

The parliamentary decision raises concerns about al-Khazali’s nomination and its ramifications for Baghdad’s relationship with Washington, especially as al-Zaidi wants to reinforce Iraq’s sovereignty and manage ties with neighboring nations.

Ministers approved by parliament

Yasser Al-Maliki – Minister of Interior

– Minister of Interior Naif Al-Shammari – Minister of Defence

– Minister of Defence Rebaz Hamlan – Minister of Construction, Housing and Municipalities

– Minister of Construction, Housing and Municipalities Qutalba Ghazi – Minister of Planning

– Minister of Planning Haider Bahaa – Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research

– Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research Yassin Al-Aithawi – Minister of Culture

– Minister of Culture Mohammed Al-Moussawi – Minister of Labour and Social Affairs

– Minister of Labour and Social Affairs Safaa al-Kinani – Minister of Youth and Sports

– Minister of Youth and Sports Mohammed Al-Daraji – Minister of Digital Economy, Governance, Science and Technology

– Minister of Digital Economy, Governance, Science and Technology Ali Al-Dakhil – Minister of Tourism and Antiquities

– Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Mehmet Seman – Minister of State

Deputy prime ministers approved

Laith Al-Khazali – Deputy Prime Minister

– Deputy Prime Minister Muhsin Al-Mandalawi – Deputy Prime Minister

– Deputy Prime Minister Mohammed Ali Tamim – Deputy Prime Minister

Political parties disagreed; therefore, lawmakers postponed a vote on the migration and displacement portfolio.

Following the voting, Al-Zaidi advised the newly appointed ministers and deputy prime ministers to do their duties with competence and integrity.

The appointments come as Iraq faces a deteriorating economic crisis, with oil export interruptions and liquidity shortages putting strain on the government’s budget.

Al-Zaidi has declared a significant depreciation of the Iraqi dinar, warning that the government confronts unprecedented economic and security problems.

The presence of a US-sanctioned militia member in the government’s high leadership may hamper Baghdad’s attempts to preserve fruitful relations with Washington.

World.title: ‘Mixed feelings’: AI cracks centuries-old ciphers
World.content:
Tokyo – Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the wartime missive written in code, creating a puzzle that went unsolved for more than 200 years — until AI cracked it in a matter of hours.

Artificial intelligence is helping non-specialists unlock the secrets of historical sources, a trend described as a “turning point” in a field previously the preserve of scholars and dedicated hobbyists.

One new sleuth is Carter Church, a 27-year-old AI engineer who decrypted a 19th-century letter to one of Napoleon’s generals.

Without digital tools, the task could have taken weeks, but the latest model from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI broke the cipher in just six hours.

“What AI mostly brings is persistence,” Church told AFP, saying he felt “an unbelievable sense of satisfaction and excitement when I saw the result”.

The message from 1809 — detailing French and allied troops’ positions in two dozen lines of symbols, numbers and letters — had lain ignored in an online academic archive.

Because traditional, low-tech methods to crack ciphers are effective but time- and labour-intensive, historians “have more important problems to solve, so many ciphers like this often sit unattended”, said Church.

To find the solution, Church, who works at US cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, needed to learn “very little” about code-breaking techniques or the historical period.

He spent some evenings going over it, then consulted Japanese patent engineer Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains an online list of unsolved ciphers, to verify it.

“2026 will be remembered as a turning point for codebreaking of historical ciphers,” Tomokiyo wrote on his website Cryptiana, a go-to resource for the small but enthusiastic global community of amateur cryptographers.

– ‘Mixed feelings’ –

Researchers were already developing AI models to break ciphers, but the public release of state-of-the-art generalist tools has unleashed dozens of new solutions.

Although Church used OpenAI’s most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, other people have used top offerings from rival US lab Anthropic instead.

Tomokiyo said that since mid-September, most of the ciphers on his list have been cracked using AI.

“There remain some tough problems” which could stay an enigma for years to come, because there is less relevant data available to help AI figure them out, the 58-year-old told AFP.

“I’m excited long-time problems are now solved, but on the other hand, I have mixed feelings, because AI seems to have solved these difficult problems so easily,” he said.

With technology draining the satisfaction of being first to crack a cipher, a fellow code-breaker told Tomokiyo: “I feel useless.”

AI is surpassing human abilities in pursuits from mathematics to computer programming, while threatening to alter or even eradicate many jobs.

The technology is transforming the work of historians not only by decoding documents, but also by analysing millions of medieval manuscripts or helping read ancient scrolls.

Too fragile to be unrolled without risking destruction, the Herculaneum Papyri — hundreds of papyrus scrolls carbonised in the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD — are now being X-rayed and analysed by AI to reveal the hidden writing inside.

Researchers in Italy announced in June the first complete virtual unrolling of a scroll, which turned out to be a treatise on ethics.

– ‘Facebook of the past’ –

AI is also being used to build a huge, searchable collection of previously inaccessible sources on Jewish history and culture by transcribing 10 million pages of Hebrew manuscripts.

“It’s gigantic. No human being could process such a quantity” of data, said project leader Daniel Stoekl Ben Ezra, of the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes in Paris.

Researchers hope the databases created using the digitised text — which he likens to a kind of “huge Facebook of the past” — could help bring to light links between people, places and ideas.

And at the French capital’s Notre Dame Cathedral, an AI system has been trained to transcribe 14,600 Latin pages from the church’s medieval archives — a task not dissimilar to code-breaking.

“These are minutes drawn up by notaries who abbreviate their decisions. The script is highly administrative, very pragmatic… with rather technical vocabulary,” said historian Julie Claustre, who leads the e-NDP project.

With character recognition rates ranging between 88 and 94 percent, the project has revealed information about the cathedral’s daily life, its building work, its staff and the care of abandoned children.

Doing the same by hand would take “several decades”, said Claustre, but “it’s not just a time-saver”.

Automation enables “inquiries that were not previously possible; it transforms the conditions of research.”

World.title: Using AI to help find Mexico’s legions of missing children
World.content:
Mexico City – Veronica Rosas is one of tens of thousands of Mexican mothers looking for a child that has disappeared into a vortex of violence fueled by brutal cartel turf wars.

Now artificial intelligence may be able to help the loved ones of Mexico’s legions of disappeared.

Two new AI tools are being developed to help in the search for the more than 134,000 people being sought.

Rosas’ son, Diego, went missing at the age of 16 in the central town of Ecatepec in September 2015 after leaving his home to meet some friends.

The state prosecutor’s office said he was kidnapped by a criminal gang but have not established which group, why, or whether Diego is still alive.

“It’s been 11 years and I still don’t know where Diego is. There’s no line of investigation leading us to find out what happened to my son,” Rosas, 52, told AFP at one of the demonstrations held regularly in Mexico City to demand justice.

Cases like Diego’s have prompted two universities to develop AI tools they hope will provide answers.

Regresa (Return) was developed by Mexico’s main public university, UNAM. It uses anthropometry — human body measurements — to create an image of how the faces of minors, which remain frozen in time in missing persons posters, may have changed over time.

With investigations generally dragging on for years, these updated likenesses are a recurring demand of the families.

Countries like the United States, India and China already use facial recognition and age progression software to search for kidnapped children.

In Mexico, some prosecutors’ offices use the technology but most software relies on open-source photo databases that don’t reflect typical Mexican traits.

Regresa’s developers took a different approach.

They created their own image bank from hundreds of photos and data from 75 Mexican volunteers to make portraits that feature more typically Mexican features.

Anthropologist Ana Juarez, one of the project’s founders, explained that Regresa also uses different technology to age the children.

“Many software programs only work with facial contours or textures, or add filters that simulate wrinkles. We seek to develop a scientific approach that shows how a person grows in craniofacial terms,” she explained to AFP, referring to imagining that predicts the developments of the skull.

– Peace boxes and posters –

In Mexico, the inaction of authorities over many years has prompted many families to carry out their own investigations.

AI is also being used by an anthropologist at the private Ibero-American University to help facilitate those searches.

Emiliano Zolla is mapping the missing by gender, age and the circumstances of their disappearance, in the hope that it will help families refine their search.

Among his observations, based on data about cases in the State of Mexico, the country’s most populous, are that many of the missing are young women who disappear either going to or returning from school or work.

The use of AI could be a game-changer, Rosas said, on learning about Regresa from AFP.

“This initiative is very important because they’re not the little people who were taken back then,” she said.

Rosas has erected a makeshift mailbox bearing a picture of 16-year-old Diego on Mexico City’s main avenue to receive clues as to his whereabouts or greetings for him on his birthday.

Karla Lechuga created a search collective after the disappearance of her 19-year-old son, Jeshua Cisneros, in 2025.

Groups like hers have installed dozens of “peace boxes” in churches across the country to gather information.

They also post photos of their missing loved ones in public spaces and urge criminal groups to provide anonymous tipoffs.

“We have found some people alive, unfortunately others not,” Lechuga said.

World.title: Man Utd teetering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League
World.content:
Manchester – Manchester United travel to historic rivals Leeds on Sunday with pressure mounting on manager Michael Carrick, while Manchester City aim to extend their perfect Premier League start despite the uncertainty over their future.

Brighton could be one of the big winners should City suffer severe sanctions for breaking financial rules.

The Seagulls riding high, just two points behind second-placed Arsenal, ahead of their grudge match against Crystal Palace.

AFP Sport looks at the pick of the action from the English top-flight this weekend.

Man Utd’s worst start for 40 years

United are off to their worst league start in 40 years and were plunged further into chaos by defender Lisandro Martinez’s attack on the club’s hierarchy over a lack of investment in the squad after Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid.

The Argentine took aim at technical director Jason Wilcox after the Red Devils only added three midfielders during the transfer window.

But Martinez himself has been one of those most culpable for a miserable start to the campaign for his part in goals conceded to Fulham and Tottenham in recent weeks.

United have won just one of their opening six league games and were also dumped out of the League Cup last month by Brighton.

Leeds last beat the Red Devils at Elland Road back in 2002, but did inflict the only home defeat of Carrick’s interim spell in charge last season when the sides met in April.

Carrick is increasingly at risk of becoming just the latest manager unable to turn around a sharp decline at Old Trafford since Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013.

But he said the hostile atmosphere that will await his side presents the perfect chance to bounce back.

“What a great game (on) Sunday to prepare for. It’s a fantastic game for us, for the club, for the history, for the supporters,” said Carrick.

“Everything to do with the game is a great game so we’ll be ready for that.”

City case leaves league in limbo

Manchester City sit pretty at the top of the table with six wins from six league games, but that may all count for nothing if they do not successfully overturn a guilty verdict on over 100 charges of breaking Premier League rules.

Enzo Maresca’s men shut out that distraction to win 3-0 at Liverpool last weekend and rallied impressively in the second half despite losing 4-2 to Paris Saint-Germain in a thrilling Champions League tie on Tuesday.

But the uncertainty over their future has left the entire league in limbo.

City deny any wrongdoing and a case that began eight years ago has at least a few months left to run before the appeal is heard and a potential sanction announced.

“My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners,” said former England manager Gareth Southgate.

City can stretch their lead at the top to six points when Ipswich visit the Etihad on Saturday, with Arsenal not in action until 24 hours later at Nottingham Forest.

‘Ruthless’ Brighton eye Champions League

Arsenal’s only defeat this season came in a 3-0 trouncing by Brighton, whose remarkable rise could reach new heights this season with many of the other established giants struggling.

Brighton have soared through the divisions and into Europe on the back of owner Tony Bloom’s expertise in data analytics.

But they are yet to play Champions League football.

Despite routinely selling their prized assets to wealthier clubs, Brighton’s smart recruitment of both players and coaches has allowed them to continue to thrive.

That has also made them a neutral’s favourite but manager Fabian Hurzeler wants his side to show their nasty side against rivals Palace on Sunday.

“We want to be ruthless. We want to create this energetic atmosphere where it makes it so hard to come to this place,” said Hurzeler. “We have to keep building this together with our fans and not be the nice football club anymore.”

Fixtures (all times GMT)

Saturday

Everton v Chelsea (1130), Fulham v Hull, Brentford v Liverpool, Manchester City v Ipswich (all 1400), Newcastle v Aston Villa (1630)

Sunday

Brighton v Crystal Palace, Leeds v Manchester United, Bournemouth v Sunderland (all 1300), Nottingham Forest v Arsenal (1530)

Monday

Tottenham v Coventry (1900)

World.title: Trump’s new press secretary defends ‘lawyer’ title
World.content:
Washington – New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, under scrutiny over her legal credentials, seemed to acknowledge Thursday that she had failed the bar exam, but argued she was accurate in presenting herself as a lawyer.

Appointed by US President Donald Trump, Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

But there is no evidence to suggest that the 41-year-old press secretary has ever passed the bar exam, required to obtain a license to practice law in the United States, after graduating from Pepperdine University with a law degree.

When questioned Thursday by conservative media outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move with her husband to China.

“We just said, ‘Let’s take this time, and I’ll take the bar and see what happens.’ The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter,” she said.

In Beijing, Zacharia worked as a lawyer at a major Chinese law firm.

She explained that she didn’t retake the bar exam upon returning to the United States due to the birth of her first child.

Zacharia said that “many people in the field” had assured her that she could “label myself a lawyer, not attorney at law…and provide legal analysis, not legal advice,” given her law degree and experience in business law gained in China.

“I was very careful how I executed this,” she said.

The Campaign for Accountability, a political ethics organization, on Wednesday called for the California Bar Association to launch an investigation.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” the organization stated in a press release.

Zacharia held her first White House press briefing on Tuesday with an unusually short press conference where she answered questions from three journalists.

She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, a loyal Trump supporter and often combative press secretary, who stepped down in August to care for her young children.

World.title: Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen’s Aden
World.content:
Aden – The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government’s interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.

The attack hit command centres located inside the Al-Maashiq presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.

Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.

Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said Thursday’s attack left five people dead and 16 injured “among those working to guard the site and civilian employees”.

An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.

Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani denounced the “cowardly” act on X, calling it a “continuation of its criminal pattern of striking civilian sites and civilians”.

A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Zindani had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”.

The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted “the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them”.

Yemen’s civil war — in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 — reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.

Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.

Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.

“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” said Dr. Rayed Krimly.

The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.

Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired “several ballistic missiles” at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.

– Oman meeting refused –

In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.

The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.

“At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused,” he added.

The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.

Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month.

Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said “the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure”.

He added the group had “worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors”, saying they now had “ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats”.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country’s infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.

Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.

In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.

World.title: UniCredit says receives ECB green light for Commerzbank takeover
World.content:
Milan – The European Central Bank has authorized the takeover of Germany’s Commerzbank AG by UniCredit, the Italian bank said Thursday, calling it an “important milestone” that underscored confidence in its bid.

By acquiring Commerzbank, valued at 35 billion euros ($39 billion), UniCredit plans to cement its status as a European heavyweight.

The deal — long contested by Commerzbank — should enable UniCredit to merge Commerzbank with its German subsidiary HypoVereinsbank, acquired in 2005.

UniCredit said it had received the authorization from the ECB to “cross the 30% equity participation threshold in Commerzbank AG… and to increase its stake further without upper limits”.

“The decision represents an important milestone in UniCredit’s acquisition of Commerzbank, underscoring the ECB’s positive assessment of the transaction and the confidence in UniCredit’s solid fundamentals and strong standing within the European banking sector,” it said.

The final regulatory steps are expected around year-end, by when “UniCredit will have approximately 50% of Commerzbank’s voting rights and be able to take control of the bank,” it said.

UniCredit is notably proposing to make cuts in Commerzbank’s international network, deemed too complex and inefficient, and to refocus the bank on its activities in Germany.

Commerzbank declined to comment when contacted by AFP.

European officials have been multiplying calls for greater integration in the banking sector, arguing that the persistent fragmentation of the European Union is hampering the continent’s competitiveness.

– ‘Vital role’ –

In a surprise move in September 2024, UniCredit took a stake in Commerzbank and thereafter built up a stake of nearly 50 percent, despite fierce resistance from the German lender and Berlin, with the German state still owning 12 percent of the capital.

Commerzbank slashed thousands of jobs and hiked its financial targets in an effort to convince shareholders to back its campaign to remain independent.

But these efforts failed and, with UniCredit closing in on a controlling stake, Commerzbank’s CEO Bettina Orlopp called in late July for “constructive” talks with the Italian lender.

Berlin has, for its part, asked the head of the Italian bank, Andrea Orcel, to preserve the role of Germany’s second-largest private bank in the country’s economy.

Last month, German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil met with Orcel seeking guarantees over the bank’s future. He said it was of “paramount importance” that Commerzbank “continue to fulfil its vital role in financing the German economy”.

UniCredit wants to create a European banking behemoth better able to take on bigger US rivals, arguing that a merger would strengthen the region’s fragmented banking sector.

That is why despite resistance in Germany, some policymakers in Brussels and at the European Central Bank have been more supportive of the possible takeover.

World.title: Stent safety concerns reach Centre after reports of complications with Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka
World.content:
Rajya Sabha MP Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade has urged a review of coronary stent safety standards after reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat has taken up concerns over the safety and quality of coronary stents with the Union health ministry after a Rajya Sabha MP sought intervention following reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka.In an October 5 letter, Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan acknowledged a representation from Rajya Sabha MP Dr Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade, a medical doctor, said it had been forwarded to the department of health and family welfare for appropriate action and a reply.Gopchadeâs September 28 representation cited media reports that Sri Lankaâs regulator had directed the withdrawal of three models of Indian-manufactured drug-eluting stents over concerns including improper positioning, stent dislodgement, acute stent thrombosis and failure to expand properly. The reported issues were identified during an investigation by Sri Lankaâs Medical Device Evaluation Committee, according to the letter.The MP cautioned that the reported concerns might not all ultimately be substantiated, but said they warranted scrutiny of existing safeguards for device performance, clinical appropriateness and the detection of complications after implantation.The representation calls for more stringent pre-market testing of stents and delivery systems, including assessments of durability, deployment, expansion and dislodgement.It also seeks stronger clinical documentation to ensure stenting is performed only when medically indicated and alternatives are considered where appropriate.A key recommendation is end-to-end traceability through batch and serial numbers for every implanted stent, allowing affected devices and patients to be identified quickly if a safety alert emerges. The MP has also sought stronger adverse-event reporting, particularly for stent thrombosis, migration, incomplete expansion, deformation and delivery-system complications.The representation further calls for a mechanism to swiftly review safety alerts, recalls and withdrawals issued by foreign regulators when the same or similar devices are marketed in India. Better patient follow-up and long-term safety data collection have also been proposed to detect emerging risks early.Citing regulatory guidance from the US, the UK and Canada, Gopchade highlighted the importance of engineering and durability testing, clinical evidence, traceability and timely regulatory action when safety signals emerge. He urged the health ministry and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) to examine the issues with cardiology experts and other stakeholders.The Cabinet Secretariatâs communication does not establish that the government has accepted the allegations, ordered a formal investigation or approved new regulatory measures. The reported concerns also do not, by themselves, establish that similar complications have occurred in India.

World.title: Stent safety concerns reach Centre after reports of complications with Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat has taken up concerns over the safety and quality of coronary stents with the Union health ministry after a Rajya Sabha MP sought intervention following reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka.

In an October 5 letter, Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan acknowledged a representation from Rajya Sabha MP Dr Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade, a medical doctor, said it had been forwarded to the Department of Health and Family Welfare for appropriate action and a reply.

Gopchadeâs September 28 representation cited media reports that Sri Lankaâs regulator had directed the withdrawal of three models of Indian-manufactured drug-eluting stents over concerns including improper positioning, stent dislodgement, acute stent thrombosis and failure to expand properly.

The reported issues were identified during an investigation by Sri Lankaâs Medical Device Evaluation Committee, according to the letter.

The MP cautioned that the reported concerns might not all ultimately be substantiated, but said they warranted scrutiny of existing safeguards for device performance, clinical appropriateness and the detection of complications after implantation.

The representation calls for more stringent pre-market testing of stents and delivery systems, including assessments of durability, deployment, expansion and dislodgement.





It also seeks stronger clinical documentation to ensure stenting is performed only when medically indicated and alternatives are considered where appropriate.

A key recommendation is end-to-end traceability through batch and serial numbers for every implanted stent, allowing affected devices and patients to be identified quickly if a safety alert emerges. The MP has also sought stronger adverse-event reporting, particularly for stent thrombosis, migration, incomplete expansion, deformation and delivery-system complications.

The representation further calls for a mechanism to swiftly review safety alerts, recalls and withdrawals issued by foreign regulators when the same or similar devices are marketed in India. Better patient follow-up and long-term safety data collection have also been proposed to detect emerging risks early.

The effigy will be set alight at the committee grounds in Pitampura. Devaraha described it as a 30-foot-tall structure shaped like a cockroach, adding that the aim was to draw attention to the need to rid homes, neighbourhoods and society of dirt and unhygienic conditions.

World.title: Fees for professional courses can be hiked midstream only in exceptional cases: SC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a relief to students pursuing professional courses like engineering and medicine in private colleges who have to face a fee hike midstream, Supreme Court has held that any change in fee structure after admission can be allowed only in exceptional circumstances.

While appreciating the contribution of self-financing institutions to the education sector, a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said there should be certainty regarding fees, and students must not be forced to pay more than that prescribed at the time of admission.

"For the overwhelming majority of households, the fee payable for a professional course constitutes a substantial part of the family's income and savings; it is not a matter of incidental expenditure.

The parents make provisions for the fees... with the aspiration that their children will acquire better qualifications, secure better opportunities and build a future that may be better than their own. Many students and families also depend on educational loans to finance professional higher education," SC said, noting fees charged in professional courses are reported to be 711% higher than in general courses.





The court said it was a matter of good governance for the state and its regulatory bodies to create an ecosystem in which there was certainty about the financial obligation that students and their families need to undertake to acquire professional qualifications.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"Adverse variations in financial commitment, and the insecurities that it may create, will impact the student and the family, and, in the long run, have an adverse effect on the quality and character of the professionals in the making.

We are of the opinion that it is not difficult to formulate a scheme through which such uncertainties can be avoided," it said.

SC quashed a 37% fee hike for BTech courses for the 2023-27 cohort at Dr BC Roy Engineering College in West Bengal. The college had also imposed a new development fee.

Passing an order in favour of students who had challenged the fee hike, the bench said, "The regulatory regime for fixation of fees, as contemplated in the decisions of this court, AICTE regulations, National Education Policy 2020 coupled with principles of certainty, necessitates the relevant authorities to notify fee payable for the entire course before a student takes admission... Variation is permissible only in exceptional instances such as unforeseen increase in the expenditure.

"

World.title: Civil Services Preliminary Examination 2026: tough by design or default?
World.content:
The story so far:

The Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination, introduced in 1979 following the Kothari Committee’s recommendations, was designed as a screening mechanism — a ‘filter and funnel’ — to shortlist candidates for the descriptive Main examination. In its original format, it consisted of two components: an optional subject paper at the graduate level and a General Studies paper, with the optional paper carrying greater weight. For many years, this system functioned smoothly with minor changes.

Break-up of marks needed to aid prep, say UPSC candidates

The Alagh Committee set up in 2000 observed that the preliminary exam should have an optional paper to assess the intellectual competence of the aspirant and maintain its connection with the university system. It also proposed a Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) which would evaluate skills such as general awareness, problem-solving, data analysis and decision-making. The committee also recommended that the questions at the preliminary exam should be made challenging and a case-study approach should be adopted.

In 2009, the S.K. Khanna Committee recommended that the Preliminary Examination should be renamed as the Civil Services Aptitude Test with two common papers at the Preliminary. The preliminary exam was reconstituted to comprise two papers — General Studies Paper- I and General Studies Paper- II. The Paper I covers all conventional areas in ‘Humanities’, while Paper- II has questions on quantitative aptitude, reasoning, comprehension, interpersonal skills and communication, decision-making and problem-solving. The components of Paper- II were designed to test whether the aspirant had the ability to imbibe new technologies. Both the papers had equal weightage and the combined marks in both the papers were taken to determine merit. This change practically delinked the Preliminary Examination with the university system. After a few years, due to protests, Paper-II known as CSAT was made qualifying in nature. In practice, this meant that nearly five lakh aspirants were narrowed down to about 10,000 candidates solely based on their performance in the 100 questions attempted over two hours.

Bringing down the vast pool of aspirants to a manageable number through a paper comprising just 100 questions is an inherently difficult task. As a result, examiners were forced to constantly reinvent and compile the most unpredictable questions. Over time, it became quite evident that the objective of selecting candidates was being overshadowed by the need to eliminate them. Even the qualifying paper became a tool for rejection, with overall difficulty level of questions rising.

What changed this year?

Against this evolving backdrop, the Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination held in May has come under widespread criticism for the perceived inequity in the distribution and format of questions. Many aspirants found the paper unusually difficult and unpredictable — concerns that were publicly acknowledged by the UPSC Chairman, who expressed empathy with candidates.

This has sparked a broader debate on whether the nature of the paper was an unintended outcome of systemic constraints or a deliberate shift in examination design, and more importantly, what course corrections are needed to ensure fairness, balance and credibility in the screening process.

This year, UPSC committed itself to greater transparency, and agreed to release the answer key of the preliminary exam immediately after it. Openness also meant that the questions had to be set from verifiable authoritative sources. The questions were framed using carefully curated information drawn from government websites.

Attempting the question paper entailed sifting through 55 pages and comprehending 40,000 words in two hours. In addition to this, the subject-wise distribution of questions was distorted and the style of questioning underwent a noticeable shift. Consequently, the aspirants found no link between their preparation and the questions. They had to make guesses, “some informed” and “some wild”. Solving previous years’ questions, which was considered as the gold standard was also of no help.

This gap between the preparation and examination, coupled with the element of surprise, prompted the aspirants to voice their concerns. The democratisation of expression through social media platforms further amplified the protests, creating a snowballing effect.

The nature of the question paper, thus, appears to be less a matter of a deliberate design and more a consequence of systemic constraints — a by-product of a short-sighted examination pattern established 15 years ago. In retrospect, the committee which introduced the pattern overlooked a dictum that is crucial in policy formulation; that anticipation is the highest form of competence. It failed to adequately foresee the challenge of balancing the increasing number of aspirants with a relatively static number of vacancies.

What is the way out?

The perceived unfairness of the Preliminary Examination has been widely voiced by aspirants and has also been recently flagged by a Parliamentary Committee. However, the Chairman’s acknowledgement of the paper’s difficulty should not remain a mere instance of proverbial “ventilation therapy.” Many crises in governance are not sudden surprises; they are warning signals that were noticed but not acted upon in time. This appears to be one such signal — one that calls for deeper reflection and timely course correction.

It is time for the government to appoint a committee to revisit the examination pattern and make suitable long-term changes after public consultation. The UPSC has been collecting information regarding the socio-economic profile of the aspirants. They have information about the distribution of applicants based on place of birth, schools and colleges attended, status of parents etc. as they are collecting this information at the preliminary stage itself. This information should be used as an input to align the scheme of examination to the background of the aspirants.

Questions may be unpredictable by design, but aspirants should not feel that they are incapable of rising up to the required level of the questions or the highest positions in the country are beyond their reach. The government must undertake reforms both in the examination system and the university framework by introducing ‘bridge courses’ along the lines of the recommendations of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission. Such measures would help restore visible alignment between education and assessment.

The education system and public employment emanate from the same source — the government. Any disconnect between the two risks eroding their trust in the system. Respecting the aspirations of this generation and sustaining their faith is the order of the day. It is better to prevent a crisis rather than ‘firefight’ one.

The writer is the Director of Brain Tree, Hyderabad, an institute training candidates for the civil services examination.

World.title: Tamil Nadu wants Namma Shale app that flagged infrastructure issues in 1,300 government schools across Karnataka
World.content:
Namma Shale, a citizen-based online platform, has received reports of 1,300 schools across 30 districts in Karnataka concerning the bad shape of government schools. It includes dysfunctional toilets, lack of clean drinking water, collapsed ceiling or walls in classrooms, broken windows and doors, and more.

Dhruv Jatti, founder of Namma Shale, said: “We launched the platform on August 27, 2026, and have geotagged all 47,000 government schools in the State. Anyone can go to NammaShale.in, upload pictures and explain the issues in government schools in their respective districts, taluks, and villages.”

In order to make it easier for people to report issues, Mr. Jatti and his team has ensured that there is no need for login details. He explained: “There is only one condition to upload the details of the school. A person reporting issues on school infrastructure has to be present within 600 m of the school premises. It aims to prevent bogus or fake photos from being uploaded on the website. The main users of our platform are teachers, principals, and parents in tier 2 and 3 cities. The identity of the person who reports is displayed as anonymous to viewers. Our backend team verifies if the reports are genuine by visiting the respective school.”

When a report is verified, it enters the public map in ‘Pending’ status. If the issue remains unaddressed after 30 days, its visual status automatically escalates to ‘Overdue’ to provide transparent public visibility.

Namma Shale team is now preparing a list of 50 schools that are in critical condition and needs urgent attention. “We will be partnering with a private real estate company that is ready to improve the infrastructure of schools through Corporate Social Responsibility funds (CSR),” Mr. Jatti said.

He also noted that the platform is free either to the government or those who want to report the issues but will help companies get in touch with the government for investment via CSR. “Companies can actually register on Namma Shale and pick the schools they want to spend their funds on,” he said.

So far, Bagalkot district has the highest number of schools reported, which is 700 followed by Ballari and other districts.

He said: “The highest number of schools reported in Bagalkot doesn’t mean that only this district has issues. But it is due to more awareness among people, teachers, and students to report the issues. We are working in other districts too with teachers to report the issues.”

When asked about the infrastructure issues in government schools across Karnataka, a senior official from the Department of School Education and Literacy, said: “Whenever infrastructure issues come to our attention, we make sure to address them. In addition to this, we have our own Praja Seve-Integrated Public Grievance Redressal System (iPGRS) where citizens can report grievances of government schools. The government also has a CSR portal through which we are aiming for funds to improve 1,000 government schools.”

T.N. keen on Namma Shaale

Tamil Nadu is reportedly keen on using Namma Shaale platform to improve infrastructure in the State’s government schools. Recently, Mr. Jatti and his team met J. Innocent Divya Thomas, secretary of Tamil Nadu Education Department. “Their response has been positive. They are eager to use the platform in Tamil Nadu to improve the condition of government schools, access to education, and more,” he said.

World.title: Bengaluru-based educator starts new community library in the city
World.content:
As a child growing up in the ocean-girdled port town of Kochi, Mather (who goes by only one name) just did not have access to as many books as she would have liked. “Our parents thought it was a waste of money,” recalls the Bengaluru-based educator, a fellow with Teach For India, a non-profit working towards educational equity in India.

This led to her and some of her friends at school deciding to set up a system “where we would make sure that no two people in the group were purchasing the same book. That way, all of us got to read multiple books by rotating them,” she says, fondly recalling the books she ended up reading this way: the Percy Jackson and Hunger Games series as well as all the John Green books. “This is how a lot of us read back then,” she says.

These memories of circulating and sharing books among friends played a big role in her decision to create the Open House Library, a free community library that recently opened its doors to the public. “I wanted to start a library as long as I can remember,” says Mather, who has catalogued and made her own sizeable collection of books, around 500-odd titles, available for anyone who wants to read them. “I really enjoy it when friends come over, go through my bookshelves and pick up something. So, I thought, why not start at some scale now.”

Beginnings

On August 26, Mather, who “just couldn’t stop fantasising about having a library”, got two friends to film and edit a reel of her declaring that she was starting one very soon. “We posted it the same day, and it ended up being super popular, which was very shocking to all of us. It got something like 80,000 views,” she remembers, with a smile.

She had not really catalogued the books or set up the website yet, but the number of views the reel garnered forced her to speed up the process. “I had 14 days to catalogue all my books, set up the website, create a sign-up process and figure out how the library would work,” says Mather, who officially opened the library on September 10.

While anyone can view the collection on the website, you need to sign up on a Google form to access it, which then imports the sign-up data to the library website. Once you fill out the Google form and become a member, you can also log in to place holds and checkouts, attend reading circles or browse the physical collection, she explains.

Since she operates out of her house and is away at work during the first half of the day, customers can pick up books at the location or have them delivered by courier between 5 and 10 pm on weekdays. “And once you check out a book, you can keep it for a month,” says Mather, a member of the Free Libraries Network (FLN), a collective of grassroots organisations and practitioners that builds, operates, and advocates for free libraries in India.

Curating her collection

Some of the books, which are part of her collection, include classics like George Orwell’s 1984, Mark Twain’s The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Leo Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina, Sylvia Plath’s The Bell Jar and J.D. Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye, as well as the contemporary literary fiction of Haruki Murakami, Miranda July, Fredrik Backman, Sally Rooney, Paul Murray, Toni Morrison and Kamila Shamsie, among others.

“I am an avid reader of classics and modern classics, so that is a big part of my collection,” says Mather. She also owns a lot of anti-caste writing, feminist and queer literature, and translations, all of which library members can borrow.

However, she has steered clear of popular genres like self-help, romance, and fantasy, a conscious choice she knows could risk alienating some readers. “I don’t read those, but a lot of people have offered those as donations. But I’ve had to deny them for space and curatorial reasons.”

In her view, these genres are both accessible and affordable, unlike literary fiction or queer literature, which is often “very expensive to access in India,” Mather says, adding that she decided early on to offer a curated collection of books. “It is very important for me to maintain my collection as an anti-caste, feminist, queer collection.”

Reading circles and more

Another aspect of the Open House Library is its reading circles, which members can join voluntarily. So far, she has held three editions in her house, where people can bring their own books or choose one from the library. “We just sit quietly and read for an hour, and after we finish, sit in a circle and share our thoughts,” says Mather, who believes the circles offer a chance to slow down, quiet the mind and articulate thoughts on what one is reading.

“I’ve really enjoyed having those discussions with people. In fact, more people want to join, but we are limited by space right now, so I have started reaching out to other public spaces asking if they can host us.”

Mather’s bigger goal now is to recreate, on a larger scale, what she and her friends did in school years ago: rotating books within a circle of people. “When I set up the library, I did not want to get other people’s books involved, because I wanted to check, with my own books, how safe this is, whether books got lost or damaged.”

Right now, Mather is working on a website that will facilitate this exchange, allowing people to sign up as both a borrower and a lender, if they want to. “This would allow each member to also upload their own personal libraries onto the website. This way, even if I don’t have the book, someone else may,” she says, pointing out that book exchanges are already happening between members, in an informal way.

For her, having the library has been a “heartwarming” exercise so far, one she hopes to sustain and expand. “Because we are only a month in, I am trying not to get too ahead of myself. But in my head, the long-term goal is to have a huge library space that can house a much bigger collection in Bengaluru,” says Mather.

To know about the library, log in to libib.com/u/openhouselibrary

World.title: Electric car crashes into divider, triggers multiple vehicle commission on Hyderabad’s PVNR Expressway
World.content:
A speeding EV car that lost control and crashed into a divider triggered a multiple-vehicle collision involving around six cars on the PVNR Expressway in Hyderabad on Thursday (October 15, 2026) night, leaving several motorists stranded in a traffic jam.

The accident occurred around 10 p.m. near Pillar No. 135 when the driver of an electric car reportedly lost control of the vehicle and rammed into a pole on the central divider. Around five other cars subsequently collided, resulting in a pile-up on the busy expressway.

The occupants of the first car reportedly sustained minor injuries. No fatalities were reported.

#HYDTPinfo #AccidentAlert🚨 An accident has been reported near Pillar No. 131 on PVNR Expressway towards Aramghar. our mobile staff of @shotr_rjnr have reached the spot to clear the vehicles. Commuters are requested to proceed with caution and follow traffic personnel instructions. #HyderabadTraffic — Hyderabad Traffic Police (@HYDTP) October 15, 2026

The collision disrupted vehicular movement along the expressway, with traffic slowing considerably as the damaged vehicles obstructed the carriageway. The Hyderabad Traffic Police issued alerts about the accident near Pillar Nos. 131 and 140 on the stretch towards Aramghar and deployed personnel to regulate traffic and facilitate the removal of the vehicles.

Further details about the circumstances leading to the collision were awaited.

World.title: TPCC chief reiterates demand for BC/OBC column in Census-2027, assures greater political share for BCs
World.content:
Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee (TPCC) president B. Mahesh Kumar Goud said that the Congress was committed to securing a greater political share for Backward Classes (BCs) and asserted that a BC leader would become Chief Minister of Telangana in future.

He reiterated the demand for inclusion of a BC/OBC column in the nationwide Census-2027 and called upon BCs to unite and fight for its inclusion.

Addressing a public meeting, organised under the chairmanship of TPCC OBC cell chairman and MLA Veerlapalli Shankar at Shamshabad on Sunday (October 4, 2026), Mr. Goud said that Rahul Gandhi had given the Congress the political confidence to take up the cause of BC rights and social justice.

Telangana had set an example by conducting a caste survey, he said and slammed the Centre for exclusion of OBCs from its surveys while retaining the Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) categories.

He said the Congress government had begun increasing BC representation in local bodies and would expand their representation in the Cabinet, Legislative Council and State corporations. He called upon BC communities to unite and demand their share in political power and welfare benefits.

Expressing confidence that Rahul Gandhi would become Prime Minister, he said the Congress would conduct a nationwide caste census if voted to power at the Centre and described social justice as a legitimate political demand.

Transport and BC Welfare Minister Ponnam Prabhakar said Telangana had emerged as a national example by conducting a caste survey. He said Telangana and Bihar had gained recognition for undertaking the exercise.

Mr. Prabhakar said a nationwide caste census was necessary to determine reservations, welfare measures and political representation on a scientific basis. He urged the BCs to mount pressure on the Union government by taking the Telangana Assembly’s resolution on the issue to the grassroots.

AICC OBC cell chairman Anil Jaihind, All India Professional Congress president Madhu Yaskhi Goud, State government Adviser V. Hanumantha Rao and other BC legislators spoke at the meeting.

World.title: Kuwait Airways flight grounded in Thiruvananthapuram airport due to technical issues returns to Kuwait
World.content:
The Kuwait Airways flight that was grounded at Thiruvananthapuram International Airport on Thursday (October 15, 2026) after it was suspected to have hit a bird returned to Kuwait on Friday.

According to airport sources, the aircraft reported technical issues after it was suspected to have hit a bird and remained grounded at the airport soon after landing.

The aircraft was scheduled to fly back to Kuwait with passengers from Thiruvananthapuram on Thursday morning itself. However, airline authorities aborted the return journey and arranged another wide-bodied aircraft to carry passengers booked on Thursday and Friday. The replacement aircraft departed for Kuwait at 7.30 a.m. on Friday with passengers of both services.

Meanwhile, airport authorities said the aircraft had been under ‘Aircraft on Ground’ (AOG) status since it landed on Thursday morning, as it could not fly back due to technical issues. The aircraft was later flown back to Kuwait without passengers at around 10.30 a.m. on Friday, the authorities said.

World.title: Congress attempted to turn Supreme Court premises into protest site: BJP
World.content:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Thursday (October 15, 2026) accused Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and his allies of attempting to turn the Supreme Court premises “into a protest site” and using “mob pressure to intimidate the judiciary”.

On Monday, Mr. Gandhi and other Opposition leaders marched to the Supreme Court and submitted a petition on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls issue.

At a press conference, BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said that, in protest against the “serious act”, Supreme Court advocates submitted a signed memorandum. “Rahul Gandhi has been named as a respondent in the petition, and the Supreme Court has issued a notice in the matter seeking a response from him,” he said.

Referring to a controversial post uploaded on the official X account of the Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee on Monday, which was subsequently deleted and the person responsible removed from the position, Mr. Bhatia alleged that such an act reflected Mr. Gandhi’s “mindset”.

He also targeted Mr. Gandhi and Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra over allegations of misconduct towards female police personnel during the protests. “Concern for women’s dignity arises only when the women belong to the Gandhi family,” he alleged.

During the press conference, the BJP leader welcomed the Supreme Court’s judgment upholding the Madras High Court’s ruling that “a person who embraces Islam cannot claim the status of backward class (Muslim)”.

“The Supreme Court has clarified that only individuals professing Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism can be recognised as members of a Scheduled Caste,” he said. The BJP leader accused the Congress and its allies of playing “appeasement” politics.

World.title: Trump banking on ‘swift end’ of Iran war to bring down fuel prices
World.content:
• Pezeshkian decries US blockade, insists ‘military force’ will not compel Tehran into submission

• Washington weighs using ‘Mother Of All Bombs’ against Iranian energy sites, CNN reports

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump once again predicted a swift end to the war with Iran, and a sharp drop in oil prices once the conflict concludes, even as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that military action cannot force them into submission.

“The Iran war will end very soon … Soon, as they want it to end,” Trump told reporters in Montana. “They’ll never have a nuclear weapon, and oil prices will drop like a rock.”

According to Anadolu Agency, Trump also expressed uncertainty over which Ira­nian officials the US was negotiating with.

“They don’t have a navy. They don’t have an air force. Their army is decimated. Their leaders are gone,” Trump said. “I should have probably left their leaders because I don’t know who the hell we’re negotiating with.”

“Iran was the bully of the Middle East,” he said, adding that the country was no longer as powerful as it had been.

Trump also claimed that US strikes had destroyed Iran’s naval fleet and rendered its military aircraft unusable. He said Iran had 159 ships and asserted that none remained operational, while also claiming that its fighter jets had been destroyed on the country’s runways.

‘Iran won’t submit to force’

Meanwhile in Tehran, President Pezeshkian warned that military action cannot force a country into submission, adding that his country “must find a way to strengthen national cohesion and unity”, Al Jazeera reported.

He said that the country was facing its most intense blockade since the 1979 Revolution, accusing the United States of seeking to provoke public protests.

“Over the 48 years since the Revolution, we have never faced such intense blockade, war and difficulties as we are facing now,” Pezeshkian said in a speech broadcast by state television.

He accused Washington of seeking to make life difficult for Iranians to fuel public anger and trigger unrest. Pezeshkian said the US was focusing its efforts on making “the people become upset and face difficulties, and then for social protests to emerge so that they can achieve their sinister objectives”.

‘Mother Of All Bombs’

Meanwhile, the US is considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb — better known by its nickname, the “Mother Of All Bombs” — against Iran if Trump decides to renew combat in the deadlocked war, CNN reported on Thursday.

The military is planning for the potential use of the weapon to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to the news outlet, which quoted officials familiar with the matter.

“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the plans told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”

Trump is trying to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November’s midterm elections, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and the fuel and other price rises it has caused are hurting his Republican Party.

Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been at an impasse since the summer, and Washington has in recent weeks dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.

However, officials have raised doubts over the efficacy of the bomb if deployed, particularly its ability to destroy suspected underground nuclear sites in Iran, as well as concerns over possible civilian casualties from such a huge weapon.

Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

World.title: Shooter kills four at Oregon elementary school before being shot dead by community member
World.content:
A 16-year-old shooter opened fire on Thursday at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing four people including three children, before being killed by an armed member of the community who had pursued the assailant into the school, police said.

The shooter entered Silver Rail Elementary School by firing through locked doors, police said, without offering any details beyond the suspect’s age.

The dead were children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher. In addition, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told a press conference.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, appearing at the same briefing, thanked the community member who “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life.”

“No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we’re probably going to cry privately,” Kotek said.

Krantz said the community member, whom he did not identify, saw the suspect enter the school and pursued him.

School shootings have become a recurring feature of American life, including high-profile attacks such as those at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018, and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.

Each shooting revives debates over gun laws in a country where gun rights are protected under the Constitution’s second amendment. Gun rights advocates have argued for arming teachers as a means of defence.

Police trained for mass shooting

Krantz said every Bend police officer went through a full day of active shooter training in August.

“Unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis, and we must,” Krantz said.

“This is going to be a long investigation.”

Thursday’s shooting took place in Bend, a city of about 100,000 people in rural central Oregon, 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest.

Silver Rail Elementary School serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.

Gun control advocate Gabrielle Giffords, a former congresswoman who survived a mass shooting in 2011, said in a statement she was “heartbroken” by the shooting in Bend.

“This cannot continue to be a reality in our country. Leaders at every level must step up and act,” Giffords said.

Emergency responders received a call at 12:59 p.m. PDT (1959 GMT) from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.

In the minutes afterwards, dozens of calls were received saying the shooter had entered the school, Krantz said. Law enforcement immediately directed the school to go into lockdown, he said.

Officers arrived at 1:02 pm and moments later an officer reported the suspect had been shot, Krantz said. Police entered and confirmed the suspect was dead, he said.

World.title: Two killed as rain, snow disrupt life across Gilgit-Baltistan
World.content:
• Babusar Pass road closed to all traffic; Diamer police rescue tourists stranded after heavy snowfall

• Karakoram Highway remains open despite blockages along route

GILGIT: Two young men were killed on Thursday when a landslide struck their vehicle on the Karakoram Highway, as intermittent rain and snowfall disrupted routine life across Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) and blocked the Babusar Pass road and other links to remote areas.

Local police said Arif Hussain and Kashif Ali, residents of Gul­mat in the Nagar district, were travelling on Karakoram High­way when a rock struck their vehicle in a landslide-prone area near the Pissan section, early on Thursday. Both men were seriously inj­u­red and later succumbed to their injuries. They were shifted to a nearby government hospital, where doctors pronounced them dead.

According to the local administration, rain caused landslides at multiple locations in the Nagar section on Wednesday and Thursday.

“Heavy rain is currently continuing in the Nagar district, leading to landslides at various locations along the Karakoram Highway. However, the highway remains open to traffic,” a GB police spokesperson said.

“The public is advised to contact the Police Helpline at 15 to check the latest status of the highway before travelling.”

Meanwhile, authorities said upper areas of GB received intermittent snowfall, while lower areas received rain.

“The Babusar Pass road has been temporarily closed to all traffic due to heavy snowfall at Babusar Top,” the police spokesperson said in a statement. “All travellers and tourists are advised to avoid unnecessary travel and to choose alternative routes.”

A large number of tourists travelling through the Babusar Pass road toward GB were stranded near the Babusar Top area on Wednesday night.

Diamer police personnel rescued the travellers stranded in the snow and brought them safely to Babusar Top, the police spokesperson said.

Tourist Police said heavy snowfall received at Khun­jerab Top made the Karakoram Highway potentially dangerous. Traffic between Pakistan and China through the Khunjerab Pass remained disrupted following slippery conditions.

Snowfall also continued across the upper areas of the Astore, Skardu, Ghanche, Shigar, Kharmang, Hunza and Nagar districts, creating difficulties for local residents. Many link roads have been blocked.

Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

World.title: IHC seeks PTI response in case about Imran’s X account
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Isla­mabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday granted PTI interim chairman Barris­ter Gohar Ali Khan additional time to submit a written response to a petition seeking a ban on party founder Imran Khan’s official X account, adjourning the hearing until Nov 23.

Justice Arbab Muham­mad Tahir heard the petition, filed by Ghulam Mur­taza, while Barrister Gohar appeared in person.

The court observed that Barrister Gohar could have submitted his response in writing.

The PTI leader told the court his party did not cla­im ownership of the X ac­­c­ount in question. However, citing a change in circumstances, he sought additional time to submit a detailed response.

Meanwhile, Judicial Magistrate Shaista Kundi issued arrest warrants for the accused who failed to appear in cases registered against the PTI founder and others in connection with the 2014 sit-in.

Mr Khan could not be produced in court as he is currently incarcerated in Adiala jail. The magistrate then adjourned proceedings till Nov 25 and directed that evidence be presented at the next hearing.

World.title: AJK assembly speaker calls for consensus on future of refugee seats
World.content:
MUZAFFARABAD: Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq has called for a broad-based consensus on the future of refugee seats in the assembly, urging political leaders to help resolve the current crisis through dialogue and reforms.

Speaking to journalists at the Speaker House on Thursday, Mr Fa­­rooq said political leaders had an opportunity to align themselves with national objectives and provide guidance by finding a way forward rather than dwelling on the past.

“Learning from mistakes is wisdom. We need to explore new avenues for the future,” he said, adding that he supported reforms in all institutions.

AJK could not progress with its large administrative structure and high expenditure, he said, while maintaining that the newly elected government, comprising young people, should be given an opportunity to move in the right direction.

Backs institutional reforms, says electricity and flour subsidies will continue

He also said subsidies on electricity and flour would not be withdrawn, though relief and concessions should be targeted on the basis of data.

Distinguishing between constitutional offices and the executive, he claimed that although power was influential, the assembly speaker was not part of the government, just as the state president was not. “The assembly is not the government; the cabinet and the prime minister constitute the government,” he said.

The government had been in office for only a few weeks, and the second phase of cabinet formation was still pending. It would be completed upon the return of PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif to Pakistan, he said.

Mr Farooq said the government and cabinet had not been expanded because elections in seven constituencies of Poonch division were still pending. Without representation from these areas, he added, the government could not be considered complete and fully functional.

Poonch situation

Mr Farooq said informal negotiations were under way through the AJK president to improve law and order and ease tensions in Poonch. He expressed the hope that backchannel contacts would produce positive results and urged the media to avoid speculation until the talks yielded an outcome.

He accused the PPP of attempting to exploit the Poonch situation for political gain during its brief stint in power, adding that the phased elections had been held with the party’s consent.

The speaker said the state president and the entire political leadership should come forward to find solutions through dialogue. Political parties and their leaders had a responsibility to play an effective role, he said, adding that the process of rendering them irrelevant and ineffective had begun during the previous assembly.

Mr Farooq recalled that he and some other PML-N leaders had called for a fact-finding commission a year ago to examine the circumstances contributing to the current situation, but no political party had supported the proposal.

Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

World.title: Judicial commission on Mir Raza’s murder  hands over sealed report to Sindh govt
World.content:
KARACHI: A sealed report prepared by the judicial commission formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in Mir Raza Ali’s murder investigation was handed over to the provincial government on Thursday.

The commission, headed by Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court, concluded its proceedings last week after examining 49 witnesses during 15 hearings, including inspection of the crime scene.

The inquiry report along with associated documents was handed over to focal person of the provincial government and additional secretary of home department Javed Ahmed Abro by registrar of the commission Abdul Majid on the premises of the SHC.

As Justice Sial was hearing cases at the SHC Hyderabad circuit court, the registrar of the commission handed over the sealed report along with the entire record of the proceedings to the provincial authorities.

It’s up to provincial authorities whether to make the document public or keep it secret, says official

According to a communication sent by registrar Abdul Majid to the chief minister of Sindh through the focal person, since Justice Sial has been sitting at SHC Hyderabad pursuant to the roster commencing from Oct 12, the registrar has handed over the sealed report to the focal person along with executive summary, statements of witnesses and other supplementary documents.

After receiving the record, Mr Abro told reporters that he would hand over the sealed report along with other record to the provincial government and it was the prerogative of the government to decide whether the inquiry report was to be brought into the public domain or otherwise. In August the provincial government formed the commission, which was tasked with making recommendations for further investigation and forensic analysis or legal/departmental action and it was required to submit its findings and recommendations to the Sindh government within 30 days.

However, the commission had struggled to meet its deadline and sent an application last month to the Sindh government for an extension in its tenure till Oct 15. Therefore, the provincial cabinet granted an extension.

Besides examining 49 witnesses and available record, the commission had also sent questionnaires to Karachi police chief Azad Khan, head of current investigation team DIG Amir Farooqui and DIG East Farrukh Lanjar after dismissing an application of aggrieved family to summon the senior police officers to testify before the commission.

Therefore, the three police officers had submitted written answers before the commission through a commissioner appointed by the commission.

The 25-year-old businessman and Institute of Business Administration graduate, Mir Raza Ali, had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS and his body with gunshot wounds was found a day later in bushes in a Gulistan-i-Jauhar’s locality.

Initially, the police built the case around suicide on the basis of the first autopsy, which indicated a bullet entry wound on the chest, and by pointing out business losses and money borrowed by the victim.

However, police surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had disputed the findings of the first post-mortem conducted by medico-legal officer Dr Osama Sheikh.
