World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: CoreWeave’s slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
World.content:
Shares of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave steadied on Thursday after a sharp slump, as investors worried about the debt financing behind the artificial intelligence build-out.

The loss-making cloud company has about $50 billion in debt and has become a focus of concerns that the data-center boom is being fueled by credit, straining newer players and pressuring cash flows even at giants such as Alphabet and Meta Platforms.

CoreWeave’s slump fueled a global rout in AI stocks, underscoring investor doubts about whether future revenue from the technology can keep pace with the spending.

World.title: Singapore probing firms over haze-causing Indonesian fires
World.content:
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has vowed to investigate firms responsible for fires that have shrouded the city-state in haze for weeks, warning that those found culpable could face legal action.

“We are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” Wong said in a Facebook post late Thursday. “Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries.”

The city-state and neighboring Malaysia have been blanketed for weeks by toxic smog from a severe wildfire season in Indonesia that’s been exacerbated by a powerful El Nino weather pattern, bringing dry weather to the region. Governments are under increasing pressure to respond to what is the worst bout of haze since 2015.

World.title: Red Wings owner responds to backlash from fans calling for team to be sold
World.content:
The Detroit Red Wings entered Thursday near the bottom of the NHL standings.

Captain Dylan Larkin requested a trade this summer, and one of the team’s top defensemen remains without a contract. The Red Wings also don’t have a permanent general manager after removing franchise legend Steve Yzerman from the role in July.

Through it all, Red Wings owner Chris Ilitch said he understands why fans have begun chants directed at him to “Sell the team.”

World.title: Yakuza member found not guilty in fatal shooting of Gyoza no Ohsho president
World.content:
A senior yakuza member was found not guilty on Friday over a fatal shooting of the president of Gyoza no Ohsho restaurant chain operator in a high-profile case that took nearly a decade for the suspect to be arrested.

The Kyoto District Court found Yukio Tanaka, 59, not guilty of killing Takayuki Ohigashi, the then-72-year-old president of dumpling chain operator Ohsho Food Service, in the early morning of Dec. 19, 2013, at a parking lot in front of Ohsho’s headquarters in the city of Kyoto.

As the murder went unresolved in the following months and years, there was rampant public speculation about the culprit. The case was considered one of Japan’s most captivating unsolved crimes alongside the 1984-85 Glico Morinaga corporate blackmail case and the slaying of a family in Tokyo’s Setagaya Ward in 2000.

Yukio Tanaka | JIJI

Nine years after Ohigashi was killed, Tanaka, who had been in prison over a separate case, was arrested in October 2022 in connection with the crime and was on trial for murder and violation of a weapons law.

Tanaka is a senior member of the Kudokai gangster organization based in Kitakyushu, Fukuoka. The trial began in late 2025, and Tanaka pleaded not guilty to the charges.

“I am absolutely not the culprit,” Tanaka said when the trial opened last November. “As a person who aims to follow the code of chivalry, I would be able to accept one or two false accusations, but I can’t allow myself to be implicated in such a sensational crime.”

Information from Jiji added

World.title: Katayama says G20 should monitor markets with urgency
World.content:
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has called for Group of 20 policymakers to closely monitor financial markets, speaking against a backdrop of renewed pressure on Japan’s currency and a selloff in bonds around the world in recent weeks.

“We reaffirmed our existing commitments on foreign exchange at the Group of 20 and other meetings,” Katayama told reporters Thursday after meetings in Bangkok with finance chiefs and central bankers from key developed and emerging markets. “I stressed the need to monitor financial markets with a high sense of urgency there.”

Earlier in the day, Katayama warned speculators that Japan was prepared to take action in the currency market again if necessary, after the yen weakened to its lowest level against the dollar this month — following hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data. She also said there’s been no change in the stance of Washington and Tokyo since their joint intervention to prop up the yen in July.

The yen weakened after U.S. consumer price data Wednesday showed inflation accelerating to its fastest in five months. The currency briefly touched ¥158.95 per dollar, but later pared its losses as U.S. Treasury yields declined. The yen rose in Thursday trading.

Katayama said Group of Seven and G20 finance chiefs discussed in Bangkok a range of challenges facing the global economy, with G7 members agreeing to conduct tabletop exercises to prepare for frontier AI-related incidents.

In terms of surging global bond yields, Katayama said earlier Thursday that Japan is among the few advanced economies in a position to make a credible case for fiscal sustainability. She said Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and her administration have repeatedly made clear their commitment to steadily reduce the nation’s debt-to-GDP ratio and keep government bond issuance at appropriate levels.

Katayama said that some officials at the Bangkok meetings cited massive private investment in AI and data centers as an unavoidable factor driving bond yields higher globally. She told her counterparts that governments needed to set credible fiscal sustainability targets and create budget space for growth-enhancing investment to address the problem.

Katayama also confirmed her official appointment as chair of the Development Committee, a joint ministerial forum of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. She will serve a two-year term and is expected to preside over her first meeting during the institutions’ spring gatherings in Washington next April.

“I am deeply honored by this appointment and feel a profound sense of responsibility,” Katayama said. “As chair, I will work to make the Development Committee an even more meaningful forum for dialogue and cooperation, and contribute to addressing development challenges with the support of member countries.”

World.title: Emergency alert for magnitude 9.9 quake withdrawn minutes later
World.content:
The Japan Meteorological Agency withdrew an earthquake early warning issued Friday afternoon after initially sending an alert for a magnitude 9.9 earthquake, forecasting strong shaking across northern, eastern and central Japan. In reality, a smaller quake was recorded, but no strong shaking was felt in Japan.

A magnitude 6.9 earthquake centered off the Kamchatka Peninsula occurred at around 12:38 p.m., with an emergency warning issued at 12:40 p.m. setting off alarms on public speakers and mobile phones. The agency called off the alert at 12:48 p.m. No tsunami warnings or advisories were issued.

A JMA spokesperson said at a press briefing that the agency’s system had erroneously placed the quake’s epicenter off the Kuril Islands and overestimated its magnitude, triggering the initial warning. The agency ruled out a possible cyberattack.

“We are currently investigating the cause and will provide an explanation as soon as it is determined,” the spokesperson said.

The 12:38 p.m. quake, which struck at a depth of 160 kilometers, registered shindo 1 on Japan’s seismic intensity scale in Hakodate, Hokkaido, according to JMA data.

World.title: Three children, one teacher killed in Oregon elementary school shooting
World.content:
Three children and one teacher were shot dead at an elementary school Thursday in the northwestern U.S. state of Oregon, police said, adding that the assailant was a 16-year-old who was killed by an armed bystander.

Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary school in Bend, a city of about 100,000 people.

Mike Krantz, police chief of Bend, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun.

World.title: Japan, South Korea agree to extend $10 billion currency swap arrangement
World.content:
Japan and South Korea agreed Thursday to extend their $10 billion currency swap arrangement, reportedly for another three years, preserving a source of U.S. dollars that either state can draw on during a financial emergency.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and her South Korean counterpart Lee Hyoung-il reached the agreement in Bangkok, where they were attending international financial meetings.

Both ministers acknowledged that their countries had sufficient foreign currency liquidity but recognized the swap’s significance as a symbol of sustained cooperation.

The swap agreement, set to expire at the end of November, is expected to run through November 2029, with its size unchanged. Japan’s Finance Ministry did not immediately confirm its duration on Friday.

The extension comes as Seoul faces substantial U.S. investment commitments under its tariff deal with Washington last year. The $350 billion package includes $200 billion in strategic investments, capped at $20 billion per calendar year, and $150 billion for shipbuilding.

Buying dollars to fund the investment deal could weaken the South Korean currency, making imports and dollar-denominated debts more expensive. The extension preserves an emergency source of dollars for Seoul, which has fewer financial safeguards and smaller foreign exchange reserves than Tokyo.

The swap works as an emergency borrowing facility. If South Korea faces dollar shortages, its authorities can exchange won for dollars held in Japan’s foreign exchange reserves. Japan can similarly obtain dollars from South Korea in exchange for yen.

Transactions are temporary, with the borrowed dollars to be returned later.

Access to dollars matters because banks and businesses need them to repay overseas debts and make international payments. During financial turmoil, lenders may become reluctant to supply dollars, making those obligations harder to meet.

The previous bilateral swap arrangement expired without being renewed in February 2015, amid strained relations over historical and territorial disputes. Both governments at the time explained that the decision reflected economic and financial considerations.

The two countries agreed to revive the swap deal in 2023 as ties gradually improved, signing the current three-year agreement in December that year.

American athleisure brand Alo Yoga generated nearly HK$20 million (US$2.6 million) in sales during its first week in Hong Kong, breaking an opening-week record at a luxury waterfront shopping centre and highlighting growing appetite for premium wellness products amid an uneven retail recovery.

The brand, which soft opened its first Greater China flagship at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui on September 25, recorded the highest first-week sales among new stores at the mall, excluding jewellery and watch retailers.

The store is set to hold its official grand opening on Friday evening.

The nearly HK$20 million haul came from its two-storey, 7,000 square foot flagship, which occupies the former premises of British luxury food retailer Fortnum & Mason. The British brand closed its Hong Kong outlet in January.

World.title: More than music: Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra strikes a chord across generations
World.content:
For nearly five decades, the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra has worked to bring its music to a wider audience, including people who might never have considered entering a concert hall.

Executive director Celina Chin Man-wah said the orchestra had long sought to ensure Chinese music was not seen as distant, formal or difficult to understand.

That has meant commissioning new works, exploring different musical styles and developing programmes for younger audiences.

“We cannot rely on the old repertoire alone,” Chin said. “New works are essential if Chinese music is to keep developing and speak to future audiences.”

World.title: Hong Kong vies for role in robotics boom with launch of embodied AI hub
World.content:
The Hong Kong Productivity Council (HKPC) opened the city’s first experimental hub for embodied artificial intelligence on Thursday with the participation of seven mainland and Hong Kong companies, including industry leaders Unitree Robotics and Galbot, as the city looks to carve out a role in the global robotics boom.

Located at the HKPC Building in Kowloon Tong, the Embodied AI International Applications Hub, housed under the HKPC’s industrial AI and robotics centre, features simulated real-world environments where the companies can test and optimise their latest robotic designs, ahead of potential global roll-outs.

“Hong Kong’s application scenarios have an international characteristic,” said Sunny Tan, HKPC chairman, at the opening ceremony. “For many mainland robot manufacturers, they can train their robots for international application scenarios without leaving the country here.”

Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong said that the hub marked a major milestone in Hong Kong’s efforts to align with national initiatives to advance in embodied AI and robotics, and pledged further government support to promote development in the field.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.title: The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.content:
In 2016, two groups of Chinese livestreamers began feuding on Kuaishou, a short-video platform popular in China’s countryside and lower-tier cities. Their leaders, Brother Hu and Captain Shamate, were both grassroots streamers from Northeast China, or Dongbei. Video after video, they traded insults, accusations, and challenges. These gang-style exchanges were loud, theatrical, and unmistakably regional, full of Northeastern Chinese dialects, bravado, and the kind of chaos that early Chinese livestreaming platforms thrived on.

The feud was widely believed to be staged, a scripted collaboration designed for dramatic effect. But that did little to diminish its appeal. Audiences couldn’t stop watching, and clips of the confrontations soon took on a life of their own. Over time, they spawned an influential body of memes that spread across various media, even video games, one of which has now become an unlikely hit on Steam.

The phenomenon emerged against the backdrop of Dongbei’s changing cultural identity. Once the heartland of China’s heavy industry, the region is often referred to as the country’s Rust Belt after decades of industrial decline. Locals have turned that history into both tragedy and comedy. TV dramas such as “The Long Season” have tapped into nostalgia for the region’s industrial heyday, helping make the “Dongbei Renaissance” a cultural buzzword. Northeasterners have long played an outsized role in Chinese comedy. On television, Zhao Benshan’s sketches made the Northeastern accent familiar to audiences nationwide; on Kuaishou, Northeastern dialects and slang became a rich source of humor and memes.

It was in this context that the feud between Brother Hu and Captain Shamate gained traction. Fans recorded and reposted clips to streaming site Bilibili, where they were remixed, quoted, and jokingly treated as “classics.” The saga became known as “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.”

Seven years later, those memes were turned into a video game. A Summer in Northeast China (DongBeiZhiXia), released for free on Steam on Jan. 9, 2023, was developed and published by Zhuangbuchun Studio, led by Zhuangbuchun, a Bilibili content creator with over 2 million followers. Up till today, the game has since accumulated more than 12,000 positive reviews on Steam, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating despite being available only in Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Its success shows just how far a regional internet joke can travel when platform dynamics, an existing fan community, and a developer’s instincts align at the right moment.

A Summer in Northeast China is a “gal game,” a genre typically centered on interactions with female characters. Set years after the original Kuaishou incidents, the game follows Xiaoliang, who must recover her memories with the help of a cast of female companions, each loosely inspired by figures from the “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” phenomenon. The game’s most conspicuous adaptation is its gender-swapping: the male roles at the center of the original memes are reimagined as women, retaining their names, signature visual traits, and personalities while being reshaped to fit the conventions of the gal game and ACGN (anime, comics, games, and novels) aesthetics.

In effect, the game translates its source material across cultural registers. “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” ran on masculine confrontation, local bravado, and the rough-edged authenticity of Kuaishou livestreaming. A Summer in Northeast China recasts that material through the softer, character-driven lens of the gal game, while keeping enough recognizable references to reward those who remember the source. Events from the original memes return as callbacks for longtime fans, while the first-person linear narrative gives newcomers an accessible way into Xiaoliang’s story.

The game also draws on subcultures Zhuangbuchun knows well, including shamate — a Chinese youth subculture known for its flamboyant hairstyles and fashion — and otaku — intense fandom of anime, manga, games, and related media, originating in Japan — while its use of Northeastern dialect keeps it rooted in Dongbei. Together, these influences reflect the game’s broader approach: combining distinctly Northeastern humor and internet culture with the appeal of manga and anime.

Zhuangbuchun made the game the way many Chinese indie developers do: on a limited budget and in public. The project was self-funded, with a crowdfunding campaign on domestic creator-sponsorship platform Afdian covering part of the cost. He handled much of the design and direction himself, outsourced some work, and recruited voice actors for the female cast.

But developing the game in public was not simply a funding strategy. It also became central to how Zhuangbuchun built an audience around the project. Nearly a year before the game’s launch, in April 2022, he posted a video announcing his gender-swapped take on “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” The video received over 1.5 million views, 71,000 likes, 23,000 saves, and 11,000 reposts.

From there, Zhuangbuchun kept followers closely involved in development. He posted early character designs, solicited feedback on voice acting, and explained delays. When viewers complained about an accent or suggested a different look, he listened and sometimes changed the game accordingly. In that sense, the project was not simply marketed to its eventual players. It was partly shaped by them.

Zhuangbuchun also visited Shenyang, the capital of the northeastern Liaoning province, several times to document where the original Kuaishou events took place. On one return trip after the game’s release, he even ran into some of its fans. These travel vlogs reinforced the sense that the game was being made by someone invested not only in the memes but also in the places and culture from which they emerged.

The steady updates kept the project visible on Bilibili and positioned Zhuangbuchun as part of the internet culture that turned the original Kuaishou videos into “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” His existing followers helped attract attention, while the project’s local roots kept audiences engaged. The original Kuaishou streamers added another layer to this relationship, posting reaction videos and engaging with Zhuangbuchun’s posts, further blurring the line between the game and the people who inspired it.

A Summer in Northeast China is neither the first game to adapt internet memes nor the first to blend Chinese regional culture with global subcultural aesthetics. What makes it unusual is the particular combination: a free gal game with a gender-swapped cast, a distinctly Northeastern setting, a developer who was already a prominent Bilibili creator, and source material rooted in the unruly world of early Kuaishou livestreaming.

For indie developers working with limited resources, A Summer in Northeast China offers a distinctive example of how online culture can move across platforms and media. The same platforms that provided the game with its source material also supplied an audience, feedback, publicity, and a community willing to participate in its development. Rather than simply adapting an existing meme, Zhuangbuchun used the participatory culture surrounding it to carry the material far beyond its origins.

That process creates tensions between local authenticity and internet marketability, and between the crude energy of the original memes and the game’s polished presentation. Yet, A Summer in Northeast China never loses sight of its regional origins. Zhuangbuchun, who has told me he loves Dongbei despite not being from the region, is part of that story: an outsider drawn into its culture who now helps reshape it for new audiences. The game has traveled from Kuaishou to Bilibili to Steam, changing along the way. But for all the distance it has traveled, it has never really left Northeast China.

Zhu Siheng, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Rochester, and Han Yisong, a postdoctoral researcher at the City University of Hong Kong, also made contributions to this research.

(Header image: Promotional art for the video game “A Summer in Northeast China” on Steam.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.title: Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.content:
Users in China who “sold their faces,” or licensed their likenesses, for use in AI short dramas and livestreams months ago report receiving few or no requests for their use, and consequently almost no related income.

Domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily reported Monday that many users on multiple domestic face-licensing platforms, such as NCAIGC, Mirafans, and ActID, which promise steady income and payment after use of a person’s likeness in their licensing agreements, have not received remuneration.

Face-licensing platforms first emerged around May this year, fueled by the growth of AI-generated content, particularly ultrashort dramas. At a September press conference held by the State Council Information Office, it was announced that more than 90% of the 430,000 ultrashort dramas released in China in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated.

The platforms attract users by advertising a low barrier to entry and high returns, with claims such as “earn nearly 2,500 yuan ($370) in three days with face selling” going viral on social media, state broadcaster CCTV reported Tuesday.

Face licensing lets individuals license their digital likenesses — otherwise protected from use by others under China’s Personal Information Protection Law — to a platform for use in AI ultrashort dramas and ads, among other content.

According to CCTV, registration on face-licensing platforms usually requires users to undergo real-name authentication, upload photos of themselves, and set a desired price for each use of their likeness. Some platforms also require users to specify which roles and scenarios they allow companies to use their likenesses for, such as villains, death scenes, or romance.

Buyers can select single-use or single-project authorization, and the licensor must accept within 24 hours, after which authorization documents are generated and materials released. Platforms take about a 30% cut.

Regular users can earn about 100 yuan per short video that uses their likeness, with some platforms setting a 500-yuan minimum, while professional actors may reportedly receive up to 10,000 yuan.

Wang Jinlin, a model based in the southern city of Guilin, licensed her face on ActID in May. If a buyer selects her portrait for commercial use, she says they’ll typically offer a one-time payment of 500 to 1,000 yuan. But so far, no studio has asked to use her likeness, she told Sixth Tone.

“There are probably few companies making AI live-action short videos right now — there’s no complete pipeline yet,” Wang said. She sees joining the platform as a way to protect her portrait: storing her portrait data should flag unauthorized use, and require any creator to apply for authorization through the platform before using her likeness.

That many report never receiving payments after licensing their faces could be because demand for non-celebrity likenesses is low. The head of AI production at a film and television company, surnamed Zheng, told CCTV that companies mainly seek celebrity and short-drama influencer likenesses, leaving little opportunity for regular people.

Liu Xiao, founder of ActID, told Southern Metropolis Daily that the platform ultimately provides users with an entry point to be seen and selected by buyers, rather than a contract that guarantees monetization.

Criminals may also steal others’ likenesses for AI use rather than go through official channels like face-licensing platforms. On Oct. 8, Beijing’s market regulator warned that lawbreakers tend to scrape selfies, videos, and voices from social platforms and use AI to generate avatars and clone voices from this material for commercial and livestream use.

“Many celebrities cannot fully guarantee their portrait and voice rights, let alone facial licensing in the AI field,” Zheng said. “It’s hard for ordinary people to define how large the gray area (of legal portrait use) is.”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An authorization page on face-licensing platform NCAIGC, Aug. 26, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.title: A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.content:
HEBEI, North China — It began with a “crazy” idea: use yoga to lift the village out of poverty. And it worked.

In 2016, yoga put Yugouliang on the map. Tucked away in the northern Hebei province, about 300 kilometers from Beijing, the village began attracting experts, journalists, and advertisers to watch its mostly elderly population perform stretches, headstands, and the splits beside crop fields, chicken coops, and sheep pens.

New revenue streams followed: livestream sales, online classes, yoga festivals, TV appearances, and even a movie. By 2020, the annual per capita net income for households under the national poverty alleviation program had reached 12,335 yuan ($1,840), up from 2,800 yuan in 2015, taking the village above the poverty line.

Today, a large stone marker proclaiming Yugouliang a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village” still stands at the village entrance, but the national attention has long faded.

As the officials who drove the trend departed and the locals aged, the streets fell quiet, and the young people who had returned to help with social media marketing and sales left once again for better opportunities in major cities.

Yet 10 years on from that viral fame, yoga remains a force in many households here, either as a source of income or simply as a memory of how it opened a door to another world.

Stretching the imagination

When Jin Xiuying, then Yugouliang’s director of women’s affairs, was first tasked with going door to door to promote yoga in March 2016, she didn’t even know how to write the word in Chinese.

Naturally, she had a hard time convincing villagers. She recalls typical responses like, “Are you crazy? Farm work is exhausting enough. Who has time to exercise?” Others were confused and thought she was offering free fish, as the phrase sounds similar to “yoga” in Mandarin.

“Do me a favor, have a try,” she urged them. “The new official wants us to do it.”

She was referring to Lu Wenzhen, then 50, who had recently been appointed the village’s resident first secretary as part of a national program that dispatched officials from major cities to help develop impoverished rural areas. He’d previously been the Party secretary of a vocational college in Shijiazhuang, the Hebei capital.

Lu arrived that February, taking a seven-hour car ride to a village so remote that he couldn’t locate it on his map app.

Its 100 or so residents — mostly the middle-aged wives and elderly parents of migrant workers — survived by farming crops, raising cattle and sheep, or renting out their land. More than half survived on incomes of less than 2,952 yuan a year, below the official poverty line, while chronic illnesses like bronchitis, arthritis, and rheumatism were common due to years of physical labor and the cold climate.

In early 2016, the village still had no internet access, and playing mahjong or card games were among the few forms of entertainment. While visiting people’s homes, Lu observed that many elderly women would sit cross-legged for long periods on their kang, a traditional heated brick platform.

It reminded Lu of the lotus position in yoga — and that’s when he struck on the idea that this 5,000-year-old Eastern exercise could be the village’s ticket out of poverty. The locals could learn through movements they already knew: sitting on a kang, pulling weeds from the fields, and pushing a stone mill to make tofu.

The only issue was that Lu had never practiced yoga. So he watched instructional videos online, then taught others what he’d learned on an open field outside the village committee office.

He started with breathing exercises, getting villagers to stand with their legs bent, extend their arms in a circle in front of their chests, and make long “woo woo” sounds. Then they would crawl on all fours to strengthen their shoulders and backs and improve their balance. Yoga poses came later.

Lu bought 50 pairs of white gloves to protect his students’ hands during floor exercises, as well as 100 red foam yoga mats. Soon, nearly 70 villagers were showing up to his twice-daily training sessions, mostly women aged over 65.

At first, Jin received complaints from villagers about soreness, and she was still convinced that “Lu was just trying something out and wouldn’t stay long.” But after three months, the symptoms from her herniated disc began to ease, potentially saving her tens of thousands of yuan in medical costs, and others were reporting that they also felt healthier. So she persisted.

In March 2017, a producer from Hebei TV called to invite the village’s “yoga grannies” to perform in its studio. A month later, the state broadcaster CCTV broadcast a clip of Yugouliang residents in various poses.

The unprecedented attention inspired the locals to train harder to master tougher positions, such as the one-legged tree pose, the Sirsasana handstand, and lateral splits. More men began joining Lu’s sessions, and even the village’s superstitious hawks stopped suggesting that female yoga practitioners would bring about poor harvests by “pointing their backsides at heaven.”

Rising fortunes

In the summer of 2017, Jin’s daughter returned from university for the holiday and helped register an account on the Kuaishou short-video platform to promote “China’s yoga village.” In just over a year, it gained more than 300,000 followers.

Then came livestreaming. Most evenings, villagers would gather beside a concrete road to film themselves practicing yoga under the streetlights. They sold local products — potato noodles, red beans, soybeans, oat flour, and quinoa — and prerecorded yoga courses, which brought in thousands of yuan on a good day.

The income was divided according to how often each villager took part. Frequent participants were making more than 1,000 yuan a month, five times the rural pension at the time.

The group practiced year-round. In winter, they filmed in an abandoned single-story house after blocking holes in the walls and windows with old clothes and installing two coal-fired stoves to stay warm.

Wu Qilian, 83, who then practiced yoga with her husband, said that her grandson quit as a gig worker in Beijing to return home and run a social media account for the family. Livestreaming helped them earn several thousand yuan a year in additional income.

Yoga competitions and festivals were organized to attract visitors, while the village women continued to perform on TV shows across the country, wearing their signature blue headscarves and red athletic outfits.

“If you couldn’t do a headstand, if you weren’t good enough, they wouldn’t take you out to perform,” Li Xiufang told Sixth Tone. The 69-year-old returned to the village from Beijing after retiring at 55 and found “everyone was doing yoga, so I just joined in.”

Netizens dubbed Yugouliang “China’s No. 1 Yoga Village,” while the national sports authority designated it as a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village.”

In 2022, the Chinese media giant Tencent released the movie “Welcome to Yoga Village” via its streaming service. A dramatized account of Lu’s poverty-alleviation efforts, it features several locals in minor speaking roles.

“Look at this. I’m a movie star,” said Zhang Xiying, 72, who had a few lines of dialogue. Pointing to a wall of photos in her home dedicated to her on-screen appearances, she added, “If I didn’t do yoga, who would invite an old woman like me anywhere?”

The village also secured more than 2.69 million yuan in government funding to build a small quinoa processing plant, creating 16 jobs. Many locals had switched to growing the grain because of its popularity among fitness enthusiasts.

On Feb. 29, 2020, Yugouliang was officially declared out of poverty.

Twist of fate

The boom times didn’t last long. Compared with other crops, quinoa requires deeper and more intensive tilling, so the aging villagers soon stopped growing it. Lu’s attempts to introduce a new variety of potato also failed when negotiations to secure a wholesale buyer broke down.

Livestream sales, which led to competition as well as resentment from families not sharing in the revenue, saw a sharp drop-off. After only a year back home, Wu’s grandson returned to Beijing to look for work.

Meanwhile, several members of the yoga group died, including Wu’s husband, or moved away to live with their children. Many of those remaining in the village are either too old to achieve difficult positions or have debilitating health issues.

Jin stepped down as the village’s director of women’s affairs in 2021. Residents say her successor promised to pay for yoga participation, but the money never materialized, so they stopped attending.

Liu Runtao, 58, took the role this year and has been struggling to put the team back together. She’d never practiced yoga before returning to the village in recent years. Now, when she posts notices about training sessions, usually only her relatives show up.

In villages like Yugouliang, organizing events and upgrading infrastructure often depend on approval and funding from town or county authorities. However, as officials change, so do their offices’ priorities.

Lu told Sixth Tone that he would sometimes win a higher official’s backing for a project only to see them transferred out before anything was finalized, taking things back to square one. Even when the village was at its most popular, funding to update its tourism facilities was slow to come.

Lu stepped down as resident first secretary in 2023 and returned to the vocational college in Shijiazhuang. Now 60, he still returns for major events and helps promote Yugouliang, but he feels it’s now someone else’s responsibility to keep the “yoga village” narrative alive.

Winding down

On one sunny July afternoon, a group of villagers sat chatting at a bus stop. Services pass through here just twice a day. Apart from the occasional truck carrying agricultural supplies, the main road is largely silent.

Liu had arranged a yoga training session, but just nine elderly women showed up. Most residents can no longer achieve the poses that made them famous. Only the septuagenarian Zhang can still balance with both feet off the ground.

The new resident first secretary, Li Jidong, who worked for the same Shijiazhuang college as Lu, watched from the sidelines. He has little interest in yoga, apparently seeing it more as a liability. “What if someone has a brain hemorrhage while doing it?” he said, after interrupting the session to suggest the elderly women attempt a safer activity.

Li believes that Yugouliang’s remote location and climate make Lu’s vision of building a tourism industry here difficult to realize.

“I don’t have that kind of ability. No single institution or person can solve a problem this big on their own,” he said. Li has only been in the job for two years but admits that he already wants to leave.

During a recent yoga event, Li asked people to help with livestream sales of local farm products, but the results were disappointing.

The village Party secretary, Zhang Pengcheng, who took over from his father in 2021, said he has also tried encouraging residents to make short videos and livestream, but many struggle even to use smartphones, let alone speak standard Mandarin with viewers online.

Yet he sees the remaining yoga team as the “embers” to spark a tourism boom. In 2025, he organized a gala in which the team performed on ice beside a bonfire. A livestream of the event drew about 100,000 viewers.

But for now, the priority is improving infrastructure. In July last year, the township government and local businesses funded the opening of a guesthouse with room for up to 86 guests. It has yet to turn a profit. When Sixth Tone visited, its doors and windows were shuttered.

The village has also built a canteen for pensioners, with dishes starting at just 2 yuan. It was also temporarily closed in July because of a staff shortage.

Before stepping down, Jin earned a yoga instructor qualification in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, and has since relocated to Zhangbei Town, about 60 kilometers from Yugouliang. She offers free classes to locals and teaches online six days a week.

Of the few residents still practicing yoga in Yugouliang, Zhang Xiying, despite her age, remains the most able and enthusiastic — though not for the village’s benefit, but for her own family’s.

“Exercise keeps me healthy,” she said, after wrapping up a practice session. “And I need to take good care of my old man.”

Additional reporting: Wu Huiyuan; editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Villagers practice yoga together on a summer afternoon in Yugouliang, Hebei province, July 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.title: Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.content:
Popular Chinese TV drama “Against the Current” has sparked debate about power dynamics between divorced male characters and their female counterparts after featuring a romantic plot between a low-ranking young woman and a high-status divorced man.

The discussion began after the 48-episode drama premiered Sept. 11 on Tencent Video, its international platform WeTV, and Disney+, and was bolstered by this month’s release of a similar drama also featuring a divorcé, “Irreplaceable.”

Set in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), “Against the Current” follows Shen Jialan, whose privileged life is upended when her grandfather, a renowned academician, is falsely accused of treason, endangering the lives of her entire family.

In exchange for a previous act of kindness, a couple allows Shen to take on the name of their late daughter, Xu Lanxiang, to escape execution. Under her new identity, Shen goes to work as a maid for her former fiancé, Lin Jinqi, who has since married another woman. Lin eventually divorces his wife to marry Shen.

After its release, the series became the most popular series on Disney+ in markets including North America and Spain, and topped WeTV charts in the U.S. and at least seven Asian countries outside China. Domestically, it currently tops analytics platform Yunhe Data’s long drama most-viewed list, with over a third of market viewership on Oct. 12.

Though the drama has been applauded for its storytelling and nuanced character development, some viewers have criticized Lin’s characterization, arguing that the show romanticizes unequal relationship dynamics, fueled by his status as a male divorcee. Lin, who divorces his wife after she cheats on him, curries favor with the King, asking him to force Shen to marry him against her will.

The debate has spread to other Chinese romance dramas that increasingly feature divorced and remarried male leads, from past hits such as “The Story of Minglan” (2018) and “The Glory” (2025), to dramas like “A Splendid Match” and “Irreplaceable” released this year.

Viewers have critiqued the imbalanced power dynamics in these series, which feature powerful, wealthy divorcés who offer protection, stability, and emotional guidance, often to younger, naive heroines from lower social statuses.

The recent popularity of remarried male leads marks a departure from the decadeslong shuangjie, or “purity on both sides,” trope in Chinese romance dramas, which favors depicting couples with no prior romantic or sexual experience before they fall in love.

In these stories, male leads are usually portrayed as successful, devoted figures whose affection belongs exclusively to the heroine, while female leads are frequently portrayed as innocent and kind.

Social media users have linked the shift to changing social realities, including rising divorce rates and the growing visibility of divorce and second marriages. Others have criticized it as a cheap way to create attention-grabbing plot twists, adding that the trend risks turning divorced males into a symbol of maturity and status while reinforcing unequal relationship dynamics.

Viewers point to the gender gap commonly found in romance narratives between divorcés and their female counterparts. When dramas instead feature divorced female protagonists, the corresponding male leads are often single or younger, and the story follows them as they “catch up” to their female counterparts professionally.

In the modern drama “Sniper Butterfly,” for instance, divorced protagonist Cen Jin reunites with a younger man who later becomes a successful professional in his own right as well as her business partner.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Against The Current.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.title: Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.content:
A daylong, nationwide buy-one-get-one-free promotion by Chinese milk tea brand Chagee, launched in honor of Zheng Qinwen becoming the first Chinese woman to win the China Open title on Sunday, saw its online ordering systems crash amid inundated orders.

The company made the announcement via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo the night of Zheng’s win, saying the sales promotion would run throughout Monday, calling it a “new (moment) in history worth raising a glass to together.” The tennis player has been a Chagee brand ambassador since 2024.

The sudden traffic surge beginning around 8 a.m. Monday crashed the brand’s mini program on super app WeChat, leaving many users unable to place orders. The crash sparked heated discussion online, with a related hashtag on Weibo attracting over 180 million views as of Tuesday and rising to the platform’s trending topics list. A check by Sixth Tone later on Monday found the problem had been resolved.

At the China Open, Zheng defeated Russia’s Mirra Andreeva, the French Open champion, in two straight sets, catapulting her to the 23rd-best women’s tennis player in the world. Last June, Zheng ranked world No. 4, a career high, but injuries over the past year forced her to stop competing and caused her ranking to drop to No. 160. She entered this year’s China Open as a wildcard, invited directly by the organizing committee.

After the win, several photos of Zheng lifting the China Open trophy were posted on her official Weibo account. A caption alongside the photos reads: “The weight of this trophy is the weight of a dream, dedicated to the younger me who always worked hard for that dream.”

According to domestic media outlet ChinaStarMarket.cn, Zheng currently holds 14 brand endorsements spanning cosmetics, sportswear, luxury accessories, cars, and technology, among others. Her endorsements include international brands such as Nike, Dior, Rolex, and Wilson, as well as Chinese brands such as Chagee, Alibaba-owned digital payment system Alipay, and large language model Qwen, also owned by Alibaba.

During Zheng’s break from competition, none of her brand endorsements were terminated, according to domestic media outlet Jiemian News. Instead, many companies increased their support, with Chagee upgrading her title from Global Health Ambassador to Global Brand Ambassador, and Wilson launching a Zheng-inspired signature tennis racket.

According to Forbes’ world tennis player earnings list, released in August and covering the 12 months prior, Zheng was the only Chinese player in the top 10, ranking seventh globally with $22.6 million — with over 97% reportedly coming from brand endorsements.

Zheng also earned roughly 474 million yuan ($71 million) in prize money and endorsements between 2024 and 2026, matching in three years what Chinese tennis legend Li Na made over her entire 15-year career.

Zheng’s commercial breakthrough came in 2024, when she finished runner-up at the Australian Open, her best Grand Slam result and the second-best by a Chinese player after Li Na. She went on to win the Paris Olympics women’s singles title that year, becoming China’s first Olympic tennis singles champion.

At the Guangzhou Auto Show in November 2024, Audi’s Chinese sub-brand AUDI named Zheng a brand ambassador. In January 2025, Dior selected her as its global brand ambassador, making her the first Chinese athlete to hold the role.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: China’s Zheng Qinwen poses with the trophy after defeating Mirra Andreeva in the women’s singles final of the China Open at the National Tennis Center in Beijing, Oct. 11, 2026. Fred Lee/Getty Images/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019102/She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.title: She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019102/She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.content:
For Chinese opera fans, 2026 will surely be remembered for one thing: Mao Weitao’s triumphant return to the stage.

Few outside China may have heard of her, but the 63-year-old is a titanic figure in her chosen discipline, Yue opera, and part of that rare group of artists who transcend their field to achieve crossover fame.

Over her nearly 50-year career, Mao has fearlessly reinvented the traditional art form, dragging it back into China’s cultural mainstream through a series of daring — and often provocative — creative choices.

From shaving her head to play Kong Yiji, the poor male scholar and eponym of Lu Xun’s classic short story, to producing “The New Dragon Gate Inn,” hailed as China’s first immersive opera show, she has continually pushed the boundaries of what a Yue opera can be.

The innovations have helped her achieve unprecedented commercial and critical success. But they have also made her a polarizing figure: even today, she jokes that she feels like she should wear “a bulletproof vest” whenever she premieres a new work.

Mao’s journey began at 17 with her first bow in Yue opera — one of around 300 regional varieties of traditional Chinese opera, originating in the city of Shaoxing in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.

Yue opera is known for being the only Chinese opera style in which female performers play every role — including male characters — and Mao quickly stood out for her rare ability as a kunsheng: an actress able to infuse male roles with beauty and elegance.

Within five years, she became the first ever Yue opera performer to receive the Plum Blossom Prize, China’s highest honor for theatrical performance. She has since won the award twice more — the only Yue opera actress in history to receive the so-called Plum Blossom Grand Prize, given to those who win the honor three times.

Yet she has also sparked plenty of outrage. Her raw, stripped-back portrayal of Kong Yiji in 1998 — which saw the 36-year-old Mao appear onstage with a buzzcut and dressed in rags — violated every norm of Yue opera, which traditionally seeks to delight audiences with lavish costumes and graceful performances.

A heated debate over the merits of tradition versus modernization followed, as critics accused Mao of sacrificing Yue opera’s soul for the sake of her creative vision. But ticket sales were excellent — and Mao continued to forge her own path.

After stepping back from performing in the mid-2010s, she co-launched her own production company — Baiyue Cultural Creative — with partners including the Chinese tech giant Alibaba and a Zhejiang Yue opera troupe. More experimentation followed.

In 2023, Baiyue debuted “The New Dragon Gate Inn” — an immersive Yue opera based on a hit 1992 Chinese martial arts movie. The first Chinese opera show of its kind, it followed a format similar to immersive stage shows like “Sleep No More,” letting the audience move freely through a recreation of the inn as the actors performed around them.

When the show became a massive commercial success — turning lead performers Chen Lijun and Li Yunxiao into stars — it felt like Mao was passing the baton to the next generation. Mao, however, had other ideas.

Earlier this year, she unexpectedly returned to the stage for the first time in nearly a decade in the new show “Su Dongpo” — an opera based on the life of one of China’s most beloved poets.

With Mao in the title role of Su, it is one of her most avant-garde productions yet. The show ditches Yue opera’s traditional linear narrative structure, instead leaping from one episode in Su’s life to another in a style Mao likens to Christopher Nolan’s movie “Inception.”

Critics have complained that “Su Dongpo” looks more like a Broadway musical than a Yue opera. But Mao has grown used to such comments: after decades in the spotlight, she knows she’ll never please what she describes as “traditionalist” opera fans.

The opera’s ending even reads like Mao’s preemptive answer to the controversy she knows the show will provoke. “Who’s afraid?” she asks, echoing a line from Su’s celebrated poem “Calming the Waves.”

In this interview, Mao discusses the new show, its reception, and the broader struggle to revive Chinese opera without losing its essence. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Su Dongpo ranks among China’s greatest cultural icons. What inspired you to create a show based on his life?

Mao: Su Dongpo’s life was full of dramatic turns. He once rode high in his prime, then suddenly hit rock bottom and was driven from place to place in exile. Yet he always remained at ease with himself — he had a natural gift for dealing with hardship. As I see it, he kept his feet in the mud while flowers bloomed in his heart.

At my age, with so many years of stage and life experience, I need a role with exactly this kind of depth, dramatic expressiveness, and tension. Ten years ago, I probably couldn’t have played him. Now, the timing feels just right. My looks may not be what they were, and my voice is no longer as clean as it was — but that heavier, thicker texture happens to suit the role.

Honestly, I think I’m quite like Su Dongpo — “an incorrigible optimist.” When I run into difficulties, I get a good night’s sleep, have a good meal, and my troubles pass. A while ago, when we performed in (the eastern city of) Nanjing, I bumped into a good friend, the writer Bi Feiyu. He asked me, “If Su Dongpo were a woman, what do you think she’d be like?” I answered with one word: “Me.”

Sixth Tone: Your emotional resonance with Su is clear onstage. But is it true that the creation of this show was also a difficult process?

Mao: It was. At the lowest point — when we were rehearsing the passage built around his most famous work, “Charm of a Maiden Singer: Memories of the Past at Red Cliff,” I found I simply could not go on. I had no idea how the music should be presented, how the vocals should sound, or how it should be performed.

But this impasse ended up handing me the key to a breakthrough. I thought of the rankou technique — a tradition of using stylized false beards to highlight a character’s personality and emotional state — and decided to turn to that ancient craft for help.

Yue opera doesn’t use the rankou, so I traveled to (the northern province of) Shanxi to study beard technique under Li Yuexian, the celebrated female performer of male roles in Jin opera. What I picked up was only the basics of the art — but it mattered enormously. I had found the key that unlocked the door to Su Dongpo. I knew how to play him.

Sixth Tone: That section is particularly powerful. It’s rare to see the rankou used that way — not hanging quietly, but torn off and wielded in a fierce dance. It became more than a marker of gender and age, instead signifying Su Dongpo’s creative, social standing – and something else that resists being put into words.

Mao: I was indeed trying to transform the rankou technique into a “second face” for building the character — a vehicle for Su Dongpo’s complex emotions and the shifts in his attitude towards life. This kind of artistic grafting across opera genres is also an exploration of what might be possible when Yue opera kunsheng portray middle-aged and elderly men.

That said, although the rankou solved one of my biggest creative problems, the production was still extremely difficult to rehearse — we halted rehearsals three times before it finally premiered. That process itself was very “Su Dongpo.” The hardships I went through in rehearsals helped build the character. The closer I drew to Su’s spiritual world, the more it nourished me. Every performance I give is a process of self-growth. Playing Su Dongpo has made me grow once again.

Sixth Tone: You have said more than once that playing Su Dongpo was a healing process.

Mao: Yes — and not only was I healed; I think the audience was, too. I have been thinking a lot about one question recently: China has so many celebrated literati; why is Su Dongpo so especially beloved?

We revere the unyielding passion of Qu Yuan — who drowned himself in the Miluo River after the fall of the capital of Chu, the ancient kingdom where he served as a loyal minister — and admire Tao Yuanming’s return to a pastoral life. But we cannot live the way they did: those paths are impossible to replicate in contemporary society.

Su Dongpo’s attitude toward life, by contrast, offers practical wisdom that remains useful for anyone living today. His life went through peaks and troughs, yet he never sank. He forged a path forward through adversity and kept his composure even amid the storms. And he loved life: he loved cooking, he loved making friends.

These qualities may be exactly what comforts people today. The fast pace of life, emotional exhaustion, uncertainty — everyone suffers some degree of anxiety. And Su Dongpo’s answer is neither escape nor resistance, but acceptance.

From this perspective, I believe this play can be embraced not only by Chinese audiences today, but by international audiences as well. How can Yue opera go global? I have thought about that question for many years, and I have done a great deal of experimenting. In my view, this production can go global, because Su’s spiritual state has the power to resonate with audiences of different countries and cultures.

Foreign viewers may not understand the conventions of Yue opera, may not be familiar with Song dynasty history, may never even have heard of Su Dongpo — but they can understand how a person faces the vicissitudes of fate and maintains dignity and gentleness in adversity.

Sixth Tone: Speaking of going global, the lighting, movement, stage design, and even some of the music all feel very modern. Were international audiences on your mind while you were rehearsing?

Mao: Not at all. Our first consideration was still the domestic audience. Today’s audiences have seen so much. The traditional “one table and two chairs” staging is fine as far as it goes, but it may no longer satisfy people’s aesthetic needs when it comes to how stories are told and opera is experienced. What we have been exploring all along is how a comprehensive stage aesthetic can connect with contemporary audiences and deliver the emotional value that modern people are looking for.

Sixth Tone: You have always been a “reformer” of Yue opera. In your mind, is there anything about Yue opera that must absolutely never change?

Mao: Sure. First, the dialect of Yue opera must not change. Its language and phonology are Yue opera’s most distinctive artistic markers and a living embodiment of eastern China’s Jiangnan culture. Pronunciation gives rise to melody, and melody gives rise to vocal style; the soft, lilting local accents carry Yue opera’s original spirit and warmth. To abandon the dialect would be to lose the soul of the genre.

Second, performance style centered on all-female Yue opera troupes must not change. Since the first women’s training school was founded in 1923 and all-female Yueju opera went on to become mainstream, this uniquely captivating aesthetic has shaped the genre’s grace and vitality, and set Yue opera apart from every other form of Chinese opera. We must keep passing down and developing this distinctive artistic character.

Third, the aesthetic centered on xieyi — suggestive, imagistic expression — must not change. Xieyi is not only the aesthetic hallmark of Yue opera; it is the aesthetic hallmark of all traditional Chinese art. This beauty of suggestion runs through every detail of vocal design, performance, and stage setting, and is core to traditional Chinese art. We should always hold fast to this essence of Eastern aesthetics, and find a new national style that belongs to the present moment

(Header image: Mao Weitao (center) stars in the premiere of the Yue opera “Su Dongpo” in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, Dec. 29, 2025. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019116/On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.title: On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019116/On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.content:
SHANGHAI — The 38th annual International Business Leaders’ Advisory Council for the Mayor of Shanghai (IBLAC) convened on Sunday, with global industry leaders recommending the city build a stronger global brand through AI deployment, sports, and cultural tourism.

Founded in 1989, IBLAC brings together international business leaders annually to discuss the city’s economic development. It has grown from 12 members from eight countries to 42 members from 15 countries, working in industries ranging from sports and consumer goods to health care and finance.

In 2025, the added value of Shanghai’s service industry reached 4.5 trillion yuan ($620 billion), ranking first among Chinese cities and accounting for nearly 80% of the city’s GDP. By 2030, that figure is expected to reach roughly 6 trillion yuan, with service imports and exports exceeding $300 billion.

“Shanghai’s service industry plays a pivotal role in driving economic growth, stimulating consumption and fostering,” John Waldron, president and chief operating officer of Goldman Sachs, said in his keynote speech.

He urged Shanghai to expand its cross-border data transfer framework and give greater priority to financial institutions and applicants.

Next, Jason Furman, an economics professor at Harvard University, advised Shanghai against chasing bigger AI models and instead to leverage its service sector — financial institutions, hospitals, and law firms, among other operations — to lead AI deployment. He also recommended attracting global scientists while training Chinese workers in skills that machines cannot replicate.

“AI will not take a city’s place in the world economy, but a city that uses AI better will,” Furman said during the event’s keynote speech.

Elliott Hill, president and chief executive officer of international footwear brand Nike, said that Shanghai should increasingly capitalize on signature events like the Shanghai Marathon and F1 Chinese Grand Prix. Each event should become a citywide celebration that connects sport with commercial districts, public spaces, culture, and retail, driving greater economic impact across the city, he said.

Hill also suggested making exercise part of everyday life by creating more community sports-related gatherings, from school programs to community runs. He called for deeper collaboration among government, business, and universities to expand access, attract world-class events, and develop talent, cementing Shanghai’s status as a global sports capital.

Manny Maceda, partner and chairman at global consultancy Bain & Company, urged the city to shift tourism toward experiences over attractions, centering tourist experiences around Shanghai cultural features such as its Art Deco architecture, jazz-related history, food, and riverfront customs to strengthen the city’s global cultural brand and sharpen its identity as the place “where East meets West.”

At a Sunday afternoon press conference, Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming said attendees offered many pertinent, forward-looking recommendations. “We will work to turn this global wisdom into a ‘Shanghai solution’ for expanding and upgrading the service industry,” he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019108/China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.content:
China has drafted its first departmental rules on gig workers’ labor rights, strengthening protections for platform-based flexible employees such as food delivery riders.

The draft, released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Oct. 8, is open for online public feedback until Nov. 8.

The proposal comes as flexible employment grows in China, with the number of people in flexible employment — including those who rely on internet platforms to earn a living — projected to reach 320 million this year, according to the China New Employment Research Center. Gig work has also come under fire for subjecting workers to excessive hours, opaque algorithms, and gaps in social security coverage.

In 2021, China introduced its first guidelines clarifying platforms’ responsibilities toward gig workers regarding employment, remuneration, social security, and workplace safety. In 2024, the country issued related guiding cases, and this July, it expanded occupational injury insurance for gig workers.

Under the new draft, platforms and their partner businesses must sign labor contracts with workers that meet the legal criteria for employment relationships, such as full-time employees. It excludes people who use online platforms to run their own businesses independently or offer freelance services on their own terms.

For workers in more flexible arrangements, such as part-time work or work across multiple platforms, platforms must sign written employment agreements specifying pay, labor protections, and liability for breaking the agreement, among others. When platform companies and partner businesses jointly manage workers, all three parties must sign a written agreement.

The draft also clarifies dispute resolution procedures. Platforms bear primary responsibility for overseeing partner businesses’ employment practices, and workers involved in legal disputes may name both the platform and its partner as parties to a case. When workers challenge pay, working hours, performance reviews, or account bans, companies must investigate and respond within 48 hours.

Platforms must also build reasonable task-allocation systems and performance metrics into their algorithms, avoid encouraging excessive work through targets or incentives, and explain relevant algorithmic rules to workers and authorities.

Decisions with “significant consequences for workers,” including suspending work assignments or banning accounts, must also undergo human review.

The draft further states that employers will face legal responsibilities and penalties for violations under existing legislation. For instance, employers may be required to pay outstanding wages, overtime pay, or economic compensation. If wages fall below the local minimum wage, employers must pay the difference.

“The draft’s biggest breakthrough is placing workers who are under the management of platforms but do not fully fit into an employment relationship under protections, and applying past traditional labor laws to flexible platform-based work,” Wang Tianyu, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, wrote in a related commentary.

“At the same time, it establishes mechanisms to hold companies accountable and prevent them from evading employment obligations, such as through subcontracting or inducing workers to register as individual businesses,” he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.
