World.title: FACT CHECK: Viral photos of fire, ambulance trikes are AI-generated
World.content:
The Patient Transport Vehicles distributed by Marcos were part of a program by the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, but they do not resemble the tricycle-type 'Hospital on Wheels' shown in the viral post

CLAIM: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. distributed ambulance and fire trikes to local government units (LGUs) across the country.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post uploaded has already garnered over 172,600 reactions, 12,000 shares, and 11,800 comments as of writing.

As the caption reads, “Nagpapatuloy ang pamamahagi ng mga compact Patient Transport Vehicle o PTV sa iba’t ibang LGU sa bansa… Ayon kay Pangulong Ferdinand Marcos Jr., naging konsiderasyon sa pagpili ng ganitong modelo ang mga lugar na hindi madaling mapasok ng malalaking emergency vehicle, prinsipyong ginagamit din ng administrasyon sa ilang maliliit o tricycle-type firetruck.”



(The distribution of compact Patient Transport Vehicles [PTVs] to various local government units [LGUs] across the country continues. According to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the selection of this type of vehicle took into consideration areas that are difficult for large emergency vehicles to access—a principle also applied by the administration in the use of smaller, tricycle-type fire trucks.)

The Facts: All three pictures attached on the graphic material used in the Facebook post were AI-generated according to an analysis made by Hive Modernation. The first photo of Marcos riding the fire truck was 99.9% likely to be AI-generated; the second photo which was the ‘hospital on wheels’ was 81.7%; and the third photo of the fire trikes was 93.9% AI-generated.

On October 7, the Bureau of Fire Protection, through a Facebook post, clarified that the fire trucks being used for their operations are full-sized with varying capacities and capabilities depending on operational requirements.



Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla clarified that the 1,500 fire trucks to be procured from South Korea in 2027 are also full-sized.

Fire trikes: Remulla clarified that the circulating fire trikes were not procured by the DILG but by LGUs, particularly San Antonio, Nueva Ecija.

“To be clear, ang bumili no’n [fire trikes] ay [LGU] Nueva Ecija. Ang binibili namin ay galing South Korea, 10 million pesos each.”

(To be clear, Nueva Ecija was the one that purchased those fire trikes. The ones we are buying are from South Korea, at ₱10 million each.)

Ambulance trikes: Marcos, through the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO), distributed Patient Transport Vehicles (PTVs) to all 82 provinces nationwide, according to a press release dated July 24, 2026.

The PTVs were provided under the PCSO’s Medical Transport Vehicle Donation Program, with units distributed to LGUs free of charge and equipped with a stretcher, spine board, wheelchair, blood pressure monitor, first aid kit, and oxygen system.

However, no reports have established that the PTVs distributed by the administration resemble the tricycle-type “Hospital on Wheels” depicted in the viral post.

The Hospital on Wheels is a separate mobile surgical and healthcare facility founded by Dr. Juan “Jim” Sanchez Jr. that provides free medical, surgical, dental, and optical services to underserved communities. – Jennifer Pading/Rappler.com

Jennifer Jezreel Kaye Pading is an economics student at Visayas State University in Baybay City in Leyte. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, she is also the executive editor of Amaranth and community officer of AYEJ-Leyte Panaad Ha Sinirangan.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
World.content:
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.

WASHINGTON, USA – Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday, October 15.

Its services gave Israel’s Candiru — a spyware company blacklisted by the US government — as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia’s Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.

The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.

“The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat,” Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. “For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”

Discover-Tech’s online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.

Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.

Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users’ devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech’s overall volume.

Malicious ads shown in hundreds of sensitive networks

Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its s.

“Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech,” Dangu said.

Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.

Reuters’ attempts to reach Candiru’s owners were similarly unsuccessful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.

Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech’s ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group.

In a statement, Al Jazeera said it “condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff” and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. “Those responsible must be held accountable,” it said.

Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in “hundreds of networks in sensitive categories,” including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm’s ads.

“You go to almost any site in Palestine — any site — you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country,” he said.

Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.

In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech’s users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.

Measures against Discover-Tech taken

Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.

Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant’s investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms “for systematically violating our policies.”

IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.

Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform “following recent activity,” Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.

Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to ​war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] The weakest link may not be the subsea cables
World.content:
Keeping the system resilient cannot be treated as the work of the Coast Guard or Navy alone. It also requires action from regulators, agencies, and operators.

Subsea cables entered the Philippine news twice in the span of a week, for different reasons.

The first involved a research vessel holding position in waters that host cable corridors connecting the country to Northeast Asia. On September 28, the Philippine Coast Guard reported that the vessel did not answer radio challenges and had displayed a physically impossible Automatic Identification System trail. It later deployed a ship and aircraft, disrupted what it described as unauthorized marine scientific research, and compelled the vessel to leave its position.

The second was a network disruption.

On October 2, the C2C Philippines-Singapore link went down while its Hong Kong link was under maintenance. Providers rerouted traffic, but the disruption coincided with reports of slow or intermittent connections. The Singapore link was restored the following day. Its cause had not been made public as of writing.

No public reporting has established a connection between the incidents. They should not be treated as one chain of events. But each exposes a different part of the same problem: what can the country detect and protect, what disruption can the network absorb? They also raise a third question that becomes critical when redundancy is no longer enough: how quickly can the system recover?

Taken together, this is a question of resilience.

Archipelagic governance

For the Philippines, subsea cable resilience is a question of archipelagic governance.

This is the approach being explored by The Asia Foundation through its Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables (AGOS) initiative, which brings government and industry together to look at subsea cable resilience beyond the infrastructure itself. The cable is only one part of a wider system of infrastructure, institutions, policies, and capabilities. The system connects what happens at sea with what happens on land.

For an archipelago, these connections are shaped by geography. Connectivity crosses maritime spaces, lands in different communities and jurisdictions, and depends on institutions and infrastructure spread across islands.

A disruption at sea can affect banking, government services, businesses, and emergency communications. Suspicious activity near a cable route may force government to respond before it fully understands the risk. Delays in maritime access can also delay repair and restoration.

The connection works both ways. Decisions on permits, power supply, security arrangements, and coordination with local governments affect whether the system can expand, remain operational, and recover from disruption.

The system stretches from cables on the seabed to landing stations and land-based networks. It also includes power, network operations, repair capacity, government policies, emergency arrangements, and the institutions responsible for them.

This makes protecting cables and building cable resilience related but different tasks. Protecting a cable is about reducing the risk of damage or interference. Resilience is about whether the larger system can continue to function when disruption happens.

Across AGOS consultations with government and industryparticipants spoke about resilience in different ways: protecting the system, keeping services running during a disruption, and restoring connectivity quickly. Taken together, their inputs pointed to three qualities describing a resilient system: protected, adaptable, and recoverable. These qualities do not come from infrastructure alone. They also depend on the policies, capabilities, and coordination that allow the system to function.

A protected system can identify and manage risks. An adaptable system can reroute traffic and keep essential services running. A recoverable system can quickly mobilize maritime access, repair permits, security, technical teams, and local support.

The cable alone can do none of these things.

The question, then, is not only whether the Philippines can prevent something from happening to a cable. Not every cable fault, anchor drag, natural hazard, technical failure, or deliberate act can be prevented. The question is also whether the system around the cables can continue functioning when something does happen.

This is why keeping the system resilient cannot be treated as the work of the Coast Guard or Navy alone. Maritime authorities have distinct responsibilities at sea. But building a resilient subsea cables system also requires action from telecommunications regulators, economic and security agencies, emergency authorities, and operators.

Uncertainty over the cause of disruption further complicates the response. An incident may be accidental or deliberate, and establishing which takes time. But the response cannot wait for attribution. If services on land are already affected, continuity measures, repairs, and coordination have to kick in.

Attribution and resilience therefore operate on different clocks. Authorities may still be determining what happened while operators and government already need to keep services running and preparing for recovery.

Building a response before it’s needed

The Philippines already has laws, mandates, and mechanisms that cover parts of the system. Telecommunications and data-transmission rules govern networks. Maritime authorities operate under their respective mandates at sea. Disaster-response mechanisms can support continuity. The Konektadong Pinoy Act provides an open-access framework for data transmission, while Executive Order No. 32 streamlines permitting process for telecommunications and internet infrastructure.

The challenge is not always the lack of a policy. It is whether existing mandates can be brought together quickly enough when an incident crosses institutional boundaries.

Which agency receives the first report? What threshold triggers interagency coordination? Who verifies the incident, secures the area, prioritizes essential services, authorizes emergency access, and communicates with affected communities? Which approvals can be expedited, and under whose authority? What information should operators share with government, and what information should remain protected?

An incident protocol is one way to answer those questions before a disruption. It should connect detection to assessment, protection, continuity, repair, and public communication.

This is where an archipelagic approach becomes operational rather than conceptual. The task is not necessarily to create another institution. The task is to make sure the institutions that already hold different parts of the system know when and how to act together.

The Philippines is not starting from scratch. PCG detected and acted on unusual vessel activity. Operators shifted traffic when an international route became unavailable. Companies already invest in additional capacity, route diversity, and repair arrangements.

At the September 29 AGOS Forum, PLDT Global Corporation President and CEO, Albert Villa-Real put the industry case plainly: “Capacity without diversity is not resilience.” He also pointed to exploratory discussions among Philippine operators on shared or complementary infrastructure that could provide greater redundancy.

Route diversity makes the network more adaptable, but redundancy does not address the whole resilience problem.When redundancy is no longer enough, or when physical repair is required, maritime access, government processes, security, information sharing, and repair capacity become part of the system’s ability to recover.

Those efforts show that competition and cooperation can coexist. No single operator or government agency controls all the elements needed for resilience. Some forms of cooperation are therefore necessary, and possible, even within a competitive industry.

What is needed is a clearer way for the different parts of the system to work together. That means having a common operating picture that protects sensitive information, clear rules on when to share it, an agreed response protocol, and a process for settling government requirements before a repair vessel is ready to move.

International experience shows a growing recognition that protecting undersea infrastructure requires cooperation between government and industry. After several incidents involving damaged cables in the Baltic Sea, NATO launched Baltic Sentry to strengthen surveillance and support national authorities. NATO also works with industry through its Critical Undersea Infrastructure Network.

But the Philippines cannot simply copy the Baltic model.

Archipelagic governance must respond to the country’s own geography, institutions, communities, and risks. It does not require placing every decision under one institution. Nor does it mean treating subsea cables primarily as a military or security problem. It requires each institution to understand how its authority connects with others, what actions should follow when an incident occurs, and how consequences at sea will be managed on land.

The recent incidents point to a broader lesson. A country can patrol the waters above a cable and still lack resilience. It can add cable capacity and still lack resilience. It can have repair arrangements, permits, emergency authorities, and capable institutions, but still find that these pieces do not connect quickly enough when disruption occurs.

For an archipelago, the weakest link may therefore not be the cable itself. It may be the system around it. – Rappler.com



Kat Tolosa is director of The Asia Foundation’s Governance and Resilience unit in the Philippines. Taj Basman is a program officer in the same unit and leads the Foundation’s Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables initiative. The views expressed are their own.

World.title: Macacua secures 46-member coalition backing ahead of BARMM chief minister vote
World.content:
BARMM interim Chief Minister Abdulraod Macacua reads a message addressed to other newly elected members of the regional parliament during a gathering in Davao. Macacua is positioning for the BARMM's top post against MILF chairman and former interim chief minister Ahod 'Al Haj Murad' Ebrahim.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. welcomes the coalition's formation, emphasizing the importance of autonomy and cooperation for peace and stability in the Bangsamoro region

DAVAO, Philippines – Forty-six members of the newly elected Bangsamoro Parliament signed a coalition agreement, giving interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua the backing of a majority ahead of the October 30 vote to choose the leader of the Muslim-majority region.

The coalition has more than the 41 votes needed for a majority in the 80-member Parliament, putting Macacua in a strong position to secure the top post, said Naguib Sinarimbo, a former Bangsamoro interior minister who was elected to represent a Cotabato City parliamentary district in September.

“We have more than the simple majority needed,” Sinarimbo told Rappler on Friday, October 16, adding that this ensures that Macacua would become the first elected chief minister of the seven-year-old Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

Macacua, former commander of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s armed wing, is vying for the position against his former leader, Ahod “Al Haj” Murad Ebrahim, a former interim chief minister and the MILF’s chairman.

Macacua is backed by the months-old Bangsamoro Federalist Party, while Murad is supported by the MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party. The two parties finished in a statistical tie in the September 14 parliamentary elections, with Macacua’s party winning 31 seats against 30 for the UBJP.

The remaining seats went to other political parties and sectoral representatives.

The newly elected Parliament is scheduled to convene for the first time on October 30, when its members will choose the first elected chief minister of the BARMM.

Coalition hailed by Marcos

On Thursday, October 15, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. welcomed the announcement of a 46-member majority coalition in the BARMM Parliament even as he reaffirmed the national government’s respect for the region’s autonomy.

In a statement, Marcos called the first-ever BARMM parliamentary elections in September as a “historic milestone” in the region’s pursuit of self-governance and lasting peace.

He said the national government recognizes the coalition’s formation and its intention to constitute the regional government through parliamentary processes, adding that it respected Parliament’s authority to choose its leadership under the Bangsamoro Organic Law.

Marcos said the national government was looking forward to working with the government formed by Parliament to promote peace, stability and inclusive development.

Macacua announced the signing of the coalition agreement during a gathering of newly elected parliament members in Davao City on Wednesday, October 14, even as he emphasized the need for unity to build a free, effective and stable Bangsamoro government. He also called on other groups and parties to respect the members’ decision.

The Macacua-led BFP spearheaded the coalition, which includes representatives of political parties, local governments, ethnolinguistic groups and former revolutionary organizations in BARMM.

Macacua said the formation of the “Government of the Day” would center on the selection and election of the chief minister.

“We will reach out our hands, we will heal divisions, and we will build a government that serves everyone,” Macacua said as he thanked those who joined the coalition for their trust, as well as the national government for respecting BARMM’s autonomy.

Lanao del Sur Governor Mamintal Adiong Jr., secretary-general of the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition (BGC), said the alliance aimed to sustain the peace process and achieve lasting peace in BARMM.

Adiong said the group had asked Marcos in Malacañang to continue the decommissioning program before the end of his term, with the aim of securing a final exit agreement between the MILF and the national government.

He said the BGC was open to dialogue with other parties, including the UBJP and the BFP, to advance Marcos’ call for unity in the region’s leadership.

“Who wouldn’t want peace? We all aspire for that, which is why we have an autonomous region for Muslims. So hopefully, lasting peace will be achieved,” Adiong said.

Planning for the first 100 days

Coalition leaders also held a strategic planning workshop in Davao City to set legislative and executive priorities for the regular parliament’s first 100 days and five years. Some UBJP members came to participate.

BARMM Interior Minister Jordan Bayam said the elected parliament faces higher expectations than the interim Bangsamoro Transition Authority.

“This time, this is not just a BTA, but this is an elected parliament. So the task and the expectations of our people is so high,” Bayam said, stressing the need for unity around a common agenda.

Lampa Pandi, a parliament member-elect representing Lanao del Sur’s fourth district under the UBJP, said he attended to support a long-term direction for the region beyond partisan politics.

“I am not playing politics here, it’s more of the direction of the parliament where we aim to unite for the good of Bangsamoro,” Pandi said. He was joined by Tawakal Midting, who won in Maguindanao del Sur’s first parliamentary district. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos to summon China envoy over use of force ‘threat’
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will summon Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over a “threat” the envoy had made on the use of force in dealing with tensions between Manila and Beijing.

Asked in a chance interview if he would summon Jing over his remark, Marcos said in a chance interview on the sidelines of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) anniversary celebration, “I think that deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself.”

A summon, especially one made by the head of state, is among the highest means of communication a government can use to express concern, disapproval, or anger to an ambassador’s home office.

Should the summon push through, it would be the second time for Marcos to summon Jing to the Palace in just over 10 months of being posted in Manila. The last time was in July, after a Filipino soldier was injured in a violent confrontation with China Coast Guard (CCG) personnel in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in the West Philippine Sea.

Echoing the view of the Department of Foreign Affairs, Marcos said of Jing’s remark on Friday: “Well it sounds very much to me like a threat, and it is not a very diplomatic statement to be made. So we perhaps would like to understand what exactly it is that he means.”

In an interview with reporters on October 15, Jing insisted that China was no troublemaker in the region and blamed some Philippine officials for causing tensions between Manila and Beijing.

The veteran diplomat, who was assigned to the United States before being sent to the Philippines in December 2025, added: “We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace.”

The DFA, in a statement late October 15, criticized Jing for his “poor choice of words that would seem to convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.”

The Chinese embassy has since hit back through an October 16 statement, accusing the DFA of “selective quotation and overinterpretation” and said “diplomacy must be honest and straightforward in order to reduce misunderstandings and prevent misjudgments.”

It also claimed that “certain individuals are actively seeking to undermine normal exchanges and cooperation between the two countries” and that the DFA should “play a more responsible role in preventing such actions.” The embassy has made similar statements in the past.

Tense public exchanges between the Chinese embassy and Philippine government agencies — the DFA included, albeit rarely — have been a recurring feature in bilateral ties of the two countries, despite Marcos saying that he wants a “reset” in bilateral relations. The rhetoric is matched by maritime tensions and confrontations across different parts of the Philippines — from northern areas close to Batanes and westward in the West Philippine Sea.

Political pressure has also escalated between the two countries. Beijing sanctioned Teodoro and his family over his remarks against Beijing, including calling it unreliable in the context of South China Sea code negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which Manila chairs.

Most recently, tensions have been spurred by statements by impeached Vice President Sara Duterte who is accused to have recieved millions from China state-owned firms through businesses linked to her and her husband. In retaliation, Duterte said the Philippines is seen as a “troublemaker” in the region over tensions with China — over the West Philippine Sea, and even over scrutiny when it comes to business ties with the Asian superpower.

“Troublemaker” is how Beijing has characterized Manila in the past whenever maritime tensions rise in the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea. China claims almost all of the South China Sea, despite a 2016 Arbitral Award finding the suppose historical claim baseless. – Rappler.com

World.title: Shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school and is shot dead by citizen
World.content:
SCHOOL SHOOTING. Emergency responders operate at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, US, October 15, 2026, in this screengrab from a handout video.

(1st UPDATE) The dead were children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher

A 16-year-old shooter opened fire on Thursday, October 15, at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing four people, including three children, before being killed by an armed person who had pursued the assailant into the school, police said.

The shooter entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without offering any details beyond the shooter’s age.

The dead were children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher. In addition, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told a press conference.

RESPONSE. Emergency personnel direct traffic at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, US, October 15, 2026. Reuters

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, appearing at the same briefing, thanked the community member who “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life.”

“No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day, and as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we’re probably going to cry privately,” Kotek said.

Krantz said the community member, whom he did not identify, had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him.

The shooting took place in Bend, a city of about 100,000 residents in rural central Oregon, 280 km southeast of Portland, in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest.

Silver Rail Elementary School serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.

Police said they received a call around 1 pm (2000 GMT) that “indicated that an unknown man had shot into a car” at Silver Rail Elementary School.

Moments later, emergency dispatchers received multiple calls “reporting that a person had entered the school and begun shooting,” police said in a statement.

Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead. – Rappler.com

World.title: Shape of Pope Leo’s papacy more uncertain after cancer diagnosis
World.content:
POPE LEO. Pope Leo XIV delivers his 'Urbi et Orbi' (To the city and the world) message from the main balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, on Easter Sunday, at the Vatican, April 5, 2026.

The world's 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope

VATICAN – When US Cardinal Robert Prevost emerged on the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica in May 2025 as Pope Leo XIV, the new leader of the Catholic Church, he struck a stark contrast from his predecessor Francis.

Leo, young for a pope at 69 then, appeared energetic, spoke in a strong voice and had no known history of health issues. Francis, who died at 88, had become increasingly frail during his 12-year papacy.

With the Vatican’s announcement on Tuesday, October 13, that Leo, now 71, was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed part of his right lung that afternoon, the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope.

Leo, the first US-born pontiff, has emerged as an increasingly influential voice beyond the Church, raising alarm about the risks posed by artificial intelligence and drawing the ire of US President Donald Trump by criticizing the Iran war.

The future shape of Leo’s papacy — once expected to be dynamic with many foreign trips and the pope stepping into a leading moral role on the global stage — is now more uncertain. Medical experts say the pope’s prognosis will depend on several factors, including whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, currently unknown.

“It’s too early to say how this will affect Pope Leo’s agenda and his ability to carry on the duties of the papacy,” John Thavis, a Vatican expert and author, told Reuters.

“If his recovery is complete and no aggressive therapy is needed, the pope may be able to carry on as usual,” he said.

Planned South America trip in question

One immediate question Leo faces is whether to proceed with an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. The trip is known to be a high priority for the pope, who spent decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru.

The original schedule, announced last month, would have made it one of the most intense foreign trips ever undertaken by a pope, with Leo leading some 50 events and giving 36 speeches across a 10-city tour.

Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, said the trip may need to be postponed, depending on Leo’s recovery.

“A trip to South America that quickly is possible, if this is an early-stage lung cancer and no further therapy is needed, but it is a tight timeline, and recovery is highly variable,” said Liu.

Leo had been keeping a rapid pace of foreign travel, already making four tours in 2026 and attracting large crowds. More than 800,000 people turned out to see him in Paris last month.

‘One day at a time’

Catholics have often witnessed a pope deal with illness. Francis, who had part of one lung removed as a young adult, was prone to respiratory infections. He was also hospitalized as pope for colon and hernia surgeries.

John Paul II began to suffer symptoms of Parkinson’s disease in the 1990s, although the Vatican only confirmed his diagnosis in 2003.

John XXIII died in 1963 from stomach cancer that was not disclosed by the Vatican until after his death.

Benedict XVI, however, who succeeded John Paul, was the first pope to resign in 600 years, stepping down in 2013 after he said he no longer had the strength for the job.

The Vatican, long reticent to discuss papal health issues, has been unusually transparent in Leo’s case.

The pope himself announced to pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that a “localized nodule” had been found in his lung and he needed surgery. He also said it was detected early and was well contained.

The Vatican later provided a detailed medical bulletin hours after Leo had undergone surgery.

Another statement may be released on Wednesday afternoon, but details on the pope’s prognosis are expected to take a few days as doctors perform the necessary tests.

According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate for non-small cell lung cancer is 67% when the disease remains confined to the lung.

Dr. Giuseppe Cardillo, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome’s San Camillo Forlanini hospital, said removal of lung cancer discovered at an early stage usually results in an “excellent” prognosis.

Elise Allen, author of a biography of Leo for Penguin Peru, said people should not “jump the gun” in making conclusions about how the pope will recover.

“Let’s take it one day at a time,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kyat Slides Again as Regime Wins Approval for 2.1 Trillion-Kyat Borrowing Plan
World.content:
The kyat lost value again this week after the regime-backed parliament on Wednesday approved borrowing of up to 2.1 trillion kyats (approximately US$1 billion at the fixed official rate) for a junta struggling with ballooning defense costs.

The kyat has weakened drastically since the 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into a dollar crisis, with economic sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment, declining exports and fighting in border trade zones taking a toll on the regime’s coffers.

On Wednesday, the rubber-stamp parliament approved the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026-27. The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.

Analysts warn that borrowing from the Central Bank will accelerate inflation and the kyat’s depreciation. Currency traders report the dollar rose to 4,670 kyats in the unofficial market on Thursday, up from 4,450 kyats earlier this month, while the baht has risen from 129 to 139 kyats. Before the coup, the kyat was trading at less than 1,300 to the dollar.

“This surge is linked to the new loans. The market jumped from 4,400 to nearly 4,700 within days. Whether it will continue to increase, or decline—or if the regime will make arrests—remains to be seen,” one trader told The Irrawaddy. The regime has repeatedly arrested foreign exchange traders during currency spikes, accusing them of speculation and market manipulation.

The loan proposal has triggered fears that the revenue-deprived regime will simply print more banknotes to address the shortfall.

Deputy Finance and Revenue Minister Kyaw Htin explained that the regime has other plans to address the shortfall, apart from borrowing money. “We are working to reduce reliance on Central Bank financing to boost state revenue. We are developing taxation policies,” he told the parliament.

Recently, the regime has escalated its efforts to enforce remittance rules requiring Myanmar migrant workers to send at least 25 percent of their salaries back home at the official exchange rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar.

Officially, the Central Bank pegs the dollar at 2,100 kyats, while the trading rate between banks is 3,660 kyats and the market rate currently hovers at around 4,670 kyats. Meanwhile, the regime has restricted imports to reduce dollar spending, which has proved counterproductive for a war-ravaged economy heavily reliant on imports ranging from cooking oil and pharmaceuticals to fuel and fertilizer.

Rising dollar rates are expected to push up the cost of imported fuel, medicines, food, consumer goods and machinery, with knock-on effects for transport and production costs. Domestic industries face mounting pressure as expenses rise.

Meanwhile, the Belarus loan package, arranged through the Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, carries interest rates of between 2.25 and 9.33 percent. The loans will be used to import goods including capital goods from Minsk, but the total amount was not revealed.

Myanmar can receive loans in five currencies—the dollar, euro, Russian ruble, Belarusian ruble and Chinese yuan—said Kyaw Htin, who admitted exchange rate fluctuations would affect the amount of money Myanmar will actually receive.

Unlike concessional loans from Japan’s aid agency JICA—which carry a 40‑year repayment term at just 0.01 percent interest—analysts note that the Belarusian loan is a “tied” arrangement, warning the regime is locking itself into costly debt that will further deepen Myanmar’s economic crisis.

International organizations and Japan suspended development aid to Myanmar following the coup.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Launches ‘ASEAN Affairs’ Panel to Clinch Full Reintegration
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the regional bloc, which continues to bar his regime from summits months after it rebranded as an “elected” government.

The committee’s inaugural meeting on Tuesday was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, with representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare also in attendance.

While the Foreign Ministry normally serves as the focal point for international relations, the new body includes the defense and home affairs ministries, underscoring the junta’s bid to institutionalize its efforts to reintegrate into the regional bloc.

Reintegration is crucial for coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, who is seeking international legitimacy after installing himself as president in April following an election widely denounced as a sham by Western nations and rights groups.

While individual members including Thailand have recognized Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency, ASEAN as a whole remains divided, prompting continuous regime demands for full integration as a “legitimate elected government.”

Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” since 2021, when ASEAN excluded Min Aung Hlaing from top-level meetings for ignoring its Five‑Point Consensus agreed in Jakarta. The bloc’s peace plan calls for an immediate end to violence, dialogue among all parties, and humanitarian access—conditions the junta has refused to meet.

Tuesday’s meeting came just weeks ahead of the next ASEAN Summit in Manila. Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has made official visits to five bloc members, securing support for Myanmar’s reintegration from Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. Analysts say the committee was formed in an effort to win over the remaining five members.

“The regime is attempting to win a majority consensus through bilateral engagement with individual member states,” said political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye.

“The committee is designed for this purpose. But it remains difficult for ASEAN to allow Myanmar’s return while there is no visible progress on the Five-Point Consensus.”

Since assuming office in April, the pseudo-civilian regime has dismissed the Five-Point Consensus as a non-binding declaration, before formally rejecting the peace deal through its rubber-stamp parliament.

The regime said Tuesday’s meeting tabled “Myanmar‑led approaches” to restore the country’s role in ASEAN—a statement reiterating defiance of the Five-Point Consensus spearheaded by an ongoing military campaign that has killed over 8,500 civilians since the coup.

While rights groups warn that countries hosting Min Aung Hlaing risk legitimizing a regime still committing atrocities, others have different views after more than five years of isolation has delivered no results.

Former Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida told Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should help Myanmar rejoin ASEAN. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently hailed Min Aung Hlaing’s visits to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis. Meanwhile, Brunei and Indonesia plan to invite Min Aung Hlaing for official visits, according to junta spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe, leaving only Timor-Leste and Singapore standing firm against the regime.

As the bloc’s newest member, Timor-Leste has backed Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement while initiating legal action against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. Meanwhile Singapore, which will take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, recently affirmed that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

Mon Mon Myat, a lecturer in the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, said: “It appears that the Philippines wants to reintegrate Myanmar into the bloc before Singapore takes the chair next year. ASEAN countries that are stepping up their diplomatic engagement with Myanmar regime must exercise extra caution to avoid legitimizing war criminals.”

She added that ASEAN must set clear rules for accountability if the regime refuses to obey the Five-Point Consensus.

“Otherwise, the regime may secure full legitimacy as a leader of an ASEAN nation.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Denies Drafting College Students Into Army
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has denied reports that university students must suspend their studies for two years to serve in the army, but fears persist among students and parents.

Earlier this month, a panic broke out when rumors said that young men selected in conscription lotteries must serve in the army even if they are registered university students, and those drawing numbers under 100 would be called up within three months.

Conscripts are selected randomly at ward levels by drawing lots from a box. Those with smaller numbers are drafted first, and those with larger numbers later.

In Mandalay, even high school students who just turned 18 were forced to participate in the conscription lottery last month, according to parents.

“High school students were also told to draw lots. I drew on my son’s behalf and got a large number, over 500,” said a mother from Mandalay. “But we are still really scared because of reports that university students would be called up.”

In denying the rumors, the regime’s central conscription committee this week cited Article 15 (a)(3) of the Conscription Law, which allows deferment for students in education. It said official newspapers “repeatedly stressed this point.”

But concerns persist as township administrative offices in regime-controlled areas including major cities like Naypyitaw, Yangon and Mandalay have called in lists of university and high school students, apparently separating out those with spectacles, health problems, disabilities or on long‑term medication.

In August, the regime centralized the draft, with regional and district authorities taking over management from township and lower-level conscription offices. Since early September, a new wave of lotteries have been held in wards and villages across Mandalay but not yet in Yangon.

“Ward offices summon us according to lists from the Population Department,” one young man said. “Everyone aged 18 to 35 including students must draw. In our ward alone, over 40 students were included. One 12th grader drew a number under 100, but officials said high school students would be granted temporary deferment.”

Previously, families with eligible young men could pay a monthly fee to the authorities for deferment, in theory so someone else could be paid to take their place. But the regime abolished the substitution fee in September, declaring that all those selected must serve in order of their lottery numbers.

The department also denied reports that ward offices are confiscating ID cards and smart cards of selected youths, requiring monthly check‑ins, and demanding parents sign pledges to prevent their sons’ escape.

A Mandalay conscription official told The Irrawaddy that the process strictly follows laws and regulations.

“Students who can prove they are genuinely enrolled, with proper documents and forms, are granted temporary deferment,” the official said.

According to the 2019 census, nearly 13 million people are eligible for conscription under the Conscription Law—6.3 million men and 7.7 million women. So far, about 140,000 men have been called up by the regime, assuming that around 5,000 recruits are drafted per batch.

When the long-dormant Conscription Law was revived in 2024, it forced a mass exodus of young people, and the regime has since been struggling to meet its quotas despite barring eligible men from working abroad and even snatching young men from streets and homes.

In Yangon, an eerie quiet descends after 8 p.m. as regime-backed thugs prowl the streets on the hunt for eligible young men to abduct, a practice that has swiftly degenerated into a black economy of kidnappings for ransom.

World.title: Myanmar’s Opposition Leadership Is Holding Back the Resistance
World.content:
Myanmar’s resistance coalition has lost the political and diplomatic war but not the military campaign. The main reason lies less in the junta’s strength than in what I call an “insurgency-industrial complex” that has grown around the opposition.

This international ecosystem of diaspora communities, exiles, dissidents, donors, rights-based organizations and Western governments, with the National Unity Government (NUG) at its center outside the country, is geared towards fighting a military dictatorship rather than defeating it and governing Myanmar in a different way.

Unless the resistance regroups around leaders inside the country and mounts a convincing battlefield turnaround, perhaps led by drone warfare, Min Aung Hlaing will keep consolidating his grip even as the fighting goes on.

It is critical to separate Myanmar’s two wars. After staging elections last December and January, Min Aung Hlaing has reinvented himself as a pseudo-civilian president. Since assuming the presidency in April, he has made eight foreign trips. China, India and Russia have received him, as have four Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states in three months, namely Laos in July, Thailand in August, Vietnam and Cambodia in September, and this month in Malaysia.

Counting Myanmar itself, nearly half of ASEAN now deals with him at the top level. Each visit lowers the diplomatic cost of the next. ASEAN, which has kept him out of its leaders’ summits since the 2021 coup, is now under pressure to readmit him. Once in motion, political engagement generates its own momentum towards normalization and eventual recognition. The political war more or less has been lost.

The military war, on the other hand, is not lost. The armed forces do not control most of the country. Ethnic armed organizations remain strong and continue to take the fight to the military in borderland states, while People’s Defense Force (PDF) units are still holding on in the central dry zone. Neither side has clearly won on the battlefield.

Yet the resistance had its chance and missed it. By mid-2024, resistance forces held more than half of Myanmar’s territory. The military was pinned down in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw and appeared close to being toppled. But the coalition of ethnic armies, PDFs and the NUG lacked the cohesion and bold thrust to take over. Its battlefield tenacity was not matched by political capability.

When Beijing saw that the resistance did not have what it took to seize control, it backed the junta, leaned on the ethnic armies along its border to stand down, and endorsed the election roadmap. The tide turned, and here we are.

Why did the resistance falter when it mattered most? The NUG has been weak and ineffective, but the deeper reason is structural. Donations, aid and grants flow into the insurgency-industrial complex.

These funds sustain offices, salaries, jobs, scholarships, residencies abroad and a way of life. Its currency is opposition and its output is advocacy. A resistance victory would end its funding model and require some of its leaders to return home to govern a broken country of 55 million people, with all the risks that entails.

Put this way, the insurgency complex almost needs a military dictatorship to fight against. For many in the diaspora and among critics who live outside the country, it is not about winning and taking over the country but about keeping a four-decade struggle going. To be sure, many exiles and dissidents are authentic and sincere and have paid a heavy personal price.

At issue are incentives, not intentions. And these incentives work squarely in Min Aung Hlaing’s favor. An opposition led from abroad keeps the contest outward-facing and predictable, and it allows the regime to portray its enemies as foreign-funded “terrorists” detached from the people.

It does not help that global standards on human rights and democracy have sagged, and international aid has been slashed systematically, from the dismantling of American aid programs to deep cuts by the United Kingdom and European donors. The moral pressure that once isolated Myanmar’s generals has weakened.

The only way to change this narrative and shift direction is a resistance counteroffensive, led mainly by the PDF and the ethnic armies still willing to topple the regime. The battlefield is where the resistance still holds cards, and the decisive weapon is the first-person-view (FPV) drone. FPV drones have already allowed small, motivated units to hit armor, outposts and supply lines. Scaled up and coordinated, a drone-led campaign against strategic towns and corridors could deliver the key victories needed to convince Beijing and ASEAN that Min Aung Hlaing is not a safe bet for them because he cannot control the country in the long run.

But a counteroffensive requires a different leadership. The resistance needs to regroup away from the NUG and towards those who are actually fighting inside the country. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has been the most successful fighting force in the civil war. Its commander-in-chief, Major General Tun Myat Naing, has the battlefield record and standing to serve as the resistance’s overall military commander. Meanwhile, PDF commanders must be brought into the top leadership, not treated as foot soldiers for exiled politicians.

Their fighters came of age during the decade of opening from 2011 to 2021, with mobile phones, jobs, travel, foreign investment and elections that counted. They want that country back. Their objective is to retake Myanmar, while the insurgency-industrial complex’s goal is to oppose the regime and keep fighting the military dictatorship to no end.

A leadership rooted inside the country would also be the kind of interlocutor that Beijing and ASEAN could take seriously, one with control over territory and troops rather than offices and press releases. That is precisely what was missing in mid-2024.

Unless there is a clear and convincing military turnaround in the resistance’s favor that is accompanied by a more capable leadership from inside the country, Min Aung Hlaing will continue to consolidate politically and diplomatically. Neighbors and major powers will deal with whoever looks set to last—right now that is Min Aung Hlaing.

Until the fighters inside lead the leaders outside, the resistance may win more battles but will keep losing the regional and international politics of the civil war.

Thitinan Pongsudhirak is a professor of comparative and international politics at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty Of Political Science and a non-resident associate with the Southeast Asia Centre at the London School of Economics.

This article first appeared in the Bangkok Post.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Escalates Assault on Free Press Critical of Its Rule
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has intensified its threats against independent media critical of its rule, vowing to eliminate outlets and journalists regardless of their location.

An editorial in the junta’s mouthpiece Kyemon on Monday urged the “elimination of any destructive element inside or outside the country,” echoing the Home Affairs Ministry’s threats last week.

On October 6, Deputy Home Affairs Minister Major‑General Min Thu told parliament the regime has opened cases against independent media outlets The Irrawaddy, Mizzima, DVB, Myanmar Now, and Khit Thit under the Counter‑Terrorism Law, Telecommunications Law, and Penal Code. He claimed the regime was coordinating with international law enforcement including Interpol and Aseanapol to detain staff working for these organizations.

Interpol bans any interventions on political grounds while Aseanapol’s focus is limited to transnational crimes.

The Kyemon editorial stated that anyone inside or outside the country who “disrupts peace, stability, and development, undermines national sovereignty, prestige, and unity, or obstructs the administrative mechanism must be eliminated.”

Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing branded outlets reporting his military’s mass-killing of civilians as “nation‑destroying media” during his October 13 trip to Dawei, claiming they were misleading the public. “Those outlets do not want to see national development,” said the president, whose February 2021 coup plunged the country into turmoil.

The putsch was followed by a brutal crackdown, targeting not only peaceful protesters but also media documenting the military’s abuses. The regime revoked licenses, raided offices, and arrested scores of journalists, forcing independent outlets into exile. After establishing itself as one of the world’s worst jailers of journalists, it is now seeking to target exiled media.

Independent media groups emphasize that journalism is not a crime and note that Interpol does not act on political requests. “Interpol does not intervene in political or religious cases. Only genuine criminal matters are considered,” said Toe Zaw Latt, secretary of the Independent Press Council of Myanmar. He added that while the regime may attempt to link reporting with criminal activities, such requests are weeded out by Interpol. “So, there is no need to worry, but we should still monitor the situation carefully.”

Lower House Speaker Khin Yi—who as former dictator Than Shwe’s police chief led deadly crackdowns on pro-democracy demonstrators—has advised the Home Affairs Ministry that criminal cases must be concocted to pursue arrests abroad.

The junta’s warning comes as its propaganda apparatus struggles to discredit the resistance movement while concealing its own war crimes. Circulation of regime newspapers has sharply declined since the coup, and junta news outlets have been barred from multiple social media platforms.

A Yangon street vendor said demand for state‑owned newspapers is practically non-existent, except for once a month when lottery results are printed.

The junta’s threats come as it faces ongoing international isolation. ASEAN has barred Min Aung Hlaing from summits since the coup for failing to implement its peace plan, while he is wanted on an international arrest warrant issued by Argentina over the Rohingya genocide. Rights groups have repeatedly called on Interpol to arrest the coup leader during his overseas trips.

On Wednesday, the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and its affiliate, the Exiled Myanmar Journalists Network (Exiled-MJN), condemned the regime’s threats as a blatant abuse of international policing mechanisms.

“Myanmar’s junta will stop at nothing to try to legitimize itself in the world’s eyes and to expand its repression against the brave and determined media and journalists who continue to expose its gross violations against its own people,” IFJ stated.

According to MJN records, at least seven journalists have been killed by the regime since the coup. The International Centre for Not-for-Profit Law has documented at least 227 journalists detained by the junta, with at least 20 still in jail.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Burn Church in Bhamo, KIA Says
World.content:
Myanmar military forces burned a Christian church near Bhamo on Monday evening as the regime continues its campaign to recapture the Kachin State town, according to Colonel Naw Bu, a spokesperson for the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

“They [the regime] burned a Christian church in Three Mile Village on the way to Momauk,” Naw Bu told The Irrawaddy. “There have been periodic clashes in that area.”

He added that there has been frequent fighting between regime troops and KIA-led forces around Light Infantry Battalion 47 and near Bhamo University.

The KIA and its allies launched an attack on Bhamo in late 2024 and captured the majority of the town in 2025. This year, however, it has lost some ground there to the regime, which has been reinforcing its troops in preparation for a counteroffensive.

Naw Bu claimed resistance groups still control a large part of the town. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the claim.

Citing residents, local media reported that the arson attack on the Kachin Baptist Convention-run church followed heavy regime casualties in the face of fierce resistance defense.

Human rights activists condemned the torching of the church.

“This is a violation of freedom of religion; we condemn it,” Jacob from Kachin Human Rights Watch told The Irrawaddy. “The regime does not respect international laws and continues to violate them.”

He said the regime and allied militias have used religious sites for military purposes, carried out drone attacks on churches, and detained religious leaders. “Religious rights in Kachin State are being increasingly violated,” he said.

Mervyn Thomas, founder president of Church World Service, an international Christian human rights group, said the attack was a “grave crime” and a “clear violation” of international laws and freedom of belief, while calling on the international community to cut off the regime’s access to aviation fuel and military equipment.

In September, the regime-allied Shanni Nationalities Army used the compounds of a Baptist church and a Catholic church in Indaw as a military training ground and an office, sparking criticism from ethnic Kachin residents.

The regime and its allies conducted a suicide drone attack on another church in Mohnyin Township in October.

The regime’s attacks on places of worship do not discriminate by faith, however. Myanmar Witness in April said it documented over 300 airstrikes on religious sites, including churches, monasteries and mosques, between January 2024 and December 2025. Nearly 90 percent of them were conducted by the regime’s air force, with Sagaing Region and Shan State the worst-affected areas.

In August, 14 civilians were killed in Sagaing Region’s Myaung Township when the regime launched an airstrike on a Buddhist temple that was hosting around 100 people for a meditation retreat.

World.title: Myanmar’s Spies: A History of Surveillance, Power and Purges
World.content:
Myanmar: The Making of an Intelligence State

By Andrew Selth

ISEAS Publishing, Singapore, 2026

609 pp. US$48

This book is bound to become a classic. Never before has any international scholar described and analyzed the history of intelligence in Myanmar, from the days of the kings, through colonial rule, to democratic and military-dominated governments after independence. And no one would be more qualified to do this study than Andrew Selth, an Australian academic and former diplomat who has written extensively about Myanmar for several decades. The Burmese kings sent spies across the eastern as well as western borders before invading armies captured the old Siamese capital Ayutthaya and the old Arakan kingdom. And they developed what a British historian, quoted by Selth, has described as “a powerful and sophisticated internal espionage system” when the country was threatened by European colonial powers.

A new, entirely different intelligence apparatus emerged after the British conquest in the 19th century. In 1896, a Criminal Intelligence Bureau was formed within the headquarters of the Burma Police, and its duty was quite specific: to monitor domestic dissent and “deal with cases of a political nature.” A Special Branch of the police continued that work throughout the colonial era, and its work became especially important after the Saya San rebellion in the 1930s, which also prompted the British to send in military police officers from India.

In the years after Myanmar’s independence in 1948, Selth outlines how the new government created five main intelligence agencies, of which the Military Intelligence Service (MIS) became the most powerful, and even cooperated with foreign intelligence services. Some officers were trained by the British, and then chiefly to spy on Myanmar’s growing communist movement. The CIA also provided training on the US-held island of Saipan in the Pacific. Among those receiving instruction was “Spectacles Tin Oo,” who became a close associate of the dictator General Ne Win and, as such, one of the most feared men in the country. He collected intelligence not only on political dissidents but also, and perhaps primarily, on officers and the ranks of the military, on whose loyalty the Ne Win regime relied for its survival.

Tin Oo (not to be confused with General Tin Oo, one of the founders of the National League for Democracy) and his inner circle of followers eventually became too powerful, acting like a state within a state, which led to his downfall in July 1983 and a purge of the entire intelligence apparatus. The near vacuum that ensued has been seen as the reason why North Korean agents managed to infiltrate Yangon and, in October that year, detonate a bomb that killed 17 visiting South Korean officials and four Myanmar nationals.

With MI Tin Oo behind bars, Ne Win needed a new officer who could rebuild the country’s intelligence services, and that was his trusted protégé, Khin Nyunt. His Directorate of Defense Services Intelligence (DDSI) soon had agents all over the country, and surveillance—and repression—of the population at large became of utmost importance during and after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising. According to Selth: “The DDSI already was the largest and most powerful intelligence agency in Myanmar before 1988, but under the SLORC [the State Law and Order Restoration Council] it dramatically increased in size, sophistication and territorial presence. The refashioning of the SLORC into the State Peace and Development Council in 1997, possibly on the advice of an American public relations consultant, does not seem to have resulted in any significant changes to the intelligence structures and procedures that were set in train after the uprising.”

Selth provides detailed descriptions of how Khin Nyunt’s DDSI and its affiliated agencies were structured, and how they operated. Now, foreigners, among them diplomats and others who were suspected of having contacts with the pro-democracy movement, also became targets of its surveillance. But like MI Tin Oo before him, Khin Nyunt grew too powerful for comfort, and he was eventually ousted in October 2004 along with almost his entire intelligence apparatus. New intelligence outfits had to be created, and those were placed more directly under military command to avoid a repeat of what happened in 1983 and 2004.

During Burma’s decade of relative openness, from 2011 to 2021, the intelligence services remained wholly autonomous from the governments in Naypyitaw, and that separation became even more obvious during the years when the NLD—after an election in 2015—was allowed to appoint most ministers. I experienced this firsthand when I visited the country on many occasions between 2012 and 2019. I was under constant surveillance, and the intelligence agents often didn’t even bother to hide it.

Selth also describes how various opposition forces have treated suspected informants for the various intelligence services. In 1992, the All-Burma Students’ Democratic Front’s section in Kachin State killed 15 of their own comrades on suspicion of being spies. In 2021, 25 unarmed prisoners were executed by Karen rebels. In both cases, the opposition groups had depended on faulty intelligence, which their own agencies had provided.

Anyone who wants to understand how successive military-dominated governments have survived, and on what traditions Myanmar’s intelligence services were built, has to read this book. It contains a 43-page bibliography, which is the most extensive I have seen in any book about Myanmar. The book also lists, for the first time, military intelligence chiefs since 1959, regional military commands in 2024, and the various intelligence agencies that shaped today’s Myanmar. Its subtitle, “The Making of an Intelligence State,” could not be more appropriate.

World.title: China Sentences Myanmar Scam Clan Members to Death
World.content:
BEIJING—A Chinese court sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death on Tuesday for operating a network of brutal scam centers in Myanmar’s Kokang region on the border with China, while jailing dozens more.

China has stepped up cooperation with Southeast Asian nations to crack down on a vast industry that has flourished in the region in recent years to fleece people out of billions of dollars.

Those conducting the online scams are sometimes willing con artists. Others are trafficked foreign nationals—many Chinese—tricked into work and held in prison-like compounds.

Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court said in a statement on Tuesday that it had sentenced Wei Huairen (aka Wei San), Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang to death for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”.

The gang was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organizing prostitution, operating illegal casinos, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese citizens, the court said.

Wei Huairen was identified as one of the group’s leaders and found guilty of several crimes including murder, the court said.

The gang’s operations netted more than 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion).

Another three gang members were handed life sentences, while 55 more were given prison terms ranging from 24 years to three years and three months, the court said.

Analysts describe the Wei clan as one of the “four families” running crime syndicates in Kokang.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday called them the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar,” having created an “iron triangle of political, military and business criminal activities.”

It described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” scam compounds and luring “large numbers” of Chinese to Myanmar through fake promises of high wages.

Police had also discovered remains of victims bound with iron chains and with bullet holes in their skulls, CCTV said.

Members of the Wei family were first indicted in October 2025.

In January, China executed 11 people, including members of the “Ming family criminal gang.”

The following month, four members of the notorious Bai clan were executed for crimes including “fraud, intentional homicide, intentional injury, kidnapping [and] extortion.”

World.title: Middle Corridor Could Add $58 Billion to Regional GDP by 2040, World Bank Says
World.content:
ASTANA – The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor could increase the combined gross domestic product of countries along the route by 3.3% and generate around two million jobs by 2040 if governments invest in infrastructure and improve cross-border coordination, according to a World Bank report presented in Astana on Oct. 15.

“The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, also known as the Middle Corridor, is more than a transit route. It can help Central Asian countries connect with global markets, attract investment, diversify their economies and create business opportunities,” said Andrei Mikhnev, World Bank country manager for Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

Speaking at the New Silk Way business forum, Mikhnev noted that Central Asia’s strategic location between Europe and Asia creates opportunities, but geography alone is not enough to deliver economic benefits.

“The European Union has even nailed the term ‘Global Gateway,’ of which this transport corridor is an important part. But geography alone does not create opportunities. The challenge is to turn connectivity into economic value, and transit flows into broader development,” he said.

Countries along the corridor have invested in railways, roads, ports, logistics facilities and border crossings, while pursuing reforms to facilitate trade and strengthen regional cooperation

According to Mikhnev, further progress will depend on more closely coordinated operations, streamlined border procedures, digitalization and greater private sector participation.

Trade volumes expected to grow

Luis Blancas, World Bank’s senior transport and logistics specialist, presented the report’s findings, describing the corridor as a platform for private investment, job creation and economic growth.

He noted that the route offers distinct benefits depending on countries’ geographic locations and trade needs.

“For the five Central Asian countries, the corridor provides access to global markets and helps diversify trade routes. For the South Caucasus and Türkiye, it offers a more direct connection to Europe, Central Asia and East Asia. For China and Western Europe, it provides an alternative for containerized freight,” Blancas said.

The corridor is also complementary to other Eurasian trade routes, rather than necessarily competing with them, because each route has different costs, operating conditions and advantages for particular types of cargo.

According to the Middle Corridor Association, total freight volumes on the route grew at an average annual rate of 34% between 2021 and 2025. Containerized freight volumes increased by an average of 32% annually over the same period.

The World Bank projects that total freight volumes could rise from about 9 million metric tons in 2023 to nearly 24 million metric tons by 2040, even without additional infrastructure investment beyond projects and facilities in place at the end of 2025.

With further infrastructure investment, volumes could reach 32 million metric tons by 2040. Non-oil freight volumes could increase to about 16 million metric tons, approximately 4.5 times the 2023 level.

Without additional investment, the corridor could miss out on 33% of potential total freight volumes and nearly 90% of potential non-oil freight volumes, according to the report.

The report estimates that infrastructure investment could boost the combined GDP of corridor countries by 3.3%, equivalent to $58 billion at current prices, through increased imports and exports by 2040. The estimate does not include the potential impact of transit trade.

Infrastructure is not the only challenge

Blancas noted that although infrastructure investment remains important, the corridor’s main challenge is likely to be operational performance rather than a lack of physical capacity.

The World Bank identified 16 critical bottlenecks along the corridor, with an estimated cost of around $25 billion to address them. According to the report, 75% of the identified bottlenecks, accounting for 85% of the estimated investment cost, were being addressed.

“The remaining 25% of the projects have not yet entered the implementation phase but are firmly included in government plans and are expected to proceed,” Blancas said.

Investments have already improved capacity on key sections of the network. In Kazakhstan, for example, the double-tracking of the Dostyk-Moiynty railway line reduced its estimated capacity utilization from 100% in 2023 to about 40%, according to the report.

However, infrastructure improvements alone will not necessarily make the corridor competitive with alternative routes for containerized freight between China and Europe.

For a shipment from Chongqing, China, to Budapest, Hungary, average delivery times on the Middle Corridor currently range from 47 to 50 days, compared with about 45 days by sea and 18 days via the Northern Corridor, according to the World Bank’s analysis.

Blancas highlighted that additional infrastructure investment could reduce delivery times on the fastest Middle Corridor route to around 26-27 days by 2040, while the Northern Corridor could offer delivery in around 19 days.

“According to our modeling projections, combining infrastructure investment with improvements in trade facilitation, service delivery and cross-border collaboration would allow the fastest route along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor to close the performance gap with the Northern Corridor by 2040,” he said.

Call for closer regional cooperation

The report proposes a framework called the TCTC Assessment and Response Structure, or TARS, to improve cross-border cooperation. It includes a shared system for measuring corridor performance, a public-private advisory committee and a platform for intergovernmental decision-making.

Blancas said inconsistent data and fragmented coordination make it difficult for governments and businesses to plan effectively. A common evidence base would help participating countries identify bottlenecks, assess progress and coordinate investment decisions.

The report also calls for simplifying transport documentation.

“Moving a container between China and Europe along the corridor currently requires around 15 documents, many of which contain overlapping information,” Blancas said.

The World Bank proposes introducing a single digital Transport, Transit and Trade document, known as T3, alongside a decentralized digital system that would allow national platforms to exchange information while preserving data sovereignty.

Another recommendation is to establish a joint railway and shipping undertaking involving the corridor’s main railway operators and shipping lines. The initiative could improve coordination across rail and maritime segments and support more reliable, time-specific freight services.

World.title: Satellite Solutions for Food Security
World.content:
Global food security faces a number of pressures, including conflict, climate change, pollution and overexploitation. North and Central Asia is a region at risk, with human activity contributing to significant levels of desertification in drylands and other fragile biomes. Agriculture is a major source of employment in the region, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the working population in Tajikistan, more than 30 per cent in Azerbaijan and Georgia and more than 20 per cent in Armenia, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Agriculture underpins the livelihoods of rural populations, which are often among the poorest sectors of society.

With greater efficiency and optimization, the agricultural sector can save water and resources, increase yields and adapt to new climatic realities. That kind of innovation is the theme of this year’s World Food Day (16 October) “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” Across North and Central Asia, geospatial technology is already helping both farmers and policymakers. Making the most of it, however, depends as much on skills and on institutions working together as on the technology itself.

Geospatial technology can support farmers in decision-making processes through online platforms and applications. In Kazakhstan, the application AgroData integrates data from 226 agrometeorological stations, giving farmers real-time information on weather, soil moisture and crop health.
