World.title: ‘Whether we should ‘marry’ the EU is question for future’, Armenia’s foreign minister says about EU membership
World.content:
Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

The Armenian parliament approved a law launching the country’s EU accession process in spring 2025. However, only now has Armenian society begun to hold “serious, in-depth” discussions about membership. Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Ararat Mirzoyan made the remarks on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.

During a panel discussion entitled “Half-Readiness or a Gradual Approach: Rethinking EU Enlargement”, Mirzoyan was asked where the train taking Armenia towards Europe would ultimately stop. The minister replied that nobody knew — neither Armenia, nor the EU, nor its member states.

He said the good news was that both Armenia and the European Union were enjoying their current process of engagement.

“So let us enjoy these warm relations, discover new opportunities and explore new dimensions of cooperation. At some point in the future, we can sit down together and discuss whether we should ‘get married’,” Mirzoyan said.

During the panel discussion, the minister also addressed the reopening of the Armenian-Turkish border and the peace process with Azerbaijan.

He stressed that Armenia’s efforts to improve relations with its neighbours do not stem from its desire to integrate with European institutions.

Moreover, he assured the audience that this process would continue regardless of other factors.

“On the other hand, we should acknowledge that if our goal is to become a full member of the European Union, problems or conflicts with our neighbours are likely to become an obstacle along the way,” Ararat Mirzoyan noted.

Armenia and the EU are pursuing more than just political dialogue

“Our relations with the European Union have reached an unprecedented depth, covering a wide range of areas and forms of cooperation. We are holding a dialogue on visa liberalisation. The EU has established a monitoring mission in Armenia, which continues to operate and monitor the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. We recently welcomed a second mission. Although temporary, it operates on a permanent basis and helps us counter hybrid threats.

Although we are not an EU candidate country, the Union has granted us preferential trade access with its member states.

This is the latest development. The EU has approved autonomous trade measures to help Armenia diversify its export markets. We have also signed an agreement with the Union that will allow us to take part in various EU missions around the world.

Moreover, although we are not a candidate country, we have received a Resilience and Growth Plan and assistance from the EU, including support through the European Peace Facility.

Our cooperation therefore extends beyond support for political dialogue, the economy and trade. It also covers security, foreign policy and other areas.

Together with the European Union, we continue to explore new opportunities as we seek to strengthen our ties even further.”

On unblocking transport links, the interests of major powers align

“In my country, and probably across the entire South Caucasus region, the interests of the US and the EU do not conflict. On the contrary, they work together very well.

The United States is actively involved in the South Caucasus. In particular, it is taking part in efforts to open and unblock transport links between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

This will provide a vital transport connection, for example between Portugal and China, linking the West and the East.

I believe the EU and its member states will also benefit from this process.

Thus, many countries and major powers around the world share an interest in unblocking the South Caucasus.”

Opening the Armenian-Turkish border is entirely possible

“We are normalising relations with Turkey. The border remains closed, but I believe the process has already reached a significant level of maturity.

It is entirely possible that tomorrow morning we will wake up and see this headline in the news: ‘Armenia-Turkey border opens’.”

Peace with Azerbaijan and the situation in neighbouring countries

“In our case, Armenia’s neighbours are a critically important factor. Let us look at them.

Azerbaijan. We recently established peace and began bilateral trade. We are opening our territories to transport and transit, and unblocking regional communications. However, several sensitive issues still need to be resolved.

To the west lies Turkey, with which we are engaged in intensive dialogue. We are normalising relations, but the border remains closed.

To the south lies Iran, with its complex regional situation, specific conditions and challenges.

To the north lie Georgia and Russia […].

**As for Georgia, imagine how much easier the situation would be if it continued on its path towards EU integration. That would bring about significant changes.”

Moscow’s reaction must be managed carefully

“As for Russia, you can imagine how it might react to Armenia joining the EU, given the specific nature of our relationship with that country.

Historically, we have had very close ties, and we continue to maintain close relations to this day. However, we must manage any potential reaction carefully.

Nobody wants to make new enemies. Nor are we interested in harming any third party.”

Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

World.title: Azerbaijani government websites hit by cyberattack allegedly originating in Turkey
World.content:
Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

More than 100 government domains in Azerbaijan were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted access to several government agencies’ websites. According to the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security, the attacks began at around 22:00 Baku time on 13 October. The agency said a foreign hacking group was behind them.

The agency said technical measures had helped limit the impact of the cyberattack and keep the websites running reliably. However, it has not disclosed detailed information about how the attack was carried out, who organised it or what motivated it.

As Meydan TV reports, one theory under discussion is that the cyberattack may have links to Turkey.

The incident has prompted debate about the resilience of the country’s digital government infrastructure and the possible political motives behind the attack. Available information confirms that the websites experienced disruptions, but it is not yet possible to assess the full scale of the cyberattack or its consequences.

Clarify the agency’s responseTighten the final paragraphUse more cautious attribution

Which websites were targeted?

According to initial reports in local media, users experienced access problems with the websites of the Cabinet of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Health and the State Examination Centre. An official statement confirming a cyberattack followed simultaneous disruptions affecting several government websites.

According to official figures, the attack targeted more than 100 domains. However, this does not mean that the attackers managed to disrupt all these websites or gain unauthorised access to their systems. The number of resources targeted must be distinguished from the number of systems that actually suffered damage.

The official statement does not specify which websites became unavailable or how long the disruptions lasted. It is also unclear whether the outages affected only information pages or disrupted electronic services as well. The State Service for Special Communications and Information Security says it is continuing its cybersecurity measures.

The nature of the cyberattack remains unclear

Disrupting a website and gaining unauthorised access to its database are two different types of cybersecurity incident. In the first case, users lose access to the resource. In the second, the confidentiality and integrity of data may be at risk.

One common method of disrupting websites is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. This involves sending a large volume of requests to a server simultaneously from different sources. The resulting traffic overloads the servers or network infrastructure, leaving legitimate users’ requests unanswered. Such an attack can disrupt a website without anyone gaining unauthorised access to its database.

There is no official confirmation that the latest cyberattack in Azerbaijan used this particular method. Authorities have also published no findings from checks for possible data leaks. The available information therefore does not establish either that personal data belonging to citizens were stolen or that the authorities have fully resolved all the consequences of the attack.

The restoration of websites indicates that users have regained access to them. However, determining whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to the systems or whether any data leaked requires a separate technical investigation.

Possible motives and speculation about links to Turkey

Cyberattacks on government websites may aim not only to disrupt online services but also to express political views, attract public attention or undermine trust in state institutions. In its report on denial-of-service attacks, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) lists political and ideological objectives, as well as financial interests, among the possible motives behind such attacks.

The specific motives behind the latest cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites remain unknown. The fact that the incident occurred amid political tensions has prompted speculation about a possible link between the events. However, further evidence is needed to substantiate such claims.

According to Meydan TV, social media users are discussing a possible link between the cyberattack and Turkey. The outlet examines this speculation against the backdrop of protests by members of some religiously conservative groups in Turkey against restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools, as well as Baku’s relations with Israel. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani embassy in Ankara and the country’s consulate general in Istanbul.

However, no evidence has established a link between the cyberattack and these protests or any groups in Turkey. The Azerbaijani authorities have also refrained from naming specific countries or organisations in their official statement.

The phrase “foreign hacking group” used in the official statement does not, in itself, indicate that any foreign state was involved. Identifying those who organised and carried out the attack, establishing their motives and determining whether they have links to state institutions will require a separate investigation.

Warning about cyber threats issued five days before the attack

On 8 October, five days before the cyberattack, Azerbaijan’s Electronic Security Service published a warning about active cyber threats targeting several information systems. The statement noted that some attacks involved outdated database management software and default login credentials that administrators had failed to change.

The warning also said that attackers who gained access to inadequately protected systems could use them to launch attacks against other resources. The service advised administrators to update their software, change default passwords, restrict access to systems and monitor suspicious activity.

The service did not report any possible connection between this warning and the cyberattack that began on 13 October. There is currently no evidence to suggest that the two incidents formed part of the same operation. Nevertheless, the warning highlights that cybersecurity depends not only on responding to attacks but also on regularly updating software and controlling access to systems.

Questions left unanswered after services were restored

One of the key criteria for assessing the impact of a cyberattack is the extent to which it disrupts government electronic services. The temporary unavailability of an informational website can have very different consequences for users from disruptions to systems for submitting documents, registering applications and processing requests.

No specific data has yet been published on whether the latest cyberattack interrupted users’ transactions, caused people to miss deadlines for submitting documents or applications, or resulted in data loss. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the actual damage caused by the incident based solely on the number of domains targeted.

Future official statements will be particularly important in clarifying which services were affected, whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to internal systems, and what the security checks found regarding personal data.

The restoration of the websites demonstrates that the authorities have taken steps to respond to the cyberattack. However, a fuller assessment of how resilient the country’s digital government infrastructure proved to be against such threats will only be possible once more detailed information becomes available.

Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

World.title: Škoda plant to open in Baku: Project progress so far
World.content:
Škoda Group plans rail vehicle production plant in Baku

Czech company Škoda Group plans to establish a rail vehicle production and maintenance facility in Baku.

The project could boost local industry, create jobs and facilitate technology transfer. However, investment figures, production capacity and a timeline have yet to be announced.

Czech transport equipment manufacturer Škoda Group has announced plans to establish a production facility and maintenance centre in Azerbaijan. The company aims to eventually use the facility to serve customers not only in Azerbaijan but also across the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

The plans emerged on 12 October during a meeting between Czech Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik and representatives of Azerbaijan Transport and Communication Holding (AZCON). The meeting was attended by AZCON head Shahin Babayev, Baku Metro chairman Vusal Aslanov and Azerbaijan Railways chairman Rovshan Rustamov.

Škoda Group vice-chairman Tomáš Ignačák said the company intended to establish a joint venture with a local partner in Azerbaijan and gradually expand production.

The proposal covers not only the supply of finished rolling stock but also maintenance services, training for local specialists, the involvement of Azerbaijani companies in component supply chains and the transfer of European manufacturing technologies.

However, the project remains at the proposal stage, with no investment agreement signed so far.

What is Škoda Group planning in Azerbaijan?

Škoda Group is one of Europe’s rail transport manufacturers. The company produces metro trains, trams, suburban electric trains, trolleybuses, as well as vehicle control and drive systems.

Škoda Group should not be confused with carmaker Škoda Auto. The latter is owned by Volkswagen Group, while Škoda Group, which specialises in rail transport, is part of Czech investment group PPF.

According to the company, it has production facilities in the Czech Republic, Finland and Turkey. In 2025, the group’s revenue, including figures from Turkish manufacturer TEMSA, reached €1.45bn.

Škoda Group’s proposal to Azerbaijan focuses primarily on modernising the metro and suburban rail networks. The planned joint venture would gradually develop local production and maintenance capabilities, using local resources and facilities.

One potential benefit would be reduced dependence on foreign manufacturers for maintenance, spare parts and repairs throughout the service life of rail vehicles.

Training local engineers and technicians could also become an important part of long-term industrial cooperation. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on which production and maintenance operations are carried out at the new facility.

Baku Metro expansion creates new opportunities

Škoda Group’s interest in the Azerbaijani market coincides with the country’s plans to expand its public transport infrastructure. Under a state programme approved in January 2025, Baku plans to build 10 new metro stations, modernise existing lines and purchase 299 new carriages by 2030.

In addition to new stations, the programme includes expanding train depots, upgrading power supply systems and increasing the metro network’s capacity. According to AZCON, around $2.5bn is earmarked for the expansion.

In June 2026, Baku Metro and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signed loan agreements worth a total of $180m to finance the first phase of the expansion. The funds will primarily support ongoing work at the Darnagul and Khojasan train depots, as well as upgrades to existing metro stations.

Azerbaijan has therefore already approved a metro modernisation programme and secured funding for several projects. The Czech company’s proposal aims to meet potential demand for equipment, maintenance services and industrial cooperation arising from these plans.

How much production will take place locally?

One of the key factors determining the project’s economic significance will be the scale of production established in Azerbaijan.

Rail vehicle manufacturing involves various levels of localisation. Some facilities specialise in assembling components imported from abroad and testing finished vehicles. Others also manufacture metal structures and electrical equipment, and carry out engineering and design work. Each model requires different levels of investment, technical infrastructure and skilled personnel.

Azerbaijan already has experience assembling metro carriages at local facilities. In 2024, Baku Metro began assembling new-generation carriages using existing infrastructure. According to official figures, under a contract to supply 65 carriages between 2024 and 2026, specialists from the manufacturer also took part in assembling, commissioning and testing rolling stock in Azerbaijan.

This experience demonstrates that existing infrastructure can be used for final assembly and technical testing. However, it remains unclear how Škoda Group’s proposed model would differ from current practices.

The company has yet to disclose which stages of production would take place in Azerbaijan, what proportion of components would be locally manufactured, the terms of technology transfer or the facility’s annual production capacity. These indicators will help assess how much added value the project could generate for local industry.

Even if the facility initially focuses only on assembly and maintenance, the project could help train skilled workers and expand rolling stock repair capabilities. However, manufacturing more complex components in Azerbaijan would require additional investment and a steady flow of orders.

Škoda Group is not the only contender

Azerbaijan’s talks on purchasing new metro carriages and introducing modern technologies are not limited to the Czech company. In January 2026, Baku Metro officials met representatives of Swiss company Stadler Rail Group. They discussed the possible purchase of up to 300 new carriages, reducing operating costs and introducing modern signalling systems.

In February, a Škoda Group delegation led by CEO Petr Novotný also held talks with Baku Metro officials. Discussions focused on purchasing new carriages and prospects for long-term technological cooperation. Potential cooperation between AZCON and Škoda Group had also been discussed in May 2025.

These meetings indicate that Azerbaijan is exploring opportunities to involve international suppliers in modernising Baku Metro. However, Škoda Group’s proposal to establish a facility in Baku does not mean the company has secured orders for the carriages envisaged under the state programme.

Key criteria for selecting suppliers will include compliance with technical requirements, purchase price, energy consumption, maintenance costs and long-term operating conditions.

Localising production in Azerbaijan could bring additional economic benefits. However, its impact on procurement costs and competition will depend on the specific commercial proposals.

What does Uzbekistan’s experience show?

Škoda Group already has experience of a similar cooperation model in Central Asia. In April 2026, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the supply of 10 electric trains to Uzbekistan and their maintenance.

The project, worth more than €120m, also includes establishing a joint venture, localising maintenance services and training specialists. The company also plans to launch a Škoda Academy educational programme in Uzbekistan.

This example shows that Škoda Group’s cooperation model goes beyond supplying rolling stock to include developing local maintenance infrastructure and transferring technology. However, its projects in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are at different stages.

In Uzbekistan, the number of trains and project cost have already been agreed, and a strategic cooperation agreement has been signed. In Azerbaijan, the company has so far only announced plans to establish a production and maintenance facility.

The proposed Baku facility’s potential to serve regional markets will also depend on commercial prospects. This would require orders from neighbouring countries, compliance with technical standards and competitive production costs.

World.title: Progress or disaster? Armenia begins operations at Amulsar mine
World.content:
Operations begin at Amulsar mine

The Amulsar gold mine has begun operations in Armenia. Guests attending the official opening ceremony were shown the mining process and the production of the first gold bar. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also attended the ceremony.

The Armenian government expects the project to generate $130m annually in tax revenue and other income for the state budget.

Environmental campaigners, who have warned about the risks associated with the project for years, condemned the government’s decision. More than 60 organisations issued a statement warning that mining at Amulsar would lead to an “irreversible environmental catastrophe”.

However, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan maintains that concerns about environmental risks have been comprehensively addressed. He insists that all questions raised by environmentalists have received thorough and conclusive answers, dispelling their fears.

“There were alarming statements and concerns, including about the possible poisoning of Lake Sevan and so on. And we are here today because we are convinced that none of these risks actually exist,” Pashinyan said.

Economist Suren Parsyan expects the development of the Amulsar deposit to bring significant economic and social benefits.

He also believes that the launch of the mine will demonstrate to investors that Armenia continues to operate in accordance with international standards and is ready to implement new projects.



$750m already invested in the project

The Amulsar mining project is being implemented as part of a strategic partnership between Lydian Armenia and the Armenian government.

According to the government, Lydian Armenia has:

introduced international best practices and standards at Amulsar;

adopted the principles of modern, responsible mining;

promoted a new culture of occupational safety, environmental management, social responsibility and the use of modern technologies.

The company has already invested around $750m in the project.

The Amulsar mine is expected to produce approximately 210,000 ounces (around 6.5 tonnes) of gold annually.

“According to expert estimates, the annual taxes and other contributions paid by Lydian Armenia to the state budget as a result of the mine’s operation will amount to approximately $130m, contributing an estimated 1.5–2% to Armenia’s GDP,” the government said in a statement.

The project is also expected to create more than 4,000 direct and indirect jobs.

Under an agreement between the government and Lydian Armenia, the company will allocate 7m–9m annually to socio-economic development programmes in nearby communities throughout the mine’s operational lifespan.

Pashinyan: ‘Country is entering a new stage of development’

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described the launch of operations at the Amulsar mine not only as a successful investment project but also as a new stage in the country’s development and an important milestone in the history of Armenia’s mining industry and economic development.

“In the context of Armenia’s history, this is a major step forward. But I hope and firmly believe that in the near future, such steps will become routine and part of our everyday practice. And what we consider a major step in the future will involve projects on an even larger scale.”

According to Pashinyan, the project will provide Armenia with greater opportunities to invest in the security and well-being of its citizens.

He stressed that the country’s mineral resources belong to the Armenian people and that the government’s key responsibility is to ensure that this wealth “serves the development and prosperity” of every citizen.

Nikol Pashinyan inspected the facilities and infrastructure developed for the operation of the mine.

The prime minister said that Lydian Armenia had imported modern equipment to develop the deposit. In his view, Armenia can now boast a high-quality mining industry:

“For any developed country, mining of this calibre, carried out in compliance with environmental and social standards, is a key driver of national development.“

‘Ignoring the risks is unacceptable’: Environmental NGOs’ statement

According to civil society representatives, they have still not received information about realistic and well-founded measures to address the environmental and socio-economic risks associated with the project.

They described the ceremonial opening of the mine just days before the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), due to take place in Yerevan, as “a very bold and irresponsible step”.

“By hosting COP17, Armenia is seeking to demonstrate its commitment to the green agenda to the international community, while an environmental catastrophe is unfolding within the country. Armenia’s natural environment, water resources and the future of local communities cannot be put at risk without proper public accountability and evidence that the project is safe. We consider it unacceptable to ignore these risks,” the statement said.

Expert commentary

According to economist Suren Parsyan, Amulsar is the largest investment project in Armenia’s modern history.

In an interview with Armenpress, he said the Amulsar deposit had sufficient reserves to sustain mining operations for at least 20–25 years. He therefore believes that the mine will have a significant economic impact not only on nearby communities but also on the country as a whole.

Parsyan said the company’s turnover or exports would amount to around $930m, meaning that Armenia would gain a new “industrial giant” comparable to the Zangezur Copper and Molybdenum Combine.

“We now have the second-largest mining company, which will have a direct impact of around 2% on the economy. Its indirect impact could amount to another 1.5–2%.”

He stressed that the company would become a customer for more than 200 small and medium-sized enterprises, serving as a “driving force for regional businesses”.

The economist also believes that the mine’s operation will bring significant social benefits. Around 1,000 direct jobs are expected to be created, alongside 4,000–6,000 indirect jobs.

“Salaries here are quite high, averaging 900,000 drams ($2,356) or more. This is a fairly high figure, even exceeding the average salary at other mining companies in Armenia,” he explained.

Suren Parsyan pointed out that Vayots Dzor is one of Armenia’s poorest regions, with a poverty rate of around 25%, above the national average.

He also noted that, in addition to creating jobs, the project includes a social component aimed at supporting nearby communities.

“The poverty rate could fall significantly, by around two to three times. In Vayots Dzor, where the population is small and employment opportunities are limited, this could provide a long-term solution to the problem,” he concluded.

World.title: Azerbaijan forecasts inflation to fall to 4.3% by 2030
World.content:
Photo: Bureau of National Statistics of the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms of the Republic of Kazakhstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Average annual inflation in Azerbaijan is projected to decline to 4.3% in 2030, while investment in fixed assets is expected to reach 28.4 billion manat ($16.7 billion).

This was reflected in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework prepared by the country's Ministry of Finance for the next four years.

According to the forecasts, the average annual inflation rate, projected at 5.7% in 2026, is expected to decline to 5.3% in 2027, 4.8% in 2028, 4.6% in 2029, and 4.3% in 2030.

The forecasts prepared by the Ministry of Economy take into account several factors, including the actual inflation rate recorded so far this year; the relative decline in global commodity and food prices and its impact on import prices; the dynamics of the nominal effective exchange rate index; the assumption that the exchange rate will remain stable; and the effects of changes in tariffs for regulated goods and services.

According to the document, the manat’s exchange rate against the US dollar is assumed to remain stable at its current-year level throughout the 2027–2030 period.

Meanwhile, investment in fixed assets is projected to increase over the medium term. Total investment is expected to reach 25.4 billion manat ($14.9 billion) in 2027, 26.9 billion manat ($15.8 billion) in 2028, 27.9 billion manat ($16.4 billion) in 2029, and 28.4 billion manat ($16.7 billion) in 2030.

The non-oil and gas sector is expected to account for an increasing share of total investment. Investment in this sector is projected to amount to 17.4 billion manat ($10.2 billion) in 2027, 18.6 billion manat ($10.9 billion) in 2028, 19.7 billion manat ($11.6 billion) in 2029, and 20.9 billion manat ($12.3 billion) in 2030.

Investment in the oil and gas sector is expected to amount to 8 billion manat ($4.7 billion) in 2027, 8.3 billion manat ($4.9 billion) in 2028, and 8.2 billion manat ($4.8 billion) in 2029, before declining to 7.5 billion manat ($4.4 billion) in 2030.

According to the forecasts, nominal household incomes and expenditures are also expected to continue increasing. Household incomes, which amounted to 89.9 billion manat ($52.9 billion) in 2025, are projected to rise to 98.6 billion manat ($58 billion) in 2026, 107.5 billion manat ($63.2 billion) in 2027, 116.5 billion manat ($68.5 billion) in 2028, 126.7 billion manat ($74.5 billion) in 2029, and 137 billion manat ($80.6 billion) in 2030.

Household expenditures are projected to increase from 88.1 billion manat ($51.8 billion) in 2025 to 96.4 billion manat ($56.7 billion) in 2026, 105.1 billion manat ($61.8 billion) in 2027, 113.9 billion manat ($67 billion) in 2028, 123.9 billion manat ($72.9 billion) in 2029, and 134.1 billion manat ($78.9 billion) in 2030.

Thus, nominal household incomes are expected to exceed expenditures throughout the forecast period. The difference between incomes and expenditures is projected to reach 2.9 billion manat ($1.7 billion) in 2030.

World.title: Azerbaijan expects limited fiscal impact from inflation risks by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Deviations from Azerbaijan's baseline inflation forecast are expected to have a limited impact on the non-oil primary deficit as a share of non-oil GDP and on the consolidated budget balance over the medium term.

This was reflected in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework prepared by the country's Ministry of Finance for the next four years.

The document identifies persistent global uncertainty, price trends in major trading partners, and volatility in global commodity markets as the main external risk factors affecting inflation.

In particular, continued geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could trigger additional volatility in energy and other commodity prices. Meanwhile, a weakening of the nominal effective exchange rate could accelerate the pass-through of imported inflation to domestic prices.

Regarding domestic factors, the document assesses the likelihood of aggregate demand increasing sufficiently to significantly intensify inflationary pressures as low under the current fiscal and monetary policy framework.

According to the document, the assessment of the fiscal impact of inflation risks takes into account the potential effects of price changes on nominal GDP, budget revenues, and fiscal indicators expressed as a share of GDP.

Inflation risks were assessed under scenarios in which inflation deviates from the baseline forecast by 0.4, 0.8, 1.1 and 1.5 percentage points in either direction.

The calculations show that, under the scenarios considered, inflation is expected to have a limited impact on the non-oil primary deficit as a share of non-oil GDP and on the consolidated budget balance in 2027-2030.

In 2027, the non-oil primary deficit as a share of non-oil GDP is expected to deviate from the baseline scenario by 0.1-0.4 percentage points under different inflation scenarios.

The projected impact of inflation on the consolidated budget balance is even smaller. Under the different scenarios, the balance is expected to deviate from the baseline by 0.1-0.3 percentage points in 2027.

According to the charts, the non-oil primary deficit as a share of non-oil GDP stood at approximately 22.5% in 2022 and is projected to reach around 17.5% in 2027. The indicator is expected to improve from 2028, declining to approximately 10%-11% by 2030.

The consolidated budget balance as a share of GDP stood at approximately 6% in 2022 and 8% in 2023. It is projected to remain in deficit in 2026-2027 before gradually improving from 2028.

The Ministry of Finance considers the management of fiscal risks associated with inflation important for maintaining macroeconomic stability. According to the document, flexible budget policies and targeted social protection programs will help minimize the adverse effects of unexpected price increases.

World.title: Azerbaijan targets $99.5B GDP and 82% non-oil share by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijan's GDP is projected to reach 169.1 billion manat ($99.5 billion) in 2030, while the non-oil-gas sector's share of GDP is expected to rise to 82%.

This was reflected in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework released by the Ministry of Finance for the next 4 years.

According to forecasts, GDP is expected to reach 141 billion manat ($82.9 billion) by the end of 2027, including non-oil-gas GDP of 109.1 billion manat ($64.2 billion). By 2030, these figures are expected to increase to 169.1 billion manat ($99.5 billion) and 138.6 billion manat ($81.5 billion), respectively.

Over the medium term, real GDP growth is projected to average 3.3% annually, while non-oil-gas GDP is expected to grow by an average of 4.4%.

According to forecasts, GDP, which amounted to 129.1 billion manat ($75.9 billion) in 2025, will reach 138 billion manat ($81.2 billion) in 2026, 141 billion manat ($82.9 billion) in 2027, 147.6 billion manat ($86.8 billion) in 2028, and 158.4 billion manat ($93.2 billion) in 2029. This figure is expected to reach 169.1 billion manat ($99.5 billion) in 2030.

Non-oil-gas GDP is projected to increase from 92.3 billion manat ($54.3 billion) in 2025 to 100 billion manat ($58.8 billion) in 2026, 109.1 billion manat ($64.2 billion) in 2027, 118.3 billion manat ($69.6 billion) in 2028, 128.1 billion manat ($75.4 billion) in 2029, and 138.6 billion manat ($81.5 billion) in 2030.

The share of the oil and gas sector in GDP is expected to decline over the medium term. However, it is anticipated that production will increase from 2029 onwards, driven by the full-capacity operation of the Absheron field, thereby making a positive contribution to the sector's development.

Under the baseline scenario, the average annual export price of a barrel of oil is assumed to be $65 in 2027, remaining at this level through 2028–2030.

Furthermore, investments in fixed capital are projected to grow by 2.4% in 2027, with an average annual growth rate of 2.2% over the medium term. An increase in capital investment directed toward the oil and gas sector is expected during 2027–2028.

The forecast for fixed capital investments takes into account the investment plans of key entities within the oil and gas sector, state budget capital expenditures, reconstruction efforts in the liberated territories, targets for attracting foreign direct investment into the non-oil and gas sector, and the expansion of public-private partnerships in infrastructure projects. According to the Ministry of Economy’s estimates, the average annual inflation, projected at 5.7% for the current year under the baseline scenario, is expected to gradually decline, reaching 4.3% by 2030. This forecast takes into account the dynamics of commodity and food prices in global markets, impacts on import prices, fluctuations in the nominal effective exchange rate index, the assumption that the exchange rate will remain stable, and adjustments to the tariffs for regulated goods and services.

Over the medium term, household incomes and expenditures are also expected to increase. In 2030, household incomes are projected to reach 137 billion manat ($80.6 billion), while expenditures are expected to total 134.1 billion manat ($78.9 billion).

World.title: Azerbaijan projects state budget deficit at 2.2% of GDP in 2027-2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijan's state budget deficit is projected to average 2.2% of GDP in 2027–2030.

The forecast is outlined in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework prepared by the Ministry of Finance for the next four years.

According to the document, the upper limit for the state budget deficit is projected at 3.146 billion manat ($1.85 billion) in 2027, 3.342 billion manat ($1.96 billion) in 2028, 3.5541 billion manat ($2.09 billion) in 2029, and 3.6595 billion manat ($2.15 billion) in 2030.

The deficit is expected to be financed through privatization proceeds, domestic and external borrowing, and the balance in the single treasury account.

The document states that relevant procedures have been launched to attract external borrowing from international financial institutions to finance projects in several priority areas. Loans secured under agreements to be signed are expected to increase the share of this source in financing the state budget deficit.

In line with the objectives of the new macro-fiscal framework, domestic and external borrowing is planned to remain within approved limits over the long term. Developing domestic financial markets through the issuance of government securities and bonds will remain a priority.

The document also projects a significant reduction in the consolidated budget deficit. The deficit is expected to fall from 2.7579 billion manat ($1.62 billion) in 2027 to 442.2 million manat ($260.1 million) in 2030.

World.title: Azerbaijan projects $7.7B for liberated territories' reconstruction by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijan is projected to allocate 13.2 billion manat ($7.7 billion) for the reconstruction and restoration of its liberated territories in 2027-2030.

The forecast is outlined in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework prepared by the Ministry of Finance for the next four years.

According to the document, the allocation will account for 24.1% of the state budget's capital expenditure.

The document states that the 2027 state budget's capital expenditure will finance several strategically important measures and government programs.

These include projects under the Strategy for the Socio-Economic Development of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027-2030, the National Strategy for the Efficient Use of Water Resources, the State Program for the Socio-Economic Development of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic for 2023-2027, and the State Program for Improving Transport Infrastructure in Baku and Surrounding Areas for 2025-2030.

A significant share of state budget capital expenditure over the medium term is also expected to go toward implementing the Great Return Program and strengthening the country's defense capabilities and security.

The forecast for reconstruction and restoration spending in the liberated territories also takes into account the draft second phase of the Great Return Plan.

World.title: Azerbaijan's public debt projected to reach 20.4% of GDP by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijan's total public debt is projected to reach 34.5 billion manat ($20.2 billion) by the end of 2030, equivalent to 20.4% of GDP.

The forecast is outlined in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework prepared by the Ministry of Finance for the next four years.

According to the document, Azerbaijan's total external and domestic public debt is expected to reach 27 billion manat ($15.8 billion), or 19.5% of projected GDP, by the end of 2026.

As of January 1, 2026, public debt stood at 20.1% of GDP. This was 9.9 percentage points below the upper limit for the public debt-to-GDP ratio set for the medium term under the fiscal rule.

Last year, Azerbaijan achieved the targets set out in the updated 2022-2025 framework for its Medium- and Long-Term Public Debt Management Strategy, which called for keeping public debt below 30% of GDP and external public debt below $10 billion.

The document states that, in line with the public debt management strategy, measures have been taken to gradually reduce the share of external debt in total public debt and replace it with domestic borrowing. At the same time, financing the state budget deficit through government securities issued on the domestic financial market has led to a significant increase in domestic public debt.

In 2026, the government plans to borrow through government securities issued on the domestic financial market and by financing projects with funds from international financial institutions.

This includes attracting loans in cooperation with international financial institutions to finance priority projects under approved government programs in the water and transport sectors.

According to forecasts, the public debt-to-GDP ratio will stand at 20.4% at the end of the medium-term period covering 2027-2030. The indicator will be monitored as part of efforts to manage public debt and maintain fiscal sustainability.

World.title: Azerbaijan's parliamentary commission warns of escalating hybrid attacks
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijan’s Parliamentary Commission on Foreign Interference and Hybrid Threats issued a statement on the hybrid attacks directed at the country.

According to the statement, the emergence of our state as a "middle power" under the wise leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, along with its resolute foreign policy, growing international standing, contributions to global energy security, strategic importance within regional transit corridors, and domestic political and economic stability, has led to a significant escalation in the scale of hybrid attacks launched against Azerbaijan by foreign actors.

"Against the backdrop of ongoing wars and tensions in our region, Azerbaijan, often characterized as an 'island of stability', has recently been subjected to unprecedented and synchronized religious-ideological provocations, coordinated information operations, and cyberattacks.

Under the guise of various freedoms, our nation’s centuries-old national-moral and multicultural values, as well as its religious beliefs, are being targeted. Furthermore, through malicious activities aimed at eroding the very concept of truth within society, they are being presented with ideologies alien to the Azerbaijani people as the correct path.

Joint investigations with relevant state authorities have revealed that influence operations, aimed at manipulating public opinion, fostering societal polarization, and undermining trust in state institutions, as well as cyberattacks and acts of terror or sabotage, are being orchestrated by agents of influence and clandestine organizations both within and outside the country. In the digital sphere, these activities are carried out through hacker groups, foreign media outlets, real and fake accounts, and bots.

Regrettably, hostile forces operating from the territories of friendly and neighboring countries are injecting disinformation into digital platforms via channels that appear independent, seeking to create rifts within society along ethnic, religious, or political lines. Their objective is to sow discord within the country, turn citizens with differing viewpoints against one another, incite violence, and undermine our state from within," the statement noted.

The statement added that actors behind these hybrid threats employ "computational propaganda" to confuse public opinion and deepen societal fragmentation. They encourage individuals, across media and social networks, to actively seek out, believe, and disseminate false information that aligns with their existing views.

"Content distribution driven by algorithms creates an 'echo chamber' effect, ensuring that users encounter only information that reflects their own pre-existing beliefs, perspectives, and worldviews. Content designed to trigger emotional responses among our citizens is directed toward broad audiences through the algorithms embedded in digital platforms.

Furthermore, through the mechanism of "filter bubbles," harmful content reaches only an audience already predisposed to receive it- those who have already fallen under a specific influence. This exponentially increases the effectiveness of such manipulation.

In such an environment, the actors in question, without resorting to traditional propaganda methods, aim to promote alien values, undermine national stability, and fragment our society from within, all by leveraging the very infrastructure of these platforms.

Monitoring efforts have also revealed that, despite the scale of the malicious activities directed against Azerbaijan from certain centers, our victorious people have maintained a firm stance; they have refused to be swayed by provocations, have unequivocally supported the measures taken by the state, and continue to provide essential assistance in exposing divisive content and the individuals behind it.

We reiterate that the Parliamentary Commission on Foreign Interference and Hybrid Threats, along with relevant committees, the structural units of the Secretariat, and appropriate state institutions, are successfully countering these malicious hybrid attacks directed against our state; furthermore, we will ensure that no future hostile action goes unanswered.

Our commission also expresses its profound gratitude to the citizens of friendly and neighboring countries who have condemned these anti-Azerbaijan activities and maintained a fair stance," the statement emphasized.

World.title: Kazakhstan joins World Bank's minerals initiative, targets $20B investment
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Kazakhstan has become the first country in Central Asia to join the World Bank Group's global Metals and Minerals Compact initiative, the government of Kazakhstan reported.

The official ceremony marking Kazakhstan's accession to the initiative took place on October 16 on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund in Thailand. Kazakhstan was represented by Yerlan Galiyev, Chairman of the Management Board of the National Geological Service under the Ministry of Industry and Construction.

In line with the tasks set by the head of state in his Address to the Nation regarding the development of the mining and metallurgical sector and attracting investment into the economy, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Industry and Construction and the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, in cooperation with the World Bank, developed a country-specific Metals and Minerals Compact.

"The document defines the main areas of partnership for 2026-2030 and brings together the World Bank Group's financial, analytical and technical support instruments," the government reported.

The Compact is based on Kazakhstan's strategic documents, including the National Development Plan through 2029, the Concept for the Development of the Geological Industry for 2023-2027, and the Comprehensive Plan for the Development of the Rare and Rare Earth Metals Industry for 2024-2028.

One of its key objectives is to help attract approximately $20 billion in investment by 2031. The investment is expected to support the expansion of the mineral resource base, the development of mining and processing facilities, the introduction of modern technologies, and the construction of the necessary infrastructure.

The Compact provides for three main areas of cooperation.

The first focuses on improving public policy and regulatory mechanisms in the mining and metallurgical sector. This is expected to help establish a transparent and predictable business environment, improve the investment climate, and promote the adoption of international environmental and social standards.

The second covers the development of geological exploration, infrastructure, and human capital. Priorities include digitizing geological data, developing energy and transport infrastructure, introducing modern metal processing technologies, and training qualified personnel.

The third aims to attract private investment in mineral extraction and advanced processing. The initiative provides support for investment projects through the World Bank Group's financing and guarantee instruments, the development of higher-value-added production, and efforts to attract international investors.

"Kazakhstan is committed to the principles of responsible and sustainable development of its mineral resources sector. Cooperation with the World Bank Group supports the implementation of national priorities in developing raw material processing and expanding the production of higher-value-added goods. We look forward to further strengthening our partnership, which will help improve the competitiveness and resilience of the sector, diversify the economy, and make more efficient use of our country's natural resource potential," Kazakhstan's Minister of Industry and Construction Yersaiyn Nagaspayev said.

The implementation of the Compact is expected to promote further mineral processing, create new jobs, and strengthen Kazakhstan's position in global value chains.

World.title: Canberra man caught bringing alleged child abuse material into country
World.content:
A 42-year old Canberra man allegedly caught returning to Australia with child abuse material has been refused bail.

Support services for those affected by child sexual abuse: Bravehearts: 1800 272 831

Lifeline (24-hour Crisis Line): 131 114

Victims of Crime Helpline: 1800 819 817

Full Stop (24-hour helpline for survivors of sexual assault and abuse): 1800 385 578

Australian Border Force officers selected Nicholas Tyson Quinn for examination after he landed in Sydney on a flight from Europe in May.

It is alleged they found child exploitation images as well as inappropriate conversations on a messaging app, with further investigation uncovering multiple transfers of money to a teenager in Europe.

ACT police raided Mr Quinn's home in Chisholm yesterday, where it is alleged they found a USB storage device containing child abuse material plugged into his computer.

He faced the ACT Magistrates Court today, charged with two counts of possessing child abuse material.

Nicholas Quinn was charged with two counts of possessing child abuse material. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Applying for bail, Mr Quinn's lawyer told the court he could comply with conditions including living at home with his mother and surrendering his passports.

But the prosecutor opposed his release, alleging Mr Quinn had been in a relationship with a 17-year-old girl in Ukraine, and his mother had previously travelled there with him and met with the teenager and her mother.

The court heard Mr Quinn's employers allegedly told police about the travel to Ukraine, and that he had been trying to move his "girlfriend" to Australia.

Concerns about persistent contact with young person, dual citizenship

As an Australian and Latvian dual citizen, the prosecutor argued bail conditions could not prevent Mr Quinn from seeking a new Latvian passport in order to flee the country.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt said the prosecution had not been able to confirm whether police believe the Ukrainian girl was depicted in the child abuse material.

Despite being unable to confirm that detail, she refused bail due to the likelihood of Mr Quinn attempting to flee or endangering the safety of others.

"Ultimately, there is a degree of speculation in those risks, I accept," Magistrate Burt said.

"It is a case where the investigation is at a fairly preliminary stage.

"I am concerned, partly because of the persistence of contact after the Australian Border Force intervention and of the connection with these two people — one of which is a young person — in Ukraine … and his dual citizenship."

Mr Quinn was remanded in custody to return to court next month.

World.title: Jury to deliberate landlord's cold case murder trial
World.content:
A Supreme Court jury will soon begin deliberating in the trial of Steven Fredereick Johnson, who is charged with murdering a Warrnambool father who disappeared more than 20 years ago.

Mr Johnson, 74, has pleaded not guilty murdering Christopher Jarvis, who was 38 when he disappeared from his Wangoom home on June 13, 2006.

During the 21-day trial in Warrnambool, Crown prosecutors said Mr Johnson, a former police officer and landfill operator, orchestrated a violent attack on Mr Jarvis, his tenant, over $2,210 in unpaid rent.

But Mr Johnson's lawyers told the court he wanted to resolve the dispute lawfully and was not involved in the disappearance.

Mr Jarvis's body has never been found.

Christopher Jarvis has not been seen since 2006. (Supplied: Australian Missing Persons Register)

'No coincidence'

Prosecutors said Mr Johnson orchestrated a violent ambush on Mr Jarvis in his driveway before he left for work early that morning.

The Crown said Mr Johnson fired a starter pistol in Mr Jarvis's ear, causing him to bleed from the head, before bundling him into his own car.

Prosecutors said Mr Johnson then drove the man to the nearby Framlingham Forest, where Mr Johnson allegedly killed Mr Jarvis by hitting him over the head with a baseball bat before he buried him in a shallow grave.

They told the court Mr Johnson then organised for Mr Jarvis's car to be torched 20 kilometres away at Thunder Point, a coastal lookout near Warrnambool.

Prosecutors said Christopher Jarvis's body was dumped in Framlingham Forest. (ABC News: Kiara Angelini)

During closing arguments, Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson KC told the court circumstantial evidence supported the Crown's case.

Mr Gibson said this included that Mr Jarvis vanished the day before the men were due to appear at a contested hearing in the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) over the rental dispute.

The court heard Mr Johnson wanted to be paid the overdue rent and had sought to evict his tenant from the property, while Mr Jarvis refused to pay rent or leave as he said his landlord owed him money for plumbing works and materials.

"It was no coincidence that [Mr Jarvis] went missing the day before that court case," Mr Gibson said.

Mr Gibson told the jury hostility and friction between the men had been growing in the lead-up to the disappearance.

He also pointed to evidence that Mr Johnson inexplicably graded the gravel driveway in front of Mr Jarvis's home in the hours after the alleged ambush.

Christopher Jarvis was living at this Wangoom property when he disappeared. (ABC News: Matt Neal)

The Crown told the court this was an attempt to conceal the presence of blood and other biological matter.

Mr Gibson told the jury Mr Johnson's behaviour after a November 2022 police interview prior to his arrest implicated him in the crime.

The court heard Mr Johnson allegedly said, "If they find out I'm an ex-copper, I'm f***ed. I'm too old to go to jail".

'Speculation and suspicion'

Defence lawyer Patrick Doyle SC told the court the prosecution's case was based on speculation.

Christopher Jarvis's car was found burnt out at Thunder Point. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

"There's an inherent improbability in the Crown's case, and it involves layering one level of speculation on another," Mr Doyle said.

Mr Doyle said his client was attempting to use lawful means to resolve their rental dispute, including initiating the VCAT proceedings.

The defence also said there were a number of key issues with the prosecution's case, including unreliable and inconsistent witness evidence, an improbable timeline of events, and that Mr Johnson kept the starter pistol allegedly used in the assault for 16 years despite the claims he took other steps to allegedly cover his tracks.

He said the jury must find Mr Johnson not guilty if it has any doubt he committed the alleged crime.

The jury will commence deliberations after Justice Andrew Tinney's charge to the jury on Monday.

World.title: Awlad Hossain denied bail in foreign bribery case surrounding wife's death
World.content:
A Queensland man charged with bribing foreign officials investigating his estranged wife's alleged murder in Bangladesh has been denied bail.

Awlad Hossain, 51, is accused of transferring $97,000 to Bangladeshi associates between 2024 and 2026 in a bid to have his name removed from a police investigation into the suspected murder of Rehana Parvin in 2024.

The ABC revealed last April that the Australian Federal Police (AFP) was also investigating the death of Ms Parvin, an Australian citizen and mother-of-five, whose body was found buried in the yard of Mr Hossain's sister's home in Bangladesh.

The ABC does not suggest that Mr Hossain had any involvement in Ms Parvin's death, only that Bangladeshi police have applied for an arrest warrant.

Rehana Parvin and her estranged husband Awlad Hossain. (Supplied)

During a bail hearing on Friday, the Brisbane Magistrates Court heard both investigations in Australia and Bangladesh remain ongoing.

Commonwealth prosecutors opposed Mr Hossain's release, arguing he posed a risk of failing to appear in court, interfering with witnesses and committing further offences.

They told the hearing the alleged bribery offence occurred while Mr Hossain was already on bail for separate fraud charges.

'Prepared to give anything'

The court also heard he had allegedly enquired previously about leaving Australia without a passport.

Prosecutors further alleged Mr Hossain had expressed he was "prepared to give anything" to convince Bangladeshi officials to drop the case against him.

Mr Hossain's lawyer, Torik Dib, challenged the strength of the prosecution's argument, pointing to the absence of a police complainant in Bangladesh alleging an attempted bribe.

He also questioned the evidence surrounding the money transfers, noting that some had been made by a third party,

"It's not as clear-cut," he told the court.

Mr Hossain's lawyer Torik Dib. (ABC News)

He urged the magistrate to consider his client's family circumstances, including his responsibility to care for an 18-year-old nephew who had no other relatives in Australia.

'Unique' case

Acting magistrate Timothy Hishon acknowledged the unusual nature of the case, describing it as "unique", but ultimately found the risks of releasing Mr Hossain from custody were too great.

"It's clear to me that … there's no conditions that would ameliorate the risk of further offending and failing to appear and as such, bail is refused," he said.

Speaking outside court, Mr Dib said his client contests the bribery charge and denies any involvement in his estranged wife's death.

He confirmed he had been instructed to make a bail application on behalf of Mr Hossain in the Supreme Court, citing "anticipated delays" in the case.

"We'll be proceeding on that basis either later this year or early next year," he said.

The matter was adjourned and will return to court early next year.

World.title: Proposed Dalby data centre to harvest rainwater from roof
World.content:
The international developer that has proposed Australia's largest data centre says it would be able to operate during even the worst droughts.

The proposed $32 billion Western Downs Digital Park in regional Queensland would consist of four data centres, the first of which has been leased by Anthropic for use as early as 2027.

Zerra DC is holding community consultation session in Dalby on the Western Downs. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Planning documents by Singapore-based developer Zerra DC said each of the four buildings planned for the Western Downs Digital Park would require 21,000 litres of water a day, equivalent to the water usage of a small shopping centre.

The company's chief data centre officer Matt Ward said modelling showed that even in 2019, when Dalby received less than 200 millimetres of rain, it would catch enough rainwater to operate.

Matt Ward says the developer is committed to being a "good neighbour". (Supplied: Zerra DC)

Mr Ward said the buildings housing the data centres were "large sheds" with "35,000-odd square metres of roof space" and the facility would be entirely air-cooled and would not draw from bores or town water.

'Landlord' role on power

Mr Ward said supplying new power to the grid would be the responsibility of its artificial intelligence customers such as Anthropic, which the company has signed an agreement with.

He said Zerra DC would act like the "landlord of any commercial building", where the tenant, Anthropic, would be responsible for paying for power supply.

The data centre is proposed on the site of a feedlot outside of Dalby. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

It comes as the federal government works to establish a framework that would require data centres to bring as much power into the electricity grid as they take.

Australia's largest proposed data centre could draw a quarter of Queensland's energy use The proposed $30 billion data centre in Queensland has a peak capacity comparable to the average power requirements of 1.5 million households.

But who pays for that power production was a dilemma, according to Climate Energy Finance director Tim Buckley.

He said both sides needed to be "collectively held to account" to commit to new renewable energy generation.

"If they aren't held to account in substance over the life of the project, we will inevitably see higher power prices for everyone across Queensland as a result," Mr Buckley said.

Some in the Western Downs have questioned how the region would benefit from the multi-billion-dollar investment.

Zerra DC began community consultation sessions during the day last week, but recently announced the "drop-in" sessions would run in the afternoons from midday to 8pm.

Robyn Sheehan attended an information session in Dalby about the proposed data centre. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Dalby resident Robyn Sheehan said she took part in a session because she felt tired of big industries making "empty promises" in the area.

"It's just downgrading our farming land, ruining the lifestyle of many people out there," Ms Sheehan said.

Zerra DC has committed to 1,500 jobs per year during construction and 1,400 ongoing operational jobs at full capacity, which would transform the local economy.

"To keep this thing running, we'll need a team of skilled people across mechanical, electrical, security, engineering at a 24-7 basis," Mr Ward said.

World.title: Reserve Bank governor paid $1.2 million as RBA workers fight real wage cuts
World.content:
The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia.

RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million.

Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217.

Half of young adults living with parents Half of all young Australians are still living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001, a survey reveals.

The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543.

The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report, which was released on Thursday afternoon.

The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672.

In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3.

It was her third investment property.

Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website.

Michele Bullock says she sympathises with the plight of Australian workers. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000.

However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more.

Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant.

Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25.

RBA workers don't want a real wage cut

The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions.

Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years.

Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth, research suggests

But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years.

A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July.

The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer.

The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm.

After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers.

But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it.

"People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said. "If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline."

According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees.

It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff.

The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas.

The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions.

RBA staff numbers increased by 8 per cent in the past year. (Source: RBA annual report 2026)

Higher unemployment will help to control inflation

Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.

It is higher than the RBA forecast for this point in its rate-hiking cycle.

At a fireside chat last month, Ms Bullock said Australia may need an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to get inflation completely under control.

"[W]hat level of unemployment eases the pressure on the supply side of the economy?" she asked.

"I think between 4.5 and 5 will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that it'll ease pressure on inflation," she said.

Unemployment rate remains at 4.7pc An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, while the number of unemployed people increased by 8,900.

On Thursday, Bureau of Statistics data showed that Australia's unemployment rate has risen 0.6 percentage points (from 4.1 per cent to 4.7 per cent) since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February this year.

Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in unemployment in more than a decade.

"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August," he said.

"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."

RBA records $11.3 billion negative equity position

The RBA's annual report shows the bank had a "negative equity" position of $11.3 billion at the end of June (compared with a negative equity position of $5.3 billion in June 2025).

The deterioration in its net equity position reflected a large "accounting loss" in 2025/26, which was partially offset by valuation gains on its gold holdings.

As at 30 June 2026, the RBA had a negative equity position of $11.3 billion. (Source: RBA annual report 2026)

The RBA's Governance Board says negative equity does not affect the RBA's ability to operate effectively or perform its functions, but it is important that the equity position is restored over time.

"This can be achieved by retaining future year profits," the RBA says in its annual report.

"Based on market expectations for the cash rate as at 30 June 2026 and market prices and exchange rates at this time, negative equity is expected to diminish over the next few years.

"However, a return to target for the Reserve Bank Reserve Fund probably remains more than a decade away."

World.title: Football Queensland backflips on 2027 fee changes
World.content:
Football Queensland has backflipped on proposed changes to its 2027 fee structure after pushback from member clubs across the state.

More than 100 clubs wrote to the governing body earlier this month in solidarity against what they called an unreasonably dramatic fee hike.

The clubs said the increased fees would likely make the sport unaffordable for families.

Initially, FQ disputed the clubs' claims and added that Queensland has the lowest fees in the country.

Football Queensland 2027 fees disagreement A spokesperson for Football Queensland rejects claims fees are going up and notes that the state has the lowest fees nationally.

Today, the governing body has gone back on its proposed changes, saying it has listened to its clubs.

The statement does not include any concession that the proposed 2027 fees had resulted in a price rise.

Instead of the 2027 fees changing to a new Competition Access Fee (CAF), FQ has confirmed it will retain the existing structure for the new year.

It added there will be "modest adjustments to reflect inflation".

In a statement, FQ said it still remained confident in the initially proposed CAF model, but accepted it "represented a significant change for clubs".

"Having carefully considered the feedback and the practical challenges of implementation, the Board believes retaining the existing structure for 2027 is the most sensible way forward," the statement said.

For 2027, player enrolment fees will now be $60 for MiniRoos, $80 for junior players, and for seniors, $150.

Explaining the 2027 fees, FQ said they will include two adjustments — transaction and technology costs, and a "modest adjustment".

"After more than seven years without an increase to player enrolment fees, a modest adjustment will help maintain the delivery of statewide football services and programs while continuing to keep football affordable," the statement said.

World.title: ACT criticised for considering 'human rights' in illegal tobacco trade
World.content:
The war on illicit tobacco has generated a war of words in the nation's capital.

The saga began earlier this week when the ACT health minister said the territory government had not yet committed to laws to close illegal tobacco retailers in part because of "human rights" considerations.

The Australian Council on Smoking and Health (ACOSH) said the ACT was the second worst jurisdiction in the country for tackling the illegal tobacco market, beating out only the Northern Territory.

ACOSH CEO Laura Hunter said the territories need "to urgently lift their response".

"Australians should not be less protected from illicit tobacco simply because they live in a territory," Ms Hunter said.

Queensland was the country's most effective state or territory at tackling the trade "thanks to its nation-leading enforcement capability and strong operational results," according to ACOSH.

The ACT's health minister says that the government will also need to consider whether closure laws are "effective". (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

'Human rights' considered by ACT government

On Wednesday, the ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the government had not yet committed to laws that would shut down illegal vape and cigarette shops, because it needed to consider the human rights implications and whether the laws would be effective.

"We will work through human rights considerations in the ACT, and we will also understand the need for those laws and look at the evidence if those laws have been effective in other jurisdictions," she told 666 ABC Canberra.

"We are a human rights jurisdiction, so we will take that into consideration ... in the development of all our legislation."

The government says it will develop legislation that includes closure laws. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Two days after her interview on ABC Radio, the government announced it would develop legislation that included closure orders, strengthened seizure powers and criminal penalties for shops that sold illegal products.

'National joke': Federal MP

Prior to the territory government's announcement on Friday, Federal Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill said human rights should not prevent the ACT government from developing laws to shut down illegal tobacconists.

Mr Hill said the human right to work came with obvious restrictions.

Federal Labor MP Julian Hill says human rights should not stop the ACT government from shutting illegal tobacco shops. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"I don't think anyone would accept there's an unqualified human right to flog illegal stuff trying to get kids hooked on nicotine and vapes [and] funding organised criminals," he said.

" We're at risk of becoming a national joke here in the ACT if the national capital is the last place in the country where every strip-shopping centre and shopping mall has illegal tobacconists. "

Illegal tobacco traders 'being put ahead of the health of Canberrans'

Chief executive of the Australian Association of Convenience Stores Theo Foukkare said the health minister's comments were "nuts".

CEO of the Australian Association of Convenience Stores Theo Foukkare said the health minister's comments were "nuts". (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

"These criminals don't care about the rights of everyday Aussies," Mr Foukkare said.

" What is happening in Canberra? Since when is stopping a criminal from selling an illegal product an infringement on their human rights? "

He said closure laws in other states had made the ACT, alongside the Northern Territory, "an open playground for criminals".

Territory ministers defend comments

ACT Equality Minister Suzanne Orr defended the territory's human rights framework.

The Equality Minister says the territory is "not falling behind". (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"We are a human rights jurisdiction and we take that very seriously here in the ACT, which does mean we have a little bit more complexity to work through in our legislative reform than other jurisdictions. But we are doing that. We're not falling behind," she said.

Before the government announced it would develop the new laws, ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne said the government needed to examine how similar laws have worked in other states, and said the power to close someone's business must be proportionate.

The ACT Attorney-General says there are measures that need to be considered in closure laws. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She added that proper checks around who could order a closure, the evidence needed, and how long a business could be closed were all needed.

The ACT passed laws in December that prohibited the sale of illegal tobacco and gave authorised officers greater powers to inspect tobacco retailers' premises, issue fines and seize illegal products.

World.title: Two men die after light plane crash in NSW Upper Hunter
World.content:
Two men have died after a light plane crashed at Scone in the NSW Upper Hunter.

Emergency crews were called to a paddock on Bunnan Road near Scone Memorial Airport, 150 kilometres north-west of Newcastle, about 1:55pm.

Police said the two occupants of the plane died at the scene, with inquiries now underway to identify the men.

A crime scene has been set up and will be examined by specialist officers.

Emergency crews respond to the crash. (ABC Newcastle: Courtney Yeandle)

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said the craft involved was a kit-built aircraft on the recreational register.

Recreational Aviation Australia has also been informed.

Upper Hunter Mayor Pat Ryan said he was contacted about the incident by the local airport general manager.

"It looks like the aircraft has crashed adjacent to the airport on private property," he said.

"Police are on the scene … sounds like a very tragic accident."

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.content:
