And the red contagion spreads. The Middle East conflict took another ugly turn to start the week as more agitators piled into the fray, with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia further inflaming regional tensions and sending global oil prices soaring. A strike on Riyadh airport that killed 12 led Trump to accuse Iran’s Islamic regime of steering the attacks to push oil prices higher ahead of the US midterms. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Identifai Limited. If that was the plan, it appeared to be working, with crude surging to US$107 a barrel this week even as Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil. Meanwhile, hopes of ending the more than four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine looked just as forlorn as the prospects for peace in the Middle East. Over on Wall Street, the AI trade looks to have finally come undone. Surely it wasn’t little old Aussie AI Firmus and its failed IPO that broke the camel’s back?



More likely, it’s China’s latest memory-chip advances that are rattling the sector, with semiconductors falling for a seventh straight NASDAQ session, down 14 per cent since the start of last week. OpenAI led the pandemonium after paring back its revenue expectations, as businesses increasingly turn to cheaper Chinese alternatives for token-heavy workloads. The AI contagion spread rapidly across the Pacific, sending Korean chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung tumbling 14 and 18 per cent respectively this week alone! With both heavyweights accounting for a substantial slice of South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI, the index suffered a bone-shattering 21 per cent plunge in just seven trading sessions as doubts over the AI boom collided with fears of further interest rate hikes. Thursday alone delivered a 7.6 per cent KOSPI wipeout, triggering trading halts and liquidations countrywide, with what had been one of the world’s hottest AI-fuelled markets now looking like a leveraged investor’s nightmare. To cap off an already bruising week, surging oil prices have reignited inflation fears and sparked a bloodbath across Australia’s mining sector. With the fuel supply squeeze again rearing its ugly head, headlines of job cuts at BHP and Rio Tinto have only added to the gloom, rattling investors and raising fresh concerns about the outlook for the broader resources industry. Rio Tinto is staring down the barrel of more than $500 million in additional annual Pilbara costs from sky-high diesel prices, while its shares have shed nearly 10 per cent in under a fortnight and took another hit during Thursday’s rout. The pain may be even worse for little brother Fortescue, with early forecasts suggesting its September quarter could deliver its first loss-making quarter in years — potentially the first since 2009, as some 67 consecutive profitable periods come undone.



One bright spot amid the carnage is the continuing takeover tussle for Northern Star Resources, Australia’s biggest listed gold miner. South African giant Gold Fields is reportedly open to sweetening its $40 billion bid with more cash and is dangling the benefits of an ASX listing as its chief executive embarks on a baby-kissing tour to win over Australian investors. Gold Fields boss Mike Fraser has also reportedly discussed selling some Northern Star mines to rivals, including Raleigh Finlayson’s Genesis Minerals, should the takeover succeed. That would allow the South African miner to concentrate on its flagship Kalgoorlie Super Pit, Alaska’s Pogo mine and the undeveloped Hemi project in WA’s Pilbara. This week’s Runners list was another small serving from a harsh vintage, with the Australian small ordinaries again among the market’s biggest casualties as domestic money flow tightens thanks to a mix of housing pressures and inflation. One bright spot on the ASX lately has been the IPO market, with several fresh listings making our Runners of late. This week’s top spot went to a plucky Israeli pregnancy biotech hopeful that managed to buck the broader market’s miserable mood for its ASX debut. Israeli biotech newcomer Identifai is targeting a significant unmet medical need with its AI-powered prenatal screening technology. IDENTIFAI GENETICS LTD (ASX: ID1)



Up 170% (20c – 54c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Israeli biotech newcomer Identifai Genetics Limited, which made a stellar debut on the ASX after raising $10 million in a float at 20 cents a share. The company’s flagship Windrose platform uses a simple blood sample from the mother as early as nine weeks into pregnancy to screen for more than 280 genes linked to genetic conditions in unborn babies. By combining DNA sequencing with AI, the technology aims to flag a much wider range of potential health problems earlier in pregnancy, without the need for invasive procedures such as amniocentesis. Shares in Identifai started strong and never looked back despite the shaky market backdrop, peaking at 54 cents on Thursday for a whopping 170 per cent gain on the week, as investors latched onto the potential of its technology. The company says it is targeting a significant unmet medical need, with the World Health Organisation (WHO) estimating that between three and six per cent of babies worldwide are born with a genetic or congenital disorder. Some conditions can be difficult to identify before birth, yet early detection can help doctors and families prepare for treatment well ahead of time.



While existing non-invasive prenatal tests primarily screen for common chromosomal conditions, Identifai says Windrose can assess fetal risk across more than 280 genes linked to conditions that may be actionable during pregnancy, delivery or shortly after birth. By combining AI with advanced genetic analysis, the company is aiming to push prenatal screening well beyond its traditional limits, initially targeting the US market with a platform backed by a growing intellectual property portfolio. AVENIRA LIMITED (ASX: AEV) Up 133% (0.6c – 1.2c) Slotting into second on the week was fertiliser frontrunner Avenira, which surged 100 per cent this week after securing an $85 million funding lifeline from major shareholder and strategic offtake partner Hebang Biotechnology. The cash injection will fully fund development of its giant Wonarah phosphate project through to first shipment and ongoing operations.



The package comprises an eight-year, $50 million development facility from China - at a staggering Reserve Bank cash rate with no additional margin. A further revolving line of $35 million in working capital will also carry the same benefits and term. Principal and cash-interest payments are deferred for two years, giving Avenira breathing room as it makes the leap from developer to producer. The deal is a major vote of confidence from Chinese-based shareholder Hebang, which already holds a 60 per cent voting interest and has committed to buying Wonarah’s premium phosphate. It also gives Avenira a clearer runway towards first direct shipping ore (DSO) shipments, targeted for the first half of next year. The prize is a monster Northern Territory resource hosting a JORC estimate of 812 million tonnes at 18 per cent phosphorus pentoxide, for a whopping 146 million tonnes of contained phosphate. Avenira plans to start with a relatively straightforward direct shipping operation to generate early revenue, before potentially stepping up to higher-grade processing and, further down the track, downstream products such as yellow phosphorus and thermal phosphoric acid for battery and electronics markets.



The timing could hardly be more interesting. Phosphate has been a quiet runner amid Middle Eastern disruptions, with supply-chain risks putting the spotlight on fertiliser security and the importance of reliable sources beyond geopolitically exposed regions. For Avenira, a well-funded path to production could put Wonarah in the frame as buyers look to secure future supply. With the funding hurdle cleared and first shipments on the horizon, Avenira appears at the doorstep of turning its enormous phosphate endowment into a producing Australian asset. Image Resources’ Boonanarring mineral sands operation in WA, which helped establish the company as a zircon and mineral sands producer. IMAGE RESOURCES LTD (ASX: IMA) Up 84% (1.9c – 3.5c)



Rounding out Runners is repeat customer Image Resources, after it kicked off the week on a tear despite having no fresh news to the market. The fun police down at the ASX came knocking around lunchtime on Tuesday after shares climbed from 1.9 cents last week to a high of 3.5 cents, issuing a “please explain” speeding ticket in the process. Image responded that it was unaware of any undisclosed information that could explain the move, but pointed to an announcement last month detailing a $5 million cash advance from major shareholder and strategic partner LB Group. The advance forms part of ongoing negotiations over a potential deal involving Image’s Durack and Yandanooka mineral sands projects in WA. The proposed transaction could see LB Group acquire a significant interest in the projects for $20 million in cash, alongside an interest in certain plant, equipment and other assets expected to be used in their development and operation. However, Image’s story is about more than just mineral sands, with the company recently giving punters another reason to straighten up in their seats, after drilling at its latest Erayinia-King gold project near Kalgoorlie and returning a swag of high-grade results. The standout was a 4.5-metre hit grading 22.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 128m, including a chunky one-metre section at a whopping 98.55g/t. Other drilling returned 14m at 2.84g/t and 16m at 2.51g/t, adding further sparkle to the historic mineral sands player’s emerging gold story.



Image says it has completed a 50-hole, 5450-metre drilling campaign at Erayinia-King, with mineralisation traced to only 140m vertical depth, leaving plenty of potential at depth. The project already hosts some two million tonnes at 2.1g/t gold for 139,000 ounces, with an updated resource now being prepared. The gold story gives Image a potentially valuable second string to its bow beyond the established mineral sands business. Meanwhile, talks with LB Group could open another lucrative chapter for Image as a strategic review gathers pace at its Durack project, fresh from a hefty 43 per cent resource upgrade to 37.7 million tonnes. With a sizeable mineral sands portfolio and a potential major deal in the works, Image has plenty to explain to the ASX why investors have been piling back in for weeks. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: NSW artist becomes just fourth woman in 30 years to win major Sculpture by the Sea prize
World.content:
CultureArt & designArts NSW artist becomes just fourth woman in 30 years to win major Sculpture by the Sea prize Michaela Boland October 16, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Female sculptors with powerful feminist messages have captured the zeitgeist – and the big prize – at Sculpture by the Sea in its 30th year. NSW artist Harrie Fasher won the $70,000 acquisitive Aqualand Sculpture Award with an abstract six-metre by five-metre steel, bronze and timber artwork. Harrie Fasher with her sculpture Unveiling the Edges of the Sky. Sam Mooy “This is for all the women, there’s a lot of us female sculptors that make work that’s really outside the square. It’s a battle. I’m the fourth (woman) to have won Sculpture by the Sea (Sydney) in its 30 years,” Fasher said. She described her work, Unveiling the Edges of the Sky, installed adjacent to the cliffs at Marks Park, as being about female strength, the dissolution of the ego and following your intuition.



After a soggy installation week, Sculpture by the Sea is open, free to the public. There are 100 works on display along two kilometres of the Bondi to Tamarama Beach walk and Marks Park, until Monday November 2. Omi McCurdie, Pip Lysaght and Matty McCarron, with their sculpture Sweethearts. Sam Mooy Reinforcing the female empowerment theme is an installation by Sydney public art collective Omi McCurdie, Matty McCarron and Philippa Lysaght. The trio’s shockingly playful outsized Sweethearts candies are emblazoned with classic Aussie phrases like “He was drunk”, “She coulda left” and “Boys will be boys”. Lysaght, a social justice advocate, said the trio, working together for the first time and making their Sculpture by the Sea debut, want to challenge the traditional notions of Australian masculinity that underpin the domestic violence epidemic.



“I was so appalled about the spate of domestic violence and wanted to do something that targets bystander inaction and calls out abuse,” she said. “I want people to really experience it and there’s no better stage than Sculpture by the Sea.” McCarron, a filmmaker, said collaborating on the project was confronting. “I’ve said a lot of these phrases because it’s just so easy to minimise individual instances, but you have to call your mates out and say it’s not OK,” he said. Over 450,000 people are expected to visit the exhibition, including thousands of schoolchildren, who McCurdie, a practising artist, said are an important part of the national discussion about violence against women.



John Eager’s Blue Water Rocket. Sam Mooy Sculpture by the Sea was founded by David Handley in 1997, originally as a one-day only event because he did not have the funds at that time to pay for overnight security. Handley was inspired by the sense of community he experienced in his 20s at the free summer concerts in the Domain, Opera in the Park and Symphony Under the Stars. Clayton Blake’s Pinnacle (centre) is seen through Michael Le Grand’s Primal Echo. Sam Mooy He then capitalised on the investment in the arts being made ahead of the Sydney Olympics, resulting in offshoot events staged around Australia.



Sculpture by the Sea eventually cemented itself in Sydney’s cultural calendar in October, when after the Sydney Olympics, it proved to be a masterstroke of counterprogramming that tapped into the city’s desire to keep partying after the games had packed up. Paul Ewart’s Both Sides Now. Sam Mooy The not-for-profit stages annual an exhibition in Cottesloe, Perth and it has over the years left a legacy of sculpture trails and staged similar events around the world. In Sydney, Sculpture by the Sea now includes an access and inclusion program; its popular school program is back; and a new Indigenous Artist Prize this year provides $20,000 for the creation and presentation of an ambitious new sculpture. Tim Storrier’s Wayfarer. Sam Mooy



Inaugural recipient David Doyle is a Barkindji and Malyangapa artist based in Broken Hill whose cast iron and steel shields Kaaku-Kaakulinyа: Eternal Sentinels explores protection, resilience and continual presence. Reflecting on the past 30 years, Handley said: “Sculptor Richard Goodwin was the first to say that Sculpture by the Sea (has) represented cultural change in Australia.” Sculptor Koichi Ishino with his work Circles. Sam Mooy “Just by the number of people turning up to an art exhibition year after year, people (through) repeat visitation are developing an eye for sculpture.” Sydney’s long history of free public art shows dates to at least 1969, when Bulgaria and Morocco-born duo Christo and Jeanne-Claude created their Wrapped Coast environmental installation, where part of the Little Bay cliffs was swaddled in fabric.



Erica Zaino’s (ART) Artificial Real Time. Sam Mooy Textile businessman and arts philanthropist John Kaldor produced that event in what became the first of his long-running series Kaldor Public Art Projects. In 1973, Transfield founder Franco Belgiorno-Nettis launched Sydney Biennale at the Opera House, the third biennial art show in the world after Venice and Sao Paulo, and the first in our region. Emma Anna’s Dream_n. Sam Mooy Handley said Sculpture by the Sea is “created for Joe Public”, and as such, some of the artworks can be climbed on and touched; they are generously Instagramable; and they are for sale. The organisers, akin to a commercial gallery, take a cut of the sale price, now 40 per cent.



Handley’s quasi commercial model has resulted in what appears to be a permanent tussle for adequate funding to cover the enormous cost of staging the event and navigating public liability complexity. Andre Braun’s Surface Breach. Sam Mooy It is supported by the NSW government, Waverley Council, philanthropy and sponsorship from backers such as the NRMA and property developer Aqualand. NSW Arts Minister John Graham at the Sculpture by the Sea launch on Friday said: “If we’re honest about our city, we’ve made it too hard to do things outdoors.“ Jenny Reddin’s Why? Sam Mooy



Last year, Handley made a last-minute public pitch for sponsorship, threatening the show might not go on. It did. “This is the year we’re not going to gripe,” Handley said. Artists this year will receive modest exhibition fees of $3000 and installation support to the value of $1500. Sculpture by the Sea has been life-changing for some artists, including Japan-born sculptor Koichi Ishino. The former art teacher exhibited at Sculpture by the Sea for the first time in 2001, returning each year until 2009 when he moved here permanently. “My works nearly always sold, so I moved here and became a full-time artist,” he said.

World.title: NRL wins early skirmish in battle over Chiefs name as parties prepare to ‘duke it out’ in court
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL wins early skirmish in battle over Chiefs name as parties prepare to ‘duke it out’ in court Chris Barrett Updated October 16, 2026 — 4:01pm ,first published 2:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The NRL has enjoyed a victory in round one of the code war over the PNG Chiefs name, with a judge turning down a bid by New Zealand Rugby for an urgent injunction after hearing that it could harm the expansion team’s efforts to attract players ahead of its debut season in 2028. NZ Rugby had rushed to court ahead of the launch of the PNG team’s logo and jersey in Port Moresby next week, warning the brand value of rugby’s long-established Chiefs franchise would be “hugely damaged” by the NRL team’s use of the same name and the confusion that would arise as a result. The NRL’s new team has been championed by PNG Prime Minister James Marape and Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys. Michaela Pollock However, Justice Karen Grau rejected its injunction application following a two-hour hearing on Friday in New Zealand’s High Court in Wellington. The dispute will now be thrashed out in a New Zealand courtroom early next year.



NZ Rugby’s barrister Earl Gray said it had intellectual property protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand and the NRL had been “negligent” by not bothering to check them. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 V’landys vows to defend court action against NRL over PNG Chiefs name “They’ve brought this issue on themselves and inexplicably, now want to get away with it,” he said. “They didn’t search, they didn’t check. They’ve thumbed their noses at New Zealand and its laws.” The NRL argued its use of the Chiefs name in Australia and PNG was not a trademark breach in New Zealand, and maintained it would be “next to impossible to rebrand at this point”. Barrister Clive Elliott, appearing for the NRL, pointed to the competition’s upcoming free agency period and in which some of the game’s leading players will be available, describing it as “a critical time for the [PNG] team”.



The Chiefs are expected to embark on a recruitment spree when it kicks off on November 1, and Elliott said a ruling against the NRL on Friday could create doubt about the legitimacy of the club and its name that could hurt their prospects of securing their targets. “In this environment, there is a real potential for this club to be set back irreparably,” he said. “If there is this cloud having over this new team, people are going to say, ‘Why would I move to Port Moresby when it’s under threat’?” ‘They would have to re-brand and say, “Sorry, we probably shouldn’t have called ourselves the PNG Chiefs”.’ Justice Karen Grau on what defeat would mean for the NRL PNG chief executive Lorna McPherson provided evidence that the team was hoping to have 12 players on its books by Christmas. The court was told the NRL had on Thursday offered to geo-block Chiefs-related material from its social media channels in New Zealand to avoid exposure of the team name there.



NZ Rugby cited code-hopping PNG signing Zac Lomax in suggesting the sports could be mixed up and made the case that even New Zealand Prime Minister Chris Luxon confused rugby league’s Warriors and rugby’s Waratahs last month. But Justice Grau said she thought “the average New Zealand sporting fan might not do that”. “People who are interested in sport – surely they know their difference between rugby and league. Are you saying somebody is going to buy the wrong ticket to a game or the wrong T-shirt?” she asked. She said the parties would have to “duke it out” at in a full hearing in coming months. The NRL could still be forced to change the Chiefs name if its loses.



“They would have to re-brand and say, ‘Sorry, we probably shouldn’t have called ourselves the PNG Chiefs’,” Grau said. The NRL was contacted for comment. NZ Rugby said it respected the court’s decision but remained committed to safeguard the legacy of its team. “Today’s decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case, and the matter will still be heard in full,” chief executive Steve Lancaster said. “As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn’t changed. We remain open to working with the [NRL] on a solution.” McPherson said she welcomed Friday’s decision.



Related Article NRL 2026 Reece Walsh on James Tedesco and ‘paying top dollar’ to solve his mystery issue “The PNG Chiefs welcome today’s decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday, October 21,” McPherson said in a statement. “As the matter remains before the Court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time.” The NRL owns the PNG Chiefs, which will become the league’s 18th team in 2028, backed by a $600 million Australian government package.

World.title: Pride and Prejudice remains the undisputed blueprint for every romcom
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature Pride and Prejudice remains the undisputed blueprint for every romcom Dolly Alderton October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The email came the day before my 35th birthday. I was lying on an overcast beach in Devon with my girlfriends when my agent messaged to say that Netflix were making a new TV adaptation of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, the first in 30 years, and would I be interested in writing and producing it? I was filled with equal amounts of excitement and terror – everyone who has read Pride and Prejudice has a vivid, singular imagining of what it should look like and how it should be. How could I make my version live up to all the versions that live in millions of people’s hearts? After a few days of thrashing out all that could possibly go wrong, I decided to embrace the challenge of adapting everyone’s favourite book. My favourite Austen adaptation of all time (the 1995 Sense And Sensibility) was made by Emma Thompson when she was 35. And in my favourite portrait of Jane Austen she was 35. When I returned home I reached for my hardback copy of Pride and Prejudice. With my highlighter pen in hand, I spent the next few days re-reading and falling back in love with it. The first thing that must be said about this novel, because it’s not said enough, is how fantastically adaptable it is. Its plotting and characterisation are flawless; its dialogue full of emotion and wit. All the script glitches you would normally get notes on from a TV commissioner or film studio have already been addressed by Austen. She did 99 per cent of the screenwriting for me back in the early 1800s. Author and columnist Dolly Alderton. NYT Pride and Prejudice is the blueprint for romantic comedy: so many romcom rules originate from it. The romantic leads initially seem like opposites, and yet discover they are more alike than they thought. They begin as enemies, sparring with language, they end up as lovers. The very title of the book is in reference to the biggest obstacles in their romantic comedy, his pride, her prejudice.



Over a couple of hundred pages, they duck and dive and dance around these obstacles. Just as we think they will never see each other again, they are drawn back together. And then comes the first great reunion – when Elizabeth unexpectedly encounters Darcy in his grand, bucolic home of Pemberley. Elizabeth’s prejudice is defeated. She sees Darcy for who he really is, and who he really is, is the perfect man for her. So, of course, here comes the turmoil. God, she’s good! Just as Elizabeth realises she loves Darcy, her youngest sister runs away with a soldier, plunging her family into ruin and rendering all her remaining sisters unmarriable. Elizabeth, having been in reaching distance of all she could ever hope for – a perfect match, both in love and marriage – loses it all. The cast of Netflix’s Pride and Prejudice (from left): Emma Corrin, Freya Mavor, Olivia Colman, Hopey Parish, Hollie Avery and Ella Smith. And then! Not only is her family saved, they’re saved by Darcy in what is arguably the greatest act of romantic heroism in literature. He does not do it for glory, he does not do it to explicitly win Elizabeth back. He does it for her peace and happiness – “I believe I thought only of you.” We are left with two people who have been transformed by love; whose every preconception has been overturned simply by coming to understand each other.



Nora Ephron, the queen of this genre, said that Pride and Prejudice is “one of the greatest romantic comedies ever written” because it is “a novel about the possibility of love between equals”. Elizabeth Bennet is the magic ingredient – a flawed but fierce heroine who, in Ephron’s words “is as close to perfect as she can be and still be interesting”. The moment in the book when I fall in love with Lizzie every time I read it comes after her first meeting with Darcy, when she overhears him calling her “tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me”. Instead of feeling humiliated by this insult from a man of much higher social status than her, she laughs it off, telling the story “with great spirit amongst her friends”. Austen couldn’t be clearer – this is a woman who not only knows who she is, but likes who she is. Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet in the new adaptation. Justin Downing/Netflix So, how do you find a man to match the perfect literary leading lady? Austen had the answer – you don’t. You construct a man who is flawed – snobbish, rude and emotionally cold – and you create a story that makes him become worthy of her. But, of course, Pride and Prejudice is not just a story of romantic love, it is a story about family too. The Bennet family is a chaotic clash of characters, all of whom are deeply recognisable.



And then there is Mrs Bennet. A character so exquisitely drawn that she has become her very own archetype. “The business of her life was to get her daughters married”. Without marriage, they will be homeless when their father dies. And penniless too, as Mr Bennet has neglected to set money aside for them. It is a very, very serious business, and no one seems preoccupied by it other than Mrs Bennet. To my mind, she is the most serious character in the book. She is the true heroine. Related Article Pop culture Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions This effortless shift between the emotional, societal and trivial resonates for so many because it replicates the multi-textured experience of real life. The living world of Pride and Prejudice is so like real life that we connect with its characters as though they were our own family members and friends. In the end, it’s not its engrossing plot or its witty dialogue, it is the emotions that underpin it all. Wounded pride, fast infatuation, being lied to by a charming stranger. Embarrassment of your family. Terror that you might never get the future you’d dreamed of. The mortification of misjudging someone or being misjudged. Finding yourself falling in love with the last person you ever thought it would be. It is a book of enormous feeling. People don’t have opinions about Pride and Prejudice, they have feelings. That is why everyone has so much to say about it. That’s why this little living world will be one I return to again and again and again. This is an edited extract from Dolly Alderton’s introduction to a new edition of Pride and Prejudice published by Penguin ($25). The series premieres on Netflix on December 3.

Neha Kale’s childhood memories are of time spent at her grandfather’s home on the banks of the Baga River in Goa. There, she splashed in tidal pools as small fish darted around her, ran through a “tangle of jackfruit and mango trees” on the hillside, and poked around the Virgin Mary grottoes, remnants of the region’s Portuguese conquest. In that house and its surrounding landscape, she felt “held”, afforded an assurance of her place in the world.

That feeling didn’t last, as her memoir Foreign Return demonstrates. When her family first migrated to Perth, she was often asked if she felt settled. Suburbia signals a politics of inclusion and exclusion; a house no longer feels like it is “the sum of material” of which it was built, but something more complex. When her grandfather died and the tether to his Goa house – one that his own grandparents built – was lost, Kale was no longer certain of what home was, or if it was indeed even a place.

At the heart of Neha Kale’s book is the question of home.

The question of home, and what it is, is the central question in Foreign Return. Kale, an art critic and writer, does not only turn inwards to uncover the answer. Key to her musings is the world around her, specifically as it is captured in art, literature, photography and architecture.

She ruminates on the concept of home by keenly interpreting the works of others. There is Dayanita Singh, who has documented Indian life in Goa, Bombay and Delhi; John Brack’s 1953 painting The New House, a “study of cultural inheritance [and] the way suburban existence builds fences around middle-class whiteness”; Brett Whiteley’s legacy of work, and the way he saw places like Redfern and Bondi. Ana Mendieta’s Untitled: Silueta Series reminds her that home is not necessarily a physical place, and Albert Namatjira’s body of watercolour art challenges European perspectives of landscape. Carol Jerrems’ photographic archive, which dignifies those on society’s margins, shows her that to be “held safely by the gaze of someone who [saw] you” can be a version of home.

World.content:
CultureBooksReview Are you stupid, an idiot – or both? Philosophy has an answer Kurt Johnson October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. “Idiots are out in force again today,” uttered my father sotto voce whenever someone cut him off or flagrantly disobeyed the road rules. From the back seat, I, a young lad naive to Sydney’s road rage, interpreted this to mean the “idiots” had got themselves organised. They were deploying en masse to the great inconvenience, even danger, of us ordinary citizens. The separation between norms and idiots may not have been as impermeable as my father supposed. Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen explains in the recently translated Stupid Idiots: A Philosophy of Stupidity and Complete and Utter Downright Idiocy that at times we’re all stupid and idiotic. Svendsen’s examination has been timed to a moment when both have taken the world by storm. With social media’s reach and AI’s amplification, never before have the stupid and the idiots been so dominant. Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen. First, a distinction: the stupid are those who choose not to think, while the idiots among us think poorly. From this point, the author develops a taxonomy via a survey of philosophers and writers. Kant, who features heavily, considered stupidity a lack of judgment, while Socrates labelled the stupid as those who failed to examine life. We, of course, could not leave without mention of Harry Frankfurt’s seminal On Bullshit, who defined bullshit as a disregard for the truth (as opposed to lying, which acknowledges truth and says the opposite). This introduces us to an overlapping concept: stupid idiocy. Through its short but incisive exploration of failures to think well, Stupid Idiots paradoxically becomes a guide to rigorous thinking. For it is at the border between wisdom and idiocy that greatest insights lie. It is also an exercise in humility as those who consider themselves best informed are most likely to err – like when Schopenhauer explains that one can “read themselves stupid” by consuming only literature that accords with their opinions. Svendsen recommends the budding Marxist pick up Hayek and vice versa.



Through echo-chamber busting, Svendsen suggests a return to the fundamentals of discourse and a subtle rejection of our fractured, dug-in politics. Opinions are not sacred while the idea of “my truth” is anathema to intelligent thought. Instead, if we cultivate critical thinking, are suspicious of orthodoxy and listen to those holding opposing views, we have a real shot at avoiding idiocy, if not attaining wisdom. On the other hand, Stupid Idiots articulates how the chips are stacked to the advantage of the habitually moronic. The Dunning-Kruger effect, for example, boils down to the less you know about a subject the smarter you think you are. You simply don’t know how much you don’t know. Meanwhile, bad information (bullshit) travels further and faster than the truth. Photo: Svendsen’s work exudes tolerance and empathy on the subject of human fallibility. Great thinkers have all been idiots at times: Heidegger was a Nazi, Aristotle thought women had fewer teeth than men, and Schopenhauer believed in all sorts of paranormal nonsense. Indeed, our discourse, the basis of our political system, can and must withstand certain amounts of stupidity and idiocy. The author states that conservatives tend to be stupid, as they too readily accept authority, while progressives are more likely to be idiots as they overestimate their outside-the-box thinking. These flaws are healthy. Things only go awry when we reach a critical mass of stupid idiots. The titular Stupid Idiots are a special group. They are those who think badly and are so pigheaded they refuse to be swayed by life, experience or contradictory data. They are the conspiracy zealots, the antivaxxers. All dictators are stupid idiots as they cannot stomach dissenting opinion. Theirs is the only truth.



Related Article Review He lasted 11 days in Trump’s White House. Now the Mooch has a warning And so, in rounding its final corner, Stupid Idiots reaches the subject it had been alluding to all along: Donald Trump. So rare IRL does one meet a near-perfect archetype. Trump, who is convinced “nobody knows more about this than me”, routinely demonstrates stupid idiocy par excellence. What is special about this book is that up to now it appears more beard stroking philosophy until the revelation it has been a political script the entire time. In the end, my father was right. The idiots are out in force today as they are every day. For we are they. Through acknowledging this, Stupid Idiots is short, sharp, rigorous and avoids condescension. It is a guide to how we can all think better and an admission that fallible thinking is universal. Or in other words, to “duh” is human. Stupid Idiots: A Philosophy of Stupidity and Complete and Utter Downright Idiocy by Lars Svendsen, translated by Matt Bagguley, is published by Reaktion Books ($35). World.title: Pip Williams’ WWI novel is beautiful – but I wish it wasn’t
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Pip Williams’ WWI novel is beautiful – but I wish it wasn’t Beejay Silcox October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When is a lovely novel too lovely? Too frictionless, too perfectly smooth. It takes skill to make a book feel effortless. But when do a novel’s pleasures begin to feel like a failure of imagination? I’ve been thinking about this question all year, as some of the most beloved names in fiction have released novels of lavish and luxurious comfort. There was Ann Patchett’s Whistler, so wilfully pleasant – so stuffed with little joys – it felt like a high-end gift basket. And then Maggie O’Farrell’s Land, which promised something wild and strange but then gave us the familiar consolations of a family saga. Author Pip Williams at home in the Adelaide Hills. Roy VanDerVegt And now there’s Pip Williams’ The German Ward, the story of an English nurse and a German doctor who serve together in a field hospital in Etaples, a few miles behind the Western Front. Two restless souls, alone on the night shift – those dark, suspended hours (“There is no after. There is only now”). It is exactly the book you expect it to be. I’m tempted to leave it there and let readers bring their own appetites to the novel. The more I explain, the more my own unmet hungers gnash and gnaw. My hunger for risk, for mess – for the kind of moral ugliness that shakes my certainties loose.



Like so much contemporary WWI fiction, The German Ward is terribly beautiful, even as it tries to be honest. When it comes to the Western Front, there’s a stubborn smear of Vaseline across our cultural lens. We look at the carnage and keep spotting love stories. Some readers will find this reassuring; humane, even: a reminder that gentleness has its place in ungentle times. Others will bristle at yet another romance plucked from the fetid mud. Both can be true. In a way, that’s Williams’s point: the tension between what we choose to see and what’s there. How our perspective shifts and warps depending on where we stand, what uniform we’re wearing and who we love. To make the point, she gives us double vision: two women looking at the same story from opposite ends of a century. In 1937, an unexpected letter prompts Tilda Taylor to open a box of relics she has kept in the attic for 20 years, among them her wartime diary. It begins in August 1915, with her assignment to the titular German ward, where wounded enemy soldiers were sent to recover before being transferred to prison camps. “We had tried to kill them but they didn’t die,” Tilda’s diary reads, “so now we try to save them. How insane.” In 2025 art historian Eva LaMotte is in the archival quiet of the Australian War Memorial, studying the work of Iso Rae, an Australian artist who was based in Etaples during the war but denied a formal commission. Rae’s work carries a quiet defiance: “Someone had said no to Iso – the war is not yours to paint; it is not your story to tell – but Iso had done it anyway.” What did she see, Eva wonders, that the men did not? Only a handful of Rae’s sketches survive but some of the most tender feature the same unnamed nurse. Eva senses a story hiding in these intimate lines. As she imagines that story, Tilda remembers it. (Williams has conjured the tale from a real-life encounter in Rae’s archives.) And so we have a novel where everyone is looking at someone who is looking at someone else. Looking, longing, sketching, interpreting. The war churns on and on, breaking bodies. And we watch them all, watching – bearing witness, bearing suffering. It could be a great, unruly tangle. But Williams knows precisely what she is doing. We can feel it: the precision, the control. The mystery of Tilda’s unopened letter; the question of Eva’s anonymous nurse. The past and the present moving towards one another like two lovers reuniting.



It’s all so carefully inevitable. Tilda is a former actress, headstrong and impatient (“one of Pankhurst’s women”). The German doctor, Hugo Henning, is taciturn and proper: “a nut to crack”. We know the archetypes; we know the script. “We kissed like we knew how it might end,” Tilda tells us, and we believe her. We already know how it will end. Related Article Literature New York Times bestseller confesses: I can’t write a simple love story Readers might remember Tilda from The Bookbinder of Jericho, Williams’ last novel. The German Ward enriches that book but stands alone. I read it alongside Daniel Kraus’ Pulitzer Prize-winning Angel Down, a horror novel set at the bleeding edge of the front during the Meuse-Argonne offensive. That was an unfair pairing. Kraus’ novel is so gloriously repulsive, so feral and deranged, that Williams’ doctors-and-nurses romance felt almost obscene in its tidiness. All that finely sketched yearning. All those diligent shades of ethical grey. Tilda and Hugo clash over rules: they anchor him and suffocate her. In the ward the couple wrestles with when to bend the rules and when to break them – when protocol stands in the way of grace. “The trick is to know when the rule is worthy and when it is not,” Tilda argues. She’s right. Pip Williams knows all the narrative rules. The German Ward is perfectly lovely, perfectly readable proof. I wish she’d smashed a couple. Smashed them all. The German Ward by Pip Williams (Affirm Press, $35) is out now.

World.title: Eight gay men met in secret to rehearse a play. This Booker-nominated novel reveals the atrocities that followed
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Eight gay men met in secret to rehearse a play. This Booker-nominated novel reveals the atrocities that followed Jack Cameron Stanton October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Marlon James’ The Disappearers, shortlisted for this year’s Booker Prize, begins when eight gay men secretly meet to rehearse a queer prison play. It’s Kingston, 1988. Jamaica has been whipped into an AIDS panic. Gay bashings occur in Kingston with impunity. The actors gather to perform parts of themselves hidden away from the rest of Jamaica, all the while envisioning the play as a small act of defiance against their homophobic society. Most notable among the men are Eddy Porteous, a young man figuring out what his sexuality means in a world that persecutes it; the troubled, abrasive Jordan Brown, disowned by his rich family and hardened by street living; Matt Chin, an elusive figure who assumes multiple identities; and the director, Havelock Titus, who hopes their adaptation of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes will blow “open the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality and homophobia”. Marlon James’ The Disappearers is nominated for this year’s Booker Prize. NYT Fatefully, a gang of hateful gay bashers called the Blackjacks discover the rehearsal and commit an atrocity, killing one of the actors, leaving another with their eyes gouged out, and traumatising those who survive. From this premise James expands The Disappearers into a true maximalist novel, writing in many voices and documenting the progression of the gay men’s lives from 1988 until 2005. It comes equipped with a list of characters, something readers of James’ Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings will recognise, along with the distinct polyphonic writing style. Heavily voice-driven, the narrative constantly fuses the profane and the lyrical, Jamaican patois with bookishness.



The Disappearers isn’t dramatised. It’s documented. James uses several faux documents, such as letters, diary entries and interviews, to report the events. Post-atrocity, the brunt of the novel revolves around Jordan and Eddy searching for two actors who disappeared “like thieves in the night”. As the title declares, The Disappearers is occupied with exploring the many forms of disappearance: not only the physical but ways of self-erasure, of vanishing within a society. The documented style of the novel reveals a second, more vital thematic than disappearance: the cost of remembering. The survivors of the gay bashing are haunted by it. They are all, in their own ways, “frozen in 1988”. The play, which never occurs, is a spectre in their lives, a reverberating what-if. Jordan Brown, a loose cannon at the best of times, cultivates a warped and hateful sense of vigilante justice as he hunts down the members of the Blackjacks whose lives continued “like nothing happened”. Eddy Porteous, the only cast member absent during the attack, is racked by survivor’s guilt, while Havelock Titus, the director, whose small act of defiance exposed the boys to their suffering, finds himself their reluctant keeper. James offers complex portrayals of his gay characters. In contrast, the Blackjacks are exaggeratedly wretched to the point of grotesquerie. They are handed the microphone in the second act, in which they spout lovely one-liners such as “The Devil is a faggot and demons are in his semen” and “Sodom was the wickedest city in creation and God did have to destroy it”. The biblical references expose their broader belief: what appears to the reader as cruel, senseless violence is seen by the perpetrators as noble persecution. Or, in Jordan’s bitter words, not “a crime but a national service. Think of how many potential cases of AIDS they prevented that night.” Zooming out from their interpersonal clashes, we see James constantly engaged in situating violence and homophobia in broader discourses of class, race, sexuality and religion. This is the novel’s greatest elegance. It is the type of maximalist fiction that enlivens history into something more real than real.



There’s a long history of queer fiction embracing the transgressive powers of sexual desire. James signals the novel’s continuation of this tradition by having Jordan Brown carry around John Rechy’s The Sexual Outlaw like a manual for how to live. It emboldens Jordan’s rejection of “normality”: “normal was as broad and loose as the f---ing universe, whereas abnormal was just one thing”. It shows other ways to exist. Related Article Literature A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail I should mention that The Disappearers is an extremely horny book. The politics of pornographic representations in fiction range from gratuitous to artfully subversive; James belongs to the latter. His characters have a lot of sex and recount their sex in vivid detail, in part to provoke the heteronormative reader by making visible and explicit what has been historically repressed. On a deeper level, the characters fixate upon and self-define according to their desire because their entire subjectivity has been filtered through the prism of their own sexuality. James deftly illuminates how the characters grappling with identity are doing so within a larger system that excludes and erases them. Remembering, forgetting and disappearing are all entangled in The Disappearers. They are the traumatic responses that come to define the men’s lives. In the closing scene, one character fails to recognise another. This cruel act of forgetting is a bleak, devastating and therefore beautiful ending to Marlon James’ magisterial return to Jamaica, full of hot blood and heartbreak. The Disappearers by Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton, $35) is out now.

And the red contagion spreads. The Middle East conflict took another ugly turn to start the week as more agitators piled into the fray, with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia further inflaming regional tensions and sending global oil prices soaring. A strike on Riyadh airport that killed 12 led Trump to accuse Iran’s Islamic regime of steering the attacks to push oil prices higher ahead of the US midterms. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Identifai Limited. If that was the plan, it appeared to be working, with crude surging to US$107 a barrel this week even as Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil. Meanwhile, hopes of ending the more than four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine looked just as forlorn as the prospects for peace in the Middle East. Over on Wall Street, the AI trade looks to have finally come undone. Surely it wasn’t little old Aussie AI Firmus and its failed IPO that broke the camel’s back?



More likely, it’s China’s latest memory-chip advances that are rattling the sector, with semiconductors falling for a seventh straight NASDAQ session, down 14 per cent since the start of last week. OpenAI led the pandemonium after paring back its revenue expectations, as businesses increasingly turn to cheaper Chinese alternatives for token-heavy workloads. The AI contagion spread rapidly across the Pacific, sending Korean chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung tumbling 14 and 18 per cent respectively this week alone! With both heavyweights accounting for a substantial slice of South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI, the index suffered a bone-shattering 21 per cent plunge in just seven trading sessions as doubts over the AI boom collided with fears of further interest rate hikes. Thursday alone delivered a 7.6 per cent KOSPI wipeout, triggering trading halts and liquidations countrywide, with what had been one of the world’s hottest AI-fuelled markets now looking like a leveraged investor’s nightmare. To cap off an already bruising week, surging oil prices have reignited inflation fears and sparked a bloodbath across Australia’s mining sector. With the fuel supply squeeze again rearing its ugly head, headlines of job cuts at BHP and Rio Tinto have only added to the gloom, rattling investors and raising fresh concerns about the outlook for the broader resources industry. Rio Tinto is staring down the barrel of more than $500 million in additional annual Pilbara costs from sky-high diesel prices, while its shares have shed nearly 10 per cent in under a fortnight and took another hit during Thursday’s rout. The pain may be even worse for little brother Fortescue, with early forecasts suggesting its September quarter could deliver its first loss-making quarter in years — potentially the first since 2009, as some 67 consecutive profitable periods come undone.



One bright spot amid the carnage is the continuing takeover tussle for Northern Star Resources, Australia’s biggest listed gold miner. South African giant Gold Fields is reportedly open to sweetening its $40 billion bid with more cash and is dangling the benefits of an ASX listing as its chief executive embarks on a baby-kissing tour to win over Australian investors. Gold Fields boss Mike Fraser has also reportedly discussed selling some Northern Star mines to rivals, including Raleigh Finlayson’s Genesis Minerals, should the takeover succeed. That would allow the South African miner to concentrate on its flagship Kalgoorlie Super Pit, Alaska’s Pogo mine and the undeveloped Hemi project in WA’s Pilbara. This week’s Runners list was another small serving from a harsh vintage, with the Australian small ordinaries again among the market’s biggest casualties as domestic money flow tightens thanks to a mix of housing pressures and inflation. One bright spot on the ASX lately has been the IPO market, with several fresh listings making our Runners of late. This week’s top spot went to a plucky Israeli pregnancy biotech hopeful that managed to buck the broader market’s miserable mood for its ASX debut. Israeli biotech newcomer Identifai is targeting a significant unmet medical need with its AI-powered prenatal screening technology. IDENTIFAI GENETICS LTD (ASX: ID1)



Up 170% (20c – 54c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Israeli biotech newcomer Identifai Genetics Limited, which made a stellar debut on the ASX after raising $10 million in a float at 20 cents a share. The company’s flagship Windrose platform uses a simple blood sample from the mother as early as nine weeks into pregnancy to screen for more than 280 genes linked to genetic conditions in unborn babies. By combining DNA sequencing with AI, the technology aims to flag a much wider range of potential health problems earlier in pregnancy, without the need for invasive procedures such as amniocentesis. Shares in Identifai started strong and never looked back despite the shaky market backdrop, peaking at 54 cents on Thursday for a whopping 170 per cent gain on the week, as investors latched onto the potential of its technology. The company says it is targeting a significant unmet medical need, with the World Health Organisation (WHO) estimating that between three and six per cent of babies worldwide are born with a genetic or congenital disorder. Some conditions can be difficult to identify before birth, yet early detection can help doctors and families prepare for treatment well ahead of time.



While existing non-invasive prenatal tests primarily screen for common chromosomal conditions, Identifai says Windrose can assess fetal risk across more than 280 genes linked to conditions that may be actionable during pregnancy, delivery or shortly after birth. By combining AI with advanced genetic analysis, the company is aiming to push prenatal screening well beyond its traditional limits, initially targeting the US market with a platform backed by a growing intellectual property portfolio. AVENIRA LIMITED (ASX: AEV) Up 133% (0.6c – 1.2c) Slotting into second on the week was fertiliser frontrunner Avenira, which surged 100 per cent this week after securing an $85 million funding lifeline from major shareholder and strategic offtake partner Hebang Biotechnology. The cash injection will fully fund development of its giant Wonarah phosphate project through to first shipment and ongoing operations.



The package comprises an eight-year, $50 million development facility from China - at a staggering Reserve Bank cash rate with no additional margin. A further revolving line of $35 million in working capital will also carry the same benefits and term. Principal and cash-interest payments are deferred for two years, giving Avenira breathing room as it makes the leap from developer to producer. The deal is a major vote of confidence from Chinese-based shareholder Hebang, which already holds a 60 per cent voting interest and has committed to buying Wonarah’s premium phosphate. It also gives Avenira a clearer runway towards first direct shipping ore (DSO) shipments, targeted for the first half of next year. The prize is a monster Northern Territory resource hosting a JORC estimate of 812 million tonnes at 18 per cent phosphorus pentoxide, for a whopping 146 million tonnes of contained phosphate. Avenira plans to start with a relatively straightforward direct shipping operation to generate early revenue, before potentially stepping up to higher-grade processing and, further down the track, downstream products such as yellow phosphorus and thermal phosphoric acid for battery and electronics markets.



The timing could hardly be more interesting. Phosphate has been a quiet runner amid Middle Eastern disruptions, with supply-chain risks putting the spotlight on fertiliser security and the importance of reliable sources beyond geopolitically exposed regions. For Avenira, a well-funded path to production could put Wonarah in the frame as buyers look to secure future supply. With the funding hurdle cleared and first shipments on the horizon, Avenira appears at the doorstep of turning its enormous phosphate endowment into a producing Australian asset. Image Resources’ Boonanarring mineral sands operation in WA, which helped establish the company as a zircon and mineral sands producer. IMAGE RESOURCES LTD (ASX: IMA) Up 84% (1.9c – 3.5c)



Rounding out Runners is repeat customer Image Resources, after it kicked off the week on a tear despite having no fresh news to the market. The fun police down at the ASX came knocking around lunchtime on Tuesday after shares climbed from 1.9 cents last week to a high of 3.5 cents, issuing a “please explain” speeding ticket in the process. Image responded that it was unaware of any undisclosed information that could explain the move, but pointed to an announcement last month detailing a $5 million cash advance from major shareholder and strategic partner LB Group. The advance forms part of ongoing negotiations over a potential deal involving Image’s Durack and Yandanooka mineral sands projects in WA. The proposed transaction could see LB Group acquire a significant interest in the projects for $20 million in cash, alongside an interest in certain plant, equipment and other assets expected to be used in their development and operation. However, Image’s story is about more than just mineral sands, with the company recently giving punters another reason to straighten up in their seats, after drilling at its latest Erayinia-King gold project near Kalgoorlie and returning a swag of high-grade results. The standout was a 4.5-metre hit grading 22.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 128m, including a chunky one-metre section at a whopping 98.55g/t. Other drilling returned 14m at 2.84g/t and 16m at 2.51g/t, adding further sparkle to the historic mineral sands player’s emerging gold story.



Image says it has completed a 50-hole, 5450-metre drilling campaign at Erayinia-King, with mineralisation traced to only 140m vertical depth, leaving plenty of potential at depth. The project already hosts some two million tonnes at 2.1g/t gold for 139,000 ounces, with an updated resource now being prepared. The gold story gives Image a potentially valuable second string to its bow beyond the established mineral sands business. Meanwhile, talks with LB Group could open another lucrative chapter for Image as a strategic review gathers pace at its Durack project, fresh from a hefty 43 per cent resource upgrade to 37.7 million tonnes. With a sizeable mineral sands portfolio and a potential major deal in the works, Image has plenty to explain to the ASX why investors have been piling back in for weeks. World.title: NSW artist becomes just fourth woman in 30 years to win major Sculpture by the Sea prize
World.content:
CultureArt & designArts NSW artist becomes just fourth woman in 30 years to win major Sculpture by the Sea prize Michaela Boland October 16, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Female sculptors with powerful feminist messages have captured the zeitgeist – and the big prize – at Sculpture by the Sea in its 30th year. NSW artist Harrie Fasher won the $70,000 acquisitive Aqualand Sculpture Award with an abstract six-metre by five-metre steel, bronze and timber artwork. Harrie Fasher with her sculpture Unveiling the Edges of the Sky. Sam Mooy “This is for all the women, there’s a lot of us female sculptors that make work that’s really outside the square. It’s a battle. I’m the fourth (woman) to have won Sculpture by the Sea (Sydney) in its 30 years,” Fasher said. She described her work, Unveiling the Edges of the Sky, installed adjacent to the cliffs at Marks Park, as being about female strength, the dissolution of the ego and following your intuition.



After a soggy installation week, Sculpture by the Sea is open, free to the public. There are 100 works on display along two kilometres of the Bondi to Tamarama Beach walk and Marks Park, until Monday November 2. Omi McCurdie, Pip Lysaght and Matty McCarron, with their sculpture Sweethearts. Sam Mooy Reinforcing the female empowerment theme is an installation by Sydney public art collective Omi McCurdie, Matty McCarron and Philippa Lysaght. The trio’s shockingly playful outsized Sweethearts candies are emblazoned with classic Aussie phrases like “He was drunk”, “She coulda left” and “Boys will be boys”. Lysaght, a social justice advocate, said the trio, working together for the first time and making their Sculpture by the Sea debut, want to challenge the traditional notions of Australian masculinity that underpin the domestic violence epidemic.



“I was so appalled about the spate of domestic violence and wanted to do something that targets bystander inaction and calls out abuse,” she said. “I want people to really experience it and there’s no better stage than Sculpture by the Sea.” McCarron, a filmmaker, said collaborating on the project was confronting. “I’ve said a lot of these phrases because it’s just so easy to minimise individual instances, but you have to call your mates out and say it’s not OK,” he said. Over 450,000 people are expected to visit the exhibition, including thousands of schoolchildren, who McCurdie, a practising artist, said are an important part of the national discussion about violence against women.



John Eager’s Blue Water Rocket. Sam Mooy Sculpture by the Sea was founded by David Handley in 1997, originally as a one-day only event because he did not have the funds at that time to pay for overnight security. Handley was inspired by the sense of community he experienced in his 20s at the free summer concerts in the Domain, Opera in the Park and Symphony Under the Stars. Clayton Blake’s Pinnacle (centre) is seen through Michael Le Grand’s Primal Echo. Sam Mooy He then capitalised on the investment in the arts being made ahead of the Sydney Olympics, resulting in offshoot events staged around Australia.



Sculpture by the Sea eventually cemented itself in Sydney’s cultural calendar in October, when after the Sydney Olympics, it proved to be a masterstroke of counterprogramming that tapped into the city’s desire to keep partying after the games had packed up. Paul Ewart’s Both Sides Now. Sam Mooy The not-for-profit stages annual an exhibition in Cottesloe, Perth and it has over the years left a legacy of sculpture trails and staged similar events around the world. In Sydney, Sculpture by the Sea now includes an access and inclusion program; its popular school program is back; and a new Indigenous Artist Prize this year provides $20,000 for the creation and presentation of an ambitious new sculpture. Tim Storrier’s Wayfarer. Sam Mooy



Inaugural recipient David Doyle is a Barkindji and Malyangapa artist based in Broken Hill whose cast iron and steel shields Kaaku-Kaakulinyа: Eternal Sentinels explores protection, resilience and continual presence. Reflecting on the past 30 years, Handley said: “Sculptor Richard Goodwin was the first to say that Sculpture by the Sea (has) represented cultural change in Australia.” Sculptor Koichi Ishino with his work Circles. Sam Mooy “Just by the number of people turning up to an art exhibition year after year, people (through) repeat visitation are developing an eye for sculpture.” Sydney’s long history of free public art shows dates to at least 1969, when Bulgaria and Morocco-born duo Christo and Jeanne-Claude created their Wrapped Coast environmental installation, where part of the Little Bay cliffs was swaddled in fabric.



Erica Zaino’s (ART) Artificial Real Time. Sam Mooy Textile businessman and arts philanthropist John Kaldor produced that event in what became the first of his long-running series Kaldor Public Art Projects. In 1973, Transfield founder Franco Belgiorno-Nettis launched Sydney Biennale at the Opera House, the third biennial art show in the world after Venice and Sao Paulo, and the first in our region. Emma Anna’s Dream_n. Sam Mooy Handley said Sculpture by the Sea is “created for Joe Public”, and as such, some of the artworks can be climbed on and touched; they are generously Instagramable; and they are for sale. The organisers, akin to a commercial gallery, take a cut of the sale price, now 40 per cent.



Handley’s quasi commercial model has resulted in what appears to be a permanent tussle for adequate funding to cover the enormous cost of staging the event and navigating public liability complexity. Andre Braun’s Surface Breach. Sam Mooy It is supported by the NSW government, Waverley Council, philanthropy and sponsorship from backers such as the NRMA and property developer Aqualand. NSW Arts Minister John Graham at the Sculpture by the Sea launch on Friday said: “If we’re honest about our city, we’ve made it too hard to do things outdoors.“ Jenny Reddin’s Why? Sam Mooy



Last year, Handley made a last-minute public pitch for sponsorship, threatening the show might not go on. It did. “This is the year we’re not going to gripe,” Handley said. Artists this year will receive modest exhibition fees of $3000 and installation support to the value of $1500. Sculpture by the Sea has been life-changing for some artists, including Japan-born sculptor Koichi Ishino. The former art teacher exhibited at Sculpture by the Sea for the first time in 2001, returning each year until 2009 when he moved here permanently. “My works nearly always sold, so I moved here and became a full-time artist,” he said.

World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL wins early skirmish in battle over Chiefs name as parties prepare to ‘duke it out’ in court Chris Barrett Updated October 16, 2026 — 4:01pm ,first published 2:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The NRL has enjoyed a victory in round one of the code war over the PNG Chiefs name, with a judge turning down a bid by New Zealand Rugby for an urgent injunction after hearing that it could harm the expansion team’s efforts to attract players ahead of its debut season in 2028. NZ Rugby had rushed to court ahead of the launch of the PNG team’s logo and jersey in Port Moresby next week, warning the brand value of rugby’s long-established Chiefs franchise would be “hugely damaged” by the NRL team’s use of the same name and the confusion that would arise as a result. The NRL’s new team has been championed by PNG Prime Minister James Marape and Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys. Michaela Pollock However, Justice Karen Grau rejected its injunction application following a two-hour hearing on Friday in New Zealand’s High Court in Wellington. The dispute will now be thrashed out in a New Zealand courtroom early next year.



NZ Rugby’s barrister Earl Gray said it had intellectual property protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand and the NRL had been “negligent” by not bothering to check them. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 V’landys vows to defend court action against NRL over PNG Chiefs name “They’ve brought this issue on themselves and inexplicably, now want to get away with it,” he said. “They didn’t search, they didn’t check. They’ve thumbed their noses at New Zealand and its laws.” The NRL argued its use of the Chiefs name in Australia and PNG was not a trademark breach in New Zealand, and maintained it would be “next to impossible to rebrand at this point”. Barrister Clive Elliott, appearing for the NRL, pointed to the competition’s upcoming free agency period and in which some of the game’s leading players will be available, describing it as “a critical time for the [PNG] team”.



The Chiefs are expected to embark on a recruitment spree when it kicks off on November 1, and Elliott said a ruling against the NRL on Friday could create doubt about the legitimacy of the club and its name that could hurt their prospects of securing their targets. “In this environment, there is a real potential for this club to be set back irreparably,” he said. “If there is this cloud having over this new team, people are going to say, ‘Why would I move to Port Moresby when it’s under threat’?” ‘They would have to re-brand and say, “Sorry, we probably shouldn’t have called ourselves the PNG Chiefs”.’ Justice Karen Grau on what defeat would mean for the NRL PNG chief executive Lorna McPherson provided evidence that the team was hoping to have 12 players on its books by Christmas. The court was told the NRL had on Thursday offered to geo-block Chiefs-related material from its social media channels in New Zealand to avoid exposure of the team name there.



NZ Rugby cited code-hopping PNG signing Zac Lomax in suggesting the sports could be mixed up and made the case that even New Zealand Prime Minister Chris Luxon confused rugby league’s Warriors and rugby’s Waratahs last month. But Justice Grau said she thought “the average New Zealand sporting fan might not do that”. “People who are interested in sport – surely they know their difference between rugby and league. Are you saying somebody is going to buy the wrong ticket to a game or the wrong T-shirt?” she asked. She said the parties would have to “duke it out” at in a full hearing in coming months. The NRL could still be forced to change the Chiefs name if its loses.



“They would have to re-brand and say, ‘Sorry, we probably shouldn’t have called ourselves the PNG Chiefs’,” Grau said. The NRL was contacted for comment. NZ Rugby said it respected the court’s decision but remained committed to safeguard the legacy of its team. “Today’s decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case, and the matter will still be heard in full,” chief executive Steve Lancaster said. “As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn’t changed. We remain open to working with the [NRL] on a solution.” McPherson said she welcomed Friday’s decision.



Related Article NRL 2026 Reece Walsh on James Tedesco and ‘paying top dollar’ to solve his mystery issue “The PNG Chiefs welcome today’s decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday, October 21,” McPherson said in a statement. “As the matter remains before the Court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time.” The NRL owns the PNG Chiefs, which will become the league’s 18th team in 2028, backed by a $600 million Australian government package.

World.title: Pride and Prejudice remains the undisputed blueprint for every romcom
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature Pride and Prejudice remains the undisputed blueprint for every romcom Dolly Alderton October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The email came the day before my 35th birthday. I was lying on an overcast beach in Devon with my girlfriends when my agent messaged to say that Netflix were making a new TV adaptation of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, the first in 30 years, and would I be interested in writing and producing it? I was filled with equal amounts of excitement and terror – everyone who has read Pride and Prejudice has a vivid, singular imagining of what it should look like and how it should be. How could I make my version live up to all the versions that live in millions of people’s hearts? After a few days of thrashing out all that could possibly go wrong, I decided to embrace the challenge of adapting everyone’s favourite book. My favourite Austen adaptation of all time (the 1995 Sense And Sensibility) was made by Emma Thompson when she was 35. And in my favourite portrait of Jane Austen she was 35. When I returned home I reached for my hardback copy of Pride and Prejudice. With my highlighter pen in hand, I spent the next few days re-reading and falling back in love with it. The first thing that must be said about this novel, because it’s not said enough, is how fantastically adaptable it is. Its plotting and characterisation are flawless; its dialogue full of emotion and wit. All the script glitches you would normally get notes on from a TV commissioner or film studio have already been addressed by Austen. She did 99 per cent of the screenwriting for me back in the early 1800s. Author and columnist Dolly Alderton. NYT Pride and Prejudice is the blueprint for romantic comedy: so many romcom rules originate from it. The romantic leads initially seem like opposites, and yet discover they are more alike than they thought. They begin as enemies, sparring with language, they end up as lovers. The very title of the book is in reference to the biggest obstacles in their romantic comedy, his pride, her prejudice.



Over a couple of hundred pages, they duck and dive and dance around these obstacles. Just as we think they will never see each other again, they are drawn back together. And then comes the first great reunion – when Elizabeth unexpectedly encounters Darcy in his grand, bucolic home of Pemberley. Elizabeth’s prejudice is defeated. She sees Darcy for who he really is, and who he really is, is the perfect man for her. So, of course, here comes the turmoil. God, she’s good! Just as Elizabeth realises she loves Darcy, her youngest sister runs away with a soldier, plunging her family into ruin and rendering all her remaining sisters unmarriable. Elizabeth, having been in reaching distance of all she could ever hope for – a perfect match, both in love and marriage – loses it all. The cast of Netflix’s Pride and Prejudice (from left): Emma Corrin, Freya Mavor, Olivia Colman, Hopey Parish, Hollie Avery and Ella Smith. And then! Not only is her family saved, they’re saved by Darcy in what is arguably the greatest act of romantic heroism in literature. He does not do it for glory, he does not do it to explicitly win Elizabeth back. He does it for her peace and happiness – “I believe I thought only of you.” We are left with two people who have been transformed by love; whose every preconception has been overturned simply by coming to understand each other.



Nora Ephron, the queen of this genre, said that Pride and Prejudice is “one of the greatest romantic comedies ever written” because it is “a novel about the possibility of love between equals”. Elizabeth Bennet is the magic ingredient – a flawed but fierce heroine who, in Ephron’s words “is as close to perfect as she can be and still be interesting”. The moment in the book when I fall in love with Lizzie every time I read it comes after her first meeting with Darcy, when she overhears him calling her “tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me”. Instead of feeling humiliated by this insult from a man of much higher social status than her, she laughs it off, telling the story “with great spirit amongst her friends”. Austen couldn’t be clearer – this is a woman who not only knows who she is, but likes who she is. Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet in the new adaptation. Justin Downing/Netflix So, how do you find a man to match the perfect literary leading lady? Austen had the answer – you don’t. You construct a man who is flawed – snobbish, rude and emotionally cold – and you create a story that makes him become worthy of her. But, of course, Pride and Prejudice is not just a story of romantic love, it is a story about family too. The Bennet family is a chaotic clash of characters, all of whom are deeply recognisable.



And then there is Mrs Bennet. A character so exquisitely drawn that she has become her very own archetype. “The business of her life was to get her daughters married”. Without marriage, they will be homeless when their father dies. And penniless too, as Mr Bennet has neglected to set money aside for them. It is a very, very serious business, and no one seems preoccupied by it other than Mrs Bennet. To my mind, she is the most serious character in the book. She is the true heroine. Related Article Pop culture Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions This effortless shift between the emotional, societal and trivial resonates for so many because it replicates the multi-textured experience of real life. The living world of Pride and Prejudice is so like real life that we connect with its characters as though they were our own family members and friends. In the end, it’s not its engrossing plot or its witty dialogue, it is the emotions that underpin it all. Wounded pride, fast infatuation, being lied to by a charming stranger. Embarrassment of your family. Terror that you might never get the future you’d dreamed of. The mortification of misjudging someone or being misjudged. Finding yourself falling in love with the last person you ever thought it would be. It is a book of enormous feeling. People don’t have opinions about Pride and Prejudice, they have feelings. That is why everyone has so much to say about it. That’s why this little living world will be one I return to again and again and again. This is an edited extract from Dolly Alderton’s introduction to a new edition of Pride and Prejudice published by Penguin ($25). The series premieres on Netflix on December 3.
