World.title: Neha Kale thought she knew what home was – then she left it behind
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Neha Kale’s childhood memories are of time spent at her grandfather’s home on the banks of the Baga River in Goa. There, she splashed in tidal pools as small fish darted around her, ran through a “tangle of jackfruit and mango trees” on the hillside, and poked around the Virgin Mary grottoes, remnants of the region’s Portuguese conquest. In that house and its surrounding landscape, she felt “held”, afforded an assurance of her place in the world.

That feeling didn’t last, as her memoir Foreign Return demonstrates. When her family first migrated to Perth, she was often asked if she felt settled. Suburbia signals a politics of inclusion and exclusion; a house no longer feels like it is “the sum of material” of which it was built, but something more complex. When her grandfather died and the tether to his Goa house – one that his own grandparents built – was lost, Kale was no longer certain of what home was, or if it was indeed even a place.

At the heart of Neha Kale’s book is the question of home.

The question of home, and what it is, is the central question in Foreign Return. Kale, an art critic and writer, does not only turn inwards to uncover the answer. Key to her musings is the world around her, specifically as it is captured in art, literature, photography and architecture.

She ruminates on the concept of home by keenly interpreting the works of others. There is Dayanita Singh, who has documented Indian life in Goa, Bombay and Delhi; John Brack’s 1953 painting The New House, a “study of cultural inheritance [and] the way suburban existence builds fences around middle-class whiteness”; Brett Whiteley’s legacy of work, and the way he saw places like Redfern and Bondi. Ana Mendieta’s Untitled: Silueta Series reminds her that home is not necessarily a physical place, and Albert Namatjira’s body of watercolour art challenges European perspectives of landscape. Carol Jerrems’ photographic archive, which dignifies those on society’s margins, shows her that to be “held safely by the gaze of someone who [saw] you” can be a version of home.

World.title: Are you stupid, an idiot – or both? Philosophy has an answer
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Are you stupid, an idiot – or both? Philosophy has an answer Kurt Johnson October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Idiots are out in force again today,” uttered my father sotto voce whenever someone cut him off or flagrantly disobeyed the road rules. From the back seat, I, a young lad naive to Sydney’s road rage, interpreted this to mean the “idiots” had got themselves organised. They were deploying en masse to the great inconvenience, even danger, of us ordinary citizens. The separation between norms and idiots may not have been as impermeable as my father supposed. Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen explains in the recently translated Stupid Idiots: A Philosophy of Stupidity and Complete and Utter Downright Idiocy that at times we’re all stupid and idiotic. Svendsen’s examination has been timed to a moment when both have taken the world by storm. With social media’s reach and AI’s amplification, never before have the stupid and the idiots been so dominant. Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen. First, a distinction: the stupid are those who choose not to think, while the idiots among us think poorly. From this point, the author develops a taxonomy via a survey of philosophers and writers. Kant, who features heavily, considered stupidity a lack of judgment, while Socrates labelled the stupid as those who failed to examine life. We, of course, could not leave without mention of Harry Frankfurt’s seminal On Bullshit, who defined bullshit as a disregard for the truth (as opposed to lying, which acknowledges truth and says the opposite). This introduces us to an overlapping concept: stupid idiocy. Through its short but incisive exploration of failures to think well, Stupid Idiots paradoxically becomes a guide to rigorous thinking. For it is at the border between wisdom and idiocy that greatest insights lie. It is also an exercise in humility as those who consider themselves best informed are most likely to err – like when Schopenhauer explains that one can “read themselves stupid” by consuming only literature that accords with their opinions. Svendsen recommends the budding Marxist pick up Hayek and vice versa.



Through echo-chamber busting, Svendsen suggests a return to the fundamentals of discourse and a subtle rejection of our fractured, dug-in politics. Opinions are not sacred while the idea of “my truth” is anathema to intelligent thought. Instead, if we cultivate critical thinking, are suspicious of orthodoxy and listen to those holding opposing views, we have a real shot at avoiding idiocy, if not attaining wisdom. On the other hand, Stupid Idiots articulates how the chips are stacked to the advantage of the habitually moronic. The Dunning-Kruger effect, for example, boils down to the less you know about a subject the smarter you think you are. You simply don’t know how much you don’t know. Meanwhile, bad information (bullshit) travels further and faster than the truth. Photo: Svendsen’s work exudes tolerance and empathy on the subject of human fallibility. Great thinkers have all been idiots at times: Heidegger was a Nazi, Aristotle thought women had fewer teeth than men, and Schopenhauer believed in all sorts of paranormal nonsense. Indeed, our discourse, the basis of our political system, can and must withstand certain amounts of stupidity and idiocy. The author states that conservatives tend to be stupid, as they too readily accept authority, while progressives are more likely to be idiots as they overestimate their outside-the-box thinking. These flaws are healthy. Things only go awry when we reach a critical mass of stupid idiots. The titular Stupid Idiots are a special group. They are those who think badly and are so pigheaded they refuse to be swayed by life, experience or contradictory data. They are the conspiracy zealots, the antivaxxers. All dictators are stupid idiots as they cannot stomach dissenting opinion. Theirs is the only truth.



Related Article Review He lasted 11 days in Trump’s White House. Now the Mooch has a warning And so, in rounding its final corner, Stupid Idiots reaches the subject it had been alluding to all along: Donald Trump. So rare IRL does one meet a near-perfect archetype. Trump, who is convinced “nobody knows more about this than me”, routinely demonstrates stupid idiocy par excellence. What is special about this book is that up to now it appears more beard stroking philosophy until the revelation it has been a political script the entire time. In the end, my father was right. The idiots are out in force today as they are every day. For we are they. Through acknowledging this, Stupid Idiots is short, sharp, rigorous and avoids condescension. It is a guide to how we can all think better and an admission that fallible thinking is universal. Or in other words, to “duh” is human. Stupid Idiots: A Philosophy of Stupidity and Complete and Utter Downright Idiocy by Lars Svendsen, translated by Matt Bagguley, is published by Reaktion Books ($35). World.title: Pip Williams’ WWI novel is beautiful – but I wish it wasn’t
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Pip Williams’ WWI novel is beautiful – but I wish it wasn’t Beejay Silcox October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When is a lovely novel too lovely? Too frictionless, too perfectly smooth. It takes skill to make a book feel effortless. But when do a novel’s pleasures begin to feel like a failure of imagination? I’ve been thinking about this question all year, as some of the most beloved names in fiction have released novels of lavish and luxurious comfort. There was Ann Patchett’s Whistler, so wilfully pleasant – so stuffed with little joys – it felt like a high-end gift basket. And then Maggie O’Farrell’s Land, which promised something wild and strange but then gave us the familiar consolations of a family saga. Author Pip Williams at home in the Adelaide Hills. Roy VanDerVegt And now there’s Pip Williams’ The German Ward, the story of an English nurse and a German doctor who serve together in a field hospital in Etaples, a few miles behind the Western Front. Two restless souls, alone on the night shift – those dark, suspended hours (“There is no after. There is only now”). It is exactly the book you expect it to be. I’m tempted to leave it there and let readers bring their own appetites to the novel. The more I explain, the more my own unmet hungers gnash and gnaw. My hunger for risk, for mess – for the kind of moral ugliness that shakes my certainties loose.



Like so much contemporary WWI fiction, The German Ward is terribly beautiful, even as it tries to be honest. When it comes to the Western Front, there’s a stubborn smear of Vaseline across our cultural lens. We look at the carnage and keep spotting love stories. Some readers will find this reassuring; humane, even: a reminder that gentleness has its place in ungentle times. Others will bristle at yet another romance plucked from the fetid mud. Both can be true. In a way, that’s Williams’s point: the tension between what we choose to see and what’s there. How our perspective shifts and warps depending on where we stand, what uniform we’re wearing and who we love. To make the point, she gives us double vision: two women looking at the same story from opposite ends of a century. In 1937, an unexpected letter prompts Tilda Taylor to open a box of relics she has kept in the attic for 20 years, among them her wartime diary. It begins in August 1915, with her assignment to the titular German ward, where wounded enemy soldiers were sent to recover before being transferred to prison camps. “We had tried to kill them but they didn’t die,” Tilda’s diary reads, “so now we try to save them. How insane.” In 2025 art historian Eva LaMotte is in the archival quiet of the Australian War Memorial, studying the work of Iso Rae, an Australian artist who was based in Etaples during the war but denied a formal commission. Rae’s work carries a quiet defiance: “Someone had said no to Iso – the war is not yours to paint; it is not your story to tell – but Iso had done it anyway.” What did she see, Eva wonders, that the men did not? Only a handful of Rae’s sketches survive but some of the most tender feature the same unnamed nurse. Eva senses a story hiding in these intimate lines. As she imagines that story, Tilda remembers it. (Williams has conjured the tale from a real-life encounter in Rae’s archives.) And so we have a novel where everyone is looking at someone who is looking at someone else. Looking, longing, sketching, interpreting. The war churns on and on, breaking bodies. And we watch them all, watching – bearing witness, bearing suffering. It could be a great, unruly tangle. But Williams knows precisely what she is doing. We can feel it: the precision, the control. The mystery of Tilda’s unopened letter; the question of Eva’s anonymous nurse. The past and the present moving towards one another like two lovers reuniting.



It’s all so carefully inevitable. Tilda is a former actress, headstrong and impatient (“one of Pankhurst’s women”). The German doctor, Hugo Henning, is taciturn and proper: “a nut to crack”. We know the archetypes; we know the script. “We kissed like we knew how it might end,” Tilda tells us, and we believe her. We already know how it will end. Related Article Literature New York Times bestseller confesses: I can’t write a simple love story Readers might remember Tilda from The Bookbinder of Jericho, Williams’ last novel. The German Ward enriches that book but stands alone. I read it alongside Daniel Kraus’ Pulitzer Prize-winning Angel Down, a horror novel set at the bleeding edge of the front during the Meuse-Argonne offensive. That was an unfair pairing. Kraus’ novel is so gloriously repulsive, so feral and deranged, that Williams’ doctors-and-nurses romance felt almost obscene in its tidiness. All that finely sketched yearning. All those diligent shades of ethical grey. Tilda and Hugo clash over rules: they anchor him and suffocate her. In the ward the couple wrestles with when to bend the rules and when to break them – when protocol stands in the way of grace. “The trick is to know when the rule is worthy and when it is not,” Tilda argues. She’s right. Pip Williams knows all the narrative rules. The German Ward is perfectly lovely, perfectly readable proof. I wish she’d smashed a couple. Smashed them all. The German Ward by Pip Williams (Affirm Press, $35) is out now.

World.title: Eight gay men met in secret to rehearse a play. This Booker-nominated novel reveals the atrocities that followed
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Eight gay men met in secret to rehearse a play. This Booker-nominated novel reveals the atrocities that followed Jack Cameron Stanton October 16, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Marlon James’ The Disappearers, shortlisted for this year’s Booker Prize, begins when eight gay men secretly meet to rehearse a queer prison play. It’s Kingston, 1988. Jamaica has been whipped into an AIDS panic. Gay bashings occur in Kingston with impunity. The actors gather to perform parts of themselves hidden away from the rest of Jamaica, all the while envisioning the play as a small act of defiance against their homophobic society. Most notable among the men are Eddy Porteous, a young man figuring out what his sexuality means in a world that persecutes it; the troubled, abrasive Jordan Brown, disowned by his rich family and hardened by street living; Matt Chin, an elusive figure who assumes multiple identities; and the director, Havelock Titus, who hopes their adaptation of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes will blow “open the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality and homophobia”. Marlon James’ The Disappearers is nominated for this year’s Booker Prize. NYT Fatefully, a gang of hateful gay bashers called the Blackjacks discover the rehearsal and commit an atrocity, killing one of the actors, leaving another with their eyes gouged out, and traumatising those who survive. From this premise James expands The Disappearers into a true maximalist novel, writing in many voices and documenting the progression of the gay men’s lives from 1988 until 2005. It comes equipped with a list of characters, something readers of James’ Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings will recognise, along with the distinct polyphonic writing style. Heavily voice-driven, the narrative constantly fuses the profane and the lyrical, Jamaican patois with bookishness.



The Disappearers isn’t dramatised. It’s documented. James uses several faux documents, such as letters, diary entries and interviews, to report the events. Post-atrocity, the brunt of the novel revolves around Jordan and Eddy searching for two actors who disappeared “like thieves in the night”. As the title declares, The Disappearers is occupied with exploring the many forms of disappearance: not only the physical but ways of self-erasure, of vanishing within a society. The documented style of the novel reveals a second, more vital thematic than disappearance: the cost of remembering. The survivors of the gay bashing are haunted by it. They are all, in their own ways, “frozen in 1988”. The play, which never occurs, is a spectre in their lives, a reverberating what-if. Jordan Brown, a loose cannon at the best of times, cultivates a warped and hateful sense of vigilante justice as he hunts down the members of the Blackjacks whose lives continued “like nothing happened”. Eddy Porteous, the only cast member absent during the attack, is racked by survivor’s guilt, while Havelock Titus, the director, whose small act of defiance exposed the boys to their suffering, finds himself their reluctant keeper. James offers complex portrayals of his gay characters. In contrast, the Blackjacks are exaggeratedly wretched to the point of grotesquerie. They are handed the microphone in the second act, in which they spout lovely one-liners such as “The Devil is a faggot and demons are in his semen” and “Sodom was the wickedest city in creation and God did have to destroy it”. The biblical references expose their broader belief: what appears to the reader as cruel, senseless violence is seen by the perpetrators as noble persecution. Or, in Jordan’s bitter words, not “a crime but a national service. Think of how many potential cases of AIDS they prevented that night.” Zooming out from their interpersonal clashes, we see James constantly engaged in situating violence and homophobia in broader discourses of class, race, sexuality and religion. This is the novel’s greatest elegance. It is the type of maximalist fiction that enlivens history into something more real than real.



There’s a long history of queer fiction embracing the transgressive powers of sexual desire. James signals the novel’s continuation of this tradition by having Jordan Brown carry around John Rechy’s The Sexual Outlaw like a manual for how to live. It emboldens Jordan’s rejection of “normality”: “normal was as broad and loose as the f---ing universe, whereas abnormal was just one thing”. It shows other ways to exist. Related Article Literature A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail I should mention that The Disappearers is an extremely horny book. The politics of pornographic representations in fiction range from gratuitous to artfully subversive; James belongs to the latter. His characters have a lot of sex and recount their sex in vivid detail, in part to provoke the heteronormative reader by making visible and explicit what has been historically repressed. On a deeper level, the characters fixate upon and self-define according to their desire because their entire subjectivity has been filtered through the prism of their own sexuality. James deftly illuminates how the characters grappling with identity are doing so within a larger system that excludes and erases them. Remembering, forgetting and disappearing are all entangled in The Disappearers. They are the traumatic responses that come to define the men’s lives. In the closing scene, one character fails to recognise another. This cruel act of forgetting is a bleak, devastating and therefore beautiful ending to Marlon James’ magisterial return to Jamaica, full of hot blood and heartbreak. The Disappearers by Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton, $35) is out now.

World.title: NZ Rugby loses round one in Chiefs v Chiefs trademark dispute
World.content:
New Zealand Rugby has lost the first round of its increasingly bitter trademark dispute with the Australian Rugby League Commission, after a High Court judge on Friday turned down its bid for an injunction.

NZ Rugby is seeking to prevent the incoming Papua New Guinea NRL side from using the Chiefs name already associated with the Super Rugby franchise.

The organisation last week filed an application for urgent interim injunction ahead of the PNG side's planned jersey and branding launch in Port Moresby next Wednesday.

However, the lawyer acting for the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC), which owns both the NRL and the new PNG side, Clive Elliott, told the Wellington High Court on Friday that the launch would go ahead regardless of the outcome of the hearing.

"It's in another country and under a different jurisdiction, the only way in which the courts in New Zealand can control it is the extent to which any information reaches New Zealand," Elliott submitted.

"We say there is no use of the trademark in New Zealand."

Elliott added both the NRL and PNG Chiefs were prepared to geo-block its social media content surrounding the launch, demonstrating the ARLC was "doing everything in their power to address" NZ Rugby's concerns.

Based on those undertakings from ARLC, Justice Karen Grau declined NZ Rugby's application. The reasons for the court's decision will be released next week.

The ruling is an early setback for NZ Rugby in a dispute that pits the national body against the ARLC, against a backdrop of growing concern within rugby about the threat the NRL poses to its market share.

But the decision does not signal the end of the trademark dispute. Unless a resolution can be reached out of court, the two organisations are on a collision course for a full court hearing, likely early next year.

In outlining NZ Rugby's case for an interim injunction, lawyer Earl Gray, said the NRL club's launch next week, which, according to submissions by the ARLC, will accompanied by a $500,000 marketing spend, would lead to the entrenchment of the PNG Chiefs name.

"The genie will be very hard to squeeze back into that bottle," Gray said.

"The owner [of the trademark] has freedom to use and exploit the brand as it sees fit. It is not for infringers to dictate that result. The ARLC … are trying to take that exclusivity and freedom away by stealth."

However, Elliott argued the jersey launch was not going to "change the status quo when it's one step in a long process".

"It's been portrayed as a milestone event that's going to change everything," he said. "That is not the case. Over the next three months there is limited prospect of irreparable harm to NZ Rugby."

He said the perceived urgency was "really an edifice" which NZR had created to "try and cover up for its own inaction".

However, NZ Rugby argued it was rugby league officials that had "brought the issue upon themselves".

Gray said it was apparent from the ARLC's submissions that the organisation had not performed the "rudimentary checks" to ensure the trademark was available before announcing the name of the new NRL club.

"A responsible brand owner or business person would think 'hell we've got a problem here - we can't use this'.

"But what's clear from the defendant's evidence is that the defendants did not bother to check that the name was available to use before adopting it.

"So they've brought this issue upon themselves, and, inexplicably, now want to get away with it."

NZ Rugby argued allowing the PNG Chiefs name would create significant "confusion and brand damage", pointing out the two codes operate in increasingly overlapping sporting markets.

Gray cited Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's gaffe ahead of the NZ Warriors appearance in NRL play-offs last month, in which he wished the team luck with the refrain "up the Waratahs", as example of how there is overlap between the two codes

"The average New Zealand sporting fan might not do that," Justice Grau responded. "People interested in sport ... surely they know the difference between rugby and league?"

Elliott told the court the ARLC was confident of its position.

"We have a good and arguable defence that there is no trademark infringement. [Granting an injunction] would create uncertainty and cause reputational damage.

World.title: Affordable rentals deal a win for ratepayers and elderly, New Plymouth mayor says
World.content:
This story has been updated to corrected the Housing for Elderly Reserve balance

The mayor of New Plymouth says a deal with a community housing provider to manage 12 new affordable rentals is a win for ratepayers and the elderly.

Habitat for Humanity Central Region will lease the units at Wynyard Street in Bell Block at full-market value and offer them to tenants on the government's housing waiting list.

Max Brough said the deal would generate more revenue for the district council than it would have earned through its council-managed Housing for the Elderly scheme, which rented units direct to tenants at below-market value.

"It's a good example of a partnership with a public service provider that can attract government funding to run the housing project. And once they get up and running in an area, then hopefully we can get some more underway in the future."

Brough said the lease arrangement would eventually pay for the $4.9 million project which was being built adjacent to existing council flats for the elderly.

"There's been a bit of work going on for over a year, probably closer to two years, to get a registered community housing provider to pick up running the service and there's some benefits that come with that along the way.

"This partnership builds on the work of previous councils and community housing advocates and allows us to achieve better outcomes than we could on our own.

"Ratepayers can't be all things to all people, but they can expect council to make the most of the assets and opportunities we already have. It'll be great to see people actually moving into these new homes."

The project was being funded from the $12 million over three years included in the 2024-2034 Long-term Plan to increase the number of homes in the council's Housing for the Elderly service.

In 2014, the council investigated selling its 145 housing for the elderly units - at the time valued at $12 million - on the open market as part of a cost cutting drive.

New Plymouth mayor Max Brough said the deal would generate more revenue for the district council than it would have earned through its council-managed Housing for the Elderly scheme. LDR /Te Korimako o Taranaki

Other options included retaining them, selling them to a social housing provider or transferring them to a third party trust or manager.

Ultimately it was decided to hold onto the flats in New Plymouth, Bell Block, Waitara and Inglewood which currently had a wait list of 80 people seeking accommodation.

Under the council's Housing for the Elderly policy tenants must generally be over 65, receive a pension or benefit or be on a low income and have no significant assets.

The flats had an annual operating budget of $1.7 million - which was funded through rents - with any surplus going into the Housing for Elderly Reserve to be used for maintenance and capital projects.

The reserve currently had a balance of $600,000.

Tenants in the new flats in Wynyard Street in Bell Block would still need to be eligible for assistance under the council's Housing for the Elderly policy.

Habitat for Humanity Central Region Chief Executive Nic Greene said the partnership would help older people access safe, affordable homes while remaining connected to their local community.

"A warm, secure home provides the foundation for well-being, independence and connection.

"We're pleased to be partnering with Council to ensure more older people in the New Plymouth District can access quality housing that enables them to continue living active and fulfilling lives in the communities they know and love."

The new one-bedroom units were being built to modern standards for heat, ventilation and accessibility - including accessible bathrooms - and would also have enclosed mobility scooter parking and their own outdoor areas.

World.title: High Court declines NZ Rugby's bid for interim injunction on PNG Chiefs
World.content:
The High Court has declined New Zealand Rugby's application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL rugby league franchise using its name in New Zealand.

The NZR has been seeking to stop Papua New Guinea's incoming franchise from using the Chiefs moniker also used by the Super Rugby franchise.

The trademark dispute is likely bound for a more substantive trial next year. Meanwhile, the PNG Chiefs, who are to enter the NRL in 2028, will launch their brand and logo next Wednesday.

The NZR has held the trademark for the Chiefs name since the 1990s, and IP Australia has previously knocked back attempts by the NRL to register the Chiefs trademark because of what it identified as the potential for brand confusion.

Following the High Court decision, the CEO of the rugby Chiefs, Simon Graafhuis, told RNZ Pacific that the NZR is "absolutely" considering legal action in Australia.

Chiefs Super Rugby Pacific fan. Photosport

At today's High Court hearing in Wellington, the NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued that the PNG Chiefs made no distinction from the rugby Chiefs in its various media materials.

He argued that the NRL was seeking to take away the rugby Chiefs' brand exclusivity 'by stealth", claiming PNG Chiefs' plans for a brand launch showed the "ramping up and loss of control of this brand" which had been built up over decades by the rugby Chiefs.

But Clive Elliott, the lawyer for the defendant, the Australian Rugby League Commission, said the launch would not change the status quo and was simply the unveiling of the franchise's strip or team jersey.

He said given the NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name around a year ago, that to only now be filing an urgent application for an injunction after an "extremely long delay" weas not appropriate.

Earlier, Gray said the NRL franchise's representatives had been using the 'PNG Chiefs' and 'Chiefs' interchangably, which created confusion for sports fans and the many people who follow both union and league codes.

"Confusion can reign," he said while also warning of potential impact on sponsorship, but Elliott said the geographical qualifier of 'PNG' distinguished the franchise clearly.

Jarome Luai signs as the PNG Chiefs marquee player. Supplied / PNG Chiefs

He said that the PNG Chiefs are at a critical juncture as they try to build the club and recruit key players during the brief free agency period which opens up in November and ends by the new year.

Elliott said that a temporary injunction at this point would threaten those efforts by creating a cloud over the franchise's reputation.

World.title: Worst staffing shortage Starship Hospital nurses have seen, as cancer treatments delayed
World.content:
Nurses at Auckland's Starship Children's Hospital say this is the worst nursing shortage they've seen, as cancer treatments are delayed.

On Thursday, Health Minister Simeon Brown confirmed some treatments were delayed up to seven days.

Do you know more? Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier on Thursday morning, Health New Zealand's Starship Hospital director Dr Greg Williams said the paediatric haematology/oncology service has had to reschedule some treatments due to a shortage of nurses.

"These decisions are not made lightly and are based on clinical need," he said, adding: "Starship is recruiting experienced and new graduate nurses as quickly as possible".

But two nurses who spoke to RNZ on the condition of anonymity, said staffing had been a critical issue for over a year.

They said there was a lack of experienced staff as nurses needed to complete a certain amount of qualifications, hours and training to be competent in chemotherapies, high-risk therapies and monitoring.

"We're getting a lot of new graduates - which is brilliant - but we need the staff to support them.

"We want to keep our new nurses not scare them away.

"It doesn't really help with our workload, at the moment they can't give chemotherapy or those high-risk therapies, so we still have to do them, as well as train the new nurses.

"It's not just the amount of nurses that we're employing, its the experience we need them to have..."

The nurses said new graduates only got two or three weeks working with another more experienced nurse and observing, before they were "on their own on the floor" in a children's oncology ward.

"It's intense, it's emotional and it's a really high-risk area. I just don't think two to three weeks is enough and we're not giving them enough support that they need to keep our staff and staff retention is really important for our kids."

A spokesperson for Brown earlier told RNZ vacancies at Health NZ were the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement, but the nurses disagreed.

"That is absolutely not the case."

They said some nurses left because they felt unsupported.

One thing the nurses did want to make clear to parents and the general public was patients would still receive support and care they needed.

"We will do everything we can to make sure we get those children seen and safely cared for," they said.

"The tricky thing is we're doing that at the detriment of our nurses.

"We want to reassure parents out there that their children will get the care and the treatment they need, the children are safe."

Following media reports in recent days, the nurses said many parents on the ward were stressed, worrying their children wouldn't get the care they needed.

"We want to reassure them all - and that is what we've spent most of the day doing... their kids will get the treatment that they need."

They said they wanted to thank the parents for messages of support they had received.

The nurses said however, they weren't currently able to spend the time really getting to know families like they used to, or spend time with the children and play with them.

"We purely come in now to do the treatment... and just get through the shift safely."

The bottom line they said, was they needed more experienced nurses.

"This is not a cry for money, we are not asking for another pay rise, we're crying out for more staff - and more staff who can train up our new starters."

They encouraged Brown to come to the hospital and meet with staff, to see what it was like in person.

"We'd be interested to speak to him if he's keen to, come and have a meeting with us, we'd be happy to have conversation."

They said Brown had not been to visit them in person before.

Brown and Health NZ have been approached by RNZ for comment.

On Thursday, a spokesperson for the minister said all children at Starship Hospital were still being treated, though a handful of chemotherapy sessions have been delayed for a few days - but no more than seven.

Two bone marrow transplants were moved "slightly", but both were still going ahead.

Williams said the oncology departments are being supported by staff in other parts of Starship and Auckland City Hospital.

World.title: RNZ funder kept in dark for six days over finance chief's sudden exit
World.content:
RNZ's major funder has requested "better communication" from the public broadcaster after being kept in the dark for nearly a week about its chief financial officer's resignation.

NZ On Air confirmed it was first notified of Hilary Parker's unexpected departure in an email from RNZ's communications director on Thursday 8 October, six days after she resigned and left the building.

"We asked for better communication in future," an NZ On Air spokesperson said.

The funding agency received a further update on Monday 12 October but said it had not sought any more information.

"RNZ's financial performance is monitored by Treasury."

In response, an RNZ spokesperson said the failure to notify NZ On Air earlier had been "an omission".

"This was rectified as soon as it was brought to our attention and we apologised.

"As a Crown Entity, RNZ remains committed to keeping key stakeholders informed as appropriate."

NZ On Air is RNZ's main funding channel, providing just over $62 million of taxpayers' money in the 2025/26 financial year.

Parker's resignation on Friday 2 October triggered an emergency board meeting and the appointment of RNZ director Richard Dellabarca as interim finance chief.

Two weeks on, the circumstances of her exit remain unexplained, despite repeated requests for answers from RNZ, government agencies and ministers.

Her departure came as the publicly funded broadcaster was preparing its annual accounts, which must be completed by the end of the month.

In a company-wide message last week, chief executive Paul Thompson acknowledged the "keen interest in what is happening" and promised staff more details "as soon as we are able".

Asked for an update this Thursday, an RNZ spokesperson said there was "nothing further to add".

"We continue to be working through the normal year-end process."

Board chair Brent Impey also declined a fresh interview request, saying there had been "no other developments" since his comments last week.

Treasury confirmed it had "engaged with RNZ" over the finalisation of its annual report following Parker's resignation.

"RNZ have advised the Treasury that the annual report will be finalised within appropriate timeframes," a spokesperson said.

The Audit Office said it too was continuing to work with RNZ on its 2025/26 audit, including "asking for any relevant information" needed to complete the job.

"We cannot give specific details about the audit," a spokesperson said. "RNZ is best placed to respond to questions about this matter."

The office said only 16 of the 80 Crown entities with a usual 31 October deadline had completed their audits so far.

It said it was not unusual for many audits to be signed off close to the deadline, which this year would be treated as Monday 2 November because 31 October fell in the weekend.

The Public Service Commission also directed questions back to RNZ's board.

Broadcasting Minister Paul Goldsmith, who was notified of Parker's resignation under the no-surprises convention at the time, had no comment "at this stage".

Associate Finance Minister David Seymour, who holds shareholding responsibility for RNZ, confirmed he too had received a written briefing but referred questions to Goldsmith.

Impey last week told RNZ's Checkpoint that Parker had resigned of her own accord to acting chief executive Mark Stevens on Friday 2 October, before leaving the premises.

Thompson, who had been overseas, was informed on Saturday.

An emergency board meeting followed on Sunday, with director Richard Dellabarca appointed interim CFO.

World.title: Independent review to examine Christchurch City Mission's care of Braydon Hepworth
World.content:
An independent review will be carried out into the care Braydon Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission.

The 21-year-old father was told to leave the mission's transitional housing less than two months before he disappeared.

His body was found buried in a shed in Linwood last week. A 60-year-old man was charged with concealing his body and making a false statement to police.

Mission board chair Jane Evans said the review would examine Hepworth's time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care.

"We take our responsibilities to our clients, our staff and the wider community very seriously," she said in a statement.

"The mission is open to improving how it supports people in its care and looks forward to the outcome."

The mission did not respond to questions about who would undertake the review.

Evans said the mission was deeply saddened by Hepworth's death and asked for respect and patience because of obligations to protect client privacy and confidentiality.

Christchurch City Mission chief executive Corinne Haines earlier confirmed that Hepworth was asked to leave transitional housing in mid-July.

"Our services support many people with complex needs and there are occasions when we must ask someone to leave accommodation because important behavioural expectations have repeatedly not been met," she said in a statement.

A former staff member told RNZ that Hepworth's death pushed her to resign from the City Mission. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

However, the circumstances surrounding Hepworth's departure from the Whakaora Kāinga complex have raised concerns and questions from staff.

Former staff member Alex - who did not wish to use her surname - told RNZ Hepworth's death was the catalyst for her resignation because of serious concerns about the mission's direction.

"I believe the shift towards a more rigid, business-oriented approach contributed to the loss of experienced staff and undermined the quality of support [Whakaora Kāinga] was established to provide," she said.

In her resignation letter, seen by RNZ, Alex said Hepworth was given 15 minutes to pack his belongings and leave.

"A year of familiarity, relationships and a place to turn when life became overwhelming, reduced to 15 minutes to gather his possessions and walk away," her letter said.

"I find it difficult to comprehend how this could be considered an appropriate way to exit someone whose circumstances called for compassion, careful consideration and trauma-informed practice.

"Braydon deserved better. His daughter deserved better. And every person who comes to Whakaora Kāinga seeking safety, stability, and support deserves better."

World.title: Is it still worth having health insurance?
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/1955912%2Fis-it-still-worth-having-health-insurance

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

Are you likely to be better off taking health insurance, or saving up a sum of money to pay for any treatment you might need, yourself?

Health insurance has been back in the news this week after celebrity chef Simon Gault said he was disappointed at the way his Southern Cross policy responded to skin cancer.

He said a mark on his cheek turned out to be cancerous.

"[Southern Cross said] they'd cover me for a standard excision of it, and my surgeon specialist said 'no, you shouldn't do that, you should be getting this Mohs surgery, you'll have a way greater chance of removing all the cancer with that'," Gault told RNZ.

"But he [the specialist] said you won't meet the criteria, but they put an application in anyway, and Southern Cross declined it.

"So then I said, 'okay, well if you'll cover the standard excision, how about you pay that portion of it and I pay the difference', and they said no to that, and I think that's disgraceful, you know, they just leave you on your own."

Southern Cross tightened its criteria for Mohs surgery in December.

With health insurance premiums rising quickly, up almost 75 percent in the past five years some people have wondered whether it's worth holding on to cover.

Russell Hutchinson, whose business Chatswood Consulting provides research on insurance products, said he personally valued health insurance but he could understand why some people did not.

"Do you need to buy private health cover? If we were having a debate, we could definitely make a case for either of the propositions."

But he said anyone who planned to self-fund their own healthcare, rather than taking insurance or relying completely on the public system, would need to save quite a bit in case of a large health problem.

"That's the classic insurance quadrant. If you have a frequent event and it's low cost, you might as well cover it yourself. That's your regular doctor's visits.

"Then if you have an infrequent event at a low cost, you might as well cover it yourself because you can do that. That's fine.

"But if you have infrequent events at very high costs that's your catastrophic risk… that's the area where medical insurance helps."

He said, although Southern Cross had a surplus in its most recent annual report, it had tougher years previously and that reflected the increasing cost of claims.

Jon-Paul Hale, who founded insurance specialist Willowgrove Consulting, said the sums of money people would have to save to truly self-insure would be unmanageable for most people.

He said one recent claim he dealt with for a client was worth $265,000 in 12 months for an early stage breast cancer.

He calculated the average person who had medical insurance from the age 20 to 70 would spend about $230,000 on premiums over their lifetime, most of that in the second half.

"For the average punter they would have to save 20 to 30 years…that saving rate needs to increase in line with where the premiums would have increased. The reality is, okay, you're saving for this, putting money aside for your health for 25 or 30 years, but what if something happens at year 10?"

Hale said, as people got older, it could make sense to take on more of the cover themselves.

"Five or 10 years ago I would have said, look, you get to 65, you assess whether holding on to specialists and test cover is something you need to keep because the cost of specialist and tests against what you're claiming is likely to be there or thereabouts, if not more. But with the price rises in the last three years, that's now come back to age 55.

"Someone who's 55, as a couple, is going to spend about $250 a month just on specialists and tests [cover]. So that's basically a follow-up specialist appointment every month. The reality is, if you're not spending that, you probably should take the money, stick it in a savings account and not pay the premiums, because a lot of those specialist and test benefits have a $5000 to $10,000 maximum anyway."

"But that still needs advice from an adviser because some of those policies, if you drop out specialists and tests, you'll lose your access to MRIs and CTs."

Liz Koh, founder of Enrich Retirement, said anyone worried about their premiums could also consider taking a higher excess.

This can make a substantial difference to the premiums that are charged, but means you pay more of the cost of any procedure you claim for.

'People need to understand exactly what their policy covers'

Tim Fairbrother, founder of Rival Wealth, said it was important to note that Gault had not been declined cover altogether.

"They declined the specific surgery his specialist recommended because it didn't meet their current funding criteria, much like they don't cover non-Pharmac drugs which can be very expensive. Southern Cross will pay for surgery, just not the better surgery that was desired.

"As for the bigger question of whether you're better off having health insurance or simply saving the premiums, for most people the value of insurance isn't the smaller claims, it's protection against potentially very large and unexpected medical costs that could run into tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars. Self-funding can work if you've accumulated substantial savings, but many New Zealanders would struggle to absorb a major medical expense without insurance. So the choice is; fund one hip for $35,000, wait on the public system for possibly 18 months, or pay $500 per month for health insurance that covers the hip and all other ailments. Under this scenario you would fund all ailments for 6 years for the cost of one hip operation.

"People need to understand exactly what their policy covers, what criteria apply, and how those rules can change over time. It's a reminder to regularly review your cover rather than assuming every treatment recommended by a specialist will automatically be funded."

Southern Cross chief sales, marketing and customer experience officer Regan Savage said people could not predict the specific treatment they would need until they were diagnosed and procedures could run to tens of thousands of dollars.

A colonoscopy was up to $4000, he said, and hip replacement could be $33,000.

"People also need to think about health insurance over the longer term. As people get older, they are generally more likely to need specialist appointments, diagnostic tests, surgery or treatment for more complex conditions. That increased use of healthcare is one reason premiums tend to rise with age.

"Before cancelling health insurance because premiums are becoming difficult to manage, we'd encourage people to talk to their insurer or financial adviser about the options available to them. Depending on their policy and circumstances, there may be ways to reduce premiums while retaining some cover, rather than cancelling altogether. It is worth thinking carefully before cancelling because taking out cover again later may not put someone back in the same position they were in previously. For example, pre-existing conditions are often excluded from new policies.

"Ultimately there's no single answer that will be right for everyone. Someone considering self-funding needs to think not only about what they could save in premiums, but how readily they could meet an unexpected healthcare bill of $20,000 or $30,000, potentially more, and what level of financial risk they are comfortable carrying themselves."

World.title: Waka destined for French museum will honour 'courageous feats' of Māori Pioneer Battalion soldiers
World.content:
Audio player for " Te Puia carvers deliver Waka Maumahara " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/te-ao-maori/1956210%2Fwaka-destined-for-french-museum-will-honour-courageous-feats-of-maori-pioneer-battalion-soldiers

Te Puia carvers deliver Waka Maumahara Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

For Tiaan Greig, carving a waka for the Carrière Wellington museum in Northern France is personal.

"I'm a descendant of John Huani Ruha. He is my nan's koroua."

His ancestor was one of the Māori Pioneer Battalion soldiers involved in the Arras offensive, a major World War 1 battle in France involving British and Commonwealth troops.

"Something that really stood out was that he was 22, which is the same age I am now.

"He had finished in the last tunnels and they got transferred over to Belgium, and then that's where his final resting place is, so he didn't make it back."

A group of carvers from Te Puia, the New Zealand Māori Arts and Crafts Institute, some of whom whakapapa back to those soldiers, have been working on a special carving.

A delegation from Arras, who commissioned the Waka Maumahara, traveled to Rotorua on Friday to see its progress.

Mayor of Arras Frédéric Leturque RNZ/Rachel Moore

It's a relationship that dates back to 1916, when 500 of the New Zealand Engineers Tunneling Company, including a detachment of 43 members of the Māori Pioneer Battalion, went to Arras during World War I.

Greig said the waka's design incorporated the style from the iwi of each of those 43 Māori men.

"It's very special, these men, they went over there and sacrificed their lives. They sacrificed a lot for us and us being able to put our korero, their korero, and their mana into something like that, it's very cool."

The tunnelers achieved an engineering feat in preparation for what was the largest surprise attack of the First World War - one that historian Chris Pugsley said was very effective.

"When they got to France, really they had no experience of tunneling for war. And so they had to learn on the job, and they learned very quickly."

The men mined a complex underground network of quarries large enough to accommodate up to 24,000 soldiers, mapping sections and naming them after places in Aotearoa. They also left inscriptions and memorabilia in the tunnels.

The waka's design incorporates the style from the iwi of each of those 43 Māori Pioneer Battalion soldiers. RNZ/Rachel Moore

Pugsley said the New Zealanders played a significant role and were remembered as such, particularly at the Wellington Quarry.

"As you go in, is all the photos on the side of the New Zealand tunnelers, and there's this marvelous statue, which gives the outline of a New Zealand tunneler and you have to think, gosh, the hundreds of thousands of men who have fought at Arras, here, the smallest contingent of any nation has pride of place."

General manager of the New Zealand Arts and Crafts Institute Eraia Kiel said the waka was about halfway finished and would be shipped to Arras for next year's unveiling.

"We're very fortunate that we still have the masters of their crafts here to be able to and do something like this justice and give it the mana it deserves.

"Hopefully through this waka maumahara and this binding of our cities and our organisations, people will start to look into just what our tīpuna did in traveling that far away from home to sacrifice and serve in a battle that we had nothing to do with, really."

The waka is about halfway finished. RNZ/Rachel Moore

He wanted people to always remember the bravery of their ancestors.

"It's extremely, extremely humbling that people from far across the other side of the world, first of all, still remember the courageous feats of our ancestors and have reached out to us to acknowledge them."

Arras mayor Frédéric Leturque said he wanted the French to understand the importance of the waka to Māori culture.

World.title: Surgery giving Kiwis hope of Ponga playing again in World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga will undergo surgery on his broken arm but will remain in camp, with New Zealand not giving up on the superstar fullback playing again in the Rugby League World Cup.

Ponga failed to finish his long-awaited Test debut for the Kiwis, departing in the 70th minute of the 24-22 loss after suffering the injury earlier in the second half.

Receiving clearance earlier this year to switch his allegiance to New Zealand, Ponga delivered a stand-out performance at Western Sydney Stadium as his side fell to Australia in the Thursday night thriller.

The Newcastle skipper scored two tries while running 253 metres from 16 runs, making three line breaks and five tackle breaks.

He has been booked in for surgery after breaking the radius in his left arm but Kiwis team doctor Greg Macleod sounded hopeful about the prospect of Ponga playing again through the tournament.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

"We wish Kalyn all the best with his surgery today," Macleod said in a statement.

"We'll see how that goes but for now he will remain in camp."

The 28-year-old is viewed as critical to the New Zealand's hopes of claiming their first World Cup since 2008.

Coach Stacey Jones, whose side will face the Cook Islands in Christchurch next week before wrapping up their group stages matches against Fiji, said Ponga had played through pain.

"He couldn't catch a ball or anything like that. He was in a bit of discomfort," Jones said.

Ponga was replaced by Keano Kini as he trudged off late in the match and was seen on the sidelines with his arm in a sling.

"He's obviously disappointed, but there's a bit of upbeat about him too. He really wants to still be involved," Jones said.

If New Zealand decide Ponga's tournament is over, the Kiwis have the option to ask for clearance to add an additional player to their squad.

"He's a tough guy and obviously has a lot of pride in the black and white jersey, and he doesn't want to let his teammates down," Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"I thought he did an outstanding job. He's a freakish player, but he's also one of those tough players. We're feeling for him right now, but fingers crossed it's not too bad."

Jones said Kini would likely replace Ponga in next week's pool match.

The Kiwis' narrow loss to Australia was one that will burn Jones for a while.

Two of the Kangaroos' five tries were the result of interceptions and another two were from kicks.

The Kiwis dominated territory but lacked the polish to make Australia pay for their mistakes.

"Unfortunately, we were on the losing side, but we will learn from it, and we will get better and we will make some adjustments," Jones said.

"You go in that changing room and everyone's down, they're hurting.

"But you just bounce back and you get back into it. We know these boys, they work hard, they're professional. We'll be OK"
